British cyclist Finlay Tarling has died at the age of 19 after a crash during stage eight of the Volta a Portugal.

The race was neutralised after Tarling was involved in a “serious accident” on the 166.8km route from Melgaco to Fafe.

“The organisation of the 87th Volta a Portugal em Bicicleta Jogos Santa Casa deeply regrets to announce the passing of British cyclist Finlay Tarling, from the NSN Development Team, following a serious accident that occurred during the 8th stage of the race,” race organisers confirmed in a statement.

“At this moment of profound dismay, the organisation of the Volta a Portugal and the Portuguese Cycling Federation express their most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his teammates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones.”

Tarling was riding for the NSN Development Team having signed a two-year deal ahead of the 2025 season.

In a statement, NSN said: "We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

"Fin was a much loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend."

A highly-rated talent, particularly as a time triallst, Tarling won three bronze medals at the 2024 UCI Junior Track Cycling World Championships.

His elder brother Josh rides for Netcompany Ineos and is a world champion in the points race on the track.

News.title: Luigi Mangione confesses ‘I shot Mr. Thompson and he died’ in UnitedHealthcare CEO killing
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Luigi Mangione admitted to fatally shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in a stunning courtroom confession as he pleaded guilty to federal charges stemming from the 2024 killing in the middle of a Manhattan street.

In tan prison scrubs, Mangione told a federal judge on Friday that he traveled to New York City after reaching out to UnitedHealthcare by posing as an investor who planned to attend a healthcare conference with Thompson. Mangione said he made the decision “after years of negotiating severe pain in my back.”

“Unlike my previous interactions with insurers, I received an immediate response within an hour,” Mangione told the court.

He said he armed himself with a gun that he manufactured with a 3D printer and affixed with a silencer.

“I shot Mr. Thompson and he died,” Mangione said. “I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or bodily injury. I knew what I was doing was illegal.”

open image in gallery Luigi Mangione has pleaded guilty to two federal stalking charges in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, who was gunned down in Manhattan in 2024 ( DAVID DEE DELGADO )

Mangione then told District Judge Margaret Garnett that he is pleading guilty to the two remaining federal counts against him.

The counts — stalking resulting in death— carry a maximum sentence of life in prison. They were the last remaining counts charges him after several others were dropped, which could have carried the death penalty, if convicted.

His sentencing hearing is scheduled for December 18.

Mangione, a 28-year-old Ivy League graduate, was the subject of a days-long manhunt after Thompson’s killing outside a Manhattan hotel, sparking intense public interest, outrage and polarizing debate over the far-reaching impacts of the nation’s health insurance industry.

Thompson’s family said in a statement that Mangione’s guilty plea “marks an important step toward justice for Brian and for our family.”

“While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable,” the statement added. “Now we look to the court to ensure the sentencing reflects the severity of this crime.”

open image in gallery The family of Brian Thompson appeared in court to hear Mangione’s confession and issued a statement saying that his guilty plea ‘marks an important step toward justice’ ( Getty )

Mangione “has accepted full responsibility for the death of Brian Thompson,” his attorney Karen Agnifilo said in a statement outside federal court on Friday.

“As Luigi explained in court today, he endured years of severe, debilitating pain following a broken back, while struggling to navigate our healthcare and health insurance systems,” she added. “Like the thousands of people who have reached out since this tragedy to share their own experiences, he believed that the system had failed him and destroyed his life.”

His plea arrived roughly a month before he is scheduled to go to trial in New York state criminal court on separate charges stemming from Thompson’s killing.

In New York criminal court, Mangione has pleaded not guilty to eight charges, including second-degree murder and criminal possession of a weapon. The charges carry a possibility of life in prison.

From the start of the cases, Mangione’s defense team has argued that the charges brought in federal and state court amounted to double jeopardy — or the prosecution of a person twice for the same offenses.

open image in gallery Paulette Thompson (pictured), the wife of Brian Thompson, listened as Luigi confessed to the killing and gave details on how he was able to learn the CEO’s location ( Getty )

“He’s been treated differently from every other defendant charged with this offense in New York,” Agnifilo told reporters Friday.

Agnifilo filed a motion in state court following Friday’s hearing to argue that Mangione cannot face a state trial after pleading guilty to two federal charges.

Mangione’s lawyers had already successfully narrowed the charges against their client.

Federal prosecutors had originally sought to bring the death penalty against Mangione by charging him with using a firearm to commit murder. It was part of a directive by President Donald Trump to renew pushes for capital punishment.

But earlier this year, a federal judge dismissed two charges, including the one carrying the death penalty, against Mangione.

A judge overseeing Mangione’s state case also dismissed two charges brought by state prosecutors: first-degree murder and a state terrorism charge.

open image in gallery Mangione’s lawyers Karen Friedman Agnifilo and Marc Agnifilo arrived in federal court August 14 after unexpectedly requesting a pretrial hearing, where Mangione pleaded guilty to federal charges of stalking resulting in death. They are seeking to block his state trial from moving forward on double jeopardy grounds ( Getty )

Mangione graduated from the University of Pennsylvania in 2020 and was the valedictorian of his 2016 graduating class at the Gilman School in Baltimore.

In the early morning of December 4, 2024, hours before Thompson was slated to attend an annual investors meeting, Mangione fatally shot Thompson, 50, outside of a midtown Manhattan hotel.

Video showed the moment he was ambushed by a masked man and gunned down on a New York City sidewalk.

Law enforcement officials engaged in a multi-state, days-long manhunt for Mangione, capturing the nation’s attention and sparking intense scrutiny into the nation’s for-profit health insurance industry and Mangione’s alleged motive.

He was captured on December 9, 2024, inside a McDonald’s restaurant in Altoona, Pennsylvania.

Bullet casings found after the shooting reportedly had the words “deny,” “delay,” and “depose” written on them, referencing an alleged tactic used by insurance companies to deny claims. Police also discovered a “ghost gun” and a notebook expressing Mangione’s animosity toward the corporate healthcare system.

Mangione’s arrest and the circumstances of the shooting, driven by widespread anger over denied insurance claims and corporate greed, lionized Mangione as a kind of antihero. Fans arrived at his pretrial court hearings with signs and supportive T-shirts.

His supporters also donated more than $1.5 million to a legal defense fund and sent long letters to the jail where he is being held.

News.title: Voices: I will send in as many troops as are needed to fight tinderbox Britain
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

This summer has been a harsh wake-up call. The heat is taking its toll. Firefighters are battling the worst wildfires they have ever known. Crops are failing. Vulnerable people are at serious risk.

I was in the West Midlands, meeting families who are suffering the devastating impact of wildfires. Their lives have been turned upside down in a matter of hours. My thoughts are with everyone affected.

I also met the incredible men and women of our fire and rescue services. They have been working day and night, dealing with multiple major incidents at once. Just imagine walking towards a wildfire in blistering heat. I am in awe of them and I am going to make sure they have every support they need.

That starts with delivering an emergency funding package to support fire and rescue services facing the greatest pressure, on top of the almost £100 million we’ve already provided.

We will deploy aerial firefighting support where it is most needed. Rather than leaving local areas to source that support on their own, we will coordinate these assets nationally and get them to the places that need them most.

We will also provide military support in South Wales to support with their emergency response. Around 200 military personnel deployed on Friday morning to ease the pressure on the ground, support evacuations where needed, and strengthen the wider emergency response.

I have also asked for further military personnel to be put on standby to support other communities across the country, should they need it.

And for families who have lost their homes or suffered damage to their property, the recovery process must begin as quickly as possible. I want to see insurers doing the right thing by those who have been affected, processing their claims rapidly and getting support to affected families without unnecessary delay.

The responsibility to avoid more fires breaking out falls on us all. Everyone should follow the advice of emergency services to take care when disposing of cigarettes and avoid lighting open fires or barbecues. That’s why we have put in place a temporary ban on the sale of all disposable barbecues, starting this weekend.

The impacts of the relentless heat and drought are on a scale that we simply haven’t seen before. This week, I chaired a meeting of the emergency COBR committee to coordinate our response – and look at how we can deal with the effects on every part of our society.

That includes supporting the doctors and nurses working in wards never built for this. The A&E staff looking after those the heat hits hardest. The farmers watching a harvest go backwards through no fault of their own.

We will do what’s needed to help today and protect for tomorrow. This includes investing in nine new reservoirs, stopping leaks and making sure water companies live up to their responsibilities through greater public control.

We will ensure that our public institutions – our NHS, our schools, as well as our homes – are better adapted to deal with more extreme temperatures in future. And we will provide our farmers, our rural communities and our countryside with the support they need.

This summer has shown beyond doubt that climate change is not a far-off prospect, but with us today. None of us can pretend we cannot see it. The cracked soil, dried-out riverbeds and low reservoirs are signs that the impacts are well and truly upon us.

I know people are deeply worried about the climate crisis and what it means for them and their children’s future. So let me say again very directly – there can be no turning away from the fight against climate change. This government will hold to the target of reaching net zero by 2050 and continue to work with other countries to protect our planet.

I’m determined to build a cleaner, healthier economy with all the benefits that can bring for people across our country. That means making sure that the advantages of transitioning from fossil fuels to renewables and nuclear are passed onto working people. And it means making sure that the opportunities from good new jobs are spread fairly across a reindustrialised Britain, with good growth in every postcode.

This summer has shown everyone what is at stake. So we will not shrink from this battle. This government will rise to the moment and build a better, fairer, greener and more resilient Britain.

News.title: Apple sends alarming ‘threat’ alerts to iPhone users
News.content:
Apple has sent some users alarming notifications indicating that their iPhone could have been hacked.

“Apple detected a mercenary spyware attack targeted at your iPhone,” the message sent to users in 110 countries this week reads. “There are actions you can take now to help protect your data and device.”

The notifications are part of a relatively new set of security features that Apple has introduced aimed at detecting advanced and powerful cyber attacks on its users. And the nature of them means that anyone receiving them should take them incredibly seriously.

Apple introduced the threat notifications in 2021 and has sent them multiple times per year, to users in more than 150 countries. They are intended to “inform and assist users who may have been individually targeted by mercenary spyware attacks, likely because of who they are or what they do”, according to a support page on the company’s website.

As that suggests, the threat notifications are intended to alert users to particularly sophisticated hacks, where attackers use large amounts of resources to target specific individuals. As such, they tend to be used by attackers working on behalf of nation states, against specific individuals such as journalists, activists, politicians, and diplomats.

That means that most people are likely never to be targeted by such advanced spyware, or to receive the alert. But it also means that anyone receiving such a notification should treat it with particular urgency.

When Apple detects such an attempted attack, it shows the threat notification as well as sending them an email. Users receiving them are giving extra information on how to protect their accounts – which might include turning on Apple’s “Lockdown Mode”, which removes some of the iPhone’s features to further secure it against attackers, and getting emergency assistance.

“This warning is a reminder that even tightly controlled ‘walled garden’ ecosystems are not immune to spyware,” said Bogdan Botezatu, senior direct of threat research and reporting at Bitdefender. “Apple’s security model raises the cost of an attack, but well-funded adversaries can still use zero-day vulnerabilities, zero-click exploits and sophisticated infection chains to reach carefully selected targets.

The ideal summer spot? Away from scams. Get All-in-One Protection for Your Digital Life LEARN MORE 

The ideal summer spot? Away from scams. Get All-in-One Protection for Your Digital Life LEARN MORE 

“The fact that notifications reached users in 110 countries illustrates the global reach of the spyware industry despite the fact that these are not mass attacks. The vast majority of users are unlikely to encounter this type of attack.

“For recipients, however, the potential consequences are severe: advanced spyware may expose messages, calls, location data, credentials, files, and in some cases the device’s microphone or camera. Recipients should verify the warning directly through their Apple account, enable Lockdown Mode, install all available updates and seek specialist assistance.”

News.title: Mexican soldier at guns-for-food drive saws up shotgun without realizing it’s loaded
News.content:
A “guns-for-food drive” organized by the Mexican Army backfired when a soldier forgot to check if one of the weapons was loaded.

Video footage shows the shotgun, which had been brought in by a resident in exchange for money or food, being sawed in half with a metal saw when a live cartridge suddenly detonated.

Shrapnel was sent flying around the room, resulting in four attendees getting injured. Three people sustained minor injuries, whilst the fourth person’s injuries were more severe. All four were taken to the Regional Hospital of Pátzcuaro, a city about four hours west of Mexico City.

News.title: How to have the perfect slow-paced holiday in Zakynthos
News.content:
Zakynthos, also known as Zante, is renowned for raucous nightlife, but there’s a far more authentic side to the Venetians “Fiore di Levante” (Flower of the East). For such a small island, scenery is extremely varied: the southern coastline – home to Laganas’ notorious nightlife strip – also encompasses the pristine beaches of Zakynthos Marine Park, where loggerhead sea turtles come to nest, while some of the island’s best-known attractions, including Navagio Beach on the cliff-lined northerly coast, can only be reached by boat.

Birthplace of the man who penned Greece’s national anthem, Zakynthos was also a magnet for literary greats: Byron lay in state here and philhellene Edgar Allan Poe wrote a sonnet to the island’s “verdant slopes”.

Last but not least, food is a powerful lure here: sit in a rustic sea view tavern sipping local Verdea white wine with a plate full of traditional kouneli stifado – a garlic and tomato-soaked rabbit stew – and you’ll be hooked.

News.title: Ebola doctors ‘step back’ from WHO in drug trial ethics row
News.content:
Two leading doctors have “stepped back” from long-held positions with the World Health Organization amid a row over the ethics of an Ebola drug trial underway in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The randomised control trial, called Ebo-Pep, is testing whether an experimental antiviral is an effective post-exposure treatment.

But experts believe the study’s design puts healthcare workers on the frontline of the epidemic at risk, because it means medics exposed to Ebola might receive a placebo treatment.

“We owe them [healthcare workers] a duty of care to do the best possible thing, and a 50 per cent chance of getting a placebo tablet is not that,” said Prof Tom Fletcher, director of the Global Health Trials Unit at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. The WHO’s health emergencies clinical unit has also deployed him to Ebola ‘Red Zones’ for more than a decade.

This week, Prof Fletcher and eight other experts based in the UK, US, Uganda, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Canada published their concerns in Nature Africa, calling for a “careful reconsideration” of the trial protocol.

They said they are not against Ebo-Pep or randomised trials, but warned there are “additional ethical obligations” when including healthcare workers in studies like this, given the case fatality rate currently stands at 40 per cent.

Prof Fletcher said: “Ebo-Pep is a really good trial, it’s the trial we’ve talked about doing for years. But we’re talking about [protecting] the ‘one-per-centers’, the people who willingly step into one of the most dangerous environments in the world.”

News.title: Wildfire watch: Inside London’s fire control centre on the hottest day of the year
News.content:
“It’s been relentless, an immense number of calls,” says Yvonne Woodhams, control room commander at the London Fire Brigade’s headquarters on the morning of what turned out to be the hottest day of the year so far.

Inside a nondescript building in South-west London, dozens of fire brigade dispatchers field calls from the public and direct the city’s 5,000 or so firefighters across 102 stations to where they are most needed.

In the middle of another heatwave and on a day when temperatures rose to just above 38 degrees, the control room was busy – the scale and frequency of wildfires in London’s parks and grasslands are now considered unprecedented.

Above the dispatchers there is a live map, with red dots representing each active fire, sprawling from Enfield in the north to Purley in the south.

Wildfires nearly always have a human origin like dropped cigarette butts, glass bottles that magnifies the sunlight, or the now-temporarily banned portable barbecues.

But it’s the tinderbox that London has become which is worrying firefighters.

Scorching hot, low-humidity weather, a bit of wind, and tinder-dry vegetation can cause the smallest spark to ignite an inferno. Conditions like this have been described as “fire weather” by the author John Vaillant.

News.title: Inside the biggest collection of venomous snakes in Latin America
News.content:
On the outskirts of São Paulo, several secure serpentariums sit in forested parkland. They contain some of the most venomous creatures on earth and provide the fuel for Latin America’s biggest antivenom manufacturing and research facility.

In one corner of the grounds, huts on stilts house five of Brazil’s most endangered snakes. One, the golden lancehead, is so rare that poachers asked $20,000 for a single specimen. It is found only on a tiny uninhabited island off the South Atlantic coast.

Nearby, inside the campus’s oldest building, a dip worn into the stone floor shows wear from the original serum-producing horses housed here over a century ago. Around it hang old scientific drawings and shelves stacked with journals bound in snakeskin.

Founded in 1901 by physician Dr Vital Brazil, the institute pioneered the development of species-specific antivenoms Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

This is Brazil’s Butantan Institute. Founded in 1901 to fight an outbreak of bubonic plague, it now produces almost all of the country's antivenoms, supplying at least 350,000 vials annually. It is part of a public health system that has made snakebite in Latin America far less deadly than almost anywhere else in the world.

Now, having spent over a century perfecting antivenom at home, Brazil is expanding its global impact – sharing not just its lifesaving sera, but its world-leading snake research.

Specimens in a jar at the institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

More than five million people are bitten by snakes around the world each year. Between 82,000 and 138,000 die, while roughly three times as many suffer amputations or permanent disability, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The burden falls heaviest on poor rural communities in Asia (up to two million bites annually) and Africa (around 500,000), where farmers, women and children walk through dense vegetation without protective clothing or access to nearby hospitals.

Across the Americas, the incidence of bites is far smaller. Some 57,000 are bitten by snakes each year, with Brazil accounting for over 30,000, according to the country’s health ministry.

But what stands out is the survival rate. According to the Pan American Health Organization (Paho), the region’s fatality rate is just 0.6 per cent – compared to up to 12 per cent in some rural regions of Africa.

Latin American snakes are no less dangerous. Venom from bothrops, a genus of the pit viper known locally as “jaracas”, can dissolve blood vessels, stop clotting and cause severe flesh rot or necrosis. Bites from the viper account for up to 90 per cent of reported envenomings each year in Brazil.

One of the snakes housed by the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

News.title: ‘More pain’ to come after economic slowdown
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The economy grew at a slower pace in the second quarter of the year, official figures show, under pressure from the Iran war.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc between April and June, down from 0.6pc in the first three months of the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.

The figures underline the challenge that the conflict poses for Andy Burnham, who has pledged to deliver “growth in every postcode”.

The Prime Minister has already been warned that the economy will slow further next year if Donald Trump continues his war in the Middle East.

Treasury officials have predicted UK growth of just 0.3pc in 2027 if the Strait of Hormuz stays blocked for the rest of this year.

That is far lower than the 1.6pc predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March, based on assumptions made before the start of the war. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Iran war threatens to cripple growth, Treasury warns Burnham | Officials predict economic expansion of just 0.3pc in 2027 if Strait of Hormuz stays blocked

2) Britain facing £54bn bill for North Sea shutdown | Costs soar amid shortage of specialised ships needed to clear up abandoned oil rigs

3) Ban on zero-hours contracts to cost companies up to £3bn | Businesses face huge bill to offer workers guaranteed hours under Employment Rights Act

4) Nvidia’s AI push has echoes of Enron, says Big Short investor | Michael Burry claims chip giant is engaging in ‘circular’ financing

5) Shadow bank founder battles to stave off bankruptcy threat | Paresh Raja launches legal claim to prevent administrators from chasing him for repayment

What happened overnight

Asian shares were mostly higher, powered by gains for AI-related stocks including computer chips as regional markets tracked a rally on Wall Street.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 advanced 1.6pc to 68,601.21. In South Korea, the Kospi jumped 4pc, climbing to 6,844.65, as shares in Samsung Electronics surged 5.4pcc. Computer chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 7.1pc.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.3pc to 3,967.28, while the Shanghai Composite index added 0.5pc to 3,967.65.

In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.4pc to 9,155.80.

Data from the US on Wednesday showed consumer prices had risen in line with analysts’ expectations in July.

Wall Street stocks were boosted on Wednesday by gains made by tech companies CoreWeave and Super Micro Computer, both of which closed up by more than 19pc.

The Nasdaq Composite ended the session up 0.5pc, with the S&P 500 up nearly 0.3pc. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished the session marginally down.

Oil prices were little changed as investors weighed the deadlock in talks between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, was broadly flat at nearly $89 a barrel.

News.title: H5N1 sparks a very Australian epidemic
News.content:
H5N1 bird flu has reached Australia’s shores and is threatening to infect some of the country’s most unique wildlife.

Australasia is the last continent to be hit by the highly infectious avian influenza H5N1, a new strain of which has been circulating worldwide since 2020.

Since recording its first case in June, more than 200 wild seabirds in Australia have been infected, with fears that the highly infectious flu could quickly ‘jump’ to other species.

While H5N1 has infected animals from foxes to sea lions in other parts of the world in recent years, the epidemic now threatens some of Australia’s most iconic wildlife – many of which are found nowhere else on earth.

An Australian government assessment of more than 2,000 native species warned that nearly one in five faces a high risk from the deadly H5N1 bird flu, with hundreds of unique birds and mammals vulnerable to severe population reductions or even extinction.

Those animals include iconic species like the Tasmanian devils, quolls, and dingoes.

Other aquatic mammals, including the platypus, which is only found in Australia, are at risk of infection through contact with bird droppings in shared wetlands and coastal environments.

News.title: Selfie-seekers bring Man Utd vs Leeds match to premature end
News.content:
Aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events? Manchester United against Leeds United in Dublin always had the capacity to be lively, but try explaining the half hour that Bruno Fernandes experienced in one breath. It would be impossible.

There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.

Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.

You could say it was harmless fun but it should not have happened and the flummoxed faces that were pulled on the Manchester United bench, as an army in high-visibility jackets stood and watched it all unfold, suggested they took a dim view.

Sports.title: Tears for Fears icon Curt Smith aims to make hometown club the ‘next Wrexham’ with £6.3m Hollywood takeover
Sports.content:
TEARS FOR FEARS legend Curt Smith is hoping to help turn his boyhood club Bath City into the next Wrexham.

The 65-year-old singer has joined a consortium led by LA-based businessman Andrew Stalbow which is completing a £6.3million takeover of the National League South outfit.



Smith, who was born and raised in Bath, will become an ambassador for the club as the new owners look to transform its fortunes.

And he has already set his sights on climbing the English football pyramid – with the Football League targeted within five or six years.



Smith told The Telegraph: “The dream is to climb the ladder and get into the Football League in the next five or six years, and have a stadium which can get somewhere close to 8,000 fans again.”

Bath currently play in the sixth tier of English football, one division below the National League — the level Wrexham were playing at when Hollywood stars Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney bought the club in 2021.

Wrexham subsequently enjoyed an extraordinary rise, winning three promotions in three seasons between 2022 and 2025 to reach the Championship.

Smith admits he wants Bath to follow a similar path, although he was quick to point out he is no Reynolds.

He said: “I’m no Ryan Reynolds. His level of fame is a lot higher than mine, but I know my reputation is on the line.”

Smith, who has sold more than 30million records as part of Tears for Fears, now lives in Los Angeles but returned to his hometown to reassure supporters about the ambitious project.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Smith said: “The idea began with Andrew. A mutual friend put us in touch. We both live in LA and after speaking with him it was obvious he is a huge football fan who wanted to do this the right way for the right reasons.

“I’ve been at the Bath stadium [Twerton Park] when there were only 600 people.

“After our bid was announced, there were 1,300 at the next match, despite us just being relegated. To have that sort of effect already is very exciting.”

Smith wants Bath to become a major football force in a city traditionally dominated by rugby.



He added: “We want Bath to be known as a football city as much as a rugby city. It’s a lofty ambition, but one that should be doable. There is no reason why the clubs cannot thrive side by side.

“The community element of our bid is fundamental to it. I feel like being involved means I can give something back to my city in a tangible way.

“Without question that’s a big part of this. I was brought up on a council estate in Bath, so although I live in America now, it feels important to be able to get involved in this way.”



The new owners are also promising to clean up Bath’s finances while investing in the squad and infrastructure rather than chasing instant success.

Smith said: “We’re taking away debt and investing in the team.

“We want to become a professional club, first. That would be a huge jump for us. We’ll do it bit by bit.”

For Smith, the Wrexham blueprint proves what can happen when a club combines investment with community backing.

But the Tears for Fears star knows the hard work starts now, with the goal to make Bath a Football League club.

Sports.title: Why are EFL matches at 3pm on Saturday allowed to be broadcast on TV?
Sports.content:
THE opening weekend of the EFL kicks off on Friday night as Wolves welcome Blackburn to Molineux.

Most matches from the Championship, League One and League Two will take place on Saturday in the traditional 3pm slot.



And fear not if you can’t make it to the stadium to see your team in person, as every opening game across the EFL will be broadcast on Sky Sports – including the matches on Saturday at 3pm.

Why are EFL matches at 3pm on Saturday allowed to be broadcast on TV?

Ordinarily, matches that kick-off at 3pm on Saturday are not allowed to be shown on television.



This is more commonly referred to as the ‘3pm blackout’, where games taking place between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday cannot be aired by broadcasters.

The ruling comes from Uefa’s Article 48, which allows a nation’s football association to nominate ‘blocked hours’ for which matches played in that time period are not allowed to be shown on TV domestically.

It’s the Premier League, the EFL and the FA’s request that the ‘3pm blackout’ is enforced in conjunction with Article 48.

It has been in place since 1960 and is designed to protect attendances at lower league clubs.

Article 48 – the ‘3pm blackout’ – only applies when 50 per cent of games in the top two divisions kick off at 3pm on a Saturday.

As the Premier League doesn’t kick off for another week and only six Championship matches are scheduled for 3pm on Saturday, the ruling is not enforced, meaning all matches this weekend can be broadcast live domestically.



Sky Sports will air all 25 3pm games across the EFL on Saturday, giving more fans the chance to see their clubs’ new players in action.

The traditional ‘3pm blackout’ will return when the Premier League gets underway next weekend.

Sports.title: Salford boss Peter Cklamovski opens up on 15 years with Big Ange as he targets glory under Gary Neville & David Beckham
Sports.content:
PETER CKLAMOVSKI has vowed to bring Ange Ball to League Two with the Class of 92’s Salford.

The new Ammies boss was Ange Postecoglou’s trusted lieutenant during a trophy-laden spell, winning the 2015 Asian Cup with Australia and the J1 League title with Yokohama F. Marinos.



Big Ange went on to conquer Scotland with Celtic, winning back-to-back titles and a domestic treble. He then brought his high-octane style to Tottenham, firing Spurs into the Champions League by lifting the Europa League.

Now, after eight years carving out his own managerial path across Australia, Malaysia, and Japan, Cklamovski has landed in the EFL.



And working under the ambitious ownership group led by Gary Neville and David Beckham — with Manchester United icon Paul Scholes keeping a keen eye on the boardroom — the Australian gaffer is determined to build a legacy that will make his ultimate mentor proud.

Cklamovski opened up on his deep connection with Postecoglou — and told SunSport: “I’ve been on my own for eight years, but for 15 years I was privileged to share a journey with Ange.

“It’s something I feel truly blessed about. We shared many great moments together from football and life, but some iconic moments for Australian football as well.

“It’s a special connection for sure. He’s a special man, super coach and leader who I’m blessed to have as a mentor.

“Whatever I do, I like to always reflect back and be an extension of his legacy. That’s how much I love him, that’s how much he means to me.

“In the next 12 months, working hard for Salford City with great people around, a strong playing group, committed, hungry, ambitious, we’ll all work hard to achieve something special. I know that’ll make him proud as well.”



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The line between former boss and friend is long gone as they both both tackle new jobs with Postecoglou taking over at Saudi Pro-League side Al-Nassr

He added: “He’s always there for me. We’ll always be in contact. It’s a special connection, a special relationship that I value and he values.”

Cklamovski revealed the lessons he took working alongside the former Spurs and Celtic boss.

He said: “It’s a really difficult one to isolate separate moments. I guess in reflection, it’s a mentality and a belief to do it a certain way, the conviction in doing that, and the mindset to never stand still.



“It’s to always push yourself and each other to be better. That transmits into a playing group, staff, a club or country.”

Cklamovski arrives in Greater Manchester with vast global experience, having tested himself in some of Asia’s toughest leagues before taking the plunge into English football.

He said: “I love the English culture. It’s an honour and privilege to be here. I’ve got the benefit of more than two decades of work built in different regions to bring here and put a stamp on what we do.”

And despite Postecoglou’s trademark attacking style being forged at the top level, Cklamovski is convinced that same philosophy can turn League Two upside down.

He added: “I’ve got no doubt. It’s not just about playing a certain way. It’s about building a strong team with a mentality that goes with it.



“You want to play a brand of football that’s going to be exciting. That’s Salford City. We want to be entertaining. We want to get our fans jumping in the stands.

“But we’ll also be a team that’s ready to roll our sleeves up in any condition — whether it be rain, hail, shine, good pitches, or muddy pitches. We’ll be committed to playing strong football that has a mentality to score goals and keep clean sheets.”

That mindset is forged on the training pitch. Cklamovski has already laid down the law following an intensive pre-season, including a 10-day camp in Spain.

“You play the way you train,” he warned. “We won’t waste a second on the pitch, and we haven’t done so yet.

“We’ve not wasted a day. Everything means something to us on the field. We say ‘stay humble and hustle.’ We’ll do that on a daily basis.”



Off the pitch, Salford boasts an ownership set-up unlike almost any other in lower-league football with the Class of 92.

Cklamovski said: “There is no pressure for me. They’re absolute legends of the game, absolute gentlemen. With Scholesy, there’s knowledge everywhere.

“Importantly for me, I just focus on the football and control what we do in the training environment. The ambition is to produce a team that can play a brand of football to make them proud, and get them excited to watch the way we play.”

Salford suffered a heartbreaking 3-0 play-off final defeat against Notts County in May.

But the Aussie is using that Wembley setback as fuel for direct promotion.



He insisted: “Within a negative of a setback, you learn a lot. We must use that heartache as a foundation to springboard forward. Think about what’s next, get better every day, and keep working hard to create the team that we dream to be.

Sports.title: Jose Mourinho reveals Roman Abramovich vetoed his dream Chelsea transfer in favour of flop Andriy Shevchenko
Sports.content:
JOSE MOURINHO has revealed ex-Chelsea chief Roman Abramovich vetoed his bid to sign Samuel Eto’o in 2006.

The legendary former Blues boss was part of a golden era at Stamford Bridge after winning back to back Prem titles in 2005 and 2006.



The Special One oversaw a host of big-name transfers during his three years in west London as the likes of Didier Drogba, Arjen Robben and Michael Essien arrived.

But things started unravelling at the start of Mourinho‘s third season and the Portuguese coach has shed light on a disagreement with Russian chief Abramovich.



He said Abramovich was pushing for Andriy Shevchenko because of their “connections”, but insisted he “never wanted to sign him”.

Instead, he was after highly-rated Eto’o, who had just scored 34 goals for Barcelona ahead of the 2006-07 season.



Speaking in his Netflix documentary Mourinho, the 63-year-old said: “Abramovich has an incredible passion for football, but he had a complete lack of understanding of the situation.

“Shevchenko was on the negotiating table because of his connections with the boss, his connections with agents, and I never wanted to sign him, but I never told anyone, so that’s also my responsibility.

“Do you want to know which player I wanted? Samuel Eto’o.”

Chelsea eventually snapped up Shevchenko in a £30million deal from AC Milan in May 2006, but the Ukrainian had mixed fortunes at the club.

If a player earns a sizeable chunk of their points through defensive actions then there should be a certain degree of caution if their defensive workload is reduced.

That being said, it’s possible this transfer will benefit Anderson in other ways.

As one of the strongest teams in Europe, Man City tend to dominate possession and territory in most fixtures, which could lead to more goal involvements for the hardworking midfielder.

It’s likely he will find himself in advanced positions more regularly and he has the ability to make things happen with the ball at his feet 25 yards from goal, especially with the likes of Erling Haaland (£8.5m), Antoine Semenyo (£6m) and Jeremy Doku (£5m) ahead of him.

Risk-adverse gaffers will wait and see how Anderson fits in at the Etihad but it’s understandable why 5.4% of managers are willing to take a punt on him from the off at this stage — City’s early fixtures are relatively favourable.

Sports.title: ‘Club decided I had to leave’ – Former Arsenal and Chelsea star Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang opens up over nightmare season
Sports.content:
PIERRE-EMERICK AUBAMEYANG has opened up on his shock Marseille departure this summer.

The former Chelsea and Arsenal forward landed for his second stint with the French outfit in 2025, after a spell in Saudi with Al Qadsiah.



He quickly cemented himself as a fan favourite and was the club’s second-highest scorer in all competitions.

But despite the 37-year-old’s blistering form, he was among the number of Marseille stars to depart the club in the summer window.



Now he has revealed that decision to join LaLiga outfit Deportivo La Coruna was out of his hands, and gave his explanation for the dire season that has left the club needing to sell.

He explained, via L’Equipe: “Given the situation, the club decided I had to leave. And I wasn’t going to go against the club’s wishes.



“I’m not someone who likes to cause trouble or be a burden. I think the club already has enough problems.”

Marseille went from a second-place finish in the 2024/25 campaign to a fifth-place finish last season, while suffering a shock league-phase exit in the Champions League.

Top scorer Mason Greenwood, starting defender Facundo Medina and keeper Geronimo Rulli have all joined the Gabon international in leaving the club this window.

Aubameyang continued: “It’s been a very, very trying season. The context was quite unusual with all the changes that took place at the club.

Sports.title: Rangers boss McInnes 'doing his best', says Halliday
Sports.content:
"Derek McInnes is doing the best that he possibly can with what's at his disposal to try and get results."

Former Rangers midfielder Andy Halliday has defended the new Gers manager amid his winless start at Ibrox, accusing the club's hierarchy of "gross mismanagement".

The pressure has increased on McInnes and his players after they extended their winless run to four games, crashing out of the Europa League to Polish side Jagiellonia Bialystok.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player McInnes reflected on a disappointing result in the Europa League

But Halliday, who spent five seasons at Ibrox, does not think the blame lies with the manager.

"He's trying to find a formula, he's trying to find a solution, he's trying to find players that he trusts. Whether that's personnel or whether that's shape and he's really scratching the surface," he told Sky Sports News.

"You look at the balance of the squad and there's a real lack of pace, a real lack of creativity, no one that can dictate the tempo of a game.

"Derek McInnes is doing the best that he possibly can with what's at his disposal to try and get results. At this moment in time, he's not found that solution."

Rangers have made nine new signings this summer, while a deal for £6.5m for PSV winger Couhaib Driouech was called off after an injury was picked up during his medical.

Image: Rangers pulled out of a deal for Couhaib Driouech due to an injury

While fans have raised concerns about player recruitment, chairman Andrew Cavenagh defended the work in that department at a shareholder Q&A, adding he believes the squad is better than it was 12 months ago.

But despite that, Halliday believes the issues are continuing to come from the top.

"A gross level of mismanagement," he added when asked about the club's incoming players.

"If you've signed 27 players in the space of 12 months, then you've got so many decisions wrong.

"It is quite incredible that we've allowed this to take place. Only one left-back in the door, three centre-halves, only two wingers, a whole host of central-midfield players that all kind of fit the same profile.

"So they're right in saying they still need more players, but it has to be players that are an immediate upgrade on what they currently have, or it's obviously going to be a long season.

"They need an upgrade, and I think it's hard to say they've done that."

Sports.content:
Formula 1 returns after its summer break as the second half of the 2026 season begins with a Sprint weekend at the Dutch Grand Prix.

This is also the last Dutch Grand Prix as the event has not been renewed beyond this year, so the Orange Army will be out to support Max Verstappen racing on home soil for potentially the final time in his career.

Verstappen is yet to win a race this year but could play a key role in the title race as Kimi Antonelli looks to remain in control of the Drivers' Championship.

Antonelli leads Lewis Hamilton by 50 points and George Russell by 59 points but that advantage could quickly disappear, particularly if Ferrari continue to bring upgrades.

Image: The F1 Drivers' Championship with 12 rounds remaining

On paper, the Zandvoort circuit should suit Ferrari as it does not feature many straights but McLaren's Lando Norris won last time out at the twisty Hungaroring and should also be a threat.

Oscar Piastri won last year's Dutch Grand Prix, which is currently his last victory in F1, and the Australian needs to rediscover that form again in the second half of this season.

It is also a big race for Russell, who got engaged to his long-term partner Carmen Montero Mundt over the summer break, given Antonelli's superb recent form.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the 2025 Dutch Grand Prix from Zandvoort

Dutch GP circuit: Zandvoort track layout

Zandvoort is one of the drivers' favourite tracks thanks to its high-speed corners and banked bends at Turn 3 and the flat-out final turn.

It can be tricky to overtake with only one long straight down to Turn 1 so track position is critical and we could see a similar race to Hungary last time out.

Dutch GP weather at Zandvoort

Cooler conditions compared to much of the European summer are expected for the Zandvoort race weekend, with temperature highs in the low 20s. There is also a chance of light showers.

Sports.title: Maresca in no mood to be 'friendly' as Arteta makes bold claim
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca has revealed part of his intention in his first season as Manchester City boss is to "close the gap to Arsenal", after finishing seven points shy of the Premier League champions last term.

A first glimpse of how realistic that ambition is will be gleaned in the Community Shield on Sunday.

The Gunners have historically won all three of their Community Shield matches against City, with this weekend's heavyweight bout in Cardiff destined to be a precursor to the start of an intriguing new rivalry between Mikel Arteta and Maresca.

The fixture also signals the final countdown to the start of the Premier League proper, with Arsenal opening their campaign against Coventry five days later and City beginning two days after that vs Bournemouth - both live on Sky Sports.

According to Sky Sports' predictor, Arsenal are favourites to retain their crown, some four points clear of Man City. But there is renewed hunger from a different challenger to Pep Guardiola to disrupt those odds. Neither manager is likely to treat this introductory meeting, with silverware on the line, as cordial.

"For me personally, it's a trophy," Maresca said. "When trophies are there in a final you are there to win the game, no friendly game at all. We want to try our best to win the first trophy.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca was non-committal when asked about the future of Rodri and the club's interest in Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez

"Arsenal have shown over the last few years, they have always been there. They're a fantastic team. Well managed, well coached from Mikel, and last year they win the Premier League.

"But we are City, we want to close the gap.

"Pre-season has been good. Now we need to compete, win games, win titles. I want to see high spirit and the right mentality."

When asked if Erling Haaland is fit to feature, Maresca added: "He is ok. He had a small thing behind the heel. But he's ok. Everyone is fit, but we know some of them have just arrived [after their summer break] two days ago."

Arteta: Maresca is as good as Pep - my players are hungry

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta says the transfer window still offers an opportunity to evolve and does not rule out players joining or leaving the club

Meanwhile, Arsenal manager Arteta revealed Maresca is "just as good" as his predecessor Guardiola - while also agreeing the Community Shield is a valid trophy - that can set the marker for the season ahead.

"The best version of Arsenal has to be on Sunday. That's the intention," said Arteta. "The best performance, the best way to start the season by lifting the first trophy. That's the way we've prepared the season."

Asked about facing City without Guardiola, Arteta replied: "Now it's Enzo - who is as good as [Guardiola], because I know him well. He will provide something different to the club."

Arteta confirmed that bar the injured Jurrien Timber and William Saliba, Arsenal have a clean bill of health - which includes Bukayo Saka, Declan Rice and Martin Zubimendi who are yet to play in pre-season yet.

"It's a trophy, one that we can have because we earned last year it from winning the Premier League," added Arteta. "You can tell how hungry the players are, which is a good sign.

"I love the way the players have come back, most of them earlier as expected. Really fit, we've done all the testing. They all seem in a great condition.

"The moment they started to look at each other, I said: 'look at the squad that we have and what we're building'. There's a lot of excitement."

Team news: Haaland unlikely, Foden's big chance

Analysis by Sky Sports' Laura Hunter:

Man City's final pre-season friendly was played on August 9, a 3-1 win over Atletico Madrid, and I expect Sunday's XI to be similar. Assuming Rayan Ait Nouri is in good enough condition, he should start at left-back. And with all the speculation around Tijjani Reijnders, it is unlikely he plays on Sunday - or ever again for City.

Maresca's central-midfield options are therefore Nico Gonzalez or Rico Lewis. England duo Nico O'Reilly and Elliot Anderson are the obvious contenders to take up that position when the Premier League kickstarts but neither have had a pre-season because of the World Cup.

Omar Marmoush scored twice, both assisted by Antoine Semenyo, in that Atletico win and is likely to play through the middle as Haaland eases back into action. Phil Foden's comeback trail will also begin after a summer absent of international obligations. He has got a chance to make the No 10 shirt his.

Team news: Bruno to start but Rice, Saka on bench?

Analysis by Sky Sports' Sam Blitz:

Arteta confirmed Rice, Saka and Zubimendi are available to play - but during the pre-season friendlies, the vast majority of Arsenal players were given 30 minutes in their first outings.

It would be wise to predict that the trio are set to start on the bench, but play the final half an hour.

That means a midfield spot for Bruno Guimaraes - who made his debut against Como - is likely in Cardiff. A first real chance to see the Brazilian in the climate Arsenal brought him in for. It could also mean Myles Lewis-Skelly starts despite all the speculation about his future, with Arteta not confirming the teenager is set to stay this summer.

Another summer signing in Christos Tzolis is expected to get a run-out on the left wing - a first real microscope test for him as well - while Max Dowman's full pre-season means he could start over Noni Madueke.

Arteta has a left-back dilemma in who to pick out of Riccardo Calafiori and Piero Hincapie - the more-defensive latter may get the nod - while a more energised Martin Odegaard has a chance to lay down a marker after a stop-start campaign last term.

Sports.title: Cadillac: Why Lowdon axed suddenly and Perez’s future amid rival links
Sports.content:
A week before Formula 1’s return to action in Zandvoort, Cadillac provided the unexpected news of the sport’s summer break by removing Graeme Lowdon as team principal and replacing him with former Alpine chief Marcin Budkowski.

The decision was taken by Cadillac F1 team chief executive Dan Towriss, who spoke to the media along with new recruit Budkowski soon after the surprise announcement to address some of the main questions surrounding both that significant change and other talking points at the sport's newest team mid-way through their debut season.

Here are four things we learned...

'A narrow window of opportunity' - why did Cadillac make Lowdon change now?

While changes of team principal in Formula 1 are far more frequent than they used to be, with all teams except Mercedes changing their chief at least once since the end of 2022, mid-season exits are still not quite as commonplace as they are in football, for instance.

So the sudden nature of Lowdon's exit, which had not been the subject of any recent speculation, came as a surprise, particularly as Cadillac are just 11 races into their first season on the grid and had always warned they would likely be spending the campaign racing towards the back of the field.

Towriss said the plan had always been for Lowdon to eventually "hand the baton off to someone else" for the next stage of Cadillac's development but admitted "that the time for that change came sooner than was expected".

"I think Graeme and I always talked about that there would be a transition at some point," said team chief executive Towriss, who also runs TWG Motorsports which founded the F1 outfit with General Motors.

Image: Lowdon had been instrumental in setting up F1's newest team and getting it onto the grid from Melbourne

"This decision was mine. I think there's a very narrow window of opportunity when you look at what we're building and an opportunity to build something new and innovative.

"What I didn't want to do was build something that's already been done, something that's old and then try to improve it.

"I think that the time for that change came sooner than was expected. I wouldn't say that it's the performance or the teething issues over the last few weeks. It's really about just having a clear vision on what we're building in the future, the rate of progress and making sure that matches the ambitions of ownership."

Fixing reliability problems identified as 'urgent' task by new boss Budkowski

While Towriss downplayed the significance of what he called the rookie team's "teething issues" on track in the timing of his decision to remove Lowdon, Cadillac's progress in their maiden season has clearly been hampered by reliability problems.

The team recorded just one two-car race finish in the seven races leading up to the summer break with overheating brakes proving to be a consistent issue on the MAC-26.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Valtteri Bottas suffered brake failure in final practice at Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya.

Budkowski, who starts work at the factory on Monday, said that they needed to fix their reliability problems "very, very urgently" as it was compromising the team from getting the most out of the upgrade packages being brought to the track.

"There are also reliability issues that have marred the team in the first part of the season," said Budkowski.

"In some part it's understandable, it's a new team, it's a new group of people, they are learning together and they are failing together and failure is a part of learning in Formula 1.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cadillac's Sergio Perez made a swift escape from his car after his brakes went on fire at the end of P2 at the Monaco Grand Prix.

"It's not pleasant but these things have clearly prevented the team from understanding more because mileage at the end of the day, during a race, it's all data that you accumulate, it's all understanding of the car and I think that needs to be fixed very, very urgently.

"I'm sure there is determination in the team to do that but there will be a strong focus on sorting the issues we are having at the moment because otherwise there's no point in developing if you can't race the parts that you're bringing."

Cadillac 'very confident' of keeping Perez despite Williams links

While the US-owned team represents F1's first start-up for a decade, the outfit opted to ensure they had a shortage of experience behind the wheel for their first season by signing up Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas, who have over 500 race starts and 16 grands prix wins between them.

Perez has outperformed Bottas so far on their respective returns to the grid with the Mexican veteran since linked with potential other drives for 2027, including Williams were Carlos Sainz to move elsewhere.

While aware of that speculation, Towriss is confident Perez will stay with them into 2027.

"Checo has been a tremendous asset to the team," he said. "He's driven very well and certainly has pushed quite hard.

"I'm very confident that Checo is going to remain with Cadillac and we're not distracted by the Williams rumours for a second.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sergio Perez joins Scottie Scheffler for a round at the Cadillac Championship

"We're very confident in the relationship here and that you're going to see him piloting the Cadillac F1 car."

Cadillac themselves have been linked with other younger drivers, notably Ferrari-backed youngster Rafael Camara, the 21-year-old rising star from Brazil who is the reigning F3 champion and sits third in his maiden season of F2.

Towriss said he was "very happy" with his current experienced duo although did not shut the door on the prospect of hiring a younger gun sometime in the future.

"It's a great question, whether a younger driver would come in and push the team, it's certainly something that we think about," he said. "We've got two experienced drivers that we're very happy with, that are pushing the team and will continue to push them.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ted Kravitz was put through his paces as he cycled around the Red Bull Ring with Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas.

"I'll throw the caveat though, it's Formula 1 and things can always change. There are no changes planned at the moment for 2027, but things can always change.

"But I know there's been some of the rumours out there with some of the young drivers, they're not substantiated, so that's not something I would focus on. We're not focused on that at the moment."

'Different rules but the same game' - what next for Cadillac as they plot move up grid?

Cadillac represents the 49-year-old Budkowski's first job at an F1 team since he left his executive director role at Alpine at the start of 2022, although he has remained a regular in the paddock owing to his work with Polish TV.

It will be the fifth different team he has worked at, while he also has the experience of three years at governing body the FIA, where he headed up its technical department to 2017 before joining Renault.

Cadillac are backed by American car giant General Motors, who ultimately plan to build their own engine, and Budkowski brings experience of working on both sides of the sport's regulatory fence.

Image: Budkowski during his time at Renault in 2020

Asked how the sport had changed in his four years away from a front-line role, Budkowski said: "The fight is really, really ruthless. One thing that strikes me is how competitive all the teams are and how good and professional all the teams are.

"In other aspects, it's different rules but the same game. At the end of the day, I don't think in my role it's going to be about this regulation or that regulation, it will be a slightly higher-level view of it.

"It's how do we steer the regulations in the future in our favour? Because the regulatory process is for the good of the sport but there's also a lot of self-interest in it, and I've got experience in that from my time at the FIA.

"You have to be the best everywhere, you have to put attention to detail, and in the era of the cost cap, you can't buy performance anymore and you can't buy your way out of a mistake either."

Towriss also underlined that Cadillac are ultimately in F1 to win, making clear they needed to think both short and long-term to ensure they evolve in the best way to be on top of future developments such as the rise of AI technology.

"The ambition is to build more than a team that is there to participate, it's a team that's a winning organisation in the future," added the 54-year-old American.

"We're far from that, but I think that's the end goal for everybody, and to build a team that's focused on the future.

Image: Perez briefly scored Cadillac's first point in Monaco before a post-race time penalty dropped him down the order

"There's a lot of changes in Formula 1, huge changes in regulations this year. There's a huge societal change as well going on with AI taking over a lot of things, and I think it's coming to Formula 1, but it's the very, very beginning of that.

"And I think the teams of the future look very different from what they look now. So it's going to be about evolving what's been put in place and improving it in the short term, but also looking in the future at what does an F1 team look in the future.

Sports.title: Bunting stunned by Smith in New Zealand Darts Masters upset
Sports.content:
Stephen Bunting was the highest-profile casualty on day one of the New Zealand Darts Masters as he was dumped out of the last 16 by Raymond Smith in Auckland.

Smith reeled off five unanswered legs en route to a 6-2 victory over third seed Bunting, averaging 99.81 and converting 86 per cent of his attempts at a double and notably sealing victory with a 124 checkout on the bullseye.

"It feels pretty awesome," Smith said. "Eight years since I last played on a PDC stage, so I'm pretty stoked.

"I think I played really well. What we're doing in the ADA, DPNZ and ANZ Premier League is setting us up for this sort of stuff. What the PDC is investing in the Oceanic region is showing in the results."

Smith's reward for beating Bunting is a quarter-final tie against fellow Australian Adam Leek, who survived six match darts against Ross Smith before securing victory in a last-leg decider on his dramatic World Series of Darts debut.

Sports.title: Is Fernandez worth two Rodris? Transfer valuations explained
Sports.content:
Speculation is swirling around two of the Premier League's leading midfielders. As Barcelona push to sign Rodri, Manchester City are being linked with a move for Enzo Fernandez. But why does the Chelsea player have a much higher transfer value?

Rodri is a four-time Premier League title winner who was named player of the tournament at the World Cup with Spain. And yet Barcelona are hoping to land him for a fee in the region of £60m, while Chelsea are demanding twice as much for Fernandez.

In this edition of Between the Lines, the Sky Sports strand unpicking the data behind football's biggest stories, we explain what goes into player transfer valuations as this summer's spending continues.

Youth trumps experience

Rodri's outstanding World Cup performances for Spain, following two injury-hit seasons with Manchester City, proved the former Ballon d'Or winner is still capable of operating at his best level.

Even in a disrupted Premier League campaign last term, data from Gradient Sports shows Rodri outperformed Fernandez in five out of six key midfield metrics, including passing, carrying and tackling.

Rodri's age, however, having turned 30 at the start of the summer, puts him at a different stage of his career to Fernandez, who is heading into what should be his peak years at 25.

Factoring current Premier League midfielders who have reached a Transfermarkt value of £35m at some point in their careers, the graphic below shows that, on average, values peak at 27 before beginning a steady decline as players head towards their 30s.

Longer deal, higher value?

Contract length is another important factor in player valuations, both in relation to Rodri and Fernandez, and more broadly.

While Rodri is entering the final year of his contract, meaning Manchester City run the risk of losing him for nothing next summer, Fernandez has six years remaining on his deal at Chelsea, putting his club in a much stronger negotiating position.
