World.title: Luigi Mangione admits to shooting health care executive Brian Thompson, pleads guilty to federal charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Luigi Mangione on Friday admitted to fatally shooting health insurance executive Brian Thompson in the back on a Manhattan sidewalk in 2024, while pleading guilty to two federal stalking charges in court.

Mangione, 28, previously pleaded not guilty in April ⁠2025 to murder, weapons and stalking charges brought by Manhattan federal prosecutors, but U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett threw out the murder and weapons charges over legal technicalities in a January ruling, leaving two stalking charges in places.

That ruling eliminated the possibility that Mangione would face the death penalty, ‌though he still faces a possible sentence of life without parole if convicted on two charges: interstate stalking resulting in death and stalking through use of interstate facilities resulting in death.

On Friday, Garnett asked him a series of questions designed to make sure he understood the consequences of a guilty plea.

Mangione answered no when asked if he had ever ⁠been treated or hospitalized for a mental illness. His lawyers and prosecutors told Garnett he was mentally competent enough to knowingly plead guilty, and the judge agreed.

The judge scheduled sentencing for Dec. 18.

It's not clear what effect, if any, the guilty plea would have on the second-degree murder charges filed in a separate case filed by New York State officials. The trial in that case is scheduled to begin on Sept. 8.

WATCH | Why the judge tossed some charges earlier this year: Death penalty off the table for Luigi Mangione as judge dismisses federal murder charge | Duration 2:10 A federal judge in New York has dismissed a murder charge against Luigi Mangione, accused of killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in 2024. U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett found the charge technically flawed. Mangione will still face federal stalking and firearms charges, as well as a separate state murder charge.

Thompson led Minnesota-based UnitedHealth Group's insurance unit before he was shot from behind on a Manhattan sidewalk early in the morning of Dec. 4, 2024. The 50-year-old Iowa native was attending an investor conference at a city hotel.

Thompson's widow sat in the ​front row of the gallery on Friday with other members of his family.

Graphic footage of the killing and a five-day manhunt for a suspect made the case a media fixture and social ⁠media sensation. Mangione was arrested at a McDonald's in Altoona, Pa., on Dec. 9, 2024

Born and raised in Maryland, Mangione lived a somewhat itinerant life in the two years leading up to Thompson's killing, working a series of jobs remotely and living for a time in Hawaii and California.

Police have alleged he lashed out at health insurers in his private writings.

UnitedHealth has said there's no record of Mangione or members of his immediate family as being among its policyholders.

Mangione pleaded not guilty in December 2024 to state terrorism, murder, weapons and forgery charges brought by Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg. The terrorism charges were thrown out ⁠by a judge in September 2025.

Mangione would face 25 years to life in prison if convicted of second-degree murder.

It is possible Mangione's legal team could seek dismissal of the ​murder charge under New York's double jeopardy law, which protects people from being prosecuted twice for the same conduct. Bragg's office ​would oppose the move, arguing ⁠that the murder charge is legally distinct from the federal charges.

World.title: Trump trade rep says Washington 'not going to tolerate' retaliation as tariff deadline looms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Donald Trump's trade envoy says the administration will not accept any form of retaliation from Canada if the U.S. president follows through on his latest tariff threat.

"For us, this is not a trade war. We have domestic supply chains we're trying to protect," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters in Des Moines, Iowa, on Friday.

"It's not Canada specific, we're doing this globally. If a country retaliates against us, we're not going to tolerate that. We'll take action."

Canada and the U.S. have ramped up trade talks after Trump threatened to slap a hefty 50 per cent tariff on hundreds of Canadian goods starting on Aug. 19. Those tariffs would be on top of sectoral levies already in place.

Greer has met with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc multiple times in recent weeks and characterized the talks as "constructive."

"My sense is the Canadians, they want to have a more conciliatory approach but we'll see," Greer said.

WATCH | U.S.-Canada trade reps working on 'options': U.S.-Canada trade reps working on 'options' | Duration 2:49 Canadian and U.S. trade officials shared no new details on trade talks on Thursday. Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette urged Canada to hold the line and hold out for a fair deal.

Industry sources with knowledge of the trade talks have previously told CBC News that the Canadian side has made it clear that they see the Aug. 19 date as a cliff-type moment, meaning there would be no political appetite among Canadians to keep talks going if the tariffs come into place.

"At the end of the day, we're going to do what's best for America. If there's a way to bring Canada along with that, we're happy to do that. But we're mostly focused, first and foremost, on making sure President Trump's trade policy is executed," Greer said Friday.

On Thursday Greer said Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney will now be given "options" ahead of the Aug. 19 deadline. CBC News previously reported that the president could be presented with a potential path forward on Monday.

World.title: Ontario appeal court says Ford can rip out Toronto bike lanes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Premier Doug Ford’s government can rip out 19 kilometres of protected bike lanes in Toronto, the Court of Appeal for Ontario has ruled in a decision released Friday, reversing a lower court decision made in July 2025.

The law empowering the province to remove bike lanes along Bloor Street, Yonge Street and University Avenue was initially passed at Queen’s Park in 2024. But the infrastructure remained on Toronto’s streets after advocacy organization Cycle Toronto and others launched a legal challenge against the bill.

In the 2025 ruling, Justice Paul Schabas ruled the removal would be unconstitutional because it would put people at increased risk of harm and death, which engages the right to life and security of the person.

But a panel of three appeal court judges ruled Friday there is no constitutional obligation to regulate the use of roads in any particular manner.

"The legislature is free to legislate to remove a bicycle lane from a road — indeed, it may remove a road entirely — without implicating the Charter," reads the decision from three appeals court judges.

Michael Longfield, executive director of Cycle Toronto, said the decision is a step back for evidence-based decision making.

"I want to be clear that bike lanes do not cause traffic congestion. Removing them will put people's lives at risk," he said.

Longfield said Schabas's original ruling still found Ontario’s plans were pushed through despite its own advisers and external experts broadly agreeing the move wouldn’t accomplish its stated goal of reducing traffic congestion.

But in Friday's decision, the appeals judges wrote, "legislative policy is not arbitrary just because some or even many advisors, experts, and citizens predict that it will not work."

World.title: Montreal police take down high-powered surveillance camera after Radio-Canada story
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Montreal police are quietly growing their network of AI-powered tools to track vehicles and people across the city, raising questions about public transparency and privacy rights.

A high-powered camera able to scan and identify vehicles was spotted earlier this week by a Radio-Canada reporter, on a lamp post along Henri-Bourassa Boulevard in Montreal’s Rivière-des-Prairies neighbourhood.

It was quickly taken down on Wednesday, after Radio-Canada published an article about the camera.

The device used was a Cloudrunner CR-H2, manufactured by Montreal-based company Genetec, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) later confirmed.

Similar to the controversial Flock Safety cameras widely used in the United States, the system does more than scan licence plates.

It also captures and stores specific vehicle characteristics, including colour, make and model, according to the company’s website .

While Flock cameras in the U.S. share data in a central database accessible to multiple police forces, Genetec's system differs in that the collected information is managed by its specific operator.

SPVM spokesperson Marc-Antoine Bélanger told CBC News that access to the captured images is used exclusively for the investigators in charge of the targeted work.

Bélanger said in an email that the camera was removed to "preserve our ongoing investigative strategies."

He said the SPVM intentionally keeps its technological tools secret so as not to hinder complex investigations.

"Investigative techniques, including the means and technologies used, are governed by clear rules from the courts and constitute privileged information," Bélanger said.

But privacy advocates say there has been a lack of transparency in rolling out new technology.

WATCH | How civil liberties could be at risk as police use AI in investigations: Montreal police turn to AI to help with investigations, raising concerns about civil liberties | Duration 3:39 A high-powered camera able to scan and identify vehicles was spotted on a lamp post on Henri-Bourassa Boulevard in Montreal’s Rivière-des-Prairies neighbourhood. It was quickly taken down on Wednesday, after Radio-Canada published an article about the camera.

Dominique Peschard, a spokesperson for the Ligue des droits et libertés, a Quebec human rights group, said police need to keep the public informed about the kinds of tools they are using — and can do so without compromising their work.

“We're not asking what they are doing in detail, but what are the procedures?” Peschard said in an interview.

“Investigative techniques are getting more and more invasive with technology. You need more and more oversight to make sure it doesn’t go overboard and infringe on our Charter rights.”

Beyond licence plates

The use of the Cloudrunner cameras is part of a broader push by the SPVM into AI-driven technology.

The SPVM confirmed it is using iMotion ROC AI software, developed by Rank One Computing.

SPVM spokesperson Anik de Repentigny told CBC News the software is being used to help investigators sift through massive amounts of video, but denied that the force is using the software's facial recognition or biometric capabilities.

"This software will not be used to verify the identity of individuals in video images, but rather to identify the video passages where the targeted known element appears," de Repentigny said in an email to CBC earlier this year.

De Repentigny added that the system operates on a closed network offline from external databases.

SPVM spokesperson Anik de Repentigny said iMotion ROC AI software is being used to help investigators sift through massive amounts of video, but denied that the force is using the software's facial recognition or biometric capabilities. (iMotion)

The software analyzes footage from the SPVM's 46 marked urban security cameras, as well as private residential and commercial surveillance video manually collected by officers with citizen consent or a warrant.

An internal privacy impact assessment by the SPVM, obtained by CBC News through an access-to-information request, acknowledges the technology poses civil liberties risks, including the potential to put innocent bystanders under investigation and the risk of discrimination based on visible social characteristics.

The assessment, prepared in 2023, also says the risk of discrimination would be reduced because the software would be configured to search for objects — giving the example of a "red coat" or "green bike" — rather than identifiable traits such as ethnicity.

Lack of oversight?

The SPVM’s admission about the Cloudrunner camera on Wednesday came after a morning of confusion.

Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher initially indicated he had no knowledge of the device on Wednesday morning. Later in the day, Dagher clarified his earlier comments, stating he was distracted by separate news regarding alleged racism at a Montréal-Nord police station.

The chief confirmed the device belonged to the SPVM and was being used to target armed violence and vehicle thefts. Peschard said it was “striking” that the chief didn’t seem to be aware the SPVM was using the technology.

“Whenever new investigative tools are used, it should be under supervision of the leading staff of a police department,” he said. “It’s their responsibility to make sure there are protocols and people’s private information is protected.”

Public records show that last October, Montreal awarded a $17,134 contract with Genetec to obtain four Cloudrunner units on a one-year subscription.

While only one camera was spotted and removed, Bélanger told CBC News that more cameras could be added depending on the needs of investigations tackling armed violence, motor vehicle thefts and violence against merchants.

Cameras that can read licence plates have become increasingly common, and a source of controversy, in the United States. (David Goldman/Associated Press)

Andrew Elvish, vice-president at Genetec, said the technology is designed to respect people’s privacy and every interaction with the data gathered is logged.

“You should have an expectation of reasonable privacy,” he said, then added, “it’s a trade off. If the threat of something bad happening is high, as a community, what are we comfortable with giving up to ensure that the community is safe?”

In response to a request for comment, a City of Montreal spokesperson said it had not installed the Cloudrunner camera, and referred questions about its deployment to the SPVM.

During last fall’s election campaign, Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada championed the creation of a “voluntary” security camera registry that would allow officers to map out the locations of residents’ home closed-circuit television cameras.

In Quebec, the Commission d'accès à l'information mandates that video surveillance in public spaces by public bodies must address a "legitimate, important, urgent and real objective" and urges organizations to only collect images necessary to solve a targeted problem.

Jean-François Latreille, a lawyer specializing in data security and privacy, said the use of such tools must be tightly restricted.

If not, he said, "the individual will lose control over his privacy, at least in the public domain."

World.title: A Canadian payment giant is being sold to U.S. private equity. Is your digital privacy at risk?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A payment processing company responsible for approximately one in three payment transactions across Canada will soon be owned by an American private equity firm.

The Royal Bank of Canada and Bank of Montreal announced earlier this week they would be selling jointly owned Moneris, one of Canada's largest commerce solutions providers, to Francisco Partners for $2 billion.

So far, it's been positive for both RBC and BMO, with the companies' shares jumping after the deal's announcement. RBC expects to gain about $475 million from the sale after tax, and BMO $600 million.

However, some industry analysts are raising concerns the move could have negative repercussions for Canada's digital sovereignty amid the country's ongoing trade war with the U.S.

Wide-reaching implications

Broadly speaking, digital sovereignty refers to the power of a country, or individual, to retain control over its own digital assets.

In September, AI Minister Evan Solomon said that Canada needs to create a sovereign digital economy that is "free from coercion."

WATCH | Solomon spoke in September about why the government is acting: 'The moment is here' to modernize Canada's privacy laws: AI minister | Duration 1:29 Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon says the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act will help keep Canadians safe in the digital age. 'I think it's a common-sense approach to what Canadians and what average folks want from their digital media,' Solomon said on Monday about the new bill. 'They want some control over their personal information.'

That same month, dozens of experts and academics penned an open letter urging Prime Minister Mark Carney to swiftly "defend Canada's digital sovereignty" and protect the country from the whims of the Trump administration.

It's a sentiment Sharon Polsky, president of the Privacy and Access Council of Canada, shares.

"Canadians should be concerned because this is their information," she said.

"We're now going to have what has been a Canadian data-processing company that has access to everybody's purchasing habits ... available to other governments."

Thousands of businesses in Canada use Moneris. The processor services more than 325,000 points of commerce and processes more than five billion transactions every year, according to a press release from the company.

Polsky said the deal means Canadians' data could be available, not only to foreign governments, but foreign law enforcement agencies.

She gave an example of U.S. border agents potentially checking an individual's transaction history before allowing them to enter the country.

"Will you be stopped at the border because your purchase records indicate that you bought something with THC?" she said, referring to a chemical compound found in cannabis, which remains illegal in the U.S. under federal jurisdiction.

"It's possible these days, much more possible than ever before."

Transaction data as leverage?

That the deal is happening as the countries grapple with a trade war only heightens Polsky's concerns.

"It's easy to foresee that the rich data that comes from millions of Canadians' purchases could easily be leveraged to inform trade negotiations," said Polsky, who has advised corporations and governments for more than 30 years on privacy and access matters.

Colin Deacon, an Independent Canadian senator, is also concerned about how the U.S. government could use Canadians' data.

"[Data] under force and under request from the U.S. government could be then shared on an individual basis," said Deacon during an interview with CBC's Power and Politics.

WATCH | Deacon raises concerns over Moneris deal: Canadian senator concerned by U.S. purchase of BMO, RBC payment processor | Duration 8:39 Nova Scotia Sen. Colin Deacon is warning against further financial integration with the United States after one of Canada's biggest payment processing platforms was bought by an American bidder. Deacon joins Power & Politics to discuss why he is so concerned about this acquisition.

"There's a number of ways in which [U.S. President Donald Trump] has absolute control over services that Canadians rely on every day."

Both BMO and RBC pointed to press releases announcing the deal, refusing to provide further comment when contacted by CBC News.

"As ownership transitions to FP, Moneris's commitment to serving Canadian businesses will remain unchanged," read a separate press release from Moneris.

Privacy legislation in the works

Canada's legislation meant to protect digital privacy isn't where it needs to be, according to Polsky, who said this comes at Canadians' "collective peril."

"Canada isn't ready," she said.

Polsky argues there's a clear outcome if a company based in Canada is compelled by the U.S. to supply data as a result of this deal.

"If the choice is either to comply with the American law or go to jail, or comply with Canadian legislation that really is nowhere near as stringent … it's a no-brainer. They will comply with the American legislation."

The Canadian government has taken steps to address digital sovereignty. In June, the government introduced Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act.

It proposes a major overhaul of Canada's private sector privacy framework, updating language to establish privacy as a "fundamental right" and replace parts of the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA), which sets out rules for how businesses, including tech, airlines and banks, collect and use customers' data.

The bill also requires companies to conduct a "privacy impact assessment" before transferring personal data outside of Canada.

At the time, government officials said the legislation would cover any company that has a "substantial connection" to Canada.

But Polsky said C-36, and the Liberals' other attempts to update Canada's digital privacy laws, only "dance around the issues."

"They don't really speak to data being retained in Canada as a matter of national security or as a matter of data sovereignty," she said.

Bill C-36 represents the Liberal government's third attempt to update privacy regulations, following failed attempts in 2020 and 2023. It underwent its first reading in June, but has a number of steps to go before becoming law.

Meanwhile, the sale of Moneris still requires regulatory approvals, including clearance under the Competition Act, and is expected to close by the end of the banks' fiscal first quarter in 2027.

Where does that leave Canada?

"Behind the eight ball," said Polsky.

"[Canada is] trying to look tough, but we have a ways to go."

World.title: Northern Ontario man pleads guilty to trying to kill his 16-year-old ex-girlfriend with a sword
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains graphic details related to intimate partner violence.

A man from the northern Ontario town of Cobalt has pleaded guilty to the attempted murder of his 16-year-old ex-girlfriend with a sword two years ago.

Phillipe Rivard Gagnon, 20, entered the plea earlier this week at the Haileybury courthouse.

On the evening of Nov. 3, 2024, Kaylie Smith was on her way home from work and was getting off a transit bus in Cobalt when she was hit by an SUV.

Ontario Provincial Police say it was driven by Gagnon, who then attacked her with a sword.

In media interviews, Smith's family has said that one of Kaylie's hands was cut off and the other badly "mangled."

Gagnon, who was 18 at the time of the attack, was arrested and charged with attempted murder and possessing a dangerous weapon.

He has been held in custody since then, and has been transported from the jail in North Bay to attend court appearances in Haileybury over the past two years.

In his most recent appearance on Tuesday, Gagnon entered a plea of guilty on the attempted murder charge.

His weapons charge remains on the books and is expected to be dealt with by the courts in the coming months.

A sentencing hearing has yet to be scheduled, but the case is slated to be back in Haileybury court on Sept. 16.

Kaylie Smith, the victim of the attack, has been described as 'strong' and 'resilient' by family members. (Submitted by the Smith family)

World.title: B.C. wildfire officials plead for patience from Bald Range evacuees
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

THE LATEST:

Evacuation orders for properties from Cinnabar Creek to Westshore Estates have been downgraded to an evacuation alert for the Quilpituk Creek wildfire.

Evacuation alerts for properties south of Cinnabar Creek in the Wilson’s Landing area have been lifted for the Quilpituk Creek wildfire, according to Central Okanagan Emergency Management. There will be a phased re-entry for residents to limit traffic congestion.

The mayor of Summerland says the Bald Range wildfire is growing away from his community — but any re-entry of residents would take place in stages.

Highway 97 between Penticton and Peachland, through Summerland, reopened in a limited fashion on Thursday.

The B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) says that over 100 wildfires continue to burn throughout the province.

On Thursday morning, the province said there were roughly 18,900 people under evacuation order and roughly 10,000 more on evacuation alert across B.C.

A staged re-entry will take place for some evacuees from the Quilpituk wildfire, located north of Kelowna, as an evacuation order has been downgraded to an alert and an evacuation alert has been lifted.

Central Okanagan Emergency Management said Friday morning that there will be phased re-entry access for residents to "support an organized return home and limit traffic congestion."

Residents are advised to inspect their property and trees for any issues or damage before re-entering their homes.

No structural loss has been reported, according to the emergency management website.

The Quilpituk Creek fire was downgraded from out-of-control to being held on Thursday.

Pleas for patience near Bald Range fire

The Regional District of Central Okanagan (RDCO) is pleading for patience from residents forced to flee their homes due to the Bald Range wildfire.

It grew by seven square kilometres between Wednesday and Thursday, according to the BCWS, and covered an area of 191 square kilometres as of Thursday morning.

Crews work to extinguish spot fires near Summerland on Thursday. (Deanna Dunham/The Canadian Press)

While the RDCO says some of the thousands of evacuees from the fire may not see significant fire activity near their communities, that could change rapidly.

"The Bald Range [wildfire] remains a dynamic and challenging incident, with fire activity continuing on multiple flanks of the wildfire under extreme drought conditions and very dry fuels," the regional district said in a Thursday evening update.

WATCH | Summerland evacuees helped by faith organizations: Faith organizations step in to support Summerland evacuees | Duration 2:35

Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes said district officials had finalized much of their re-entry plans, and evacuees would return in a staged fashion once the BCWS gives the all-clear.

"The good thing for Summerland is that it's kind of moving away from the town," he said of the fire on Thursday evening.

"Not so good for the people who live in the direction that the fire is moving — but for us, it's a good development."

Premier David Eby had previously said specialized search-and-rescue crews are being deployed to conduct damage assessments, which have also taken place in the area of the Quilpituk Creek fire in the Okanagan.

There are more than 100 wildfires burning in B.C. as of Thursday night, and wildfire activity remains concentrated in the southern half of the province.

The largest wildfire remains the Pear Lake wildfire near Clinton, which covered an area of 1,574 square kilometres as of Thursday night.

In the Fraser Canyon, the Brunswick Creek fire complex around Boston Bar covered an area of more than 700 square kilometres.

Highways and air quality

Highway 97 reopened Thursday with limited daytime hours, according to DriveBC, though officials say highway conditions are subject to change with little warning and stopping isn't allowed.

The stretch between Peachland and the Pyramid Picnic Area in Kickininee Provincial Park had been closed due to the Bald Range wildfire.

Other closures to Highway 1 north of Hope and Highway 97 north of Cache Creek remain in place.

Air quality warnings were in place for many parts of southern B.C. on Thursday night, with warnings of high health risk due to wildfire smoke.

World.title: The End of Oak Street is a fun — but flat — Spielberg clone
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

What are you most concerned about as a housewife in 1982? Is it that your kids are off making flirty eyes with their fellow teens or running from the local bully? Is it that your slightly-estranged husband refuses to man the barbecue because he's off to work the second job you asked him to quit?

Or just maybe, the things you're most worried about are the blue lights pulsating around town, the oppressive heat suddenly coursing through the atmosphere — and what looks like a dinosaur tail snaking through your backyard.

Welcome to the world of Oak Street — or as our housewife Denise (Anne Hathaway) and writer/director David Robert Mitchell so forebodingly put it, The End of Oak Street — where a mild-mannered (and deeply unhappy) family's neighbourhood is mysteriously relocated back in time to the late Jurassic period where they're forced to battle both the strange creatures outside their home and all their internal estrangement inside.

As a Spielbergian tale that simultaneously feels ripped straight from a Stephen King book, it certainly does deliver on the vibe.

From aloof but loving, functional-alcoholic father Greg (Ewan McGregor), to forlorn genius elder sister Audrey (Maisy Stella), to boy-next-door little brother Brian (Christian Convery), this Detroit family reads more non-threateningly middle-American than a Leave it to Beaver fourth of July special.

And if we're to believe what everyone and their film-critic mother has decided, it's the perfect recipe for an Amblin-style, B-movie love letter. That, even if it is a bit reductive, Oak Street's frank and straightforward sentimentality plays like the nostalgic 80s romp yearned for by audiences burnt out on self-serious, trauma-infused films.

If you're looking for a good time at the movies, what could go wrong with a straight-shooting, time-travelling dino flick?

WATCH | The End of Oak Street trailer:

As it would turn out, quite a lot actually.

Because while Oak Street is at times genuinely fun and somewhat original, there seems to be something missing from what's been widely crowned as the summer blockbuster we've all been waiting for.

Instead, it's more a going-through-the-motions type film that seems very aware of how classic Spielberg films looked and felt — but isn't necessarily aware of the artistic intent behind them.

It's the exact type of movie you'd expect to find at the centre of a controversy involving an AI-version of the family's dog being used to advertise the film on a fake podcast.

An interpretation of Jurassic Park that begins and ends by looking up through brachiosaurus legs — but features none of the hubris of man, critique of capitalism stuff.

A fascination with the kids-on-bikes-solving-mysteries aesthetics of E.T. — but without any awareness of the anti-xenophobia, government paranoia theme it all rests on.

From left, Christian Convery, Anne Hathaway and Maisy Stella in a scene from The End of Oak Street. (Warner Bros. Pictures/The Associated Press)

In The End of Oak Street, that feeling catches up to you quickly.

In an almost impressive feat, the stakes set up for each character are juggled and discarded faster than pterodactyls ripping hunks from a portly man's chest cavity — a scene we do in fact get in Oak Street.

Will the movie focus on the idea of abandoned potential — set up by Denise's secretive attempts to launch a writing career with the help of an elderly retired editor down the street? Will it be about pursuing what you need to survive even in the face of overwhelming danger — a possibility brought up through Audrey's suggested crush on the neighbour girl?

Will it test how "moral" the average person really is when things get real — perhaps through Brian's borderline fanatical attention to the safety of his dog and the casual cruelty he doles out to neighbourhood friends?

The answer in The End of Oak Street is kind of yes — but actually, no. Aside from the fact that every member of this family seems to have a secret, any character trajectory is essentially thrown out the window the first time a dinosaur starts huffing and puffing.

Given the relatively truncated length (it clocks in at one hour, 39 minutes) and the protracted introductions for each family member, there's not much time left to do anything except show these half-developed characters screaming at therapods and sauropods of increasingly dubious design acting in increasingly dubious ways. Bet you've never seen dinosaurs get it on before.

But the dinosaur attacks become less and less interesting due to absent character growth, repetitive action sequences and aped visual language. After the fourth or fifth time Brian runs from the fourth or fifth identically dangerous growling feathery thing, you start to ask yourself what we're really doing here.

And during a family conversation in which literally every member gets the Jaws split-diopter treatment for absolutely no narrative reason, it starts to feel more like a Spielberg tribute band is playing than the birth of a new talent.

Though all this does raise an important question: should it matter that this dinosaur disaster movie doesn't have a point? Maybe not — we're here for the spectacle after all, and for that you just need giant lizards with giant teeth ripping apart flaming cars.

The more insufferable among us might point out that it does matter because this idea has been done before, and better.

Kazuo Umezu's The Drifting Classroom featured a school inexplicably thrust into an apocalyptic future — clearly borrowing from Japan's post-atomic bomb fears. And 1983's Testament went through much of the same isolated neighbourhood horror to tell the story of a family surviving nuclear fallout in a setting eerily similar to the first half of Oak Street.

The End of Oak Street tells the story of a suburban neighbourhood that's mysteriously transported back in time to the late Jurassic period. (Warner Bros. Pictures/The Associated Press)

But leaving out any deep examination, something still feels like it's missing.

Because despite Oak Street's more or less engaging set pieces, audiences might find themselves checking their watches since the director hasn't given them any tangible reason to root for the heroes.

Or, maybe they won't care.

Maybe the simple fact that Oak Street looks and sounds somewhat like Spielberg movies will be enough — even if it seems like nobody who made it cared what those movies were saying.

And if that's the case, at least it's good news for the future of AI-written movies.
