Brazilian food maker Dias Branco just showed how hard it is to protect profit when costs climb faster than prices. The pasta and biscuit giant, known formally as M.

Dias Branco, earned R$168.9 million, about US$33 million, in the second quarter of 2026. That was 22% less than a year earlier, even though it sold more food.

What the second quarter showed

The Ceará-based company reported its results after markets closed on 13 August 2026. The headline number was a net profit of R$168.9 million, or roughly US$33 million.

That figure was down 22% from the R$216.4 million posted a year earlier. So the company kept selling well but took home much less.

Net revenue barely moved, slipping 0.9% to R$2.70 billion, close to US$520 million. In plain terms, sales held steady while profit shrank.

The gap between those two lines tells the story. Costs and pricing, not weak demand, drove the decline.

Why M. Dias Branco earned less

The squeeze came from margins rather than sales. Operating expenses rose and weighed on the bottom line, even as the factories stayed busy.

EBITDA, a rough measure of operating cash flow, fell 17.5% to R$284.4 million, about US$55 million. Its margin narrowed to 10.5%, down from 12.7% a year earlier.

Prices also worked against the company. The average price across all categories fell 5%, from R$6.00 to R$5.70 per kilo.

Lower prices can win shelf space, yet they thin out each sale. As a result, more volume did not translate into more profit.

More food out the door

The volume story was actually a bright spot. Sales volume rose 4.4% to 477.3 thousand tonnes in the quarter.

That suggests shoppers kept reaching for the company’s pasta, biscuits and flour. Demand, in other words, was not the problem.

Cheaper prices likely helped move those extra tonnes. So the firm traded some margin for market share.

Over the first half, volumes reached 885 thousand tonnes. The direction of travel on the shelf remains upward.

A rare gross-margin gain

Not every margin moved the wrong way. Gross margin, measured before overheads, actually improved to 34.2% from 33%.

That hints at some relief on raw materials during the quarter. Better buying or milder input costs can lift the gross line.

Yet the gain stopped there. Higher expenses further down the income statement erased the benefit.

This is why EBITDA still fell even as gross margin rose. The pressure sat in operating costs, not in the cost of goods.

The bigger cost picture

Food makers live and die by a few big inputs. Wheat, energy and freight all feed into the price of a packet of pasta.

Analysts had expected a softer quarter, so the drop was not a shock. Still, the scale of the profit fall drew attention.

Management framed the period as two-sided. The company gained volume and share, while expenses pressured earnings.

For a firm this size, small shifts in cost ripple widely. A few cents per kilo, multiplied by 477 thousand tonnes, add up fast.

How this compares with recent quarters

The year has been bumpy for the company. In the first quarter of 2026 it earned R$106 million on thinner margins.

Back in February, full-year results showed profit falling about 10% on a cost squeeze. The pattern has been persistent.

This latest quarter continues that theme rather than breaking it. Costs keep testing the company’s pricing power.

Even so, the business remains solidly profitable. The debate is about the size of the margin, not survival.

What it means for shoppers

For consumers, the numbers carry a quiet upside. Falling average prices mean staples got a little cheaper on the shelf.

Pasta, crackers and flour are pantry basics across Brazil. So even small price moves reach many kitchen tables.

The company is clearly choosing volume over fat margins for now. That trade tends to favour buyers in the short run.

Whether prices stay soft depends on costs. If wheat or freight climb, some of that relief could fade.

What investors will watch next

The market’s focus now turns to margins in the second half. Investors want to see whether the squeeze eases or deepens.

The stock trades in São Paulo under the ticker MDIA3. It carries Fitch’s top domestic rating, renewed earlier this month.

That rating signals a stable balance sheet despite the profit dip. So the company has room to ride out a soft patch.

For now, the message is simple. Selling more is not enough when each sale earns less.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did M. Dias Branco earn in the second quarter of 2026?

It reported net profit of R$168.9 million, about US$33 million, down 22% from R$216.4 million a year earlier. Results were released on 13 August 2026.

Why did profit fall if sales volumes rose?

Higher operating expenses and lower average prices squeezed margins. EBITDA margin fell to 10.5% from 12.7%, so extra volume did not lift profit.

What does M. Dias Branco make?

It is a Ceará-based food company, one of Brazil’s largest, producing pasta, biscuits, wheat flour and related staples. Its shares trade on B3 as MDIA3.

Did revenue grow in the quarter?

No. Net revenue slipped 0.9% to R$2.70 billion, roughly US$520 million, even though sales volume rose 4.4% to 477.3 thousand tonnes.

Sources: InfoMoney; Estadão; Valor Econômico; Investidor10.

World.title: Light Posts a US$49 Million Loss Even as Its Earnings Jump 82%
World.content:
Brazil · Earnings

Key Facts — The loss Light reported a net loss of R$252.2 million (about US$49 million) for the second quarter of 2026.

— The earnings Adjusted EBITDA rose 82.3% from a year earlier to R$599 million (roughly US$116 million).

— The cause A one-off charge from the REFIS tax-settlement program and other non-recurring items drove the accounting loss.

— The flip side Excluding those items, the company would have booked an adjusted profit near R$150 million (about US$29 million).

— The backdrop Light is finishing a court-supervised debt overhaul and has asked to exit judicial recovery after a R$1.5 billion capital raise.

Strip out one-off tax and accounting charges and the Rio utility actually turned a small operating profit. Most of the red ink sits on paper.

Illustrative photo of Rio de Janeiro at sunset across Guanabara Bay. Light distributes electricity across the Rio metropolitan area, where it serves millions of customers. (Photo: Leandro Neumann Ciuffo, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Light, the electricity distributor that keeps Rio de Janeiro’s homes and streets lit. Reported a bruising net loss for the second quarter of 2026.

Yet the same results showed operating earnings surging more than 80%, a sign the turnaround underneath is gathering pace.

What Light actually reported

The company posted a net loss of R$252.2 million, or about US$49 million, for the April-to-June quarter. That is nearly five times the R$51.4 million loss it recorded in the same period a year earlier.

At first glance that looks like a sharp step backward. Dig into the numbers, however, and a very different picture appears.

Why the earnings figure matters more

Adjusted EBITDA, a measure of core operating cash generation, jumped 82.3% year over year to R$599 million (around US$116 million). In plain terms, the business is earning far more from its day-to-day work than it did a year ago.

Management credited a stronger distribution arm for the gain. The distributor’s adjusted gross margin rose 49.2%, and tighter operating costs across the group added to the improvement.

So why the loss?

The bottom-line loss came from charges that have little to do with everyday operations. The biggest was a one-off hit tied to REFIS, a Brazilian tax-installment program that let the company settle old liabilities.

Accounting adjustments linked to the renewal of its distribution concession also weighed on the quarter. Because these items are non-recurring, they distort the headline number without reflecting how the business is really doing.

The profit hiding in plain sight

Once those one-off and mark-to-market effects are stripped out, the story reverses. On an adjusted basis, the company would have shown a profit of roughly R$150 million, or about US$29 million.

That is a swing from an adjusted loss a year earlier. In other words, the underlying engine turned from red to black even as the reported figure went the other way.

Light’s long road out of debt

This quarter lands in the middle of one of Brazil’s most closely watched corporate rescues. Light filed for court-supervised recovery, its version of Chapter 11, in 2023 under a debt load of around R$11 billion.

Creditors approved a recovery plan in 2024, and the company has since worked steadily through its obligations. As a result, the group’s balance sheet looks far healthier today than it did two years ago.

The capital raise that changed things

In July, Light completed a capital increase of about R$1.5 billion, or roughly US$289 million, issuing new shares at R$6.29 each. The raise exceeded what the recovery plan required.

On the strength of that cash injection, the company then asked a Rio court to formally end its judicial recovery. That request is still awaiting a judge’s decision.

What it means for Rio de Janeiro

Light serves millions of customers across the Rio de Janeiro metropolitan area. A financially steadier utility is better placed to invest in the grid and keep the power flowing.

For residents, the near-term impact is limited, since tariffs are set by the national regulator. Still, a healthier operator lowers the risk of the service disruptions that plague cash-strapped utilities.

How investors are reading it

Investors tend to look past one-off charges toward operating trends. And the 82% EBITDA jump is exactly the kind of signal they watch.

The stock trades on Brazil’s B3 exchange under the ticker LIGT3. That said, the pending court ruling on the recovery exit still hangs over the shares.

Until the judge signs off, the company technically remains under protection from its creditors.

What comes next

The next milestone is the court’s decision on whether Light can leave judicial recovery for good. Approval would close a chapter that began with the 2023 filing.

After that, attention shifts to whether the operating gains seen this quarter can hold. Management has signaled that the second half of the year should keep driving the recovery in profitability.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Light really lose money in the second quarter of 2026?

Yes. Light reported a net loss of R$252.2 million, about US$49 million, for the April-to-June period.

Why did EBITDA rise if the company posted a loss?

EBITDA measures operating cash generation before financing and one-off items. It rose 82.3% to R$599 million because the distribution business earned more and costs fell, while the net loss reflected non-recurring charges.

What is judicial recovery and where does Light stand?

Judicial recovery is Brazil’s court-supervised restructuring, similar to Chapter 11. Light filed in 2023, completed a R$1.5 billion capital raise in July 2026.

How can I follow Light’s shares?

Light trades on Brazil’s B3 exchange under the ticker LIGT3. Investors are watching both the operating recovery and the pending court ruling on its exit from judicial recovery.

Sources: Valor Econômico; Estadão/E-Investidor; InfoMoney; O Globo.

World.title: Grupo Argos Preferred Share Joins MSCI Small Cap Index After 14% August Climb
World.content:
Colombia · Markets

Key Facts — The move MSCI added the preferred share of Grupo Argos to its Colombia small-cap index on 12 August 2026.

— The date The change takes effect after the Colombian market closes on 31 August 2026.

— The rally The preferred share has risen about 14% since early August; the common share about 18%.

— The company Grupo Argos is a Colombian conglomerate spanning cement, energy and infrastructure.

— Why it matters Funds that track MSCI must buy the stock, widening its investor base and liquidity.

From 31 August, funds that track MSCI’s benchmarks will have to hold the Colombian conglomerate’s stock, widening its global investor base.

Illustrative photo: a cement plant. Cement, through Cementos Argos, is the flagship business of Grupo Argos, whose preferred share joined the MSCI small-cap index on 12 August 2026. (Photo: Chday, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Grupo Argos has just earned a new badge on the world stage. On 12 August, index provider MSCI added the company’s preferred share to its Colombia small-cap index.

The change gives one of Colombia’s largest firms fresh visibility with investors abroad.

What MSCI decided

On 12 August 2026, MSCI announced the results of its regular index review. It added the preferred share of Grupo Argos to its Colombia small-cap segment.

MSCI is one of the world’s most-watched index providers. Its benchmarks act as a scorecard that international money managers follow closely.

The change is not immediate, however. It takes effect after the Colombian market closes on 31 August 2026.

MSCI reported no deletions from the Colombia list in the same review. So for the local market, the update is a clean addition.

Why the Grupo Argos inclusion matters

Index membership sounds technical, yet it carries real weight. Global funds use MSCI benchmarks to decide where their money goes.

So the move puts Grupo Argos on more radar screens abroad. As a result, more investors are likely to track and hold the stock.

The company itself framed the entry as a boost to its visibility. It said the listing strengthens its standing in the capital markets.

For a mid-sized emerging-market name, that recognition is hard to buy. In short, an index seat is a form of free advertising.

The August rally

The timing has been kind to shareholders. The preferred share has climbed about 14% since the start of August.

The common share has done even better, rising roughly 18%. Still, those gains reflect several pieces of news at once, not the index move alone.

That is an important caution to keep in mind. A single day’s move on the Colombian exchange should not be pinned on the index news.

Even so, the direction is clear enough. Investors have warmed to the stock during a strong August for the group.

How index inclusion moves a stock

Many large funds simply mirror an index rather than pick stocks. Because of that, they must hold whatever the benchmark tells them to.

So when a company joins, these passive funds have to add it. That mechanical buying can lift demand, liquidity and the share price.

Active managers pay attention too, since the index shapes their yardstick. Meanwhile, the extra trading can make it easier to buy and sell the shares.

None of this guarantees a lasting rise, though. The effect is often strongest around the date the change takes hold.

What Grupo Argos actually does

Grupo Argos is one of Colombia’s largest holding companies. It owns controlling stakes in three big businesses across the region.

Cement comes through Cementos Argos, where it holds about 55%. Energy runs through Celsia, at roughly 54%, and infrastructure through Odinsa.

Celsia generates power in Colombia, Panama and Costa Rica. Its mix spans hydro, thermal, solar and wind plants.

Odinsa manages roads and airports under long concessions. Its portfolio includes stakes in the El Dorado and Mariscal Sucre airports.

The preferred share, explained

The group trades two kinds of shares in Bogota. The common share carries voting rights, while the preferred share usually does not.

Instead, the preferred share tends to offer priority on dividends. It was this preferred class that MSCI chose to add.

Grupo Argos is already a member of Colombia’s main COLCAP index. That places it among the country’s most heavily traded companies.

The new small-cap seat sits alongside that status. Together they widen the pool of funds that may buy the stock.

A company already in motion

The index news lands during a busy stretch for the group. Earlier in August it launched a share buyback and began reshaping Odinsa.

That plan turns the roads-and-airports unit toward asset management. Together, these moves have helped fuel the recent share gains.

The company has branded the overhaul as its ACE strategy. It aims to close the gap between the market price and what managers see as fair value.

The buyback signals that leaders think the stock is cheap. For investors, that is often read as a vote of confidence.

What it means for Colombia’s market

For Colombia, the inclusion reads as a small vote of confidence. The country’s stock market is modest by global standards and often overlooked.

Getting a local name into an MSCI index raises its profile. By contrast, exits from such benchmarks can quietly drain foreign money.

Colombia has had a turbulent year on the political front. A steady inflow of index-driven cash is a welcome counterweight.

It also reminds investors that the market has real businesses. Cement, power and airports are far from speculative bets.

What happens next

The key date is 31 August, when the change goes live. After that, funds tracking the index must reflect the new weighting.

Beyond the mechanics, the test is whether the attention lasts. For now, the conglomerate ends the month with a stronger global footprint.

The next MSCI review will show whether the seat holds. Small-cap membership can change as a company’s size shifts.

Until then, the focus turns back to results and the ACE plan. Those fundamentals, not the index, will drive the shares over time.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did MSCI do with Grupo Argos?

On 12 August 2026 MSCI added the preferred share of Grupo Argos to its Colombia small-cap index. The change takes effect after the market closes on 31 August 2026.

How much has the Grupo Argos share risen?

The preferred share has gained about 14% since early August. The common share has risen around 18%, helped by several company announcements.

What does Grupo Argos do?

It is a Colombian conglomerate. It controls cement maker Cementos Argos, energy firm Celsia and infrastructure company Odinsa, which runs roads and airports.

Why does joining an MSCI index matter?

Global funds track MSCI benchmarks. When a stock is added, index-tracking funds must buy it, which can lift demand, liquidity and visibility.

Sources: Valora Analitik; Forbes Colombia; MSCI; Grupo Argos.

World.title: Grupo Energía Bogotá Profit Climbs 15% as Q2 Revenue Dips 11%
World.content:
Colombia · Business

Key Facts — The revenue Second-quarter revenue fell about 11% to roughly COP 447 billion (about US$143 million).

— The profit Net income attributable to owners rose about 15% to roughly COP 701 billion (about US$224 million).

— The reason A lower regulated return (WACC of 10.94%) and weaker gas-transport contracting cut the top line.

— The lift Bigger dividends and equity earnings, mainly from Enel Colombia, plus peso gains, boosted profit.

— The company GEB is a Bogotá-based utility moving electricity and natural gas across Colombia, Peru, Brazil and Guatemala.

Higher earnings from Enel Colombia and a stronger peso lifted the bottom line, even as regulated gas-transport income shrank.

Illustrative photo of a high-voltage transmission line. Grupo Energía Bogotá is Colombia’s number-two electricity-transmission operator and its largest gas transporter. (Photo: TagaSanPedroAko, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Grupo Energía Bogotá reported a split result for the second quarter of 2026, with revenue down but profit sharply up. Sales slipped about 11% while net income jumped roughly 15%, the company said in results released on 13 August.

The contrast came because earnings from stakes in other firms outpaced a softer core business.

What Grupo Energía Bogotá reported

Grupo Energía Bogotá, known as GEB, posted second-quarter revenue of about COP 447 billion. That is roughly US$143 million, and it marked a drop of about 11% from a year earlier.

However, the headline that mattered was profit. Net income attributable to shareholders climbed about 15% to around COP 701 billion, or roughly US$224 million.

Why revenue fell

The decline came mainly from the regulated part of the business. Colombia set a lower allowed return, known as the WACC, at 10.94%, so GEB could recognize less revenue from its pipelines.

On top of that, gas-transport contracting weakened. Reduced industrial demand and tight gas supply meant fewer volumes moved, which trimmed sales still further.

Why profit rose anyway

Even so, the bottom line improved because GEB earns a lot from stakes it holds in other companies. Dividends and equity earnings, especially from power firm Enel Colombia, came in strong.

A stronger peso helped too. As the currency firmed, GEB booked foreign-exchange gains, and as a result profit grew despite the softer core.

What GEB actually does

Grupo Energía Bogotá is an energy holding company based in Bogotá. In plain terms, it owns the wires and pipes that carry electricity and natural gas rather than selling power to homes.

It is the number-two electricity-transmission operator in Colombia. Through its unit TGI, it is also the country’s largest natural-gas transporter.

A business spread across four countries

The group reaches well beyond Colombia. In Peru, it leads gas distribution through Cálidda and Contugas, while it also runs power-distribution assets there.

Meanwhile, it operates transmission lines in Brazil through Argo and Gebbras, and leads electricity transmission in Guatemala. So a single quarter blends regulated income from several markets.

The EBITDA picture

Operating cash earnings softened during the quarter. EBITDA fell about 16% to roughly COP 315 billion, and the margin narrowed as gas headwinds bit.

Adjusted EBITDA, a broader measure GEB tracks, fell about 24% for the quarter. Still, the rolling 12-month adjusted figure held near COP 5.8 trillion, up modestly on the year.

What it means for investors

For shareholders, the quarter shows how GEB’s earnings really work. Because so much profit flows from stakes in other utilities, headline revenue can fall while net income rises.

That structure can steady returns, yet it also ties the group’s fortunes to partners like Enel Colombia. In short, dividends from affiliates now do much of the heavy lifting.

The regulatory backdrop

The lower WACC is not a one-off event. Regulators periodically reset the returns utilities may earn, and this cycle pushed GEB’s allowed revenue down.

Because pipelines and grids are long-life assets, these resets shape income for years. Therefore the current squeeze on gas-transport revenue could linger into future quarters.

How the quarter fits the wider year

GEB had opened 2026 on a firmer footing, with first-quarter revenue and profit both rising. By contrast, the second quarter split the two, as the top line turned down.

Overall, the first half still leaned on the group’s steady dividend flows. After a busy year of deals abroad, the domestic regulated business is now the part to watch.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Grupo Energía Bogotá make more or less money in Q2 2026?

Both, in a sense. Revenue fell about 11% to roughly COP 447 billion (US$143 million).

Why did revenue drop while profit went up?

Revenue fell because of a lower regulated return and weaker gas transport. Profit rose because dividends and equity earnings from affiliates, mainly Enel Colombia, and peso gains more than offset it.

What kind of company is GEB?

It is a Bogotá-based energy utility that transmits electricity and transports natural gas. It operates in Colombia, Peru, Brazil and Guatemala, and trades under the ticker GEB.

When were the results released?

GEB published its second-quarter 2026 results on 13 August 2026, covering the April-to-June period.

Sources: GEB investor materials (Q2-26 report, 13 Aug 2026); Quartr; Banco de la República (TRM).

World.title: De la Espriella Removes Five Colombian Ambassadors and Restores Ties With Israel
World.content:
Colombia · Politics

Key Facts — The removals On 14 August 2026 the Presidency declared five ambassadors ‘insubsistentes’, or removed, during the handover.

— The posts The five envoys covered Sweden, Haiti, Turkey, Paraguay and Trinidad and Tobago.

— The reason Most Petro-era ambassadors resigned as asked; these five did not, so the president dismissed them.

— The Israel turn Colombia is restoring full relations with Israel from 7 August, reversing Petro’s 2024 rupture.

— The decrees Officials say the formal removal decrees are still being processed.

In days, his government is rebuilding relations with Israel and Washington, unwinding Gustavo Petro’s foreign policy almost overnight.

Illustrative photo: the Palacio de Narino, seat of Colombia’s presidency in Bogota, from which De la Espriella’s government declared five ambassadors removed on 14 August 2026. (Photo: Mriobomorales, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

President De la Espriella has begun clearing out Colombia’s embassies abroad. On 14 August his office declared five ambassadors removed for refusing to step aside during the transition.

The decision is the sharp edge of a much wider foreign-policy reset.

What De la Espriella actually did

The announcement came from the Presidency press office on Friday, 14 August 2026. It said the government had declared the appointments of five ambassadors ‘insubsistentes’, the Colombian legal term for removed.

The measure lands one week after De la Espriella took office on 7 August. Because it targets envoys named under his predecessor, it reads as a deliberate reset of the diplomatic corps.

Who the five ambassadors are

The government named each envoy and the country they served. They are Guillermo Francisco Reyes in Sweden, Vilma Rocio Velasquez in Haiti and Yennifer Edilma Parra in Turkey.

The list also includes Juan Manuel Corzo in Paraguay and William Sidney Bush Howard in Trinidad and Tobago. All five were posted abroad under former president Gustavo Petro.

Why these five and not the others

The reason is procedural rather than personal, at least officially. When a new government arrives, ambassadors are expected to file a courtesy resignation and place their posts at the president’s disposal.

Most of Colombia’s envoys did exactly that during the handover. These five did not, so the president simply declared their appointments void instead.

The word that carries the weight

The Spanish term at the centre of this is ‘insubsistente’. In Colombian administrative law, a government can declare an appointment insubsistent when the post is one of free appointment and removal.

Ambassadors sit squarely in that category, so the president needs no cause to end the posting. Still, the government said the formal decrees to seal each removal are being drafted.

De la Espriella turns back toward Israel

The removals are only the visible part of a broader pivot. Even before taking office, the incoming team of De la Espriella agreed to restore full relations with Israel from 7 August.

That reverses Petro’s 2024 decision to break ties over the war in Gaza. As a result, Colombia is unwinding one of its most contentious foreign-policy moves of recent years.

How the Israel deal came together

The groundwork was laid in Washington in July. Foreign Minister Omar Bula met his Israeli counterpart Gideon Saar and agreed on an immediate exchange of ambassadors once the new government took power.

Israel has already confirmed Vivian Aisen as its ambassador to Colombia. On the Colombian side, an envoy to Israel is expected, though officials have not yet named the person publicly.

An embassy bound for Jerusalem

The agreement goes further than restoring normal contact. Both sides said they would scrap visa requirements and work toward opening a Colombian embassy in Jerusalem.

Recognising the city as Israel’s capital. The government also signalled it would drop Colombia’s support for genocide claims against Israel.

In short, the shift is not a small correction but a full reversal of tone.

The wider break with Petro

The Israel move fits a clear pattern in the new administration. De la Espriella campaigned as a right-wing lawyer promising a hard line on security and a warmer relationship with Washington.

He has also pledged to suspend the peace talks his predecessor pursued with armed groups. By contrast, Petro spent four years pushing Colombia toward the global left.

What is still unsettled

Several pieces of the picture remain open. The removal decrees are still in progress, and the Foreign Ministry says it will manage each handover to keep the embassies running.

The name of Colombia’s own ambassador to Israel has not been made public. Until that appears, the promised exchange of envoys remains a commitment rather than a finished fact.

What comes next

The immediate task is filling the gaps left in five capitals. Because ambassadors carry real weight in trade and consular work, long vacancies can slow everyday business.

The bigger test is Israel, where symbolism and logistics both matter. After the announcements fade, the slow work of opening a Jerusalem mission and naming envoys begins.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many ambassadors did De la Espriella remove?

Five. On 14 August 2026 his government declared the appointments of ambassadors to Sweden.

Why were these ambassadors removed?

Most Colombian envoys filed a courtesy resignation during the transition. These five did not, so the president declared their posts void.

What does ‘insubsistente’ mean?

It is a Colombian legal term. The government can declare an appointment insubsistent, or void.

Is Colombia restoring relations with Israel?

Yes. From 7 August 2026 Colombia is restoring full ties, reversing Petro’s 2024 break.

Sources: La FM; Semana; El Espectador; Infobae; El Pais; Reuters.

World.title: US Revokes Visa of López Obrador’s Son, Who Fires Back at Trump
World.content:
Mexico · Politics

Key Facts — The trigger On August 13, 2026, Andy López Beltrán said the US revoked his visa, in a letter to Donald Trump.

— The accusation He named Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau, calling the move political, not legal.

— The reason Washington gave no public, case-specific reason; his letter says there is no proof of any wrongdoing.

— The pattern Reuters reported at least 50 Mexican politicians, mostly from Morena, have lost US visas since 2025.

— The reaction President Claudia Sheinbaum called it possible political interference on August 14, 2026.

Mexico’s president called the move foreign interference, as Reuters counts at least 50 Morena-linked figures stripped of US visas since 2025.

Illustrative photo: former Mexican president Andrés Manuel López Obrador with Colombia’s Gustavo Petro. His son Andy López Beltrán said the US revoked his visa in August 2026. (Photo: EneasMx, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former Mexican president Andrés Manuel López Obrador, says the United States has revoked his visa. Indeed, he made the claim in a public letter to President Donald Trump, posted on Instagram on August 13, 2026.

His father has stayed quiet so far, but President Claudia Sheinbaum called the move possible political interference.

What López Obrador’s son says happened

First, Andy López Beltrán said US officials told him his visa to enter the country had been cancelled. Then he revealed the news himself, in a letter posted to his Instagram account late on August 13, 2026.

Notably, the letter was dated from Teapa, in Tabasco, his family’s home state in southern Mexico.

The letter to Trump

Rather than stay silent, he addressed the message directly to US President Donald Trump. In it, moreover, he named Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau.

He also said Landau styles himself ‘the visa remover,’ and that the two had ‘ordered’ his entry permit removed.

A political motive, he argues

Above all, López Beltrán framed the decision as political rather than legal. Indeed, he called it ‘petty and propagandistic,’ and compared the style to Hitler’s.

Furthermore, he insisted the officials held ‘no proof’ of any immoral or criminal act by him.

Who Andy López Beltrán is

For context, he is one of AMLO’s sons and a prominent figure in the ruling Morena party. Until May 25, 2026, moreover, he served as Morena’s national organization secretary.

Commentators often described him as the party’s ‘number two,’ although that is an informal label.

Why Washington acted, officially nobody knows

So far, the US government has not given a public, case-specific reason for the revocation. In general, State Department policy allows visas to be pulled for ‘activities contrary to the national interest.

However, no official has tied that language to López Beltrán by name.

Part of a wider pattern

Meanwhile, his case is not isolated, according to reporting by Reuters. In fact, the agency found at least 50 Mexican politicians and officials have lost US visas since 2025.

Most of them, notably, belong to Morena, the party López Obrador founded and once led.

Sheinbaum calls it interference

Soon after, President Claudia Sheinbaum addressed the case at her morning press conference on August 14, 2026. She called the pattern ‘a sense of interference in Mexican politics,’ because she saw no other explanation.

Then she added a pointed line: ‘It is the people who define recognition, not a visa.

Mexico’s line on sovereignty

Naturally, Sheinbaum tied her answer to a familiar theme for her government. ‘In Mexico, the people of Mexico decide,’ she said, stressing national sovereignty.

In short, she argued that a foreign travel document confers no political legitimacy at home.

What the letter does not prove

Still, the revocation rests largely on López Beltrán’s own account and on media reports. Meanwhile, Washington has released no document, and the reason remains publicly unknown.

As a result, his claim of a political motive is his interpretation, not an established fact.

What happens next

For now, the affair is a war of words between a Morena leader and Washington. Whether the US explains its decision, or reverses it, however, remains to be seen.

Either way, the episode adds fresh strain to an already tense US-Mexico relationship.

Frequently Asked Questions

Whose visa did the US revoke?

Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, known as Andy, the son of former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador. He said he was notified in mid-August 2026.

Did the US say why?

No. Washington gave no public, case-specific reason. State Department policy allows revocations for ‘activities contrary to the national interest,’ but no official linked that to him by name.

Did AMLO write the letter to Trump?

No. The letter was written by his son, Andy López Beltrán, and posted on Instagram on August 13, 2026. The former president himself has not publicly commented.

How did the Mexican government react?

President Claudia Sheinbaum called it possible political interference and said ‘it is the people who define recognition, not a visa.

Sources: El País; Infobae; Reuters; Le Figaro.

World.title: Milei’s Reform Package Heads to Congress as Argentina Lifts Its Dollar Ceiling
World.content:
Argentina · Politics

Key Facts — The bill Milei unveiled a central-bank charter reform in a national address on July 30, 2026, then filed it with the Chamber of Deputies days later.

— The core it would give the BCRA a single price-stability mandate and ban it from printing money to fund the state.

— The dollar ceiling Argentina’s crawling band tops out near 1,881 pesos per US$ on September 1, rising to about 1,919 by September 30.

— The cushion the peso trades around 1,490 to 1,500 per US$, roughly 20 to 25% below that ceiling, so the bank is not selling reserves to defend it.

— The fiscal rule a permanent ‘no-deficit’ law would trigger an automatic partial shutdown if Congress fails to fix a lasting deficit.

The centerpiece is a central-bank overhaul that would ban money-printing, even as the peso trades far below its rising band.

The Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) headquarters in Buenos Aires. Milei’s reform package would give the bank a single mandate to protect the peso. (Photo: Galio, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

President Javier Milei is pushing a fresh reform package through Argentina’s Congress. And its centerpiece is a rewrite of the central bank’s founding charter.

He unveiled the plan in a national address on July 30, 2026. And the government filed it with the Chamber of Deputies days later.

Lawmakers are set to take it up in August sessions.

What is in Milei’s reform package

Milei’s reform package is not one giant bill. Instead, it arrives in waves, and the current wave centers squarely on the economy.

After his October 2025 midterm win, he gained the seats to push harder. So he has moved from emergency decrees toward permanent laws.

Rewriting the central bank’s charter

The headline measure is a reform of the central bank, known locally as the BCRA. It would rewrite the bank’s founding rulebook, its Organic Charter.

Milei presented the plan on national television on July 30, 2026. The government then sent the bill to the Chamber of Deputies within days.

A ban on printing money

At its heart, the bill would give the BCRA a single job: protect the value of the peso. That reverses a 2012 change that added growth and jobs to its mission.

It would also ban the bank from financing the government, directly or indirectly. As a result, the Treasury could no longer lean on the printing press to cover deficits.

The bill scraps the old tools for that lending, such as ‘temporary advances. ‘ Milei even wants a later law to treat deficit money-printing as counterfeiting.

Locking in a balanced budget

Alongside the charter, Milei is pushing a permanent fiscal rule. Officials call it the ‘fiscal handcuffs,’ because it would outlaw deficit budgets.

If a shortfall persists and Congress does nothing, part of the government would shut down automatically. In short, the plan tries to make overspending legally very hard.

The September dollar ceiling, explained

Argentina lets the peso float inside a band with a floor and a ceiling. The ceiling is the weak point, where the bank would sell dollars to stop a slide.

That ceiling climbs higher every month. On September 1, 2026 it sits near 1,881 pesos per US$, and by September 30 it reaches about 1,919.

The band launched in April 2025 at 1,000 to 1,400 pesos. Since January 2026, it has widened at the pace of recent inflation rather than a flat 1% a month.

Why the peso is not testing the ceiling

Despite the headlines, the peso is nowhere near that ceiling. In mid-August it traded around 1,490 to 1,500 per US$.

That leaves a gap of roughly 20 to 25% before the limit bites. So the central bank has no duty to sell reserves right now.

Courts, jobs and taxes

The wider agenda reaches beyond money. Milei has long promised to fill judicial vacancies and curb political sway over the courts.

A contested labor reform already cleared the Senate in February 2026. Meanwhile, deeper tax cuts remain a stated goal, though several were trimmed in earlier deals.

He has also floated changes to the electoral system. Yet no formal electoral bill is part of this economic package.

The political math in Congress

None of this passes on Milei’s word alone. His bloc grew in 2025, but he still needs allies to reach a majority.

The central-bank bill is slated for August committee and floor debate. Because it rewrites core rules, opposition and provincial governors will push back.

What to watch next

The first test is whether the charter reform survives the August votes intact. After that, the fiscal rule and penal changes line up behind it.

For the peso, the number to watch is the gap to the ceiling. As long as it stays wide, the band is a backstop, not a battle.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Milei’s reform package?

It is a set of economic bills led by a central-bank charter reform. Plus a permanent balanced-budget rule and related fiscal and legal measures.

What would the central-bank reform do?

It would give the BCRA a single mandate to protect the peso and ban it from printing money to fund the government.

What is Argentina’s dollar ceiling in September 2026?

The band’s upper limit sits near 1,881 pesos per US$ on September 1 and rises to about 1,919 by September 30, 2026.

Is the peso close to that ceiling?

No. In mid-August 2026 it traded around 1,490 to 1,500 per US$, roughly 20 to 25% below the ceiling.

Sources: Reuters; Mercopress; Buenos Aires Times; BCRA; Infobae.

World.title: Brazil Approves US$2.5 Billion State Credit Deal, US$1 Billion for São Paulo
World.content:
Brazil · Economy

Key Facts — The package Brazil’s Treasury cleared five new state credit operations worth roughly R$13 billion (about US$2.5 billion).

— São Paulo the biggest slice is R$5.4 billion (about US$1 billion) from Banco do Brasil, backed by a federal guarantee.

— The guarantee stock since 2023 the Union has authorized R$270 billion in guaranteed credit to states and cities.

— What it funds new São Paulo metro and rail lines, plus the widening of the Rodovia dos Tamoios highway.

— The resolution the deal was signed on 12 August, hours after São Paulo asked the Supreme Court to force the minister’s hand.

The São Paulo loan was signed just hours after the state ran to the Supreme Court, defusing a rare federal clash.

Illustrative photo: Ana Rosa station on the São Paulo Metro Blue Line. Part of the R$5.4 billion loan will fund new metro and rail lines. (Photo: Wilfredor, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Brazil has approved about R$13 billion in new state credit. Resolving a standoff that had dragged São Paulo’s governor to the Supreme Court.

The Treasury signed off on five loan operations, with São Paulo taking the largest at R$5.4 billion, or roughly US$1 billion. As a result, a rare public clash between Brasília and its richest state has quietly ended.

A standoff that reached the top court

For weeks, São Paulo had waited for Brasília to sign off on a loan it said was already approved on the merits. Because the minister had not signed, the state escalated.

So on 11 August, Governor Tarcísio de Freitas asked the Supreme Court to compel the Finance Ministry to act within 48 hours. The move turned a paperwork delay into a headline dispute.

The state had first requested the federal guarantee back in November 2025. Since then, the Treasury and its legal team had already issued favorable opinions in May 2026.

In other words, the loan had cleared every technical hurdle. Still, the final signature had stalled, and that gap is what sent lawyers to the court.

How the state credit deal was resolved

The answer came fast. On the night of 12 August, Deputy Finance Minister Dario Durigan signed the dispatch granting the state credit and the federal guarantee.

The authorization was published in the official gazette on 14 August. Therefore the core of the dispute, the missing signature, simply disappeared.

The timing was striking. The signature landed only hours after São Paulo had filed its urgent request at the court.

Because the deal was already sound, the ministry framed the move as routine. Even so, few missed the speed once the court was involved.

What the São Paulo loan is worth

The exact figure authorized was R$5.453 billion, or about US$1 billion at mid-August rates near R$5.2 per dollar. The funding comes from Banco do Brasil.

The Union, through the Treasury, acts as guarantor. In short, if the state ever defaulted, the federal government would cover the debt.

That backing matters because it lowers the interest rate the state pays. As a result, borrowing becomes far cheaper than it would be on São Paulo’s own credit.

The loan itself was first requested in late 2025. Since then, it had become the biggest single guarantee in the new batch of five.

The five states in the state credit batch

São Paulo was not alone. The same batch cleared credit for Piauí, Maranhão, Pernambuco and Rondônia.

Piauí’s operation, at R$4.9 billion, was the second largest. Together, São Paulo and Piauí alone account for R$10.3 billion of the roughly R$13 billion total.

The other three loans were smaller and drew on different banks. For instance, Pernambuco’s deal runs through Caixa, while Rondônia’s uses Bradesco.

What the money will build

For São Paulo, the loan targets transport above all. It funds work on Metro Line 6 (Orange) and Line 5 (Lilac), plus several suburban rail lines.

It also pays for widening the Rodovia dos Tamoios highway. In addition, state law allows the cash to reach health and security projects.

These are long-lived assets that outlast any single budget year. That is why states prefer cheap, guaranteed credit over paying cash up front.

Metro Line 6, in particular, has been under construction for years. Because it is costly, fresh financing helps keep the project moving toward completion.

Why the guarantee stock keeps growing

Every guaranteed loan adds to a rising federal exposure. Since the start of the current government in 2023, the Union has authorized R$270 billion in such credit.

The wider stock of outstanding guarantees is even larger. By the end of 2025, it stood near R$336 billion across states, cities and their companies.

For context, states alone accounted for roughly R$230 billion of that stock. Because guarantees are contingent, they sit off the headline budget yet still carry real risk.

Why the delay became so political

São Paulo is run by Tarcísio, a likely rival to President Lula’s camp in 2026. As a result, a routine loan file carried political weight.

The state argued it was being treated unfairly. Even so, the ministry says it has approved almost R$30 billion in guarantees for São Paulo since 2023.

That figure, the ministry notes, is more than triple the state’s historical average. In short, both sides read the same numbers very differently.

What the resolution means for Brasília

The quick signature lets the government argue it plays fair, despite the rivalry. Yet the trip to the Supreme Court still exposed real friction.

For now, the guarantee is granted and the money can flow. Because the substance is settled, the court case loses its urgency.

The episode also sets a template for future fights. When a file stalls, states now know a court filing can force a fast answer.

For investors, the message is calmer. Despite the drama, Brazil kept funding subnational projects through its usual channels.

What happens next

São Paulo can now contract the loan with Banco do Brasil and start drawing funds. Meanwhile, the four other states move ahead with their own operations.

The Treasury will keep signing similar deals as demand grows. Still, each new guarantee tightens the federal government’s long-term balance sheet.

Analysts will watch how fast the metro and highway works actually begin. After all, approval is only the first step toward finished infrastructure.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much state credit did Brazil approve?

The Treasury cleared five operations worth roughly R$13 billion, about US$2.5 billion, for five different states.

How big is the São Paulo loan?

It is R$5.453 billion, or about US$1 billion, funded by Banco do Brasil and guaranteed by the federal Treasury.

Did this end the Supreme Court dispute?

Yes, in substance. The minister signed the authorization hours after São Paulo filed, so the missing signature is no longer an issue.

What will the São Paulo money fund?

Mainly transport, including Metro Lines 6 and 5, suburban rail upgrades and the widening of the Rodovia dos Tamoios highway.

World.title: Nicaragua Bishop Abelardo Mata Says He Is Well After Detention
World.content:
Catholic Bishop Abelardo Mata, a critic of Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega, said he is in good condition in an interview broadcast Wednesday by the government, which released him days earlier following his arrest over alleged corruption. Mata, 80, was detained on June 29 for questioning about the origin of his properties, which Nicaragua’s Interior Ministry said did not correspond “with his status as a priest.” Authorities officially announced his release on July 4.

“Thank you, I’m fine,” Mata said in an interview at his home with state-run Channel 6 that was circulated by pro-government media. The interview made no mention of the bishop’s detention. Mata appeared to be in good health, while the United Nations and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights had previously requested information about his whereabouts.

“Prayer helps a lot,” Mata said after the journalist repeatedly remarked that he appeared to have “a lot of vitality.” The United States denounced what it called “religious repression by the dictatorship” of Ortega and his wife and co-president, Rosario Murillo, over the case. Opposition groups accuse the two leaders of persecuting the Catholic Church, which the government blames for supporting the 2018 protests that left more than 300 people dead and for promoting what authorities describe as a Washington-backed coup attempt.

Mata was one of the most influential figures in Nicaraguan Catholicism over the past three decades and was known for criticizing the government, according to Nicaraguan media outlets operating in exile. In the interview, Mata also said that a brother and a niece visit him at his residence, although he prefers “silence, study and prayer.”

In recent years, the Ortega-Murillo government has intensified its crackdown on critics, stripping some of their nationality and expelling them from the country. Those affected have included politicians, business leaders, journalists, intellectuals, human rights activists and members of the clergy. In some cases, the government has also confiscated their property.

The government’s campaign against its opponents has been accompanied by a constitutional reform that is expected to be put to a vote in early September and would exclude opposition parties from elections.

World.title: Costa Rica Hands Macho Coca and Compadre to US Agents in New York Cases
World.content:
Costa Rica surrendered two men wanted on United States drug trafficking charges to American agents on this morning, closing extradition proceedings that had run for months and opening a fresh dispute over conditions inside the maximum-security prison.

Gilbert Bell Fernández, known as “Macho Coca,” and Gabriel Lozano Bonilla, known as “Compadre,” left Juan Santamaría International Airport at approximately 8:58 a.m. aboard an aircraft registered N387SC and operated by the United States Drug Enforcement Administration.

The flight plan filed for the aircraft listed a stop in Nassau, Bahamas, before continuing to New York. Both men are wanted by the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York in separate but parallel proceedings. Neither has been convicted, and the allegations against them remain untested in court.

Agents of the Unit for Special Intervention of the Directorate of Intelligence and Security escorted both men out of the La Reforma prison complex in San Rafael de Alajuela shortly before 6:40 a.m. Each wore the orange uniform recently introduced by the Ministry of Justice and Peace for maximum-security inmates, along with a ballistic vest and helmet. The formal handcuff exchange conducted minutes before boarding transferred both men to United States jurisdiction.

United States prosecutors allege that Bell, 63, led a structure that stockpiled and shipped large quantities of cocaine from Costa Rican territory to the United States between March 2022 and August 2023. According to the Public Ministry, Bell held contacts with undercover agents that included the sale of a drug sample and negotiations toward a shipment of 700 kilograms (about 1,540 pounds) of cocaine bound for New York. In November 2023 he became the first Costa Rican designated by the United States Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, which described him as a major trafficker operating out of Limón.

Lozano, 52, was named by Costa Rican investigators as the alleged head of the organization at the center of the case known as Corona, which authorities say converted cocaine to liquid form at a clandestine laboratory and moved it out of the country concealed in beverage bottles bound for Europe and Asia.

As part of that investigation, authorities intercepted a shipment of 150 liters (about 40 gallons) of liquid cocaine at the Israel-Jordan border in June 2023, a load that investigators traced to the APM Terminals dock in Moín. United States prosecutors allege his participation in trafficking operations running from Venezuela and Colombia toward American territory. He is the first naturalized Costa Rican surrendered under the constitutional reform.

Both handovers required prosecutors to set aside pending domestic cases. The Public Ministry applied a criterio de oportunidad to the fuel-theft investigation in which Bell had been held since October 11, 2024, and requested the same measure in the Corona file, in which Lozano had been ordered to trial alongside five other men.

A Limón tribunal initially rejected the United States request for Bell in March, ruling that the conduct alleged predated the May 28, 2025 amendment to Article 32 of the Constitution. An appeals court in San José reversed that finding in June. The final diplomatic assurances arrived on July 31, committing United States authorities to try Bell only on the charges for which extradition was granted and not to seek life imprisonment or a term exceeding 50 years, the maximum available under Costa Rican law.

In the hours before the handover, both men told prosecutors they had been tortured in the high-containment unit at the Jorge Arturo Montero Institutional Care Center, the facility widely known as La Reforma. Attorney General Carlo Díaz confirmed the complaints and said he took the men’s statements on video after obtaining their consent.

According to Díaz, the men described being woken every hour through the night and being told the practice was ordered by the attorney general. Díaz rejected any involvement, stating that his office holds no authority over the prison system. He said he would forward the recording to the Fiscalía de Ejecución Penal, the Ombudsman’s Office and the National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture for whatever action each considers appropriate.

Speaking on camera before boarding, Bell said he had lived alongside rats and pigeons in his cell, described a diet of rice and eggs, and claimed he had lost 45 kilograms (about 99 pounds) in custody. He called on President Laura Fernández, judges and prosecutors to examine conditions in the unit.

Manrique González, Bell’s attorney, said he was unaware of the formal complaint but confirmed that his client had repeatedly reported mistreatment that had damaged his physical and emotional condition. The Ministry of Justice had not responded publicly to the allegations as of Thursday afternoon.

The complaints reflect those raised by former security minister and magistrate Celso Gamboa, whose account of treatment in the same unit prompted the Fiscalía de Probidad, Transparencia y Anticorrupción to open an investigation on its own initiative into the penitentiary staff involved.

Bell and Lozano bring to five the number of alleged traffickers surrendered by Costa Rica since the constitutional reform took effect. Gamboa and Edwin López Vega were flown to Texas in March in the first handover of Costa Rican nationals in the country’s history, and José Johnny Angulo was delivered to Italian authorities in April. Roughly 20 more people remain in custody in Costa Rica awaiting transfer to foreign courts, the large majority of them requested by the United States

World.title: Corcovado National Park Placed on Red Alert Over Sewage and Crumbling Infrastructure
World.content:
A coalition of Costa Rican environmental organizations has placed Corcovado National Park under what it calls a red alert, warning that sewage discharges, decaying infrastructure and chronic underfunding at our most popular protected area point to a wider breakdown across the national park system.

The Parlamento Cívico Ambiental, an umbrella body grouping environmental organizations from across the country, issued the manifesto on August 10 under the title “For our protected areas: Corcovado on red alert.” The document is dated July 31 and is framed around the first 100 days of President Laura Fernández’s administration, a mark her government reaches on August 16.

“Corcovado is not only a national park. It is water, forest, biodiversity and a promise Costa Rica has made to the world and to future generations: that nature can stand above abandonment and economic interest,” the manifesto states. “One hundred days into the Fernández administration, as with our entire system of protected areas, that promise is at risk.”

At the center of the complaint are discharges of wastewater and fecal matter from the Sirena Biological Station into water bodies inside the park. The manifesto says the discharges were verified by the Costa Rican Institute of Aqueducts and Sewers (AyA) and the Ministry of Health. The groups argue the contamination cannot be written off as an isolated technical fault. They describe it instead as the visible signal of a deeper crisis in how protected areas are managed, maintained, financed and supervised.

What the signatories call most alarming is that the situation appears to have persisted despite health warnings, technical reports and prior institutional knowledge of the problem. “When controls arrive late and responsibilities are diluted, conservation ceases to be a guarantee and becomes a discourse,” the document states, arguing that this compromises the right to a healthy and ecologically balanced environment recognized in Article 50 of the Constitution.

The wastewater treatment plant at Sirena discharges into Quebrada Camaronal, a stream that runs behind the station inside the park boundaries. Ministry of Health inspections concluded that wastewater was being released without quality control or operating records, and the ministry ordered the situation corrected by December 31, 2025.

That deadline passed without compliance. A December 2025 report by AyA and the National Water Laboratory found the remedial plan had not been carried out and described the condition of the plant as limiting to the operation of all services at the station.

An earlier AyA inspection in November 2025 found the discharges into Quebrada Camaronal exceeded legal limits for biochemical oxygen demand, chemical oxygen demand and total suspended solids. When AyA applied the Ministry of Health’s technical guide for evaluating treatment systems, Sirena failed slightly more than 80 percent of the criteria assessed, including signage, operating and maintenance manuals, approved plans and a numbered operations log.

The same report found the discharge point had never been registered with the Water Directorate, that no operational reports were filed, and that no payments were made toward the environmental levy owed on wastewater discharges. The Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE) has said the plant was designed in 2017 to handle roughly 100 people per day but had been receiving more than 200 since 2022.

The ministry also acknowledged the plant had gone without continuous electricity for about eight years, a serious problem for a system whose aerobic stage depends on powered blowers to keep treatment bacteria alive. The question of how many visitors Sirena should receive has swung back and forth this year. On June 26, the then director of the Osa Conservation Area, Juan José Jiménez Espinoza, cut the daily limit at Sirena to 150 people, split between 100 day visitors and 50 overnight guests, citing the sanitary crisis.

Six days later, Environment Minister Mónica Navarro Del Valle reassigned him to a desk post at SINAC headquarters, a move that drew protests along the southern Pacific coast. His replacement raised the ceiling again on July 9, to 225 people per day through September, with 175 day visits and 50 overnight stays.

That resolution leaned on an AyA finding that restroom batteries installed in recent weeks at the Los Naranjos sector could operate independently of the treatment plant. SINAC acknowledged in the same document that rehabilitation of the plant itself had not been completed. The reversals follow a Constitutional Chamber ruling issued on August 8, 2025, which struck down a 2023 resolution that had raised Corcovado’s daily visitor ceiling from 560 to 700. The court found the increase lacked explicit technical grounding.

SINAC has requested more than 2.63 billion colones (about $5.8 million) from the Rural Development Institute to finance comprehensive infrastructure improvements at Sirena, and has assigned a further 50 million colones (roughly $111,000) through a REDD+ master plan covering 2026 to 2028. Sirena closes each October for seasonal maintenance, and most of the repair work is expected during that window.

The manifesto sets out four demands. The first is a comprehensive investigation into what happened at Corcovado, with responsibilities assigned, technical reports and sanitary orders made public, and damaged infrastructure repaired immediately and effectively. The second is a public, transparent national audit of sanitary, operational and environmental infrastructure across all protected areas, differentiated by management category, visitation levels and actual needs.

The third calls for a real and verifiable increase in SINAC’s budget, with sufficient staff, adequate equipment, continuous maintenance and genuine capacity to prevent, correct and penalize environmental damage. The fourth demands a review of permits, concessions and commercial activities inside protected areas, alongside open data, accountability, citizen participation and consequences for unjustified non-compliance.

“Corcovado is not the problem: it is the alarm,” the manifesto concludes. “We cannot normalize places called upon to receive the greatest protection operating with deteriorated infrastructure, precarious services, insufficient controls and late responses.” Corcovado covers 424 square kilometers (164 square miles) on the Osa Peninsula and was declared a protected wilderness area in 1975. SINAC figures put annual visitation above 60,000, with Sirena the most heavily used sector and the focus of a longer argument over how much tourism the park can absorb.

The document carries the signatures of Bernardo Aguilar González, Victoria Rudín Vega, Oscar Moya Cantero and Melanie Pérez Vargas on behalf of the Parlamento Cívico Ambiental. It closes with an appeal aimed less at any single ministry than at the public: defending Corcovado, the group argues, means defending water, biodiversity and ecological democracy, and it cannot wait.

World.title: World Surf League Returns to Costa Rica at Playa Hermosa
World.content:
Professional surfing returns to Costa Rica’s international stage today as the Garabito Surf City PRO 2026 gets underway at Playa Hermosa, bringing an official World Surf League competition back to the country for the first time in nearly eight years. The four-day competition runs from August 13 through August 16 at the well-known surf beach just south of Jacó. Surfers from 19 countries are expected to compete, including 23 representing Costa Rica.

The event features men’s and women’s QS 2000 competition. The Qualifying Series is part of the World Surf League system in which professional surfers earn ranking points as they try to move into higher levels of international competition. Winners at Playa Hermosa can earn up to 2,000 ranking points.

For Costa Rica, however, the tournament is about more than results in the water. Tourism officials and local organizers see the return of the WSL as another opportunity to promote the Central Pacific coast as an international surf destination and bring visitors to hotels, restaurants and other businesses in Garabito.

Surfing is already an important part of Costa Rica’s tourism industry. Figures provided by the Costa Rican Tourism Board indicate that about 17% of the more than 2.6 million travelers who arrive in the country by air each year surf during their visit.

Playa Hermosa is particularly well positioned to benefit. The beach was approved as a World Surfing Reserve in 2020 and formally dedicated in 2022, becoming the first such reserve in Central America. Save The Waves Coalition selected it because of its consistent waves, biodiversity, surf culture and community support for conservation.

A 2021 study commissioned through Save The Waves estimated that surfing directly contributed about $14 million annually to the Playa Hermosa economy, illustrating how much the sport already matters to local businesses.

This week’s tournament also comes as Garabito joins the World Surf Cities Network, an international group of destinations where surfing plays a significant role in tourism, employment and local culture. Garabito is now listed alongside destinations in countries including Portugal, Spain, Brazil, Chile, Peru, Ecuador and France.

Costa Rica’s 23-member contingent includes two of our best-known professional surfers, Carlos “Cali” Muñoz and Leilani McGonagle, along with Darshan Antequera, Axel Castro, Jair Pérez, Ethan Hollander, Tomás Pathenay, Malakai Martínez and several younger competitors. McGonagle is also part of a women’s field that includes American Talia Swindal, Argentina’s Victoria Muñoz Larreta, Peru’s Brianna Barthelmess and U.S. surfers Ella McCaffray, Remy Todd and Zoe Benedetto.

The last official WSL event held in Costa Rica was the Essential Costa Rica Surf Pro at Jacó in October 2018. Muñoz won the men’s competition that year, while Germany’s Rachel Presti took the women’s title. Playa Hermosa has hosted major international surfing before, including the 2009 ISA World Surfing Games, but this will be the first time the beach hosts a WSL Qualifying Series event.

For Garabito, the hope is that the benefits continue after the final surfers leave the water Sunday. Local officials have been pushing surfing as a way to attract visitors outside Costa Rica’s traditional peak tourism periods and give the area a more consistent flow of business throughout the year.

With Playa Hermosa’s reputation for powerful, consistent waves and Jacó’s tourism infrastructure only a short drive away, the return of the WSL gives Costa Rica another chance to put one of its most established surf destinations in front of an international audience.

World.title: Grammy award winning artist Shyne Barrow named 2026 Global Ambassador honoree at Caribbean Music Awards
World.content:
Grammy award winning artist Shyne Barrow named 2026 Global Ambassador honoree at Caribbean Music Awards

By Zoila Palma: Belizean Grammy Award-winning recording artist and former Leader of the Opposition Shyne Barrow has been named the 2026 Global Ambassador Honoree by the Caribbean Music Awards, recognizing his contributions to Caribbean music and his journey from international recording artist to political leader and advocate for Belize.

The Caribbean Music Awards highlighted Shyne’s rise as an internationally recognized artist who helped bring the sound and influence of Caribbean talent to audiences around the world.

The organization said his journey represents “music, transformation, leadership, and impact,” while celebrating his role in representing Caribbean culture, creativity and resilience on the global stage.

As a Belizean artist, Shyne made his mark on the international music industry with his distinctive baritone and gritty lyrical style.

He released his platinum-certified self-titled debut album in 2000, followed by the gold-certified “Godfather Buried Alive” in 2004, and has worked as a performer, writer and producer with major artists including Usher, Lil Wayne and The Notorious B.I.G.

His music career later evolved into public service, where he served as Leader of the Opposition in Belize’s House of Representatives.

The recognition comes as Shyne continues his return to music with his “2622 LGND” tour, featuring reggae icon Barrington Levy, rap legend Lil’ Cease and Belizean artists Stig Da Artist and DJ Rampage. Announcing the tour, Shyne said, “Beyond excited to announce the celebration of the legacy continues this fall with the 2622 LGND tour,” describing the shows as a continuation of his return to the stage and a celebration of hip-hop and reggae’s golden eras.

Shyne will receive the Global Ambassador Honoree recognition at the 2026 Caribbean Music Awards on Saturday, September 19, at the National Academy for the Performing Arts (NAPA) in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago.

World.title: Corozal health services promotes Breastfeeding support and awareness
World.content:
Corozal health services promotes Breastfeeding support and awareness

By Zoila Palma: The Corozal District Health Services, in collaboration with the Instituto de Nutrición de Centro América y Panamá (INCAP), hosted a breastfeeding awareness and support event aimed at highlighting the benefits of breastfeeding and providing mothers with information and encouragement throughout their breastfeeding journeys.

The event brought together a pediatrician, medical doctor, nutritionist and other health officials who shared guidance on the nutritional and health benefits of breastfeeding, while emphasizing the importance of providing mothers with adequate support from families, communities and healthcare providers.

Mothers attending the event also had an opportunity to connect, share their personal experiences and engage in discussions in a supportive environment.

The initiative formed part of activities surrounding World Breastfeeding Week, observed from August 1 to 7, which is supported by the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF, Ministries of Health and civil society organizations around the world.

The 2026 theme, “Breastfeeding for a Sustainable Start in Life: Strengthen What Works,” focuses on expanding proven approaches that improve breastfeeding outcomes and strengthening the support available to mothers.

According to WHO and UNICEF, exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months has increased globally from about 37 percent in 2012 to more than 47 percent today.

However, progress remains uneven, with many mothers still lacking access to quality breastfeeding support.

Health officials point to skilled counselling, community-based support, maternity protection and supportive workplace policies as among the measures that can help more women successfully breastfeed.

World.title: Belize listed among countries seeing surge in American visitors in 2026
World.content:
Belize listed among countries seeing surge in American visitors in 2026

By Zoila Palma: Belize is being highlighted among 10 countries experiencing a surge in visits from American travelers in 2026, as more tourists look beyond traditional destinations for affordable experiences with fewer crowds.

Belize is gaining attention for our beaches, rainforests, Maya sites and world-renowned marine attractions.

According to the article, “Belize has quietly built one of the more compelling pitches to American beachgoers looking for an alternative to Mexico’s increasingly crowded coastline.” It noted that Belize is “coming in hot for 2026,” having already been recognized as one of the best off-the-beaten-path destinations for travelers seeking a different Caribbean experience.

The article particularly highlighted Belize’s barrier reef, describing it as a major advantage for visitors interested in diving and snorkeling. “That reef access alone gives Belize a genuine edge for divers and snorkelers,” the article stated.

Belize’s growing air connectivity is also being credited for helping attract more American visitors.

The article said that the Belize Tourism Board has been focusing on new flight routes and expanding low-cost and regional connections from the United States, making travel to Belize easier and, in some cases, cheaper.

It also noted that English being the country’s official language can make Belize an attractive option for U.S. travelers.

World.title: Social Partners welcome Cabinet’s position against proposed BTL-Smart acquisition
World.content:
Social Partners welcome Cabinet’s position against proposed BTL-Smart acquisition

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BCCI), National Trade Union Congress of Belize (NTUCB), National Evangelical Association of Belize (NEAB), Belize Network of Non-Governmental Organizations (Benn), and their respective Independent Senators have welcomed Cabinet’s decision not to support the proposed acquisition of Speednet Communications Ltd. (Smart) by Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL).

In a joint statement issued on August 13, the Social Partners said they “commend Cabinet for listening to the concerns expressed by Belizeans across the country,” adding that the decision demonstrates the importance of “public scrutiny, collective action and meaningful engagement on matters of national importance.”

The groups, however, stressed that Cabinet’s position does not determine the legal or regulatory outcome of the proposed transaction.

They pointed to the Public Utilities Commission (PUC) as the relevant regulatory authority and called for the Commission to continue carrying out its legal responsibilities independently and transparently.

The Social Partners also reiterated their request for the PUC to address outstanding regulatory concerns, including the implications of the acquisition for competition and compliance with Belize’s telecommunications framework.

The Social Partners further called on BTL’s Board to comply with its legal and fiduciary obligations and respond fully to outstanding requests for information, including financial and valuation material needed to properly assess the proposed acquisition.

“Cabinet’s announcement does not remove the need for accountability regarding how a transaction of this magnitude was introduced, assessed and advanced,” the groups stated.

Reaffirming their position, the Social Partners said the proposed acquisition must withstand rigorous public, financial and regulatory scrutiny and comply fully with the law.

World.title: International News: Hundreds remain missing as Colombia’s earthquake rescue effort enters grim phase
World.content:
International News: Hundreds remain missing as Colombia’s earthquake rescue effort enters grim phase

By Zoila Palma: Hopes of finding more survivors following the powerful earthquake that struck Colombia earlier this week are fading, as rescue crews narrow their searches and families continue to wait for news of missing relatives.

In Cali, the country’s third-largest city, many teams have shifted from search-and-rescue operations to clearing debris, signaling a difficult new phase after the critical first 72 hours.

The 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck shortly after 7:30 a.m. Monday, destroying buildings and damaging homes, schools and hospitals across western Colombia, Reuters report.

Government figures released Thursday evening placed the death toll at 281, with more than 3,900 people injured and 379 still reported missing.

More than 150 aftershocks have also been recorded, complicating rescue operations and increasing risks for workers and displaced residents.

David Tamayo, head of Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management, acknowledged that the chances of finding survivors are declining but said rescue teams would continue searching for everyone reported missing. In Cali, volunteers and emergency crews continued working through unstable rubble, while residents and local businesses provided food and other assistance to rescuers, medics and displaced families.

The disaster has also exposed challenges outside Colombia’s major cities.

In some communities, residents reportedly spent hours digging through collapsed structures with their bare hands before formal rescue teams arrived.

More than 10,500 homes are estimated to have been destroyed, while some affected communities continue to face shortages of water, gas and electricity. In parts of Buenaventura, access has also reportedly been complicated by armed groups.

The earthquake represents the first major crisis facing President Abelardo De La Espriella, who took office only days before the disaster.

He has announced plans to declare an economic emergency and establish a reconstruction fund to support the rebuilding of homes, schools, hospitals and other infrastructure.

World.title: International News: New El Niño forecast warns of potential ‘Historic Event’
World.content:
International News: New El Niño forecast warns of potential ‘Historic Event’

By Zoila Palma: A strengthening El Niño could develop into one of the most powerful events on record, according to an updated forecast released by scientists at the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center on August 13.

Forecasters say there is now a greater than 90 percent chance that El Niño will become a “very strong” event during the fall and winter of 2026-27.

The forecast also places the likelihood at 69 percent that the event could reach historic strength, potentially exceeding previous El Niño events recorded since 1950. Sea-surface temperatures in the eastern equatorial Pacific are already more than 3.6 degrees above average, with scientists expecting the warming to continue through the end of 2026.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern characterized by unusually warm ocean temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. The phenomenon can influence weather patterns around the globe, contributing to increased hurricane activity in the Pacific, reduced activity in the Atlantic, shifts in rainfall and drought patterns, and higher global temperatures.

Scientists caution, however, that even a very strong El Niño does not guarantee specific weather impacts in every region.

Current conditions are already being associated with drier-than-average conditions in parts of Central America, Indonesia, India and the Horn of Africa, while wetter conditions have been observed in parts of Chile. In the United States, El Niño winters typically bring wetter conditions to the southern states and warmer-than-average temperatures across much of the country.

World.title: Belizean transmigrante involved in horrible crash in Matamoros-Victoria, Mexico
World.content:
Belizean transmigrante involved in horrible crash in Matamoros-Victoria, Mexico

By Zoila Palma: A Belizean transmigrante was reportedly involved in a horrific traffic accident along the Matamoros-Victoria highway in Tamaulipas, Mexico, resulting in the deaths of a mother and her two children.

Preliminary reports indicate that the mother and her two children were traveling in another vehicle when they reportedly entered the lane of the vehicle being driven by the Belizean transmigrante, resulting in a devastating collision.

The mother and both children reportedly died as a result of the crash.

Details surrounding the circumstances of the accident, including the identities of those involved, have not yet been officially confirmed.

World.title: Friday ends damp as showers spread across Belize
World.content:
Friday ends damp as showers spread across Belize
