World.title: France upholds assisted dying law but strikes down social media ban for children
World.content:
France's top constitutional authority approved legislation on Friday on the right to assisted dying, but struck down a ban on social media access for children under 15 in a blow to one of President Emmanuel Macron's cherished reforms.

 

Macron's office hailed the Constitutional Council's decision on the assisted dying law, seen as one of the major social reforms of his second term.

The ruling "completes an exemplary democratic debate," the Élysée Palace said, adding that the legislation "provides an essential safeguard for our fellow citizens."

At the same time his office said the president had no plans to give up on his push to bar children from apps such as TikTok and the government would work on a new draft law.

The legislation establishing a right to assisted dying for some adults suffering from an incurable condition was passed by parliament in July after years of debate.

The Constitutional Council's ruling will see France join the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland and Canada, which have already legalised the practice.

France's President Emmanuel Macron speaks to the press in Bordeaux, 27 July, 2026 AP Photo

The decision is a victory for Macron, who promised the law after his re-election in 2022, marking one of France's biggest social reforms since same-sex marriage was legalised in 2012.

At the same time the constitutional authority found that certain provisions of the legislation required clarification, including the so-called conscience clause, which allows healthcare professionals to refuse to take part in the procedure.

The clause must also apply to private healthcare facilities where assisted dying is "manifestly contrary" to their mission, provided they are not the only establishments able to meet "local needs," the constitutional authority said, meeting a key demand from Catholic healthcare institutions.

To be eligible for assisted dying, a patient must be of legal age and a French national or a long-term resident.

They must suffer from pain that is either unresponsive to treatment or, in the patient's view, unbearable if they have chosen not to receive or to stop receiving treatment.

The patient will administer a lethal substance themselves, with exceptions for those who are physically unable to do so and can be helped by a healthcare worker.

A board shows the result after France's lower house of parliament adopted a bill to allow adults with incurable illness to take lethal medication, 27 May, 2025 AP Photo

'Deadly poison for children'

But in a major setback to Macron, the constitutional authority struck down a ban on social media access for children under 15.

The Constitutional Council found that Article 1 of the legislation "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of those under 15.

In its ruling, the Constitutional Council also expressed concern about the potential impact on privacy of introducing an age-verification system for all users.

The law, which was due to take effect on 1 September, would have barred younger users from social networks such as TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram, among other restrictions.

The French government had promoted the ban as a way to better protect young people from the harmful effects associated with social media platforms, including anxiety, depression, sleep disorders and online harassment.

A view of the TikTok app logo in Tokyo, 28 September, 2020 AP Photo

Macron had thanked members of parliament in July for backing the legislation and pledged to enforce it by September.

After the ruling, the Élysée said Macron had tasked Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu with working on a new "legally robust draft" of the legislation.

Lecornu will have to work "as quickly as possible" on a draft that takes into account both the Constitutional Council's ruling and the European regulatory framework, the Élysée Palace said.

The presidency said Macron's determination to see the reform implemented remained undiminished.

Macron's former prime minister Gabriel Attal, who backed the proposal, expressed his disappointment.

"We take note of it and respect this decision, which applies to everyone," he said in a post on X, vowing to continue fighting against what he described as "a deadly poison for our children."

The Constitutional Council did not rule on a separate provision banning mobile phone use in high schools from 1 September.

A growing number of countries are taking steps to restrict social media access amid multiplying warnings over its harmful effects on children.

World.title: Croatia wildfire near Omiš injures residents and disrupts holiday travel
World.content:
Fourteen people were taken to hospital, with seven reportedly in a life-threatening condition early on Friday. Parts of Omiš lost power as the fire approached the town centre, while homes, cars and boats were damaged or destroyed. Evacuees spent the night in a sports hall, sleeping on beds and floors.

 

Residents described chaotic scenes as they fled the advancing flames. Omiš fire brigade commander Slavko Tučaković said numerous homes and vehicles had been destroyed, causing extensive damage to property, the natural environment and wildlife.

Firefighters brought the blaze under control by Friday, while crews were also deployed to another wildfire on the Pelješac peninsula. Authorities said there were no fatalities.

The fires came at the height of Croatia’s summer tourist season, threatening to disrupt travel and put further pressure on the local economy. Sections of the main coastal road near Omiš were closed, affecting links between Split and Dubrovnik as well as day trips and coach tours. Damage to homes, cafés, restaurants, cars and boats could also reduce the area’s tourism capacity at a time when demand is at its peak.

World.title: Ash clouds, lava flows and fertile soil: What are the effects of Mount Etna’s eruptions?
World.content:
Europe’s most active volcano has been putting on a fiery show, and experts predict that this is just the beginning.

 

Tourists have flocked en masse to see molten lava spewing out of Mount Etna, a stratovolcano located on the east coast of Sicily.

As the eruption enters its seventh consecutive day, plumes of thick black smoke have continued to trigger travel chaos in the region, grounding dozens of flights at Catania–Fontanarossa Airport and temporarily suspending arrivals.

And yet, for all the fiery force Etna is displaying, the environmental consequences of its eruptions are not necessarily as far-reaching or devastating as they appear.

Eruptive activity continues on Mount Etna, where lava flows continue to descend on the slopes of the volcano, as seen from Serracozzo near Catania, Italy, Aug. 11, 2026. AP Photo/Simone Genovese

Etna is almost always erupting

For one, this kind of activity is not unusual for Etna. The volcano erupts several times a year, and sometimes multiple times a month. In fact, it erupted in late July.

The Sicilian landmark is one of the world’s most active volcanoes and has produced more than 70 paroxysmal eruptions in the past six years, Giorgio Costa, a PhD student at the University of Catania’s Department of Biological, Geological and Environmental Sciences, tells Euronews Earth.

These intense bursts of activity can send lava fountains hundreds of metres into the air and ash clouds several kilometres high. They typically last several hours.

“In reality, the volcano’s activity is currently perfectly normal,” says Costa.

Eruptive activity continues on Mount Etna, where lava flows continue to descend on the slopes of the volcano, as seen from Serracozzo near Catania, Italy, Aug. 11, 2026. AP Photo/Simone Genovese

Is Mount Etna an environmental disaster waiting?

Volcanic eruptions send a cocktail of debris and emissions into the air. The most obvious is ash, but volcanoes also emit carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, as well as small amounts of hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen chloride and hydrogen fluoride.

That might make Etna’s regular eruptions seem like potential environmental catastrophes, but the truth is more complex.

The US Geological Survey explains that gases such as sulfur dioxide can cause global cooling while carbon dioxide has the potential to promote global warming.

The impact is minimal, however. NASA says that human activities generate 100 times the carbon dioxide of the planet’s volcanic eruptions.

And climate change itself doesn’t influence eruptions. “There is no correlation between meteorological events, including climate change, and the Earth's volcanic or tectonic activity,” Costa tells Euronews Earth.

Eruptive activity continues on Mount Etna, where lava flows continue to descend on the slopes of the volcano, as seen from Mareneve near Catania, Italy, Aug. 13, 2026. AP Photo/Salvatore Allegra

Ash is a bigger – but still small – concern

“The main issue currently associated with the eruptions of Etna concerns the fallout of pyroclastic material, mostly ash and small lapilli, which can be carried by the wind to the slopes,” says Costa.

Lapilli are small fragments of rock, which typically range from two to 64 millimetres.

Costa explains that while ash and small lapilli are not dangerous to human health, they can become so when fine particles produced by the ash are lifted into the air.

“Inhaling large amounts of this material is certainly not healthy for the respiratory system, so wearing a mask is recommended,” he adds.

It can also pose a serious problem for aircraft.

If a plane flies through an ash cloud, the particles can enter its engines, where they can melt and damage components and, in some cases, cause engines to lose power. This is why ash in the airspace around Etna can force Catania Airport to close.

The airport is currently closed until 2am on Saturday, and hundreds of flights have been cancelled or diverted over the past week.

Smoke billows from Mount Etna volcano, Italy, Monday, June 2, 2025. AP Photo/Giuseppe Distefano

Why Etna’s ash is also a boon for human life

They may have a negative impact on aeroplanes, but these same materials can benefit the planet.

Etna’s ash acts as a mineral-rich fertiliser and can improve soil drainage and water retention, helping farmers produce Sicily’s renowned wines, pistachios and citrus fruit.

Research from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography in San Diego found that volcanic ash can do morethan simply add nutrients to soil, too.

In experiments, ash helped revive microbial communities in degraded soil, increasing the activity of organisms that play a key role in breaking down organic matter and making nutrients available to plants.

The researchers also found that plants grown in ash-rich soil developed larger root systems and produced more biomass.

Volcanic ash can also improve soil drainage and water retention.

Etna’s frequent eruptions mean it repeatedly deposits fresh layers of ash, creating a long-term cycle of destruction, enrichment and renewal. Even if ash causes problems when it falls, it eventually becomes part of the soil supporting new life, if not important crops for Sicilian farmers.

Eruptive activity continues on Mount Etna, where two lava flows continue to descend on the slopes of the volcano, as seen from Nicolosi near Catania, Italy, Aug. 26, 2025. AP photo/Salvatore Allegra

The dangers of getting too close

While some might be worried about Etna’s impact on the environment, the biggest immediate risk may come from people getting too close to the action.

“The greatest risk factor is the presence of large numbers of onlookers who set out along Mount Etna’s most rugged trails to watch the ongoing eruption, completely lacking in mountain gear,” says Mirko Messina, the co-founder of Bùum, a specialised tour service that leads excursions of Italian volcanoes, including Etna.

“The Alpine Rescue Service has already carried out numerous rescues, especially at night when law enforcement checks are not in place.”

Messina adds that Etna’s northeast slope – which has just one small, uphill road – has become “gridlocked with hundreds of cars, preventing normal traffic flow and hindering rescue efforts”.

While Etna erupting might be business as usual, Messina says, it should be anything but that for those looking to witness it up close.

“It is impossible to predict in advance how the eruption will evolve in the coming days,” he explains, “but it will be constantly monitored.”

World.title: War in Ukraine: Deadly Russian air raid on Kramatorsk leaves 1 dead and 17 wounded
World.content:
Emergency crews worked through the night on Friday to rescue residents trapped under rubble and extinguish fires after eight FAB‑250 guided aerial bombs hit the city, local authorities said. Several private homes and a garage caught fire, while an apartment building suffered extensive damage.

 

The strike caused sections of the ten‑storey apartment building from the first to the sixth floors to collapse, the emergency service said. Rescuers were filmed pulling a woman and a man from the rubble and helping residents leave damaged buildings. Firefighters also tackled flames at several sites across the city, while cars were damaged near the impact areas. The Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office has opened a war‑crimes investigation into the attack.

Kramatorsk has repeatedly come under Russian attacks during the war because of its proximity to the front line. The injured, aged between 47 and 85, were treated for blast and traumatic brain injuries, shrapnel wounds, cuts and abrasions, officials said.

World.title: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal stalking charges in Brian Thompson death
World.content:
The plea resolves the remaining federal charges tied to the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and could affect a separate New York state case.

Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty in a Manhattan federal court to a stalking charges tied to the death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

"I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died," he told the court,

Prosecutors said Mangione traveled to New York City and fatally shot Thompson outside a Manhattan hotel on December 4, 2024, as he walked to UnitedHealth Group's annual investor conference.

The judge has accepted his guilty plea and said sentencing would take place in December. Mangione faces a possible sentence ‌of life without parole on the two counts of stalking.

Mangione seek dismissal of state murder charges

Mangione had previously pleaded not guilty to federal murder, weapons and stalking charges. Earlier this year, the judge dismissed the murder and weapons counts on legal technicalities, leaving only the stalking charges and eliminating the possibility of the death penalty.

Mangione still faces separate murder, weapons and forgery charges in New York state court. His federal guilty plea could prompted defense arguments that some state charges should be dismissed.

Now, "state charges must be dismissed under New York's double jeopardy protections,"Mangione's lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, told reporters outside the federal court.

Under double jeopardy protections, defendants are protected from being prosecuted for the same crime twice.

World.content:

08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 Farmers fear drought will wipe out this year's harvest

German farmers fear they could see harvests wiped out entirely by ongoing drought and unseasonably high temperatures, says German Farmers' Association (DBV) President Joachim Ruckwied.

"We expect below-average grain harvests, especially when it comes to wheat and rapeseed," he said during an interview with Germany's Redaktionsnetzwerk media group.

"As far as fall crops are concerned, the trend suggests we must expect significant yield losses here as well."

Potatoes, vegetables and sugar beets, as well as grain maize and soy could be affected.

Ruckwied warned that although farmers in the north could hope for "acceptable" if "below-average" harvests thanks to occasional rains, farmers in drier southern Germany could be facing "total harvest loss."

"What's becoming a problem, especially in southern Germany, is that feed crops aren't coming in," he added, noting that this would force farmers to slaughter animals earlier than usual.

The threat adds to the financial pressure farmers already face when it comes to buying seed, fertilizer and pesticides, says Ruckwied.

"The economic situation is brutal… on the one hand high investment costs, and on the other, lower market prices for agricultural products."

World.title: France: Top court blocks social media ban for children
World.content:
Denying access to platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and YouTube for under-15s would infringe upon freedom of expression, the Constitutional Council has said.

France's highest constitutional authority on Friday struck down the ban on social media for children under 15.

The Constitutional Council ruled that the flagship policy of President Emmanuel Macron's second term infringed on freedom of expression.

"By prohibiting minors under the age of 15 from accessing certain online services, the law inherently requires every person, even an adult, to prove their age before accessing them," it said in its decision.

Macron still wants social media ban for children

French lawmakers last month approved legislation that barred children under 15 from opening social media accounts from September 1. Beyond that, platforms would have until the start of 2027 to close children's existing accounts.

The law would also have banned the use of mobile phones in high schools and required social media platforms to introduce age-verification measures in accordance with France's privacy regulator.

France: First EU country to ban social media use under 15 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Council, however, found lawmakers had failed to set out clear rules on how people should prove their age and what limits should apply, meaning there were not enough legal safeguards in place.

Macron has instructed Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to revise the bill to address the Constitutional Council's concerns, the Elysee Palace said. It added the president wanted the reform in place before France's 2027 presidential election.

Social media bans for teens and children also considered elsewhere

Australia became the first country in the world to ban social media for under-16s in 2025. France was the first in Europe.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen last month pledged to pursue an EU-wide social media ban for children following a recommendation by an expert group to restrict access for under-13s.

"Our children need time in the real world. Time to play, time to build friendships, time to make mistakes. Time to shape their own identity, their own personality, before an algorithm shapes them instead," von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels.

"This is not about whether children can access social media. It is about whether and when social media can access our children," she said.

A number of other countries have announced plans to consider similar bans, including Brazil, the UK, Canada, Norway and Denmark.

World.title: Eco wins: A Dutch gym for crops, a climate-ready city and a beaver comeback
World.content:
Dutch crops hit the "climate gym," a German city is constructing for more extreme weather, and beavers are restoring rivers across Europe. This week's eco wins are all about building for a changing climate.

The Netherlands is putting plants through their climate paces

How will the world feed 10 billion people with less land, less water, and unpredictable weather? The Netherlands, also known as agriculture's 'Silicon Valley', knows a thing or two about it.

It's already the world's second biggest exporter of agricultural products after the United States, despite being a fraction of its size.

Now, in some of the country's greenhouses, scientists are using high-tech means and reams of data to figure out which crops will be resilient in a changing climate.

Can we build a climate-proof crop? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A German city is building for the new climate reality

In October 2023, the northern German city of Kiel saw the worst storm surge in more than 150 years. It destroyed dikes, collapsed coastal cliffs, and devastated marinas. It shocked city officials into reimagining infrastructure to cope with more frequent and intense weather extremes linked to human-made climate change.

Ideas range from cool city corridors and green facades to flooding soccer pitches at certain times of the year and adapting daily schedules to heat. Find out more about what Kiel is doing, alongside other cities worldwide.

Turtles are ready for their close-up

Ever dreamed of becoming a wildlife photographer? Destinations in Egypt are getting tourists to snap photos of sea turtles to help with conservation efforts.

These underwater creatures have unique markings on their faces — almost like human fingerprints. Researchers use them to identify individual turtles and even track injuries. If they spot a turtle that's recovering, they can alert authorities to steer boat traffic away from that area.

Beavers make a comeback to help fight wildfires, drought and flood

After being hunted to near extinction for their fur, meat and scent glands in the early 20th century in Europe, beavers are so back.

Thanks to major long-term rewilding efforts across the continent, populations have skyrocketed from about 1500 wild Eurasian beavers in 1900 to 1.5 million today.

Beavers are the engineers of the animal world. They build dams that help filter water pollutants, reduce the impacts of flooding, wildfire and drought, and recharge underground aquifers. And they're fixing wetlands and rivers across Europe — from Spain to Russia.

World.title: Taliban pressured by insurgents after 5 years in power
World.content:
The Taliban managed to retake power in Afghanistan on August 15, 2021. Now, they face armed factions who challenge the Taliban rule and strain their central claim of providing security.

Less than a month before the five-year anniversary of the Taliban retaking power in Afghanistan, the Islamist regime lost control of the Yaftal-e Payeen district capital in the northeastern province of Badakhshan. The disruption was temporary, but it nevertheless marked the first time the Taliban lost control of a district center since returning to power in August 2021.

Reports from Badakhshan also indicated internal clashes among Taliban fighters and fatal attacks on high-ranking Taliban officials.

On August 2, some two weeks after the brief loss of the district center, former Afghan army general Sami Sadat ordered his forces to launch attacks against the Taliban across the country.

"Today at 5:00 AM, I ordered all military members of the United Front to begin military operations," General Sadat said in a video message released from the US, where he has lived since the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban.

Other armed groups, including the National Resistance Front led by the son of the late commander Ahmad Shah Massoud, have been engaged in a continuous armed struggle against the Taliban since 2021. While armed insurgents have not been able to pose a major threat to the Taliban's overall grip on power, experts are questioning whether the clashes in Badakhshan could pave the way for more impactful resistance.

"In these five years, this opposition existed in two forms: political and military... As the five-year mark approaches, both forms of opposition have taken shape," former Afghan Interior Minister Mohammad Umer Daudzai told DW.

5 years of Taliban rule: What has changed in Afghanistan? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fear of new proxy wars in Afghanistan

The Taliban have reigned with an iron fist since the collapse of the US-backed Afghan government five years ago. The Islamist regime denied basic human rights and imposed strict restrictions on women, banning them from work and education beyond the sixth grade. Women are mostly banned from public life in Afghanistan as well, and have few rights at all.

Most former government officials are in exile. While the Taliban maintain that all Afghans are free to return and lead ordinary lives, opponents counter that return is only viable if political activity is permitted.

While the regime managed to cultivate some contacts internationally, they are still viewed as illegitimate by most of the world's governments. To date, only Russia has acknowledged the Taliban as the official government of Afghanistan.

Facing pressures both within and outside of the country, the Taliban repeatedly pointed to the restoration of nationwide security as their primary claim to legitimacy. However, experts warn that their governing style could in fact enable armed rebels to challenge them in various parts of Afghanistan.

Exiled Afghanistan envoy still advocating for women's rights To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"If this policy of the Taliban continues, armed forces will emerge against them, opposition will emerge, interference from neighbors will arise, and ultimately the ground will be prepared for proxy wars," former Acting Minister of Defense Shahmohammad Miakhel told DW.

Beyond political opposition, the regional branch of the "Islamic State" (IS) remains active in Afghanistan. The group has claimed responsibility for several high-profile attacks against Taliban officials, including a January explosion at a Chinese restaurant in central Kabul that killed at least seven people, and a December 2024 suicide bombing in Kabul that killed the regime's Minister of Refugees Khalil Ur-Rahman Haqqani.

Taliban claim Pakistan supports insurgents in Afghanistan

The strongest challenge to Taliban control could originate from outside Afghanistan's borders. Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan — once considered one of the Taliban's closest allies — have been fraught with tension since 2021, erupting in full on clashes this year. According to a United Nations report from May, cross-border hostilities during the first three months of 2026 resulted in at least 372 Afghan civilian deaths and nearly 400 injuries .

EU-Taliban talks spark debate over normalizing Taliban rule To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"When Mr. Sami Sadat issues such an order from America to those who must fight the Taliban, he has certainly seen a green light. And remember that in Afghanistan, no group and no one can carry out any activity without the support of one or more foreign countries," former defense ministry spokesperson Mohammad Radmanish told DW.

While the Taliban publicly downplay the threat posed by rebel groups, they also allege that external support for armed resistance is rising.

"We are aware that lame ducks were invited to Pakistan [...] A large group has been invited to Islamabad who are now discussing where they can have an office and center and refuge," Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid told DW in an interview.

When pressed by DW to provide evidence for these claims, Mujahid offered no proof.

'Islamabad has used all its options'

Pakistan accuses the Taliban of providing safe havens to militants executing attacks inside Pakistani territory, particularly the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). The Taliban deny these charges, in turn accusing Pakistan of harboring hostile elements and violating Afghan sovereignty.

Qamar Cheema, an Islamabad-based security expert, told DW in February that it is Pakistan that is targeting the militant groups.

"Pakistan wants the Afghan people to understand that the Taliban are harboring terrorists. Therefore, Pakistan will continue targeting military sites associated with the Taliban, TTP and ISIS-K hideouts," Cheema said.

"Islamabad has used all its options, including regional diplomacy and direct communication, but nothing has been honored," he added. "As a neighboring Muslim country, Pakistan appears to inflict damage in an attempt to alter Taliban behavior."

World.title: Congo: Ebola cases are rising at record pace
World.content:
The Ebola virus is spreading rapidly in the DRC. In Kinshasa, a city of millions, fears of a serious health crisis are growing. Hospitals are scrambling to prepare for emergencies as best as they can.

The Ebola epidemic in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo has now spread to a sixth province in the country. Concerns are growing that the life-threatening infectious disease could reach the capital, Kinshasa, which is home to 19 million people.

Facilities for isolating patients are ready for the event that a public health alert should hit the capital, says Jean-Jacques Muyembe, Director General of the National Institute for Biomedical Research (INRB).

"If there is a suspected case, the epidemiological services and the INRB laboratory are ready to quickly identify and confirm cases," he told DW.

"The Ministry of Health has set up the Cinquantenaire Hospital so that it can admit and fully isolate patients if necessary. We are prepared. We can quickly contain an Ebola outbreak here in Kinshasa."

The peak of the Ebola outbreak is expected to arrive in six months Image: Badru Katumba/AFP

A health crisis still in the making

However, the virus has been spreading faster than health authorities can contain it. This Ebola outbreak is driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which no vaccine or treatment has yet been approved.

According to Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO), the outbreak, given its rapid rise, could surpass the West African Ebola outbreak of 2014 – 2016. .

At that time, 11,000 people died, while the current health crisis has claimed 2,000 lives so far, with more than 4,300 cases recorded to date. Authorities officially announced the outbreak on May 15; three months later, the country remains on edge.

The WHO meanwhile expects the current outbreak to only peak in six months.

The initial infections meanwhile can be traced back to as early as February, according to reports. The epicenter of the outbreak was identified as the northeastern province of Ituri, which has been plagued by insecurity for years, and is home to a large number of internally displaced persons.

Many other cases have meanwhile also been reported in the provinces of North and South Kivu, where the security situation is an even bigger problem; authorities have effectively lost control over entire areas in their years-long conflict with M23 rebels and affiliated groups.

Fear among Kinshasa's massive population

Fear among the population of contracting the virus is also growing every day. A week ago, the threat came close to the capital when a boat was stopped at the port of Maluku, about 65 kilometers upstream from Kinshasa.

One of the passengers had previously disembarked in Mongala Province to seek medical help, presenting with typical Ebola symptoms such as fever and diarrhea.

Shortly thereafter, the patient died, prompting more than 200 passengers from the vessel to be placed in isolation. Teams from the Ministry of Health and the WHO tested them using a mobile laboratory — but the results came back negative.

But with its population of millions, this did not mean the all-clear for Kinshasa: Every day people come and go between cities and provinces, leaving potentially lethal traces behind.

In fact, the rapid spread of the current outbreak has been positively attributed to large-scale population movements as well as ongoing violence in main affected areas.

Not enough beds for worst-case scenario

Beyond the diagnosis of the disease and isolation of patients, capacity remains one of the biggest challenges for Kinshasa if the virus were to make its way there.

However, the Center for Public Health Emergency Response (COUSP) says that it plans to further expand its capacity to be able to meet the onset of any outbreak.

Emergency preparations have already been taken at Cinquantenaire Hospital: "We have set up twenty beds for this purpose. However, this capacity is flexible and can be expanded to 200 or 250 beds," Christian Ngandu, the hospital's coordinator, told DW.

However, according to the WHO, several thousand beds would need to be ready in the worst-case scenario.

"We are currently exploring the possibility of providing additional beds. We have trained more than 120 people from various facilities, including the Vijana, Sino-Congolais, Kinkole, Kintambo and Cinquantenaire hospitals. These professionals are capable of treating any potential Ebola case," Ngandu said.

DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Is enough being done?

According to Carlos Mupili, president of the Supreme Council of Civil Society, current capacities are insufficient.

"Twenty beds are insignificant in this city, and a single hospital is not enough. Several health facilities should have been mobilized to prevent the outbreak effectively," he told DW.

Mupili has been calling on authorities to provide more resources to avoid unpleasant surprises: "The authorities must act swiftly and provide the necessary resources so we are not overwhelmed and... forced to make hasty decisions."

WHO Director-General Ghebreyesus cautioned that an unexpected surge in infections could ensue anywhere, as contact-tracing of infected individuals has been slow. He expressed "concern" about the fact that many people dying from the virus have not been registered on the official Ebola contact lists before being buried.

Furthermore, he stressed that many infections originate from from funerals.

Passengers on a boat were tested for the deadly virus, but the results all came back negative Image: Xinhua/IMAGO

Ngandu meanwhile emphasizes the fact that there has not been a single case of Ebola in Kinshasa so far, and that the primary strategy is to keep things that way.

To break the fast-moving chains of transmission, 95% of all contacts must be tracked; currently, that rate is believe to be around only 80%.

Scientists meanwhile are scrambling to find a cure: Clinical trials of two anti-viral treatments are underway, and work on vaccines is also in progress. The results — so far — look promising.

To date, there have been no mutations of the virus observed in the current DRC outbreak, commented Sylvie Briand, the WHO's chief scientist, which has been a small source of hope amid the growing crisis. After all, mutations of the virus could be highly dangerous, with the potential of becoming more lethal or increasing the transmission rate, thus jumping across borders faster.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Fact check: False claims target US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed
World.content:
Abdul El-Sayed, who could become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate if he wins in November, has been targeted by false claims online following his victory in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary.

On August 4, Abdul El-Sayed, a leading progressive candidate, won Michigan's Democratic primary for the US Senate.

The 41-year-old will face Republican Mike Rogers in the November 3 midterm elections. The winner will succeed retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.

Michigan is a battleground or so-called "swing" state, where both parties have a strong chance of winning. The large Arab American and Muslim population plays a key role.

If El-Sayed wins in November, he would become the first Muslim US senator in history.

Soon after his primary victory, several false claims about El-Sayed were spread online, including claims promoted by prominent political figures.

Michigan is a key swing state in the upcoming midterm elections Image: Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP

According to Lawrence Pintak, a journalism professor at Washington State University and author of America & Islam, El-Sayed is an ideal target for political disinformation.

"He checks off all the boxes: He's a Muslim, he's a progressive, and he is vocally critical of Israel," Pintak said in a written statement to DW.

DW Fact check examined claims about voting irregularities during the primaries, El-Sayed's political ideology and whether he said the US deserved the 9/11 attacks.

Alleged ghost votes

Claim: "Of course they cheated. Nobody actually votes for communists," a Facebook post claimed, linking to an article headlined: "Abdul El-Sayed got three times as many votes in Detroit as there are registered voters."

The article states that El-Sayed "received 1.4 million votes in Detroit alone — a city with approximately 480,000 registered voters."

Originally published as satire, the false claim spread as disinformation after being reposted on other pages Image: Facebook

DW Fact check: False

The Facebook account that shared the claim, "America's Last Line of Defense," states that "nothing on this page is real." The page has around 748,000 followers and is linked to a website run by Christopher Blair, a well-known creator of fabricated political content. The BBC once described him as the "godfather of fake news."

However, this disclaimer is often lost when the content is reposted on other pages, allowing the false claim to spread without context.

The invented story echoes a claim shared by US President Donald Trump days earlier about a county in Michigan: "Miracles happen in Wayne County, including more votes being cast than there are voters, by a lot."

Trump did not provide any evidence to support his claim of alleged voter fraud.

According to the Michigan Voter Information Center , Michigan has approximately 7.3 million active registered voters, while El-Sayed received 743,455 votes statewide in the Democratic Senate primary, not 1.4 million votes in Detroit alone.

Michael Hameleers, an associate professor of political communication at the University of Amsterdam who researches misinformation and disinformation, warned about the impact of such allegations.

"It is a prominent delegitimization technique to put democratic institutions and the fairness of elections in question," he said.

"Especially in a context where people perceive disinformation and fraud as highly likely, it may be a fruitful strategy to cast doubt on elections."

A 2023 US study found that exposure to unfounded claims of voter fraud can significantly undermine confidence in elections, particularly among Republicans and Trump supporters.

Claims about political ideology

Claim: US President Donald Trump has repeatedly described Abdul El-Sayed as a communist, most recently in a Truth Social post published shortly after El-Sayed's primary victory.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed Abdul El-Sayed is a communist Image: @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social

DW Fact check: False

El-Sayed's campaign has focused on government-sponsored health insurance, taxing billionaires and reducing the influence of corporate money in politics.

In the past, he has rejected claims that he is a socialist or a communist by stating he is a capitalist . "I'm not a socialist. I'm just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works," he said.

El-Sayed emphasized his views on capitalism as a point of difference from self-described democratic socialist Bernie Sanders.

In a recent interview with The New York Times , he responded to Trump's claims that he is a communist by saying: "The man is so clearly a joker."

In a comment to DW, Lawrence Pintak also called the claims historically bizarre. He sees it as part of systematic attempts by the Republican Party "to spin 'progressive' and 'democratic socialist' to be synonyms for 'Communist.'"

An analysis by Reuters found that Trump has significantly increased his use of the term in recent weeks.

Pintak told DW that the loaded term works well on social media.

Misattributing views on 9/11

Claim: After El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination, his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, posted a statement on X , calling him "someone who believes America deserved 9/11."

Abdul El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers during the general election in November Image: @MikeRogersForMI/X

DW Fact check: False

9/11 refers to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, in which planes hijacked by militant ​al-Qaeda Islamists struck the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon near Washington, killing nearly 3,000 people.

The allegation has come up repeatedly but conflates previous remarks made by El-Sayed supporter Hasan Piker with El-Sayed's own views.

Piker has supported El-Sayed during his 2026 US Senate campaign, appearing with him at rallies and in livestreams.

American Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has been a vocal supporter of Abdul El-Sayed's 2026 US Senate campaign Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance

During a 2019 livestream, Piker said America had "deserved" 9/11, a remark that generated widespread criticism. Since then, however, he has walked back this statement .

When asked by US-based fact checkers PolitiFact for evidence to support his claim, the Rogers campaign pointed to a video clip of El-Sayed refusing to disavow Piker's 2019 comments.

Pintak, who researches Islamophobia, described "guilt by association" as one of the disinformation tactics used against El-Sayed.

He points out that El-Sayed has become a target of disinformation at a time when the Republican Party has shifted from an anti-immigrant focus back to an anti-Muslim narrative.

"Attacks on Muslim candidates, and El-Sayed himself, are nothing new," Pintak said, pointing to Islamophobic reporting during El-Sayed's 2018 campaign for Michigan governor and false claims portraying New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an extremist.

During the 2018 midterms, Pintak led a research team that found Muslim candidates, from local school boards to Congress, were systematically targeted by "a social media narrative of manufactured outrage [that] was disproportionately Islamophobic, xenophobic, racist, and misogynistic."

The researchers concluded that such attacks were often aimed at undermining candidates' legitimacy and reducing trust among voters.

World.title: Can a giant Madonna help slow secularization in Poland?
World.content:
Europe's largest statue of the Virgin Mary will be inaugurated on Saturday in the Polish village of Konotopie. What will the monument mean for the village it towers over and for the Catholic faith in Poland in general?

With its grain fields, meadows and lake, the countryside around the tiny village of Konotopie in central Poland is idyllic. Now there is a monumental statue of the Virgin Mary towering above all this.

Home to just 120 residents and situated about 160 kilometers (99 miles) northwest of the capital, Warsaw, the previously little-known village of Konotopie has been in the headlines for weeks now as a result of the massive statue.

The snow-white structure, which is visible for miles around, is more than 55 meters (180 feet) tall. The statue itself is 40.6 meters high and stands on a 15-meter-high pedestal shaped like a crown that is intended to serve as a viewing platform.

The figure dwarfs Rio de Janeiro's famous statue of Christ the Redeemer, which reaches a total height of 38 meters including its base.

'Pile of concrete' or 'fantastic achievement?'

The statue will be officially inaugurated on Saturday, August 15, the feast of the Assumption of Mary, a major holy day in the Catholic calendar.

Although final construction work is still underway and the site remains fenced off and guarded, thousands of people — both pilgrims and sightseers — have been flocking to see it for months.

Opinion about the project is divided.

"It's a nightmare," one critic of the statue told the weekly magazine Newsweek, "a complete waste. Instead of investing that money in useful projects, they financed a giant pile of concrete."

"This Mary is absolutely beautiful. My utmost respect. A fantastic achievement," said one devout woman visiting the site, according to the right-wing conservative weekly Sieci.

Madonna statue financed by Poland's Warren Buffett

The benefactor behind the statue, 75-year-old Roman Karkosik, hails from a nearby village and is one of Poland's wealthiest individuals.

Nearly 40 years ago, when the shortage economy of socialism gave way to free-market capitalism after the collapse of communism in eastern Europe, Karkosik was a young graduate from technical high school.

He started out as a bartender, but moved on to buying and selling scrap metal, producing soft drinks and later became the first entrepreneur in Poland to manufacture plastic bottles.

People have been coming to see the statue of the Virgin Mary in Konotopie even before it is officially opened to the public on Saturday Image: Mateusz Kaczmarek/REUTERS

Karkosik made a name for himself on the Warsaw Stock Exchange. Some journalists have compared his role in Poland to Warren Buffett's influence on Wall Street.

His fortune is estimated at roughly €442 million ($511 million), and he ranks 44th on Wprost magazine's list of Poland's richest people. He lives in an 18th-century manor in the town of Kikol, just two kilometers from Konotopie.

A 'gesture of gratitude'

Karkosik and his wife, Grazyna, avoid both public appearances and contact with the media.

The cost of the statue remains a closely guarded secret. Media reports speculate that the project may have cost as much as €23 million.

The Karkosiks have described the Marian statue as a "gesture of gratitude."

According to media reports, the devout businessman wanted to thank the Virgin Mary for his recovery from a serious illness. His two brothers, who were also successful businessmen, both died prematurely after illnesses.

This is not the first time Karkosik has provided money for a religious structure. Back in 2011, he funded the construction of a church at a nearby pilgrimage site.

Artist feared seeing the finished statue

"I was afraid to come to Konotopie to see what had become of my design in reality," sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski told Polish media. Worried that the hands and face of the Virgin Mary might appear distorted, Matejkowski only visited the site in July.

"I opened my eyes and was stunned. The Mother of God is opening her arms to embrace us," he said with satisfaction. "That was exactly my intention: for the figure to have a human character, to come toward us."

The statue of Jesus Christ the King of the Universe, one of the tallest Jesus statues in the world, is also in Poland Image: Monika Skolimowska/ZB/dpa/picture alliance

Matejkowski says the statue has the facial expression of his 11-year-old daughter and the delicate facial features of his wife.

Polish region hopes for economic boost

Konotopie is situated in one of Poland's economically weak regions. There are no major industrial employers here, and jobs are scarce.

Local leaders hope the Marian statue will stimulate economic growth.

"The monument is not only a spiritual landmark but also a strategic asset for the region. We expect it to attract more investors and tourists, which will benefit the local economy," Krzysztof Kowalewski of the authorities in the nearby town of Kikol told Polish media.

Mayor Renata Golebiewska has said that revenues at local restaurants and bars have already broken local records.

Not the first statue of its kind in Poland

Poland is well known for its monumental Christian structures.

Following Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, a massive basilica was built in the village of Lichen in central Poland, overshadowing even the cathedrals of Paris and Cologne in scale.

The basilica is 138 meters (453 feet) long, 77 meters wide, and features a dome with a diameter of 35 meters. It can accommodate 20,000 worshippers.

Since 2010, Poland has also been home to the world's tallest statue of Jesus. Located in Swiebodzin near the German border, the 36-meter-high statue stands on a 17-meter-high mound.

Rising secularization

Whether all these gigantic monuments can stop the ongoing secularization of Polish society, however, remains highly questionable.

Although Poland is still one of the most Catholic countries in Europe, public trust in the Church continues to decline.

For centuries, the Catholic faith was a key part of Polish identity.

A huge statue of Pope John Paul II, who was born in Poland and was head of the Catholic Church from 1978 to 2005, in Czestochowa Image: Waldemar Deska/dpa/picture alliance

In the 19th century, when the territory that now makes up Poland was not an independent state and was divided up among foreign powers, Catholicism played a major role in the resistance to Protestant Prussia and Orthodox Russia.

After World War II, despite ideological differences, the anti-communist opposition and the Catholic Church in Poland worked together against the communist dictatorship.

During this period, churches became refuges for persecuted dissidents, and several priests were murdered by the secret police.

Pope John Paul II, himself Polish, also played a significant role in the struggle against the regime.

Catholicism in modern-day Poland

Since Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, however, the Catholic Church has experienced a crisis similar to that seen across Europe.

According to a September 2025 survey conducted by the Polish polling institute IBRIS, only 35% of Poles still trust the Church, down from 58% in 2016. Distrust rose from 24% to 47% over the same period.

In 2026, the annual number of priests ordained in Poland fell below 200 for the first time since 2000. Church attendance has also been steadily declining, especially among young people.

Even a gigantic Madonna is unlikely to reverse that trend.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: El Gobierno amplía la vida de la central nuclear de Almaraz hasta 2030 por la “volatilidad de precios” originada en Oriente Próximo
World.content:
El principio del fin de la energía nuclear en España se gana una prórroga de dos años y medio mientras las guerras en Oriente Próximo y Ucrania se enquistan y no dejan de alborotar los precios energéticos mundiales. El Gobierno ha autorizado la ampliación de la vida útil de la central de Almaraz (en Cáceres), tal y como había recomendado el Consejo de Seguridad Nuclear hace un mes y habían solicitado desde el otoño pasado sus propietarias: Iberdrola, Endesa y Naturgy. Según se publica en el Boletín Oficial del Estado de este viernes, el Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico concede la renovación de la autorización de explotación de la Central Nuclear Almaraz, Unidades I y II, y prorroga “la vigencia de la autorización de explotación de ambas Unidades hasta el 8 de junio de 2030, teniendo en cuenta que la central nuclear cuenta con una Revisión Periódica de Seguridad (RPS) vigente hasta dicha fecha”. El apagado programado debía comenzar en noviembre de 2027 y no se cambia el resto de los previstos hasta 2035. Desde el Gobierno se subraya que la extensión es “acotada y limitada”, y que se pretende defender al sistema energético y a los consumidores de la volatilidad de los precios internacionales.

El alcalde de Almaraz, Juan Antonio Díaz Agraz (segundo por la derecha), junto con otros alcaldes de la zona se han concentrado para mostrar su satisfacción por la prórroga de la central nuclear, este viernes. EDUARDO PALOMO (EFE)

El Ministerio justifica la decisión por el nuevo contexto energético internacional y la volatilidad del precio del gas derivada de la crisis en Oriente Próximo, según el texto de la orden. “La crisis en Oriente Medio ha supuesto una disrupción en el contexto energético global, incrementando y añadiendo volatilidad de forma significativa a los precios de los combustibles fósiles, entre ellos el gas natural. Según indican organismos internacionales, el contexto geopolítico y los daños en infraestructura de producción y exportación de combustibles extienden el riesgo y la incertidumbre a los próximos años”, indica el texto publicado en el BOE.

Según los cálculos incluidos en la resolución, mantener Almaraz hasta 2030 tendrá un efecto “acotado y poco significativo” sobre el despliegue renovable y contribuiría a reducir la dependencia del gas. El Ministerio no quiere que la decisión se entienda como un paso atrás y deja clara cuál es su estrategia en la misma orden de prórroga de Almaraz: “La política energética aprobada y en ejecución en España, alineada con la normativa y objetivos europeos, tiene como base la apuesta por la generación renovable como forma más competitiva de producir electricidad, aprovechando asimismo las ventajas competitivas del país en términos de recurso, tecnología y capacidades. Esta apuesta ha permitido mejorar la posición de España en cuanto a costes energéticos en el contexto europeo, proteger a los consumidores ante subidas de precio, y generar un contexto inédito de atracción de proyectos industriales y de electrificación”.

Fuentes del Ministerio subrayan las “circunstancias extraordinarias derivadas del conflicto en Oriente Medio y de la continuidad de la guerra en Ucrania”. “Hay una situación energética internacional excepcional y sobrevenida que está generando un escenario de elevada volatilidad y precios altos de los combustibles fósiles, cuya duración es actualmente imposible de prever”, se subraya como punto de partida. Y como remate, se incide en que “la volatilidad y la incertidumbre son significativamente mayores a las anticipadas hace tan solo unos meses”. El cierre efectivo del estrecho de Ormuz provocado por la guerra de Irán ha ocasionado que se dispare el precio del gas en Europa.

Sala de turbinas de la central nuclear de Almaraz, en 2025. Alex Onciu

Por lo tanto, se actúa en consecuencia: “En el contexto actual, la prórroga, coyuntural, puede contribuir a moderar la exposición de los consumidores a unos picos de precios de los combustibles fósiles no previstos anteriormente. Ello permite seguir protegiendo a la población ante la volatilidad de los precios y la incertidumbre en este periodo, mientras se sigue ampliando la respuesta estructural frente a la dependencia de los precios de combustibles fósiles: el despliegue de renovables”, explica el Gobierno.

La orden señala igualmente que la continuidad de Almaraz aporta estabilidad al sistema eléctrico, según el propio operador, aunque la prórroga no “cambia la necesidad de continuar con las actuaciones ya en curso dirigidas a fortalecer la seguridad y estabilidad del suministro”.

Una extensión “acotada”

El Ministerio insiste en que la extensión es “acotada y limitada”, y que se otorga tras comprobar el cumplimiento de las tres condiciones que siempre exigió para concederla: que fuera segura para las personas (como avala el CSN en su informe preceptivo anterior), que no comprometiera la seguridad de suministro y que no suponga ningún coste para los ciudadanos. Es decir, no hay “ningún tipo de rebaja fiscal ni contraprestación económica para las empresas eléctricas”.

“La extensión solicitada del periodo de explotación para las Unidades I y II de la Central Nuclear Almaraz se limita en torno a 31 y 19 meses respectivamente, lo cual representa una proporción reducida de la vida media prevista del parque nuclear español, no alterándose el resto del calendario ni la fecha de cese definitivo del conjunto del parque nuclear a 2035. De acuerdo con los análisis realizados, dicha extensión tiene un impacto muy limitado sobre los objetivos de política energética del país”, explica la orden del departamento dirigido por Sara Aagesen.

El protocolo firmado en 2019 entre las propietarias del parque nuclear español y la Empresa Nacional de Residuos Radiactivos (Enresa), sociedad dependiente del Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica, contemplaba el cierre ordenado del parque hasta 2035, empezando en ese año 2027 que ahora se traslada a 2030 para el recinto extremeño. Las dos unidades de Almaraz eran las primeras en echar el cierre y, pese a contar desde 2020 con el visto bueno del CSN para funcionar durante 10 años (los permisos del organismo de seguridad se dan por una década), el calendario fijaba el cierre de las plantas cacereñas en siete y ocho años, respectivamente. Esto es, ya tenían permiso para funcionar 10 años, por lo que era de esperar que el CSN no se pronunciase en contra.

Finalmente, y tras muchos meses de debate soterrado, presión social en la comarca implicada, declaraciones públicas para testar la posición de la otra parte y negociaciones sobre el alcance de la posible medida, las eléctricas decidieron pedir la ampliación de la vida de ambas unidades de Almaraz hasta 2030, por mucho que su primera intención apuntaba a una extensión de diez años. Iberdrola, con una participación del 53% y Endesa con un 36%, eran partidarias de esta mayor ampliación, si bien, Naturgy, con un 11%, se opuso, y ganó la partida toda vez que, al estar constituidas las nucleares como comunidades de bienes, las decisiones deben adoptarse por unanimidad.

Vista del exterior de la central nuclear de Almaraz (Cáceres), este viernes. EDUARDO PALOMO (EFE)

Además, Endesa e Iberdrola habían venido batallando para lograr un recorte de los impuestos que gravan a estas plantas, esencialmente, el del combustible nuclear gastado, que el Gobierno de Mariano Rajoy aprobó en 2013 para hacer frente a la deuda del sistema eléctrico. Pero, a medida que se acercaba el plazo límite para solicitar la prórroga al CSN (un año antes del cierre previsto), las compañías renunciaron a los recortes fiscales que venían reclamando y que el ministerio, y el Gobierno en su conjunto en no pocas declaraciones, siempre consideró “una línea roja”. Con todo, mantienen recurrida en los tribunales la tasa de gestión de residuos de Enresa.

La decisión del Ministerio pone fin al trámite y evita que el cierre escalonado de los dos reactores se active para sus fechas previstas: el 1 de noviembre de 2027 para la Unidad I y el 31 de octubre de 2028 para la Unidad II.

En cualquier caso, y según recoge la orden ministerial de este viernes, la prórroga de funcionamiento estará subordinada al cumplimiento estricto de las condiciones e instrucciones de seguridad dictadas por el CSN. El Consejo de Seguridad Nuclear emitió ya el pasado 16 de julio un informe favorable a la renovación solicitada, condicionado al cumplimiento de los límites y exigencias de seguridad nuclear y protección radiológica recogidos ahora en la orden. El aval técnico del organismo regulador certificó y acreditó que la instalación nuclear cacereña reúne las condiciones de seguridad necesarias para operar de manera segura durante dicho periodo de prórroga. Tras este pronunciamiento del CSN, el expediente fue remitido al Gobierno, abriendo un plazo para que el Ejecutivo tomara una decisión definitiva sobre su continuidad.

La orden obliga a las empresas a mantener las dotaciones de personal de plantilla con funciones relacionadas con la seguridad previstas para los años 2028 a 2030. También señala que la prórroga “deberá facilitar la mayor implicación de las empresas propietarias en alternativas industriales y de empleo en el territorio y debe ser utilizada por las mismas para avanzar en el diálogo social para una transición justa”, aunque sin imponer condiciones explícitas al respecto.

World.title: 16 pueblos españoles que piden manga larga cuando cae la tarde
World.content:
Vielha (Lleida). La gran baza de los pueblos seleccionados radica, sobre todo, en la posibilidad de tener que taparse para descansar, algo que se ha convertido en todo un lujo durante la canícula. Es un requisito que cumple Vielha, a la vera de los ríos Garona y Nere, con su casco histórico construido a la manera aranesa, a golpe de piedra, pizarra y madera. Sus mínimas descenderán hasta los 12ºC la noche del domingo; las máximas alcanzarán picos de 33ºC en las horas centrales del jueves y viernes, pero bajarán a los 24ºC (y con probabilidad de lluvias) el lunes, según la Aemet. La capital del Valle de Arán se presenta como un buen campamento base para conocer este territorio del Pirineo catalán, con sus 33 núcleos de población, sus algo más de 10.000 habitantes y sus iglesias románicas. Es recomendable acercarse a la cascada Saut deth Pish, probablemente la más bonita de la zona. Más información: visitvaldaran.com/descubre-la-val-daran/pueblos/vielha/.

Toni M (GETTY IMAGES)

World.title: Shell and Philips hit by Russian ransomware attack
World.content:
The Russia-linked ransomware group Cl0p claims to have hacked global corporations Shell and Philips. The two are among nearly 50 companies Cl0p has listed on its website, alongside General Electric and payments firm Fiserv.

From the oil giant, the group says it has taken some 89 gigabytes of material, including technical drawings, facility images, scans of test reports and project plans. They claimed to have stolen another 13.5 gigabytes from health technology company Philips, mostly diagrams and blueprints.

Both companies are investigating, with Shell saying it is “aware of a possible incident”.

Philips said it had “identified and contained an attempted cybersecurity compromise of a specific enterprise server related to internal data”. A spokesperson told NOS that the incident is now under control and has no impact on its customers.

Russian hackers

Cl0p, which has been active since 2019, is a Russia-linked ransomware group that has likely already extorted $500 million from other victims.

It operates by stealing files and other sensitive data from companies and then threatens to publish them online unless a ransom is paid.

There’s no word yet on how much money the hackers are asking for in exchange for not selling or releasing the stolen data.

Security researchers have linked the campaign to a flaw in Windchill, engineering software made by American firm PTC, which was patched on June 17. Neither Shell nor Philips has said how it was breached.

Writing about the attacks, TNW editor-in-chief Ana-Maria Stanciuc said the pattern carried an uncomfortable lesson: “When enough of the corporate world standardises on the same enterprise platform, one shared supplier quietly becomes everyone’s single point of failure, and no amount of internal security spending can fully patch a hole in someone else’s code.”

World.title: Jetten tells farmers to get off motorways after two die in crash
World.content:
Prime minister Rob Jetten has said it is “unacceptable” that tractors were driving on the A59 motorway on Friday, after two people were killed and six injured in a crash. The collision happened at the back of a queue that had built up as the tractors drove to a protest in Den Bosch.

“It is unacceptable and incomprehensible to demonstrate on the motorway because it leads to very dangerous situations,” Jetten said during a press conference.

Jetten also said the decision not to stop the tractors earlier was not a good signal and would have to be reviewed. News agency ANP reported that 50 tractors were driving on the A2 towards Utrecht as he spoke. “Don’t do it, get off the motorway,” Jetten said.

Police said four cars were involved and that they were still investigating what caused the collision, but no tractors were involved.

The victims have not been identified. The tractors had been in the right-hand lane and other traffic could pass on the left, but a traffic jam still built up.

Disputed agreements

Tractors are not permitted on Dutch motorways. Earlier this week the public prosecution department (OM) and the police said they would not stop farmers who drove onto them, citing the right to demonstrate.

A spokesperson for the OM in Oost-Brabant told broadcaster NOS that this had not been agreed. The authorities help demonstrations go ahead, the spokesperson said, but once a tractor is on the motorway it is up to the local mayor, police and prosecutors to decide when and how to step in.

“A tractor on the motorway is never allowed, and is a criminal offence” the spokesperson said. The OM did not answer questions from NOS about what had been agreed instead, or why nobody intervened.

Provincial council members held a minute’s silence for the two dead. Mark van den Oever of Farmers Defence Force called on farmers at the provincial offices not to travel home by motorway.

What the protest is about

Noord-Brabant’s provincial executive intends to revoke the nature permits of five poultry farms close to protected nature areas, after environmental groups won a court case in April 2025.

The court found the protected areas were overloaded with nitrogen, and that the farms were a significant cause. But it stopped short of ordering the permits withdrawn, giving the province, the farmers and the environmental groups a year to come up with a plan that would cut nitrogen levels for good.

The farmers sent in their plans in November 2025 but in July were told their permits would be revoked, although that decision is not yet final. The provincial executive has admitted it never gave them a proper response to those plans, Omroep Brabant reported.

Members of the provincial council, which oversees the executive, broke off their summer break on Friday for a debate on the plan demanded by seven opposition parties, led by farmers’ party BBB. Saskia Boelema, the executive member responsible, told them the province should have sat down with the farmers earlier and apologised for the way the process had been handled.

World.title: Mouse invasion plagues Friesland farmers
World.content:
A mouse plague has been destroying fields in Friesland in the northwest of the country, depleting crops as the rodents eat entire patches of land.

According to Omrop Fryslân, recent weeks have seen the mice mostly causing damage in peat meadows, but they have now also infiltrated clay areas.

“They eat the roots and then the grass dies,” farmer Jan Brouwer from Koufurderrige told the broadcaster. He estimates that it reduces his grass yield by up to 20%.

Drought

The outbreak comes on the heels of a countrywide drought, which has also affected the farmers.

But as there’s no irrigation ban in Friesland yet as compared to other areas of the country, Brouwer was able to flood his fields to flush out the mice. The critters drown in their burrows, and those that try to escape are easy prey for birds.

The water has also helped his land come back to life. “We were making silage today and the grass is starting to come back quite nicely in those spots,” said Brouwer.

The nearby Ijsselmeer still has plenty of water, but that could change if the drought persists.

There have been several mouse plagues since 2015 in the region. And with them, comes an owl invasion, including the short-eared owl. “I have seen at least six short-eared owls here in the past few weeks,” says Brouwer.

Researchers expect the number of mice to decrease substantially next year. “With such a plague, at a certain point there are simply too many,” said Niek Bosma of the regional waterboard. “Then a disease sets in, and within a few weeks all those mice are dead.”

But a few ultimately remain, meaning another mouse plague is inevitable.

World.title: Care homes, prisons and asylum centres hit by night-time heat
World.content:
As daytime temperatures continue to soar during the Netherlands’ fifth heatwave this year, night-time heat, where temperatures stay above 20 degrees, has lagged behind in public discourse despite its effects on the population.

“Night-time heat is an under-examined aspect of heatwaves,” Lisette Klok, researcher at the Climate Adaptation Services foundation, told broadcaster NOS and NRC.

Especially for vulnerable people – including the elderly and those living in asylum seeker centres and prisons – “night-time temperature is important because your body needs the chance to recover from the heat at night. Poor sleep [due to the heat] makes that more difficult.”

Hot nights, which are defined from 11pm to 7am, affect how well people are able to cope during daytime heat. People tend to sleep worse, making them less functional during the day. In addition, homes build up heat because they can’t cool down during the night, meaning neither do their inhabitants.

Climate atlas

The foundation puts out the Climate Impact Atlas, which maps climate effects – from threats of flooding, waterlogging, drought and heat – throughout the country. Using the Atlas, NRC and regional broadcasters found that on average, there are some six tropical nights per year in the Netherlands, although there are regional differences.

Going neighborhood by neighborhood, the journalists found that in parts of South Limburg, there is an average of 15 “sticky nights” annually.

Maastricht has the most hot nights in the country, while the Randstad also has a higher number. The north of the Netherlands sees less than the national average. Urban areas also take a heat hit, with city centres becoming “heat islands” on hot days. Heat in these areas is even worse at night.

“As a result, homes can be cooled less effectively by ventilation,” said Marjolein van Esch, urban microclimate researcher at TU Delft. “This depends on the difference in air temperature between indoors and outdoors. The greater that difference, the easier it is to cool. Due to the urban heat island effect, that temperature difference is smaller.”

Elderly

The high night-time temperatures have a particularly strong effect on older people, who are more vulnerable to heat.

That led some nursing homes being evacuated earlier this summer, including the De Taling care home in Den Bosch and a facility in Raalte whose systems temporarily failed in July.

“Many buildings are designed for a different climate,” a spokesperson for the care organization Carinova told NOS. “The climate systems were tested to the limit at some locations this summer.”

Temporary portable air conditioners and moving residents to cooler rooms helped ease the problems.

Asylum seekers and prisoners

Since 2021, new homes must meet certain requirements to prevent overheating, but the rules don’t apply to existing houses and also usually not to care homes, prisons and asylum seeker centres. Requirements also vary depending on the region.

But residents of asylum seeker centres and prisons, who have nowhere else to go, are not allowed to install air conditioners on their own. Refugee settlement agency COA allows only one fan per room.

According to NRC, the Dutch Correctional Institutions Agency said increasing temperatures in prisons in recent years mean it needs more resources to cool things down. “Many buildings are due for major maintenance or renovation.”

Ajax and Twente both reached the play-off round of the Conference League on Thursday, despite drawing both away games.

Ajax drew 2-2 away at Shelbourne in Dublin, going through 5-3 on aggregate after winning the first leg 3-1 in Amsterdam.

The Amsterdam side led twice in the first half, the second time through Anton Gaaei, but the Irish club equalised on both occasions. Substitute Sean Moore scored the second in the closing stages.

Twente had the easier night, leading 6-0 from the first leg, they drew 3-3 away at DAC 1904 in Slovakia to go through 9-3.

NEC chase Champions League

Every result in Europe counts towards the Uefa coefficient, the ranking that decides how many Dutch clubs qualify each season. The Eredivisie lost sixth place on the Uefa coefficient to Portugal in March, costing it a direct Champions League spot from 2027.

NEC, meanwhile, play Bodø/Glimt on August 19 for a place in the Champions League league phase.

The Conference League draw is on August 28.

World.title: Fifth heatwave confirmed as temperatures reach 37°
World.content:
Temperatures will reach 37° on Friday, after forecaster Weeronline confirmed the fifth regional heatwave of the year.

Temperatures will range from 33° in the north to 37° in the south and southeast, the national weather service KNMI said.

Five heatwaves in a single year have happened only once before, in 1947. Then it was Maastricht alone – this year several southern stations have reached the tally.

There will be no national heatwave, which is measured at the KNMI station in De Bilt, near Utrecht. Most of the country, including the Randstad and the north, will fall below the threshold.

KNMI has issued a code yellow warning for heat across the country. The national heat plan, run by public health institute RIVM, puts care homes and health services on alert. It covers the whole country on Friday and only the southeast on Saturday.

Friday night will stay warm, with temperatures holding near 20° in towns and cities.

Saturday will be cooler, with a chance of thunderstorms, although the southeast may still reach about 32°. Sunday will peak at 24°, and next week will be cooler and wetter, with maximums of 21 to 25° and rain likely from Tuesday.

The weekend rain will do little for the drought. Weeronline says short showers run off ground that is baked too hard to absorb water.

World.title: Illegal gambling ads on Meta target vulnerable gamblers: BNR
World.content:
Unlicensed gambling sites are running adverts on Facebook and Instagram that target vulnerable people who have signed themselves onto the national register barring them from gambling, an investigation by radio station BNR has found.

More than 100,000 people in the Netherlands have registered with Cruks, the self-exclusion scheme set up when online gambling was legalised, which requires every licensed casino, arcade and betting site to turn them away.

BNR found that searching Facebook for terms such as “Cruks”, geen Cruks or zonder Cruks (without Cruks) – surfaces a stream of adverts from casinos that hold no Dutch licence, promising large bonuses and offering routes around the register.

The adverts follow a consistent pattern, BNR reported: they suggest Cruks is restricting the user, then point them towards unlicensed alternatives. One features an AI-generated woman who tells viewers that international casinos do not consult the Dutch register and invites them to play the same day.

The accounts placing them carry names such as Betrouwbare Spelsites (reliable gaming sites). Users who encounter the adverts on Facebook go on to see them on Instagram and Threads.

Addiction specialists told BNR they were concerned that people registered with Cruks were being singled out, because seeing gambling adverts can trigger strong urges in addicts.

Meta removed adverts

Meta pulled a large number of the adverts from its public ad library after BNR put questions to the company, and the accounts that were identified were taken offline.

In a written response, Meta said it takes enforcement seriously and that advertisers must comply with the law. It declined to tell BNR what it earns from the adverts.

An estimate published in May by two gambling industry bodies KVA and VNLOK put Meta’s annual revenue from illegal gambling adverts aimed at the Netherlands at between €7.3 million and €13.6 million.

The figure is modelled from publicly available advertising data rather than confirmed by Meta, and the report states that it is not suggesting Meta knowingly allows the adverts.

VNLOK took Meta to court in June in an attempt to force it to act faster, and complained to the European Commission that the company is not meeting its obligations under the EU’s Digital Services Act.

The cabinet set out plans in June for a complete ban on online gambling advertising and bonuses. Junior justice minister Claudia van Bruggen has said the rise in gambling addiction, particularly among young people, is deeply worrying.

If you are concerned about your own or someone else’s gambling, OpenOverGokken, the national gambling helpline run by regulator the Kansspelautoriteit, can be reached free on 0800 24 000 22, day or night.

World.title: Man admits bomb attack on D66 office, calls it protest
World.content:
The man who set off a firework bomb at the D66 headquarters in The Hague in May has admitted the attack, telling a court it was a protest against Dutch asylum policy and what he called the dismantling of the country.

The 37-year-old, identified as Berry van D., appeared at a preliminary hearing at The Hague district court on Thursday. He is accused of causing an explosion with terrorist intent.

About 30 people, most of them members of the party’s youth wing, were inside the building when the firework bomb went off shortly after 9pm. No one was hurt.

Van D. said he had not known anyone was there because he had seen no lights on and that he never intended to hurt anyone.

Prosecutors said he acted alone and told the court he had a political message and wanted to silence people who think differently, ANP reported.

Van D. was arrested about an hour after the blast in the Grote Marktstraat, the city’s main shopping street, carrying two knives. NOS reported that he has a previous conviction for setting fire to city buses in Tilburg, where he had worked as a driver.

He told the court he had turned to violence because voting and peaceful demonstration had achieved nothing.

Psychiatric assessment

Thursday’s hearing was procedural and no trial date has been set yet. Van D. will be transferred to a forensic psychiatric clinic to assess whether he can be held responsible for his actions.

NOS reported that Van D. presents himself on social media as a supporter of the anti-immigration PVV, and described D66 leader Rob Jetten being sworn in as prime minister in February as a black day for the country.

The office on the Lange Houtstraat was also attacked in September last year, when rioters from an anti-immigration demonstration smashed its windows.
