World.title: Hungary unveils huge EUR 3 billion housing plan as new government takes aim at controversial mega-projects
World.content:
The Wekerle Sándor programme could deliver affordable rental homes and student accommodation, while the government also moves to revisit the M6 motorway deal and several controversial investments

Hungary could launch a multi-billion-euro rental housing programme by the end of the year, with the Wekerle Sándor Housing Construction Programme potentially reaching a value of up to EUR 3 billion, partly financed through EU funds, Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy said at Friday’s government briefing.

The government has not yet approved the programme’s detailed framework. For now, it is drawing up a list of tasks and the legislative changes needed to implement the scheme.

Vitézy said the Hungarian property market had slowed significantly and argued that the government needed to stimulate new housing construction. The planned programme would focus on affordable rental homes and additional student accommodation, with developments primarily targeted at brownfield and underused urban areas with good public transport connections.

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy speaking at 14 August’s government briefing. Photo: MTI

Former Fudan University site could become housing development

One of the locations being considered is the Budapest site originally earmarked for the planned Fudan University campus. According to Vitézy, the government wants to prioritise brownfield sites and underused urban areas in Budapest and other major Hungarian cities. Choosing locations with existing public transport connections would make it possible to develop new housing without creating entirely new transport infrastructure.

The minister said the detailed development of the Wekerle Sándor programme could get under way by the end of December, with the overall programme potentially worth as much as EUR 3 billion.

Vitézy also criticised the housing policy of previous governments, arguing that the emphasis had been placed on helping people purchase their own homes rather than developing a sizeable rental housing sector. He said this had contributed to difficulties with social mobility, as people could become tied to the location where they own property.

Government to retender controversial M6 motorway project

The government is also planning to retender a major project connected to the M6 motorway, after Vitézy raised questions about the price and legality of a previous decision. The minister said that a section of the M6 between Dunaújváros and Érd had been awarded to MKIF, a motorway concession company linked to businessmen Lőrinc Mészáros and László Szíjj.

According to Vitézy, competing bidders were prepared to carry out the work for approximately HUF 50 billion, while MKIF quoted HUF 149 billion for the same work and services. The minister described this as a threefold overpricing and said the government would now put the project out to tender again, with the cheapest bid to be selected.

Vitézy also claimed that the original order had been unlawful because, in his view, the decision should have been made by then-Economic Minister Márton Nagy rather than by former Construction and Transport Minister János Lázár.

The ministry will file a criminal complaint in connection with the M6 case, Vitézy said. He also argued that the entire motorway concession system should be reviewed. The minister further criticised additional costs paid to the concession company, which he said had been requested on the grounds of the war in Ukraine.

Vanda Szondi government spokesperson. Photo: MTI

Tougher environmental rules for battery factories

The government is also preparing changes affecting battery factories operating under special investment status. According to Vitézy, the government will review which battery plants have been granted priority status and will amend the relevant decrees.

If a factory violates environmental or nature conservation regulations, its special status could be suspended for at least six months. If the violation is not remedied, the suspension could remain in place for longer. Vitézy stressed that the aim was not to prevent battery factories from operating, but to ensure that companies comply with Hungary’s environmental regulations.

Several controversial projects lose priority status

The government has also decided to withdraw national economic priority status from a number of projects that have attracted controversy in recent years. The projects include:

a brownfield development on the site of the former brickworks in Törökbálint;

redevelopment of the former Lang factory site in Budapest’s 13th district;

the Club Aliga development in Balatonvilágos;

the planned Tihany Castle Hotel and Training Centre;

the Fiatalokért Központ project in Sukoró;

the National Tennis Competition Centre on Margaret Island;

a logistics and general economic property development in Soroksár and Gyál;

the Pázmány Campus development; and

the planned National Circus Arts Centre near Nyugati railway station.

The withdrawal of priority status means these projects will no longer benefit from the special framework previously granted to them.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

New national transport bodies established

Another major change concerns Hungary’s public transport system. The National Transport Organiser and the Train Fleet company were established at the beginning of August following legislation adopted by the Tisza-majority parliament.

The National Transport Organiser is intended to perform functions similar to those of Budapest’s BKK, but on a national level. The Train Fleet company, meanwhile, could play a key role in planned rolling-stock purchases.

In particular, the new structure is expected to facilitate the planned procurement of new HÉV suburban trains and InterCity trains, for which the government intends to make use of around EUR 1.8 billion in EU funding.

The announcements form part of a broader overhaul of Hungary’s investment, housing and transport policies under the new government, with several large-scale projects inherited from the previous administration now being reviewed or reconsidered.

World.title: PM Magyar: Hungary begins sinking two huge barges to raise Danube water levels near Paks
World.content:
Hungary is set to begin the controlled sinking of two 80-metre-long barges near Paks on Friday afternoon in an extraordinary effort to raise water levels in the Danube and help safeguard the operation of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced the latest stage of the emergency construction project in a video filmed at the site of the Danube’s temporary bottom sill.

According to the prime minister, all of the anchoring piles, drilled eight metres into the riverbed, have now been installed. The two barges will be secured to them using steel cables approximately four centimetres thick before being deliberately sunk.

80-metre barges to be lowered into the Danube

The controlled sinking of the two vessels was expected to begin at around 3 PM on Friday, according to Magyar. The operation forms part of a major project designed to increase the Danube’s water level near Paks amid prolonged drought and exceptionally low river levels.

Work is continuing around the clock, involving the Hungarian Defence Forces, industrial divers, water management specialists, contractors and staff from the National Defence Authority. The scale and complexity of the construction work has been described by Magyar as unprecedented in Hungary in recent decades.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Government invites opposition leaders to Paks

Magyar has invited the leaders of Hungary’s parliamentary parties to Paks at 10 AM on Saturday. The prime minister said he wanted to show them the construction site and explain why the government had been forced to undertake such a complex and large-scale project.

He also intends to discuss what he described as failures over the past decade that contributed to the current situation.

However, the leaders of Fidesz and Mi Hazánk declined the invitation, citing holidays and other reasons.

If you missed it: Government press conference: Paks nuclear power plant faces shutdown risk

Magyar attacks Orbán over absence

The prime minister sharply criticised former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán for declining to attend. Magyar accused Orbán of remaining silent despite the prolonged drought, low Danube water levels and Hungary’s energy situation.

He argued that the current circumstances required national cooperation regardless of political differences, and said Orbán should have visited Paks to see the work being carried out and hear about the government’s efforts to stabilise the country’s energy supply.

Magyar also suggested that Orbán could have brought contributions from business figures to help with the project. The prime minister concluded by thanking everyone involved in the emergency construction effort, saying that around 145,000 cubic metres of rock will ultimately be used for the temporary and permanent structures.

World.title: Orbán fails to block return of billions in state assets as Hungary’s top court rejects Fidesz
World.content:
Hungary’s Constitutional Court has rejected a petition submitted by Fidesz challenging the constitutional amendment concerning public interest asset management foundations, known as KEKVAs.

The court dismissed the petition without examining its substance, ruling that it did not have the jurisdiction to review the challenged constitutional provision. The decision concerns the 16th amendment to Hungary’s Fundamental Law, adopted under the new Tisza government,

which abolished the public interest asset management foundations into which the previous Orbán government had transferred thousands of billions of forints in state assets.

Constitutional Court says it lacks jurisdiction

According to the Constitutional Court’s decision, the full bench rejected the Fidesz petition because the court lacks the necessary jurisdiction to carry out a substantive review of constitutional amendments. The issue stems from the Fourth Amendment to Hungary’s Fundamental Law in 2013, when

the Fidesz-led parliamentary majority removed the Constitutional Court’s power to conduct substantive constitutional reviews of amendments to the Fundamental Law.

Since then, the court has generally been limited to examining whether constitutional amendments were adopted in accordance with the required procedural rules, rather than assessing their substantive constitutional content.

Fidesz had argued in its petition that the disputed provision did not establish a general constitutional institution for the future. Instead, the party claimed that it introduced transitional rules specifically concerning identifiable foundations that were already operating when the amendment entered into force.

The Constitutional Court nevertheless concluded that it could not examine the substance of the challenge.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Two constitutional judges dissent

The decision was not unanimous. Outgoing Constitutional Court President Péter Polt and Constitutional Court Judge Tünde Handó issued separate opinions, arguing that the petition should have been examined on its merits.

Their dissent sets them apart from the majority of the court, which considered itself unable to rule substantively on the constitutional amendment.

The decision is particularly significant given the political and financial importance of the KEKVAs. Under the previous government, substantial amounts of public assets were transferred to such foundations, including assets connected to Hungarian universities and other public interest institutions.

Separate decision on Sulyok still pending

The Constitutional Court has also been asked to consider another politically significant constitutional amendment. According to 24.hu, the court has not yet ruled on the challenge seeking to annul the constitutional amendment that ended President Tamás Sulyok’s mandate. A decision on that case has been postponed.

World.title: Croatia wildfire forces at least 58 Hungarians to evacuate: foreign minister monitors the situation – UPDATE: 4 injured
World.content:
At least 58 Hungarian citizens have been evacuated from areas affected by the devastating wildfire on Croatia’s Dalmatian coast, Hungary’s Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said on Friday.

Around 45 of those evacuated were accommodated in a sports hall, while another 13 were taken to a separate location. Croatian authorities and the Red Cross are providing them with assistance. The wildfire broke out near Omiš on Thursday evening and spread rapidly through dry vegetation and pine forest before reaching residential areas.

One Hungarian tourist injured

According to the Foreign Ministry, one Hungarian citizen was taken to a hospital in Split with a minor limb injury. No other Hungarian injuries are currently known. The Hungarian consular service remains in contact with the hospital and is monitoring the situation in case additional Hungarian citizens require medical assistance.

Hungarian consular officials spent the entire night responding to calls from citizens in the affected area and contacting people registered for consular protection. The exact number of Hungarians seeking consular assistance is not yet known, as officials are still contacting affected citizens individually to establish what help they require.

The ministry’s 24-hour consular emergency number is +36 80 36 80 36.

Seven Hungarians escaped on foot

The requests for assistance have mainly concerned evacuation, accommodation, safe onward travel and personal belongings or vehicles left behind.

Two Hungarian families, consisting of seven people in total, reportedly had to escape the affected area on foot. Their vehicles may have been destroyed by the fire, according to the Foreign Ministry.

Two Hungarian police officers currently serving in Zadar are also assisting with the consular response. Following consultations with Hungary’s Interior Ministry, they have been asked to remain in the area and continue supporting the operation. Their accommodation is being provided by Hungary’s embassy in Zagreb.

More information on the wildfire: Hungarian tourists flee as huge wildfire engulfs Croatian coast near Omiš

Minibuses sent from Hungary

Two minibuses have been sent from Hungary to collect the 13 Hungarian citizens evacuated to the second location. The Hungarian embassy in Zagreb and the Consular Service are currently contacting all known Hungarian citizens affected by the fire, assessing their individual needs and coordinating with Croatian authorities.

Where necessary, Hungarian officials will also help organise onward travel, accommodation and other consular assistance.

Fire contained, but firefighting continues

According to Anita Orbán, Croatian authorities have managed to prevent the fire from spreading further, although firefighting operations are continuing with the assistance of specialised aircraft. No further evacuations are currently known to have taken place.

The wildfire near Omiš forced around 1,000 residents and tourists to flee the affected area. At least 36 people were injured, seven of them in life-threatening condition.

The fire spread to residential areas overnight amid strong winds, causing significant disruption along the popular Dalmatian coast. Hungarians still in the affected region are advised to follow instructions from Croatian authorities and contact the Hungarian Consular Service if they require assistance.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

UPDATE: 4 injured

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs received reports that four Hungarian citizens were injured in connection with the forest fire in Croatia, according to a post on Facebook. Two Hungarians are currently in the hospital and are expected to be discharged today. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs took immediate action to provide assistance to the injured Hungarians.

World.title: Hungary’s new president Baka already more popular than predecessor Sulyok ever was, poll finds
World.content:
Hungary’s newly elected President András Baka has already achieved a level of public support that his predecessor, Tamás Sulyok, never managed to reach, according to a new poll commissioned by Telex.

The survey, commissioned by Telex and conducted by the 21 Research Centre on 11 and 12 August – the day Baka was elected and the following day – examined how well Hungarians knew the new president and whether they considered him suitable for the position.

The findings suggest that although Baka was largely unknown to the public before his nomination, he quickly won substantial support, particularly among voters of the governing Tisza Party.

Most Hungarians have heard of Baka

Some 84% of respondents had heard about Baka’s nomination as president. However, only 57% felt sufficiently familiar with him to say whether they considered him suitable for the role. Among those who expressed an opinion, 72% said Baka was suitable for the presidency, while 28% disagreed.

Across the entire sample, 41% considered him suitable for the post, compared with 16% who said he was unsuitable. The remaining respondents either did not know enough about him or declined to answer.

Baka’s initial level of recognition is difficult to compare directly with previous presidents because of the unusual circumstances surrounding his nomination. His name only became widely known after Prime Minister Péter Magyar posted a photograph of himself with Baka and Tisza politician Ruff Bálint on 5 August.

Before that, relatively few voters were likely to have remembered Baka as the former head of Hungary’s Supreme Court, a position from which he was removed in 2011.

András Baka. Photo: MTI

Baka starts with stronger ratings than Sulyok

Despite his relatively low public profile, Baka appears to be starting his presidency from a considerably stronger position than Sulyok ever enjoyed.

The 21 Research Centre’s earlier research found that Sulyok’s popularity remained relatively low throughout his presidency. By contrast, Baka has already attracted a significantly higher level of support just days after becoming president.

That does not necessarily put him among Hungary’s most popular political figures, however. Former presidents János Áder and Katalin Novák both reached much higher levels of popularity at their peaks. Still, Baka has already surpassed Sulyok’s highest recorded level of popularity, according to the polling data.

Tisza voters overwhelmingly back the new president

Baka’s support is strongly connected to current party preferences. Among Tisza voters, 69% consider him suitable for the presidency, while just 1% believe he is unsuitable. By comparison, only 8% of Fidesz voters consider Baka suitable, while 47% consider him unsuitable.

Among voters of other parties and those without a party preference, 20% consider him suitable and 17% unsuitable. A much larger 63% in this group either do not know enough about him or did not express an opinion.

The figures suggest that Baka has managed to attract some sympathy outside the Tisza camp, despite being nominated by the party at a particularly politically polarised moment.

At the same time, the researchers caution that Tisza voters were much more likely to have heard about Baka’s nomination and therefore much more likely to form an opinion about him. A large proportion of those who remain uninformed are Fidesz, Mi Hazánk or unaffiliated voters, meaning winning over these groups could prove considerably more difficult.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Is Baka independent or close to Tisza?

The poll also asked respondents how they viewed Baka politically. Some 37% considered him independent, while 15% believed he was close to Tisza. Another 47% could not decide, while just 1% considered him a Fidesz politician.

There is a clear link between perceptions of Baka’s independence and his perceived suitability for the presidency. Among those who consider Baka suitable, 88% see him as independent, while only 7% regard him as a Tisza-aligned figure.

Among those who consider him unsuitable, the picture is almost reversed: 76% believe he is close to Tisza, while just 9% consider him independent.

Have you read this? New President Baka could stand up firmly to PM Magyar – so why is the opposition attacking him so viciously?

Baka also tops the list of preferred presidential candidates

Respondents were also asked to name, without being given a list, the person they considered most suitable for the presidency. The question produced highly fragmented results, with 62% unable to name anyone. Among those who did provide a name, however, Baka came out on top, with 14% mentioning him. Sulyok was named by just 5%.

Other names receiving one or two percent of mentions included chess grandmaster Judit Polgár, Péter Márki-Zay, Ákos Hadházy, Viktor Orbán, Mi Hazánk’s presidential nominee Máté Tóth, Katalin Novák, historian Ignác Romsics, former justice minister Péter Bárándy, Ágnes Forsthoffer and András Schiffer.

Fidesz voters were more likely to mention Sulyok, Orbán, Schiffer and former justice minister Judit Varga, although they were generally less likely to name anyone than Tisza voters.

The fact that Sulyok received just 5% of spontaneous mentions is also notable. According to the analysis, this suggests that even among Fidesz voters, relatively few appear to have a strong personal attachment to the outgoing president. Much of their opposition to his removal may therefore be connected to the procedure itself rather than support for Sulyok personally.

World.title: Hungarian tourists flee as huge wildfire engulfs Croatian coast near Omiš
World.content:
A major wildfire has swept through the Croatian Dalmatian coast near Omiš, forcing around 1,000 residents and tourists to evacuate overnight – including Hungarian holidaymakers.

The blaze broke out on Thursday evening near Lokva Rogoznica, south of Omiš, and rapidly spread through dry vegetation and pine forest amid strong and changing winds. The flames reached residential areas and parts of Omiš, destroying homes, cars and other property.

The situation was described by Croatia’s national fire chief as one of the most serious wildfires in the country’s history.

Dozens injured as flames approach Omiš

The fire started at around 8.20 PM on Thursday near the main coastal road. Strong winds quickly pushed the flames through the dry vegetation and forest, eventually bringing the fire into the Omiš area.

According to the latest information from Split hospital, 36 people required medical treatment, with 14 remaining in hospital. Seven of those injured were in life-threatening condition, while most of the casualties suffered burns or smoke inhalation.

The fire also caused significant damage to property as flames reached residential buildings and vehicles.

The rapidly changing wind has made the firefighters’ work particularly difficult, with the flames spreading in different directions. Some parts of Omiš were also left without electricity overnight.

Požar koji je počeo u Lokvi Rogoznici stigao je u noći do Omiša a u ranim jutarnjim satima očekuje se dolazak kanadera. pic.twitter.com/bWSy4Opzgb — HINA (@Agencija_HINA) August 14, 2026

Nearly 300 firefighters battle the blaze

By Friday morning, 286 firefighters and 93 vehicles were involved in the firefighting operation. Crews were sent from several Croatian counties and Zagreb to reinforce local teams.

Four Canadair CL-415 firefighting aircraft were also deployed in the early hours of Friday, while a Croatian Navy vessel was placed on standby in case a sea evacuation became necessary.

Emergency accommodation centres were opened in Omiš, Dugi Rat, Makarska and Split. Around 1,000 people spent the night at the sports hall in Omiš, while people from the most endangered areas were evacuated both by road and by boat.

The main coastal road, the Jadranska Magistrala, was closed on the affected section, as was part of the Omiš bypass towards Makarska. The evacuations and road closures caused major traffic congestion in the town.

Hungarian tourists among those forced to flee

The wildfire has also affected Hungarian holidaymakers staying in the area. Hungary’s Foreign Ministry said that Hungarian nationals known to the consular service and those who had contacted the service were currently safe. Hungarian officials reportedly liaised directly with Croatian authorities overnight to help Hungarian citizens leave the affected areas safely.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said the situation was being monitored continuously and that the Hungarian consular service remained in contact with affected Hungarian citizens and local authorities.

Hungarians currently in the area are being urged to follow instructions from Croatian authorities and contact the Hungarian Consular Service immediately if necessary.

The ministry’s 24-hour consular emergency number is +36 80 36 80 36.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Fire continues to threaten the area

The blaze has been particularly difficult to contain because of the strong, shifting winds and extremely dry conditions. Reuters also reported that the fire forced hundreds to evacuate and that emergency services provided shelter for around 1,000 people.

Authorities continue to work to prevent the flames from spreading further around Omiš and the surrounding settlements. For tourists still in the region, the authorities’ evacuation instructions should be followed without delay, particularly as the direction and intensity of the fire can change rapidly.

World.title: Warning at Lake Balaton: Experts urge swimmers to take precautions
World.content:
Algae levels in Lake Balaton have continued to rise, with the highest concentration recorded in the Keszthely Basin. Experts are now urging swimmers in the area to take extra precautions and shower after bathing due to the growing dominance of filamentous cyanobacteria.

According to the latest measurements by the HUN-REN Balaton Limnological Research Institute, the increase in algal biomass that began in the second half of July has continued in recent weeks. However, significant differences remain between the various parts of the lake.

Algae levels highest in the Keszthely Basin

Measurements taken on 10 August 2026 found the highest a-chlorophyll concentration in the Keszthely Basin, at 80 micrograms per litre (µg/l), according to the institute.

The Szigliget Basin followed with 54 µg/l, while 32 µg/l was measured in the Szemes Basin. The water was considerably clearer in the Siófok Basin, with concentrations of 19 µg/l recorded near Tihany and 21 µg/l near Balatonfűzfő.

This means a clear west-to-east gradient in algal biomass continues to be visible along the lake. The pattern was also confirmed by the latest Sentinel-2 satellite imagery taken on 9 August.

Filamentous cyanobacteria are taking over

Researchers have also observed a significant change in the composition of the lake’s algal community.

The algae previously found in large quantities have declined considerably, while filamentous cyanobacteria have become dominant across the entire length of Lake Balaton.

One species in particular, Raphidiopsis raciborskii, has become widespread. The species is characteristic of late-summer conditions and is capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen. Researchers have also noted the presence of Planktothrix, which cannot fix atmospheric nitrogen.

Despite the increased algal biomass, the situation may not look alarming to people on the beaches. Unlike earlier in the summer, the algae are not currently accumulating in large visible patches in sheltered areas. Instead, they are mostly distributed evenly throughout the water column.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Experts advise swimmers to shower after bathing

Although there is currently no visible mass accumulation of algae, researchers are urging people swimming in the Keszthely Basin to take precautions.

Experts recommend showering after every swim in the Keszthely Basin.

Researchers stress that monitoring will remain particularly important for the rest of the summer, as a considerable part of the bathing season is still ahead.

It’s important to note that the latest findings do not mean that Lake Balaton’s beaches are unsafe across the board. However, the rising algal biomass and growing dominance of filamentous cyanobacteria mean that swimmers in the most affected areas should pay particular attention to the latest guidance from researchers.

World.title: Romanian executive to submit fifth payment request under Recovery and Resilience Facility
World.content:
The Romanian government is set to submit the fifth payment request under the EU-backed Recovery and Resilience Facility, or PNRR, according to an announcement from European Investments and Projects minister Dragoș Pîslaru.

Payment no. 5 is worth EUR 2.84 billion, and is the penultimate request that Romania will submit within the PNRR. Once approved, the fifth payment will bring Romania’s absorption rate of PNRR-related grants to 78%, from 66% currently.

“One final request remains, request no. 6, worth EUR 2.58 billion in grants and EUR 1.76 billion in loans. From a total of EUR 13.57 billion allocated at the time the PNRR was signed, we will reach EUR 10.56 billion after request no. 5,” Pîslaru said during a press conference.

Initially, the European Commission planned for a single final payment request, reuniting the now separated requests no. 5 and 6, the minister noted.

The final payment request will be submitted at the end of September, and with it “we could reach 97.2% of the PNRR,” he said, referring to the grants component.

“47% was the percentage of the PNRR when I came to the ministry, after four years since the program was launched. The annual average was about 10.4% of the PNRR. In one year and two months, under the Bolojan government, we added 31% of the PNRR,” the minister also said.

Romania’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan is financed through EUR 21.41 billion under the EU mechanism, including EUR 13.57 billion in grants and EUR 7.84 billion in loans. The fourth payment request, worth EUR 2.62 billion, was approved by the European Commission in May of this year.

(Photo source: gov.ro)

World.title: Drone crashes in Romania’s Tulcea County
World.content:
A drone crashed on Friday, August 14, in the area of Luncaviţa, a locality in eastern Romania’s Tulcea County, about five kilometers from the border with Ukraine, the Defense Ministry (MApN) announced.

The drone crashed in a wooded area and caused no casualties, according to preliminary information provided by MApN.

The drone was not detected by MApN’s radar surveillance systems as it was flying at a very low altitude, the ministry said.

The crash resulted in an explosion followed by a fire, which has been extinguished, the Emergency Situations Inspectorate of Tulcea announced.

A MApN team, using an IAR 330 PUMA SOCAT helicopter, will investigate the area.

A day earlier, drone remains were discovered in the sea, close to Romania’s Costinești beach, on the Black Sea shore. Five drones were tracked nearing Romanian territory on the night of Wednesday, August 12, to Thursday, August 13, around 1 AM. One drone briefly entered Romanian airspace in Tulcea County but then exited and headed to Ukraine. Another drone was detected in Romanian airspace around 9 AM. Earlier this week, two Gerbera-type drones were destroyed by divers of the Romanian Army in the exclusive economic zone, approximately 165 kilometers from Constanța, in the Neptun Deep exploitation area.

At the end of the August 14 government meeting, prime minister Ilie Bolojan said the country’s military was doing “everything in their power to combat the drones.”

“We have a reality that we cannot deny, namely that the war resulting from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is having an impact, including along our borders, and we can expect drone debris, drones reaching the river areas along Romania’s border, in the vicinity of ports, to stray into Romania,” the PM said.

“It is regrettable that we are facing such situations, but given what has happened in recent months, we are beginning to see that this is becoming something of a constant; it is not just in Romania, we have seen what has happened in other areas as well. It is becoming clear that equipping our Armed Forces as quickly as possible with counter-drone systems is a necessity,” he added.

(Photo: Trentinness/ Dreamstime)

World.title: Romanian telco Digi reports 10% higher revenues in Q2 2026
World.content:
Romanian telecommunications company Digi (BVB: DIGI) reported consolidated revenues of EUR 608 million in the second quarter of 2026, representing an 11% YoY increase.

Adjusted EBITDA (ex. operating leases) for Q2 2026 increased by 23% compared to the result from Q2 2025, reaching EUR 169 million. Consequently, in the first semester of 2026, the group recorded consolidated revenues of EUR 1.2 billion, a 10% increase versus 6M 2025, and adjusted EBITDA of EUR 398 million, up 17% YoY.

“Spain continues to be our primary growth engine, maintaining strong commercial momentum and progressing in line with our long-term plans, while Romania continued to perform well,” said Serghei Bulgac, CEO of Digi Communications.

Last month, Digi successfully completed an initial public offering for its Spanish subsidiary. The Spanish IPO was multiple times oversubscribed, showing investor appetite for the company’s shares.

In Q2 2026, Digi reached 33.9 million revenue-generating user agreements (RGUs) across Romania, Spain, Portugal and Italy, a 14% increase compared to Q2 2025.

The mobile segment stands out for generating the most RGUs within the group’s array of services, accounting for 51% of the overall clients across the four markets. In Q2 2026, the mobile segment saw its RGUs climb to 17.3 million, a 19% YoY increase, covering mobile telephony clients across Romania, Spain, Portugal and Italy.

In Romania, the mobile service segment remained the largest, reaching 8.4 million RGUs as of the end of Q2 2026, a positive evolution of 20% compared to Q2 2025. Broadband services registered an increase of 4% in Q2 2026, compared to Q2 2025, up to 5.2 million RGUs, while the segment of Pay-TV services (cable and satellite) increased by 2% YoY, up to 6.1 million RGUs. Together with fixed-line telephony, the total number of RGUs in the Romanian market amounted to 20.5 million customers as of Q2 2026, a 9% increase versus Q2 2025.

Spanish operations continued the strong performance in Q2 2026, with the number of users of fixed services, internet, and mobile telephony increasing by 23% compared to Q2 2025, to 11.9 million RGUs. Mobile users increased by 19% to 7.8 million RGUs, while broadband users increased by 28% to 2.9 million.

In Portugal, the number of RGUs amounted to 960k, up 22% YoY, of which 545k were mobile, and 186k were broadband users.

In Italy, mobile users increased by 4,5% YoY, reaching 535k RGUs as of the end of Q2 2026.

In the United Kingdom, Digi launched its fiber broadband services and continued expanding its network footprint during the second quarter of 2026, while onboarding its first customers.

World.title: Romania’s Presidential Administration to host summit on animal welfare
World.content:
The Presidential Administration will host the second edition of Animal Summit Romania on September 29 - 30, Diana Pungă, a state adviser for relations with civil society at the institution, announced on Friday, August 14.

The event, organized by the non-profit Sache Vet Association and Bucharest’s Animal Protection Administration ASPA, will take place at Cotroceni Palace.

Over two days, it will gather public administration representatives, veterinarians, legal and education specialists, non-governmental organizations and other experts to discuss animal protection and welfare and solutions to challenges in the field.

“Romania continues to face major challenges in the field of animal protection. Beyond the issue of abandonment and the lack of education about responsible pet ownership, civil society frequently raises concerns about the non-transparent operation of some private shelters, suspected abusive euthanasia practices and difficulties in uniformly enforcing existing legislation. In many communities, volunteers, NGOs and active citizens end up compensating for the lack of coherent institutional mechanisms by becoming directly involved in animal rescue, shelter monitoring and the promotion of responsible sterilization and adoption,” an announcement from the organizers reads.

All of these aspects point to an urgent need for clear standards and consistently implemented public policies protecting both the communities and the animals, the organizers said.

World.title: Central Romania: EBRD extends EUR 120 mln loan for PV plant, battery system near Brașov
World.content:
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced on Friday, August 14, that it has extended a financing package of up to EUR 120 million for the development, construction, and operation of Econergy’s Părău 2 project in Romania.

The project includes a 342 MW solar photovoltaic plant and a 150 MW/300 MWh battery storage system in Brașov, according to a statement by the lender.

The financing consists of an EBRD A loan of up to EUR 57 million and an EBRD B loan of up to EUR 63 million, which includes a EUR 3.6 million debt service guarantee provided by commercial banks Privredna banka Zagreb and NLB.

According to the EBRD, the Părău 2 project will increase renewable energy production, help improve grid flexibility, and strengthen Romania’s energy security.

The project is co-financed by BSTDB (the Black Sea Trade and Development Bank), OTP Bank, and Exim Banca Românească, as part of a debt financing package of up to EUR 229 million.

“By financing one of the country’s pioneering solar and battery storage investments, the EBRD is helping to increase the generation of renewable energy, strengthen energy security and support a more resilient and flexible electricity system. The support of the European Union through InvestEU demonstrates how public and private partners can work together to mobilize financing for the green transition,” said Georgios Gkiaouris, the EBRD’s Head of Energy Europe.

The project is backed by Romania’s Contract for Difference scheme, which was developed with EBRD technical assistance and aims to unlock 5 GW of solar and onshore wind capacity. The solar plant has secured a 125 MWac allocation in the first auction at a strike price of EUR 49.4/MWh for 15 years, while the remaining capacity will operate on a merchant basis.

The European Union supported the EBRD A/B loan through a first-loss portfolio guarantee provided by the InvestEU programme, which covers up to EUR 115 million and helps mitigate the risks associated with the project’s substantial exposure to merchant revenue.

World.title: Romanian consumer goods distributor AQUILA reports slightly higher revenues amid challenging context
World.content:
AQUILA, one of the largest players in the fast-moving consumer goods distribution sector from Romania and the region, reported revenues of RON 1.6 billion in the first half of 2026, amid an economic environment marked by declining consumption, according to a report submitted to the local stock exchange.

The figure represents a 6.4% increase compared to the same period last year.

Revenue from the distribution segment increased by 6% in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025, driven by the organic growth of this business line. The main contributor to this performance was the traditional retail channel, which grew by 22%, followed by the HoReCa channel with 7% growth, and the gas station channel with 1%, evolutions that offset the 19% decline recorded in the organized retail channel.

Revenue from the logistics segment increased by 6%, driven by higher operating volumes and the expansion of logistics activities across multiple temperature categories, particularly in the frozen products segment. Revenue from the transport segment increased by 13%.

The company's own brands continued to strengthen their contribution to the group’s performance, with revenues of RON 78.5 million in the first half of 2026, up 23% compared to the same period in 2025.

The results for the first half of the year were affected by a more challenging operating environment, marked by weaker consumer spending in Romania, an approximately 30% increase in fuel costs, and unfavorable foreign exchange movements, as well as by the temporary impact of the group’s market share expansion strategy and continued investments in the development of our operating platform.

In this context, EBITDA amounted to approximately RON 61 million, down 33% compared to the same period in 2025, while the net result was negative, at approximately RON 21 million.

During the first six months of the year, the group invested EUR 3 million in the development of its logistics infrastructure, process digitalization, operations automation, and equipment modernization, in line with its growth strategy and commitment to improving operational efficiency.

“Our distribution segment continued to deliver growth, supported by the expansion of the traditional retail and HoReCa channels, the consolidated contribution of our own brands, and the commercial synergies generated through the integration of the acquired companies. At the same time, we chose to prioritize strengthening commercial relationships and increasing market share, which play an essential role in supporting long-term growth and value creation,” said Cătălin Vasile, CEO of AQUILA.

The company head noted that the strategy had a temporary impact on commercial margins and profitability but created “a foundation for capitalizing on the investments made and supporting sustainable performance in the period ahead.”

World.title: Raiffeisen Bank Romania issues a new series of bonds denominated in RON
World.content:
Raiffeisen Bank, one of the largest banks in Romania, issued on August 13, 2026, a senior preferred eligible bond issue maturing in 2033, with a total value of RON 750 million.

The tranche represents the bank’s 0th series of eligible bonds, the financial institution informs through a statement sent to Economica.net.

The bond issue was addressed to institutional investors and was placed at a fixed coupon of 7.538% for the first five years, respectively 0.85% above the yield of the benchmark Romanian government bonds denominated in lei.

The bonds received a Baa1 rating from the rating agency Moody’s, two notches above Romania’s sovereign rating (Baa3).

After obtaining approval from the National Bank of Romania, the bonds are set to be included in the bank’s own funds and eligible liabilities base and listed on the Luxembourg and Bucharest stock exchanges.

In Romania, Raiffeisen Bank serves approximately 2.4 million individual and corporate customers. The bank has been active in Romania for more than 25 years.

World.title: Central Romania: Winners Holding Investments, Finas Group commission 100 MWh energy storage battery after EUR 25 million investment

Cluj-based companies Winners Holding Investments and Finas Group have commissioned the second energy storage battery in their joint portfolio, with a capacity of 100 MWh, following an investment of more than EUR 25 million.

The project, located in Glodeni, in Mureș County, comes several months after the companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding with China’s equipment producer Sieyuan Electric Co., Ltd., the companies said.

World.title: Albania Ruling Party Documents Highlight Country’s Ageing Demographic
World.content:
Documents produced by governing Socialist Party experts for a reform of the country’s municipal set-up, seen by BIRN, reveal an ageing population that could have adverse economic consequences for Albania.

The “Administrative-Territorial Reform 2.0” documents, prepared by experts on a special parliamentary committee, also show how emigration and internal migration have emptied out small towns and rural areas while concentrating the population in a few urban centres.

At one end are several urban centres where both population and economic activity are increasingly concentrated. At the other end are peripheral areas, particularly in the northeast, southeast and mountainous regions, which are caught in a vicious cycle of population decline and subsistence economies, with few formal jobs.

In these areas, municipal budgets survive largely on central government transfers, with funds often used mainly to cover the salaries of local administration staff.

The Urban Mass Index, UMI, one of three analytical documents underpinning the proposed new map of 46 municipalities – which would merge 15 local government units with larger municipalities – documents the territorial transformation of Albania since the 1990s, with a few centres continuing to grow as an increasing number of municipalities lose residents.

The “dependency ratio” in the index, which measures the burden that children and elderly people place on the working-age population, shows that in 51 municipalities out of 61 in total, this burden is higher than the national average. In many of them, the number of elderly residents exceeds the number of children.

The data highlights an Albania divided into three distinct realities: a small group of municipalities that continue to attract population and economic activity; a group of municipalities with intermediate potential; and a majority of the country’s territory, which is losing the critical mass of population needed to sustain local economies and public services.

The analysis is based on data from the 2023 census and, as part of the technical report accompanying the reform proposal, suggests that Albania is experiencing a growing concentration of its population in an ever-smaller number of urban centres, while the rest of the country is losing residents, functions and development capacity.

The index results show that only 13 municipalities are classified as having a high level of urban mass and are home to 62.5 per cent of the population.

By contrast, 30 municipalities – covering almost half of the country’s administrative map – are classified as having a low level of urban mass and account for just 14.2 per cent of the population.

Another 18 municipalities fall into the intermediate or medium category.

According to the data, the country’s population is concentrated in the capital, which is home to more than half a million people, followed at a considerable

distance by the municipalities of Durres, Vlora, Elbasan, Shkoder, Fieri, Kamza and Berat.

At the other end of the scale, municipalities such as Pustec, Libohova, Himara, Kelcyra, Memaliaj, Selenica, Dropull, Finiq, Delvina and Kolonja have the smallest populations.

The ruling-party experts did not build the index solely on population size. It also combines other indicators, including population density, the spatial distribution of residents, the demographic dependency ratio and the level of urbanisation.

This means that a municipality may cover a large area, but if its population is concentrated in a small town while the rest of its territory is largely empty, it is considered structurally weak.

One of the most significant findings is that, on average, 57 per cent of Albania’s territory is uninhabited.

The analytical document notes that the country no longer has the same population distribution it had in 2014, when the current administrative-territorial division was introduced with the aim of creating larger and more efficient municipalities.

“Some areas have grown, while others have lost a significant share of their population,” the report says, arguing that some municipalities are struggling to secure sustainable finances, qualified staff and adequate administrative capacity.

The Socialists have submitted a bill to parliament proposing a new administrative-territorial map that would merge several smaller municipalities with larger neighbouring ones – without explaining how the proposed map would address these underlying problems.

The proposal has faced opposition from residents in the affected areas. Some fear mergers will leave them with even more limited access to public services.

World.title: Kosovo Detains Man Suspected of Spying for Serbian Intelligence
World.content:
Fehim Sali, second left, at a court hearing in Pristina on August 14, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Pristina Basic Court on Friday ordered 30 days of detention for a dual Kosovo and Serbia citizen, Fehim Sali, who is suspected of spying for Serbia’s intelligence agency, the BIA.

It is alleged that he passed the BIA information about Kosovo officials, politicians and Islamist radicals, including potential recruitment targets, and received money in return.

Sali, a resident of Kosovo’s southern Dragash/Dragas municipality, was arrested on Thursday at the Merdare border crossing point while entering from Serbia. He appeared before the Basic Court in Pristina on Friday.

“The court’s assessment took into account the circumstances relating to the risk of absconding, the risk of influencing witnesses and evidence, and the risk of repetition or continuation of the criminal offence,” the court said in a statement.

According to the prosecution file, Sali is suspected of “maintaining contact with BIA officers using four different mobile phones”, which were found during raids at his house on Thursday, alongside around 40,000 euros in cash.

The prosecution file alleges that Sali “worked as a recruited agent for Serbia’s Security Information Agency, BIA, in exchange for material benefits”. The file alleges that he acted on the instructions of a senior BIA officer identified as Zelimir Matovic, nicknamed Zeljko.

It alleges that Sali provided the BIA with information about Kosovo’s political situation and helped it identify officials of Kosovo’s own intelligence agency, the AKI. According to the case file, he photographed some of its officials to facilitate their identification.

Sali is also accused of providing information about members of the radical Islamist Wahhabi movement as well as other people whom he allegedly proposed to the BIA officer as potential targets for contact and recruitment.

According to prosecutors, Sali also “mediated matters and documents connected to Serbian state institutions and maintained contacts with people with political and social influence in Serbia and Kosovo, particularly members of non-majority communities”.

The prosecution stated that he provided some of these people with “guidance on political activity, with the aim of gathering and transmitting information of interest to the BIA”.

Prosecutors argue that these activities were carried out against the state interests of Kosovo and endangered its constitutional order and national security.

The prosecution also alleges that the 40,000 euros found and seized during a search of Sali’s home came from his alleged activities on behalf of the BIA.

According to the case file, the evidence against Sali includes his own statement.

Prosecutors claim he described in detail his alleged activities, including how and where he communicated with BIA officials, exchanged information and provided assistance to the Serbian intelligence service.

Prosecutor Bekim Kodraliu told media that Sali admitted having been recruited and maintained regular contact with BIA officials.

“The suspect himself stated that he had been recruited and had ongoing contacts with BIA officials,” Kodraliu said.

The case comes two months after another Kosovo espionage conviction involving Serbia’s intelligence service.

In June, the Pristina Basic Court sentenced a Kosovo Albanian man, Hysri Selimi, a former Islamic State member, to six years in prison for espionage.

Prosecutors said Selimi had provided the BIA with information about religious radicalisation in Kosovo, former members of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, and people who had joined Islamic State.

World.title: Week in Review: Between the Absurd and the Unexpected
World.content:
Kosovo’s governance drama is beginning to border on the absurd. Weeks after the June election results were certified, two months after the elections were held, MPs have yet to elect a parliamentary speaker and deputies and, in doing so, constitute the new parliament.

The winning party, Vetevendosje, has the votes to elect a new speaker, and indeed a new government. But it has conditioned the election of a speaker on reaching a wider agreement with the opposition on the election of a new president. With deadlines imposed by the Constitutional Court passing, is Kosovo heading to a fourth parliamentary election in two years?

World.title: Thousands Flee, 14 Hospitalised as Wildfire Menaces Croatian Coastal Town
World.content:
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said on Friday that 14 people have been hospitalised, with ten in intensive care, after a wildfire that reportedly forced some 2,000 people to evacuate homes around the Dalmatian coastal town of Omis overnight.

“The government and all relevant services are coordinating to protect people and rectify the consequences of the large fire in Omis,” Plenkovic wrote on X.

The fire swept through forested areas to destroy property and vehicles. Chief national fire officer Slavko Tucakovic told media that he had “never experienced anything like this in my career”.

“Unfortunately, many houses were damaged or burned down. A large number of vehicles were also burned up,” he said.

The Croatian coast has seen record high temperatures this summer. The heatwave left dry vegetation as fuel for the fire, and the flames were spread by high winds, Tucakovic explained.

World.title: Kosovo’s LDK Drops Demand to Choose President in Bid to Resolve Crisis
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku addresses media on August 13, 2026. Photo: BIRN .

The opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, said on Thursday it had withdrawn its demands to name the country’s new president in an attempt to end the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since parliamentary elections in June.

Lumir Abdixhiku, the LDK leader, said that while talks with the poll-winning Vetevendosje party’s leader Albin Kurti over a government partnership had not yet produced results, he was offering new talks about the election of a new president – which is crucial to avoid new parliamentary polls.

“From this moment, no one has any reason, alibi or the right to delay the inauguration of parliament, the formation of the government and starting negotiations on a new president. We are late and should not waste any more time,” Abdixhiku said in a video message after a meeting with the party’s parliamentary group.

“The constitutional uncertainty is a reality we cannot ignore … The crisis does not seem to have an end and it’s getting worse and worse,” he added.

“We are ready to discuss the election of a president who defends our republic’s interests and its constitution, represents people’s unity and exercises the constitutional responsibilities. We are not asking for any posts or any political compensation in return,” he continued.

In the June elections, Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, well ahead of the Kosovo Democratic Party, PDK, which won 22. The LDK won 18 seats and has until now insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority in the Assembly to form a new government, by again relying on the support of MPs from various ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk, Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved; the parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new parliament, or it will trigger another election.

Speaking on Friday, Kurti did not specifically say if he will accept the LDK offer, but welcomed Abdixhiku’s willingness to include other parties in negotiations over the presidency.

“We are open to further discussions in order to come to a name or names [for the presidency], someone who is out of the current political scene, out of daily party polemics, and who is a unifying figure,” Kurti said.

“We want to agree in advance in order to avoid new elections. The election of a parliament speaker and a cabinet is not a challenge, so we have to agree on the election of a president,” he added.

Meanwhile a group PDK MPs protested on Friday for the second day in a row in front of acting premier Kurti’s office, demanding the resumption of parliament’s inaugural session. This was interrupted last Saturday when Kurti asked for “more time” to discuss the issue of a new president with other parties.

So far, Abdixhiku and Kurti have met twice but have not found a common ground on new institutions. In his video address, Abdixhiku disclosed that the LDK was offered three ministries in Kurti’s next cabinet – “a disproportion we could not afford”.

World.title: Democracy Digest: US Charges Mexican Cartel Members over Czech Weapons Deal
World.content:
Russia on the radar; Slovakia picks a fight with Brussels over same-sex marriage

Slovakia’s Interior Ministry has been forced into an embarrassing retreat over speed cameras with suspected Russian links, a week after dismissing opposition warnings about their origin. The National Security Authority (NBU) confirmed on Tuesday that the two devices in question contain Russian components. The finding vindicates concerns raised by Progressive Slovakia (PS), the country’s strongest opposition party, which had warned that the cameras could pose a security risk. There were red flags from the start. Journalists found that the cameras closely resembled equipment made by the St Petersburg-based company Simicon. More strikingly, the measurement software listed in the Slovak certification had the same digital fingerprint as software used in a Russian CORDON speed camera. The ministry’s story has shifted ever since. It first insisted the cameras were not Russian, then conceded it could not prove their origin, before ordering IT supplier Soitron to remove the test devices. It now says two ministry employees will lose their jobs and cooperation with Soitron will end. Interior Minister Matus Sutaj Estok, of the governing Hlas party, has resisted calls to take political responsibility. “We were lied to,” he said on Thursday, blaming the Slovak Institute of Metrology, which certified the cameras. The institute says checking cybersecurity risks, supply chains or the origin of components is not its job. Soitron also denies misleading the state. Soitron obtained the devices from a Slovak distributor whose CEO had worked in Russia for many years and had previously imported similar equipment to Slovakia through another company. The ministry will not publish the NBU analysis, and it is unclear why the country’s security services failed to spot the potential problem before opposition politicians and journalists did. The General Prosecutor’s Office has now said it will examine the case.

There was another controversy this week involving the Interior Ministry, and Interior Minister Sutaj Estok in particular. His ministry has refused to register same-sex marriages legally concluded abroad. Several Slovak same-sex couples applied in December to have their foreign marriage certificates entered into Slovakia’s special registry. After waiting eight months, they received an answer not from the registry, but directly from Sutaj Estok. He argued that registering the unions as marriages would conflict with Slovak law and the constitution, which has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 2014. Among those affected are former diplomats Ivan Novotny and his husband Metod Spacek. They argue that the minister intervened in a procedure that should have been handled by the registry and are now preparing an administrative lawsuit. At the heart of the dispute is a 2025 ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union involving a Polish-German same-sex couple. The court ruled that an EU country cannot refuse to recognise a same-sex marriage legally concluded in another member state if doing so interferes with rights guaranteed under EU law, particularly freedom of movement and residence. The ruling does not require member states to introduce same-sex marriage into their domestic law. The European Commission has reminded Slovakia that EU law, as interpreted by the EU’s top court, takes precedence over national law and that member states are required to implement its judgments. It told the SME daily that it would continue to monitor the situation and could use the tools at its disposal if needed. The ministry argues that EU law may require Slovakia to recognise same-sex marriages for specific purposes, but does not oblige the country to enter them in its registry as marriages with the same legal status as marriages recognised under Slovak law. Novotny, Spacek and other couples dispute that interpretation. Their planned legal challenge could now put that question before the Slovak courts.

World.title: Montenegro’s Menstrual Leave Law Won’t Succeed Without More Gynaecologists
World.content:
Imagine a woman called Milica. She is 29, on a fixed-term contract, and every month menstrual pain keeps her from working for several days.

Milica has not seen a gynaecologist in two years. There aren’t enough appointments where she lives and she cannot travel to the capital, Podgorica, because of work.

When she finally gets a diagnosis, she learns a law offering paid leave exists, and she must renew her medical diagnosis certificate every year.

But she wonders whether her employer will extend her contract if he learns why she has been absent.

World.title: BIRN Reality Check: What Has Albania’s AI ‘Minister’ Achieved So Far?
World.content:
According to Rama, Diella was to serve as Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, with a specific task: to eliminate corruption from public procurement tenders – a key issue for Albania as it seeks to push forward its EU accession process.

But a year later, the actual role of the bot ‘minister’ role remains unclear.

At the Public Procurement Agency, where the bot’s skills were expected to be tested, work still appears to be at the preparatory stage.

“There is a project to develop an AI-powered procurement system, but it is still in progress,” said Reida Kashta, the Agency’s director, when asked whether it had begun using AI in public procurement.

According to Kashta, the agency has “just completed the drafting of the terms of reference”. This is a document that sets out the technical criteria for launching the tender that will select the company responsible for building the system.

The public procurement system has for years been considered one of the sectors most exposed to corruption in Albania. Investigations by the Special Prosecution Office for organised crime and corruption, SPAK, have uncovered several cases involving schemes to manipulate tenders, in which winners had been predetermined before the procedures were launched. Contracts for the construction of roads, incinerators and other public investments have been subject to investigations over allegations of favouring economic operators and violating competition rules.

The government’s ambition to integrate AI into the sector has been met with scepticism by both opposition politicians and public policy experts, mainly because of the security risks it entails, its lack of human capacity and various legal uncertainties.

Opposition Democratic Party MP Klevis Balliu told BIRN that the use of AI could serve as an assisting tool for the administration, but could not replace the legal responsibility of institutions, nor guarantee the fight against corruption.

According to Balliu, without a clear constitutional and legal basis, the creation of a virtual minister raises questions about who bears responsibility for decision-making, particularly in a sensitive sector such as public procurement.

“Diella does not solve corruption. On the contrary, she raises a fundamental question: who bears responsibility for decisions influenced by a system that has no legally defined status?” Balliu said.

He argued that a virtual system could help increase efficiency and identify irregularities, but “it cannot replace transparency, oversight and human accountability.”

Public policy experts are also concerned about the use of AI in procurement without a comprehensive legal, institutional and technical framework in place.

Alba Brojka, an independent digital policy expert, said artificial intelligence should not be treated as a “magic wand solution” to complex problems such as corruption, but only as a tool to increase efficiency and automate administrative processes.

“Under [UN culture agency] UNESCO’s principles on the ethical use of AI, decision-making ultimately belongs to the expert or human, not the technology,” Brojka said. She sees this particular use of AI as “an excuse for a problem [corruption] that has existed for years”, and that what needs addressing first is the “legal gap and institutional capacity”.

For Aranita Brahaj, head of the Albanian Institute of Science (AIS) the use of AI in procurement cannot be seen as a solution to tendering problems without first consolidating the legal framework and developing a new methodology to monitor the efficiency of such systems.

“Albania still lacks a complete, secondary legal framework and, above all, this process is taking place at a time when public contracting is showing significant problems,” Brahaj said.

World.title: Nearly 200 People Rescued From the Sea as Fire Ravages Omiš Area
World.content:
August the 14th, 2026 – An utterly devastating wildfire in the Omiš area has left a trail of destruction along the Croatian coast, with nearly 200 people rescued from the sea.

Those rescued headed for the safety of the sea and boats, fleeing the flames during a dramatic overnight evacuation. The enormous fire rapidly spread across the Omiš area on Thursday night, forcing residents and visitors to seek safety wherever they could. Index reports that as the flames approached the coastline, dozens of people, including children, entered the sea or boarded vessels in an attempt to escape the fire.

A large-scale maritime rescue operation was launched after authorities received reports at around 23:40 that a significant number of people were in the sea and on boats without supervision. The National Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Rijeka coordinated the operation together with the Split Port Authority and its stations in Makarska, Milna and Hvar.

Police vessels, the Croatian Coast Guard, customs officials and the Croatian Mountain Rescue Service were also involved. Members of the public and a private passenger-boat company joined the rescue effort.

The most intensive phase of the operation took place between 12:15 a.m. and 2:45 a.m., with rescuers moving between the coastline, the sea and vessels where people had taken shelter.

According to the latest information, port authority crews rescued 194 people, mainly from the areas between Nemira and Ruskamen. Authorities noted that the final number of people rescued could be higher, as other emergency services, private citizens and companies were also involved in the operation.

The fire has also resulted in a serious number of injuries. According to KBC Split, 36 people sought medical assistance, with 14 subsequently hospitalised. Ten of those patients are being treated in intensive care, and seven are in life-threatening condition.

Most of the patients in intensive care suffered serious burns. Doctors described the treatment of burn victims as particularly complex and said that preparations were already under way to transfer some patients to hospitals in Zagreb to ensure they receive the best possible care. Among those seriously injured is a 17-year-old, according to information reported by Index. Further details about individual patients have not been released because of medical privacy.

The response to the disaster is continuing on the ground.

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković has already arrived in Omiš together with several government ministers. A crisis meeting is being held with senior firefighters, local officials, Civil Protection, police and representatives of KBC Split. President Zoran Milanović is also scheduled to visit Omiš today. According to the Office of the President, he is expected to meet with the mayor of Omiš and representatives of the firefighting service before visiting areas affected by the fire. His arrival is scheduled for 14:00.

Following the overnight rescue operation, maritime authorities continued monitoring the affected coastline as the emergency response moved into a new phase. For many caught in the path of the flames, however, the night will be remembered for the extraordinary decision to escape into the Adriatic, and for the rescue crews who went out into the darkness to bring them back to safety.

World.title: Should Croatia Send SRUUK Messages to Tourists Before Danger Strikes?
World.content:
August the 14th, 2026 – Should Croatia send out SRUUK messages to tourists before danger strikes? With more and more incidents of mountain, sea and other rescues taking place, some believe the country be doing more to warn visitors of potential risks.

Four Portuguese nationals recently went missing at sea after strong bura winds took control of their 1.5 metre inflatable boat. Index reports that this is one incident in an increasingly long list of issues that take place every single summer. From flip flop-donning “hikers” on Biokovo to people trying to cross the Adriatic to Italy on an inflatable flamingo, there’s never a drama-free tourist season in this regard.

The question for some is whether Croatia could be doing more, such as sending out SRUUK messages to tourists about specific dangers they may face during their stay. The latest case of the Portuguese tourists being swept away has once again raised the question of how well tourists are actually warned about the dangers of a strong and stormy bura. This is especially true in the area of the Velebit Channel, where rescue operations for people blown away from the shore by the wind are commonplace during the season.

sruuk messages specifically for bura winds

A similar case occurred at the end of July, when the bura carried a foreign national on a SUP board from Karlobag across the Velebit Channel all the way to Pag. After a multi-hour night-time operation, the Croatian Mountain Rescue Service (HGSS) found him uninjured on an inaccessible part of the Pag coast.

Because of the frequent occurrence of such cases, an inquiry was sent to the Ministry of the Interior, which is responsible for Civil Protection, asking why warnings about a strong and stormy bura on the Adriatic are not sent to citizens and tourists via the Early Warning and Crisis Management System (SRUUK). The ministry was also asked whether the introduction of such warnings is being considered, when they could start being sent, and whether there are any obstacles that prevent strong and stormy bura from being among the events for which citizens receive SRUUK messages.

From the response of Civil Protection it follows that Civil Protection itself doesn’t actually decide whether an SRUUK message will be sent due to a severe weather issue. They explained that the sending of SRUUK messages is regulated by the Ordinance on the procedure for early warning of the population.

warnings for severe weather events

“The early warning of the population is the provision of timely and useful information on the basis of which the competent institutions mobilise communities and individuals exposed to dangers to take measures to avoid or reduce risks and to carry out timely preparations for an effective response to threats,” they replied.

Information for early warning is collected by institutions responsible for meteorology, hydrology and flood defence, fire protection, seismology, ionising radiation, public health and geology. Operators of facilities with hazardous substances and hydro-accumulations, inspection services and scientific institutions also participate in the system. These institutions use their websites, social media channels, the traditional media and other methods as the basic channels for warnings so that the information can reach citizens as quickly as possible. Data on immediate danger are also forwarded to the Civil Protection Directorate.

who can actually issue a sruuk message urgently?

The Ordinance defines the persons who can decide to initiate the procedure for sending an SRUUK message, depending on the type of danger. In the case of floods, the decision is made by the chief flood defence manager or a person authorised by him, and in the case of large-scale fires by the chief fire commander or an authorised person.

For natural disasters and severe weather warnings, which include dangerous weather phenomena such as a strong and stormy bura, the decision is made by the director of the Croatian Meteorological and Hydrological Service (DHMZ) or a person authorised by him. In the case of a threat from military means, the decision is made in accordance with the Defence Act, while in the case of an immediate terrorist threat or other security reasons of a larger scale the decision is made by the chief police director or a person authorised by him.

There is also the possibility of activating the system due to an extraordinary event in the area of a particular county, city or municipality. In that case, a request with the text of the message can be submitted to the competent county 112 centre by the head of the civil protection headquarters of the local or regional self-government unit affected by the event, or a person authorised by him.

Civil Protection therefore emphasises that SRUUK is not an institution that assesses whether citizens should be warned, but a technical system by which the decision of the competent body is transmitted to people in the threatened area. “From all of the above it is clear that SRUUK is only an information tool by which early warning messages are sent to all mobile devices located in the area that the decision-maker has designated as threatened,” they state.

After receiving the decision, the Civil Protection Directorate enters the message composed by the decision-maker and sends it via mobile operators to users in the designated area.

World.title: Temperature Records Broken in Three Croatian Cities
World.content:
August the 14th, 2026 – Temperature records have been well and truly broken in three Croatian cities as the summer heat causes an array of issues nationwide.

Index reports that on the 12th of August, the City of Split recorded the highest air temperature since official records began. At the Split-Marjan measuring station at 14:00, the temperature reached a staggering 39.7 degrees Celsius.

According to official DHMZ data, this officially breaks the previous record of 39.5 degrees measured on the 30th of June this year. It still hasn’t broken the record measured back in 2017 at the Split-Kaštela meteorological station, which still stands at a horrendous 42.2 degrees Celsius.

HRT meteorologist Zoran Vakula reported that the record was also broken on the same day in Senj. 39.8°C was measured, breaking the 2015 record of 39.7°C. On the same date at 12:00 in Dubrovnik, 39.1°C was measured, breaking the 2025 record of 38.6°C.
