World.title: Govt scraps 12-minute ad cap for TV channel
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Television channels will no longer be restricted to 12 minutes of s per hour, with the government deciding to scrap the two-decade-old cap in a move it says will put traditional broadcasters on a more level footing with digital platforms.The restriction, introduced in 2006 under the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, will cease to apply once the amended rules are notified in the Gazette, the information and broadcasting ministry said.The government has argued that the television landscape has changed substantially since the cap was imposed. India had only 62 TV channels in 2006, compared with more than 900 now. Cable television, then the dominant distribution platform, was largely analog and offered limited capacity and consumer choice.With digitisation, platforms including cable TV, direct-to-home, HITS and IPTV can now carry 300 to 500 channels or more, significantly expanding viewer choice and competition, the ministry said.The decision could give broadcasters greater flexibility to determine advertising inventory, an important consideration for an industry that remains heavily dependent on advertising revenue across both pay and free-to-air channels.The ministry also cited the growing competition television faces from digital media, where there is no comparable statutory cap on advertising duration.It said the existing restriction had created a ânon-level playing fieldâ for conventional television broadcasters and that removing it would promote âfair competitionâ and ease of doing business.The change, however, will become operational only from the date the amendment to the Cable Television Networks Rules is formally notified.

World.title: Pew survey: What US, UK and others think about India at 80
World.content:
As India completes 79 years of independence, its global standing presents a striking study in contrasts.

A Pew Research Center survey conducted across 36 countries between February and May 2026 reveals an international community divided down the middle: a global median of 45% of respondents hold a favorable view of India, while 41% express an unfavorable opinion.



Behind this median lies a complex tapestry of geopolitical shifts, historical rivalries, and evolving regional alliances.

From enthusiasm in Western Europe and East Africa to frosty hostility in parts of the Middle East and South Asia, public perception of the worldâs most populous democracy depends heavily on where you ask.

Neighbourhood contrasts & global scorecard

Nowhere is this divergence more intense than in India's immediate backyard.

While proximity can foster cooperation, in South Asia it has produced antithetical attitudes.

Sri Lanka has the most favourable view of India, with 79% of adults expressing a positive opinion.

Pakistan sits at the opposite end, with just 7% viewing India favourably. The gulf between the two countries reflects decades of conflict, political rivalry and competing national narratives.

Turkey is another major outlier. Only 15% of Turks have a favourable opinion of India, while a majority hold an unfavourable view.





In the West Bank and East Jerusalem, just 18% express a positive opinion.

Yet beyond these pockets of hostility, India finds considerable goodwill across much of the world.

as India enters its 80th year as an independent nation, what does the world think of it?

Kenya and the United Kingdom rank alongside Sri Lanka among the countries most positive towards India, with roughly seven in 10 adults expressing favourable views.

Majorities in Germany, Israel, Italy, Sweden, Japan and Thailand also see India positively.

In contrast, Latin American publics express mixed-to-negative views, alongside substantial shares of respondents who offer no opinion.

The findings suggest that India's global image is not simply a reflection of its diplomatic alliances.

Economic ties, strategic partnerships, cultural familiarity and perceptions of India's growing global role all appear to shape how people view the country.

India's image is changing

The bigger story is perhaps not where India stands today, but how its image has changed.

In most countries surveyed, opinions have remained relatively stable since Pew last asked the question. But in 10 countries, the change has been statistically significant â and in seven of them, India's favourability has fallen.

Turkey and Nigeria have recorded the sharpest declines since 2025, with the share of people expressing a favourable opinion of India falling by 10 percentage points in both countries.

India has also lost ground in the United States, Indonesia, South Africa and Mexico.

The decline is particularly striking in Bangladesh.

Pew's previous survey there was conducted in 2024. Since then, the share of Bangladeshis with a favourable opinion of India has fallen by 15 percentage points, leaving fewer than half with a positive view.

At the same time, the number of Bangladeshis who do not express an opinion has also fallen sharply, from 24% to just 7%. In other words, more Bangladeshis now appear to have a defined opinion of India â and that opinion has become considerably less favourable.

The trend is not uniformly negative, however.

India's image has improved significantly in Germany, Britain and Sri Lanka.

The share of Britons with a favourable opinion of India has risen 11 points since 2025, while Germany has recorded a six-point increase. Sri Lanka has seen an even bigger jump, with favourability rising 14 points since 2024.

Looking further back to 2023 reveals another interesting divide.

Across several European countries, India's image has strengthened substantially since the first post-pandemic survey.

In Germany, for example, only 47% had a favourable opinion of India in 2023. That figure has now climbed to 63%.

France has followed a similar trajectory. India's favourability there has risen from 39% in 2023 to 50% today.

Outside Europe, however, the picture is less encouraging.

South Korea is one example. In 2023, 59% of South Koreans viewed India favourably. Today, that figure has dropped to 44%.

Latin America also tends to lean more negative, although large numbers of people in several European and Latin American countries do not express an opinion at all.

Politics matters too

India's global image is also shaped by domestic political ideology in some countries.

The United States and Canada show a striking pattern: people on the political left are more likely than conservatives to view India favourably.

In the US, 54% of liberals express a positive opinion of India, compared with 40% of conservatives. In Canada, the corresponding figures are 58% and 45%.

Israel presents almost the exact opposite picture.

There, 68% of people on the political right view India favourably, compared with just 46% on the left.

The ideological divide underlines how perceptions of India can be tied not only to India's own policies, but also to how different political constituencies interpret its role in the world.

A mixed but largely positive global image

So, as India enters its 80th year as an independent nation, what does the world think of it?

The answer is neither uniformly celebratory nor overwhelmingly negative.

Pakistan and Turkey may give India the stink eye, but they represent the more hostile end of a much broader spectrum.

From Sri Lanka and Kenya to Britain, Germany and Israel, India enjoys strong positive sentiment in several strategically important countries.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

At the same time, the declines in Bangladesh, the US, South Korea, Turkey, Nigeria and other countries show that India's global image cannot be taken for granted.

India's international reputation is therefore becoming more consequential â and more contested.

As New Delhi seeks a larger role in global affairs, its challenge will not simply be to build economic and military power, but also to shape how that power is perceived abroad.

At 80, India is increasingly a country the world has an opinion about.

World.title: Sunil Amrith On 'The Burning Earth' And The Unequal Costs Of Environmental Destruction
World.content:
Sunil Amrith

Excerpts from the interview.

Q: Why did you feel this book needed to be written?

A:

Q: You also bring in a kind of storytelling which positions itself in different geographies as if to say, the inherited narratives of Eurocentric histories are not what we're going to look at.

A:

Q: How do you bring in a methodology which ensures that what you're positioning and presenting can be as accurate as possible?

A:

Q: You use the word 'elite' a few times when you're talking about social stratification for a very specific economic growth touted as well-being of a community, but usually you see it as exploitative.

A:

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Q: You point out that there are these rather horrific incidents which are almost genocidal.

A:

Sunil Amrith is the Renu and Anand Dhawan Professor of History at Yale University with a secondary appointment as professor at the Yale School of the Environment. He serves as Director of the Macmillan Centre for International and Area Studies and Yale's Vice Provost for International Affairs.He has received the 2016 Infosys Prize in Humanities, a 2017 MacArthur Fellowship, and the 2025 Toynbee Prize in Global History, among others. He has authored five books that put Asia at the heart of global history. In this conversation, he discusses his book, 'The Burning Earth'.It was a coming together of my academic life and the rest of my life. For close to 20 years, I had been researching some of the themes that do make it into 'The Burning Earth'. I've particularly been interested in the relationship between migration, the movement of people and environmental change. So I wrote a book more than 10 years ago called 'Crossing the Bay of Bengal', which I think was my first foray into environmental history, in which I was really thinking about the enormous movement of people, particularly from Tamil Nadu, to southeast Asia in the 19th and 20th century, many of them to work on rubber plantations, but also to work in port cities, places like Singapore and Penang and Rangoon, and understanding that that was actually a moment of fundamental transformation in the environment... At the same time, as a teacher, but also as a parent, as a citizen, the climate crisis became quite unavoidable in my own consciousness. And so for me, that prompted me to scale things up beyond my areas of specialisation towards perhaps the biggest question, which is how did we get to this point of planetary crisis? And that's really what's at the heart of 'The Burning Earth'.If the question is what is it about my own perspective that may make this book a little bit different from some of the other books out there on this big theme of the environment, it is the fact that my own training is not in European and North American history. And I think most of what is called global history continues to take as its starting point and as its default, a kind of familiar North Atlantic history. And so by starting the book in China and ending it in Indonesia, I was really trying to write it anchored in Asia. .. Asia has always been home to the majority of humanity. It still is today. And so it seemed to me completely fitting to really think about the history of this planet with a firm anchor in the part of the world, the part of the planet which has been the most inhabited by most people throughout the longest period of time.That's the biggest challenge of a book like this. There's no possibility that I can have the primary expertise in all of these areas that I write about in the book. And so in some ways that was a leap that I took. Academia is a collective enterprise. And this is very much a book that builds on my own work in some areas. And in other areas, it's really sort of bringing together my reading in multiple fields of scholarship and different disciplines as well. So I'm a historian, but some of the most exciting new scholarship which I draw on and interpret is actually coming from the physical sciences.There's some phenomenally interesting work in paleoclimatology, for example, which is trying to reconstruct past climates using ice cores, using lake bed sediment, using tree rings. And of course, these disciplines traditionally and even still within the walls of the university barely meet. But what's been very interesting about recent work on climate and environment in particular, is you have this forcing together of completely different ideas of what the archive is.I don't use the word that many times, but when I do, I think it's doing a lot of work for me. 'The Burning Earth' is not an activist book, which is to say that it is just that bit muddier and less clear about the villains of the piece than activist writing necessarily has to be. And yet there is such a strong core in my own thinking of awareness of just how stark environmental inequalities are and just how much the scale of planetary destruction that has been achieved over the last two centuries has been disproportionately, not exclusively, but disproportionately driven by the elite pursuit of luxuries and of accumulation. .. There is a story of human need in this book and there's also a story of human greed... I think we need to think about desire, we need to think about states, we need to think about liberation, we need to think about the genuinely liberatory promises that led to some of this environmental destruction which can't be reduced to a question of greed or even of capitalism...There's no question that the social and economic system that has been a driving force in the climate crisis is the capitalist system. But the socialist system in some sense was even more environmentally profligate and wasteful. It was just less successful. And so in terms of its longevity, in terms of the scale on which it was operating, it kind of doesn't compare with what a particular capitalist mode of production does to our ability to treat all of nature as commodity and to lead to this kind of constantly expanding frontier of production.But my question is really a different one, which is, where were the alternatives? Who was thinking differently?I think that's one of the key narratives in the book to show that the moments of the most intensive and accelerated environmental destruction over the last several hundred years have almost always gone together with moments of intense violence. And violence is at the core of 'The Burning Earth'. Not just violence against the earth or against nature, but against other people... Wars that are going on all around us in the world today are part of a very long pattern where armed violence and militarism and military destruction have been inextricably bound with massive environmental destruction.

World.title: 'Greatest threat': How India, Pakistan view each other; data lays bare deep animosity
World.content:
A survey has revealed that a majority of adults in Pakistan and India view the other as their single greatest threat.

' Greatest threat ': India and Pakistan point at each other

The data paints a stark picture of two neighbours frozen in mutual distrust.

Mutual hostility runs deep

The numbers on bilateral perceptions are stark.

Lack of trust

When asked whether the Indian and Pakistani governments and people are committed to good relations with each other, the clear pattern is that people only have faith in their own country Pew Research report

Beneath the geopolitical differences lies a more fundamental problem: the absence of trust.

How Bangladesh, Sri Lanka view the rivals

The India-Pakistan divide extends beyond bilateral relations.

Divergent worldviews

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Two countries, two very different worlds

Nearly eight decades after the 1947 Partition of British India gave birth to two independent nations, deep-seated historical trauma, and territorial disputes that have led to multiple military confrontations continue to shape the mindset of citizens on both sides of the border.As the two countries celebrate their independence, a major survey by the Pew Research Center reveals that an overwhelming majority of adults in both nuclear-armed rivals view the other as their single greatest geopolitical threat.Conducted across South Asia between February and May 2026, the findings highlight a persistent, deep-rooted mutual hostility that shows little sign of thawing. These sentiments reflect not merely political disagreements, but deeply entrenched unfavourable opinions among general populations, extending into perceptions of global superpowers, regional allies, and the long-term prospects for bilateral peace.The data paints a stark picture of two neighbours frozen in mutual distrust.In India, 54% of respondents named Pakistan as the greatest threat to their country.Conversely, 43% of Pakistanis identified India as their primary security threat.For Indians, China is the next most cited threat at 21%. For Pakistanis, Israel and the US each register at 24% as major threats â though still far below India.These threat perceptions align closely with how each public judges the otherâs commitment to peace.Most Indians believe their own government and people are committed to good bilateral relations, but a majority say Pakistanâs government and people are not.Pakistanis mirror this: they express confidence in their own sideâs commitment but doubt Indiaâs.The numbers on bilateral perceptions are stark.Nearly nine in 10 Pakistanis have an unfavourable view of India, with 73% describing their opinion as 'very unfavourable'. The sentiment cuts across demographic groups, suggesting that hostility toward India is not confined to any particular section of Pakistani society.The picture in India is similarly bleak. As many as 78% of Indians have an unfavourable view of Pakistan, including 65% who hold a very unfavourable opinion. There is, however, a notable internal divide in India. Indian Muslims are somewhat more favorable toward Pakistan (21%) than Indian Hindus (6%), and they are also less likely to name Pakistan as their top threat (34% vs 57% among Hindus).Pew's polling also shows that this is not a temporary shift in sentiment.Indian views of Pakistan have remained overwhelmingly negative for more than a decade, with the share expressing a favourable opinion never rising above 20% since 2013.Historical Pew surveys also show that Pakistanis have long held predominantly negative views of India. Pakistani respondents expressing favourable views of India have generally ranged from single digits to around one-third.The survey further suggests that hostility is not simply about how Indians and Pakistanis perceive each other. It also extends to whether they believe the other side genuinely wants better relations.A clear pattern emerges: people tend to believe that their own government and population are committed to good bilateral relations, while doubting the intentions of the other side.A majority of Indians believe both the Indian government and Indian people are committed to maintaining good relations with Pakistan. But a majority of Pakistanis reject that assessment, saying the Indian government and people are not committed to good relations.The mirror image appears in Pakistan.A majority of Pakistanis say their government and people want good relations with India.Most Indians, however, believe Pakistan's government and people are not committed to improving ties. About a quarter of Indian respondents were unsure.This mutual lack of trust creates a difficult cycle: each side sees itself as willing to improve relations while viewing the other as unwilling to reciprocate.Indian Muslims again stand apart to some degree. Around a third say the Pakistani government and people are committed to good relations, significantly higher than the corresponding share among Indian Hindus.The Pew findings become even more revealing when India and Pakistan are placed alongside Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.Of the four South Asian countries surveyed, Sri Lanka is the only country that receives more positive than negative ratings from respondents in all three of the others.India, meanwhile, has the widest range of perceptions.Sri Lankans are overwhelmingly positive toward India, with 79% expressing a favourable opinion. In Bangladesh, 42% view India favourably. In Pakistan, however, the figure plunges to just 7%.India is also seen as Sri Lanka's most important ally by a clear majority: 63% of Sri Lankan respondents name India.The picture is very different in Bangladesh and Pakistan, where India is most often identified as the greatest threat.Views of Prime Minister Narendra Modi follow a broadly similar pattern. Seventy percent of Sri Lankans express confidence in PM Modi to do the right thing in world affairs, compared with 42% in Bangladesh and 4% in Pakistan.The survey also finds that Pakistan is not universally viewed negatively across South Asia.Fifty-seven percent of Sri Lankans and 54% of Bangladeshis have a favourable opinion of Pakistan, compared with only 8% of Indians.Bangladesh itself receives broadly positive views in Pakistan and Sri Lanka: 66% of Pakistanis and 56% of Sri Lankans express favourable opinions of Bangladesh. Only about a quarter of Indians do so.Sri Lanka emerges as the region's relative outlier. Around half or more of respondents in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh view the island nation positively, while significantly fewer hold negative views.The India-Pakistan divide extends beyond bilateral relations to the way each country views the global order.For Indians, Russia remains a particularly important and popular partner. Thirty-six percent identify Russia as India's most important ally, while 16% name the United States.Russia's favourable image in India is particularly striking. Fifty-eight percent of Indians have a favourable opinion of Russia, while 51% express confidence in Russian President Vladimir Putin.Pakistanis are considerably less positive: 39% have a favourable view of Russia and only 32% express confidence in Putin.India's relationship with the United States is also reflected in public opinion. Indians are substantially more favourable toward the US than Pakistanis are and are more likely to express confidence in US President Donald Trump.The picture is almost completely reversed when it comes to China.An overwhelming 90% of Pakistanis have a favourable view of China, while 83% express confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping. Three-quarters of Pakistanis identify China as their country's most important ally.Saudi Arabia is a distant second, named by 12%.In India, however, only around a quarter of respondents view China or Xi positively. Even Indian Muslims, who are more favourable toward China than Indian Hindus, remain negative toward both China and its president on balance.Nearly 80 years after Partition, the survey suggests that the India-Pakistan rivalry remains deeply embedded not only in government policy and military strategy, but also in public perceptions.The most striking finding may therefore not be that Indians and Pakistanis dislike each other. It is that both overwhelmingly believe the other side sees them as the problem.That mutual conviction â reinforced by decades of conflict, competing national narratives and geopolitical rivalry â remains one of the biggest barriers to changing the relationship between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.Yet beneath these geopolitical differences lies a more fundamental problem: the absence of trust.Both populations believe their own side is committed to better relations, while doubting the intentions of the other.

World.title: 'Cannot imagine': Rajnath Singh's sharp 'Gandhi surname' attack on Rahul Gandhi over PM hug jibe
World.content:
Defence minister

has hit back at Congress leader

over his remarks on Prime Minister

and the government's foreign policy, calling them âpetty and condemnableâ and warning that such language could damage democratic discourse.

Singh said he was particularly upset that the comments came from the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha. He accused Gandhi of lowering the dignity associated with the post and questioned whether such conduct was appropriate for someone holding a key constitutional position.

"The remarks made by LoP Rahul Gandhi on PM Narendra Modi and India's foreign policy yesterday are petty and condemnable. It is painful for me personally, too.

In my long political life, I had never seen such indecent and unimaginable conduct from any LoP. Such conduct is a grave sign of a threat to a healthy democracy," Singh said.

The defence minister also defended Modi's record as Prime Minister and his standing abroad, while arguing that political differences should not lead to what he described as disrespectful remarks.

"Rahul Gandhi might have frustration with PM in his mind, but such indecent remarks are unacceptable, especially when PM Modi has been a Prime Minister who has brought prestige to India nationally and internationally, and paved the way for Viksit Bharat. "

"In 12 years, working with full dedication, he did not take any leave.





Such indecent remarks against such a PM pain every Indian," he said.

Singh then turned his criticism towards the Congress, questioning whether the party could continue to claim the legacy of several of India's prominent leaders after Gandhi's remarks.

"I would also like to humbly tell the

Congress party

that after such language and conduct, can they have any claim over the legacy of Lal-Bal-Pal and Gandhi, Patel and Nehru, from Subhas Babu to Rajendra Babu and Shastri ji and Narasimha Rao ji to Pranab Mukherjee?" Rajnath Singh said.

He further accused Gandhi of not only targeting Modi but also damaging India's image and the dignity of the Leader of Opposition's office.

"With this conduct, Rahul Gandhi has not only insulted PM Narendra Modi but also the international prestige of India. He has shredded the dignity of the post of Lok Sabha LoP. I cannot even imagine that someone with the Gandhi surname can make such a shameful remark."

The exchange followed remarks made by Gandhi at the Congress's Rachnatmak Congress National Convention in New Delhi on Thursday.

Gandhi criticised the government's approach to foreign policy and argued that India's international relations should be driven by national interest rather than personal relationships between political leaders.

"I don't know where it came from; this idea got into their heads. I don't know who put it there or where it came from, the idea that foreign policy means hugging politicians. I was young. We went to America.

Since we're talking about expressions, I'll share this. We went to America. I was twelve years old. Priyanka, myself, my mother, and my grandmother - my grandmother was the Prime Minister. There was a state dinner - an official dinner.

My grandmother and mother went to the official dinner," he said.

He added, "You aren't just visiting a friend's house. In this role, the Prime Minister of India doesn't engage in mere friendship.

They have no interest in friendship; their job is to protect the country."

Gandhi also accused the Modi government of damaging India's foreign policy, using the ongoing conflict involving Iran, the US and Israel as an example.

"War broke out in Iran. For India - had it recognised its own strength and had its leader been someone like Indira Gandhi--this presented the greatest opportunity in the world. What kind of opportunity? Iran was our old friend, America was our friend, and Russia was our friend.

We could have stepped up, become relevant, and leveraged these friendships. But what actually happened? Nothing of the sort. Instead, Pakistan stepped in and took our place; Pakistan became the mediator, while India and Modi-ji simply looked on," he said.

Rahul Gandhi claimed he receives "information directly from Modi ji's office these days; there is a full-blown revolt going on inside".He also referred to certain claims in videos on social media about China's actions concerning patrolling along the LAC in a border area of Arunachal Pradesh.

He also raised allegations concerning Chinese activity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh and accused the government of pressuring the media not to report certain claims.

"In our patrolling areas--specifically in Arunachal--China blocked us from patrolling. They essentially said, 'Look, all that is fine--it is indeed your land--but you cannot patrol here.' Rajnath Singh, Amit Shah, and Narendra Modi have been completely deflated.

They are calling up all the media editors, telling them, 'Don't publish this in your newspapers; suppress the story.' They are causing direct harm to the country without a second thought," he said.

Gandhi also revisited the dispute over India's handling of the border situation with China following the Galwan clash.

He alleged that conflicting statements about whether Indian territory had been lost weakened India's position during negotiations with China.

"After the Galwan incident, the Prime Minister held a meeting--a Zoom call. He stated that China hadn't taken a single inch of Indian territory. The Army said that our land had been taken. Just think about the message sent to China: Chinese negotiators asked our negotiators, 'What nonsense are you talking about? Your own Prime Minister said no land was lost.' So, internally, they have destroyed the country; they have wrecked our foreign policy.

And they did all of this solely to finance their political structure, to secure funds from Adaniji," he alleged.

Duty of every person associated with judicial system to ensure that no one is deprived of justice due to lack of resources.

Operation Sindoor demonstrated Indian Armed Forces' capability for precision strikes against terror networks.

Free ration programme ensuring food security for more than 80 cr beneficiaries.

World.title: 'Unprecedented transformation': Rajnath hails fourfold rise in defence production in message to soldiers
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Defence Minister

on Friday said India's defence sector had undergone an âunprecedented transformationâ over the past 12 years, with domestic defence production rising nearly fourfold to a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26.

In his message to soldiers on the eve of Independence Day, Rajnath said India had reduced its dependence on defence imports while strengthening indigenous manufacturing under the

and

initiatives.

""You all know that under the leadership of the Hon'ble Prime Minister, our government has always accorded the highest priority to self-reliance in the defence sector. Over the past 12 years, you have witnessed unprecedented transformation in the defence sector through Aatmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India," he said.

âOur domestic defence production, which stood at around Rs 46,000 crore in 2014, reached a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in FY 2025-26. This means that over the past decade, our domestic defence production has increased nearly fourfold. This is proof of the structural changes that have taken place over the past decade," the defence minister added.

The union minister further highlighted recent tests and developments in indigenous defence technology, including the MIRV-equipped Advanced Agni missile, Rudram-II air-to-surface missile, Long Range Land Attack Cruise Missile and Pinaka Long Range Guided Rocket.





âWe have also made major advances in hypersonic technology. The successful demonstration of Solid Fuel Ducted Ramjet technology is equally significant,â he said.

He also said the first successful test of the indigenous Kusha Long Range Surface-to-Air Missile had strengthened India's air-defence capabilities.

91% indegenisation in Army ammunitions

As Rajnath hailed the growth in defence sector, the ministry of defence said India's defence production reached a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, nearly four times the level of 2014.

The government said defence exports have grown 56-fold, from Rs 686 crore in 2013-14 to Rs 38,424 crore in 2025-26, with Indian defence products now reaching more than 80 countries.

The defence budget has increased 3.1-fold, from Rs 2.53 lakh crore in 2013-14 to Rs 7.85 lakh crore in 2026-27, while capital expenditure has risen 2.3-fold to Rs 2.19 lakh crore. Defence R&D spending has more than doubled to Rs 29,100 crore in 2026-27 from Rs 13,716 crore in 2014-15.

World.title: AIADMK functionaries stage protest in Dindigul, Theni
World.content:
AIADMK functionaries staged protests in Dindigul and Theni districts on Friday, condemning the TVK-led government for failing to fully waive crop loans for farmers. They also criticised the State government for its handling of the Mekedatu issue.

In Dindigul district, the protests were led by Senior AIADMK leader Dindigul C. Sreenivasan. He said the TVK-led government had failed to fulfil the poll promises made to the people, particularly the farmers. The government failed to fully waive crop loans for farmers. The farmers suffered crop loss. The State government has betrayed the farmers, he said.

He criticised the government for its handling of the Mekedatu issue. The government should take necessary steps to prevent Karnataka from proceeding with the construction of the Mekedatu dam across the Cauvery river, he said. He also criticised the government for not securing the State’s share of Cauvery water.

In Theni district, AIADMK functionaries conducted a protest condemning the TVK government. They said the government had failed to implement its poll promises, including the full waiver of crop loans for farmers.

World.title: Vocalist Ramakrishnan Murthy enthrals audience at music festival
World.content:
Energetic, elaborate and explorative concert by vocalist Ramakrishnan Murthy at the 58th anniversary of Ragapriya Chamber Music Club, with the percussion support from Sivateja Mallajoysula on the violin and NC Bharadwaj on the Mruthangam drew an applause from the rasikas.

Murthy began with the varnam “neranammitinayya nityamuga” in Kannada, worshipping Lord Srinivasa, who is incomparable (“nir-upama”) and in whom Goddess Sri lives (“nivasa”). He exhibited his vocal flexibility for complex rhythm with deep emotional expression.

His next rendition was “Vatapi Ganapatim” by Muthuswami Dikshitar in hamsadwani in praise of Lord Ganesha—specifically at Vatapi (modern Badami), the supreme remover of obstacles which set a positive tone for the concert.

Thyagaraja’s “Seetamma Maayamma” in Vasanta, in which Tyagaraja states all Bhagavatas are his most intimate relatives, was very elaborate and expressive.

He infused positive energy and set the mood with elaborate improvisation in Kalyani, which was equally mirrored by the violinist. The niraval “ sidambaram ena manam” evoked devotion (bhakti), and profound peace.

The vocalist then in quick succession rendered “Vazhi maraithirukkuthe malai pole” on Tirupunkur temple by Gopalakrishna Bharathi (Nandanar charitram) in Nattakurinji.

Then he chose to sing a Navagraha Kriti on Mercury, to seek refuge through “Budhamaashrayaami Satatam” by Dikshitar in Nata Kuranji. Our real status is devotion to Lord. This was well expressed in his rendition of “Padavi ni sadbhaktiyu galgute” by Thyagaraja in ragam Saalaka Bhairavi.

Thodi, the main raga of the evening for “kartikeya kangeya gowri” by Papanasam sivan, Murthy expressed deep emotion, devotion and endless creative scope. The niraval “maruvum amalakara aarumugaa” was applauded by the rasikas.

Throughout the concert, the violinist mirrored and expanded upon the vocalist’s improvisations. The mridangist, who took centre stage to show his skill and speed during the solo Mridangam Tani, came in for a big round of applause.

World.title: NALSAR row: Can BCI freeze enrolment of an entire graduating batch?
World.content:
The story so far: On 13 August, Bar Council of India (BCI) Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra issued a direction to all State Bar Councils not to enrol any NALSAR (National Academy of Legal Studies and Research) 2026 graduate until further orders. The direction came amid an inquiry into a campaign by some students opposing Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant’s participation in NALSAR’s convocation. The Chairman sought a factual report from NALSAR identifying those who initiated, organised, coordinated or mobilised the campaign.

“A student of Law, having no regard or respect for the highest Judicial Office of the country, is not expected to be a responsible or sensible advocate, teacher or judge. Such persons shall always be a liability on the profession...Our experience is that such people are always indulged in strikes and boycotts and tarnish the image of the legal profession,” the letter said.

Subsequently, the BCI modified the direction and said all NALSAR 2026 graduates could enrol with the State Bar Council of their choice, while the inquiry would continue.

This raises several questions about the statutory powers of the BCI, the authority of its Chairman and the legality of imposing a batch-wide restriction when individual responsibility has not yet been established.

What powers does the BCI have over State Bar Councils?

The Bar Council of India is a statutory body constituted under the Advocates Act, 1961. Section 7(1)(b) entrusts the BCI with laying down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for advocates, while Section 7(1)(g) entrusts it with general supervision and control over State Bar Councils. Sections 7(1)(h) and 7(1)(i) concern the promotion and standards of legal education and recognition and inspection of universities whose law degrees qualify for enrolment, respectively. Section 49 empowers the BCI to frame Rules concerning, inter alia, professional conduct and etiquette and standards of legal education.

Section 48B is the power to give directions. It states, “For the proper and efficient discharge of the functions of a State Bar Council or any committee thereof, the Bar Council of India may, in the exercise of its powers of general supervision and control, give such directions to the State Bar Council or any committee thereof as may appear to it to be necessary, and the State Bar Council or the committee shall comply with such directions.”

Rule 15 of the Bar Council of India Rules provides that, subject to the resolutions of the Council, the Chairman shall exercise general control and supervision over the affairs of the Council. Rule 18 further provides that the Chairman has the power to pass interim orders in revisional and other matters arising out of the supervisory jurisdiction of the Council.

“The blanket direction stopping the entire 2026 NALSAR batch from enrolling has no statutory basis. Enrolment is primarily the statutory function of the State Bar Councils under the Advocates Act, and there appears to be no specific provision empowering the BCI Chairman, acting individually, to suspend the enrolment of an entire batch.” said advocate N. Manoj Kumar, BCI and Bar Council of Kerala member.

What does the law say about enrolment?

Section 6(1)(a) entrusts the State Bar Councils with admitting persons as advocates on their rolls. Section 24 of the Advocates Act sets out the qualifications for admission to a State roll, while Section 24A provides for certain disqualifications for enrolment. Sections 25 and 26 deal with the authority and procedure for admission as an advocate, while Section 26A empowers a State Bar Council to remove a name from its roll.

“No blanket restrictions can be imposed by the BCI. Every application has to be dealt with independently and if they meet the statutory requirements, they are entitled to be enrolled,” said advocate Yeshwanth Shenoy, member of Bar Council of Kerala.

“The conduct of a person has nothing to do with his eligibility to be enrolled as an advocate. The Bar Council can only regulate the conduct of advocates, which means that they have to be enrolled with any of the bar councils.” said Mr. Shenoy. He also said the BCI had no authority to direct NALSAR to conduct an inquiry into students’ conduct, arguing that neither the BCI nor the State Bar Councils could initiate disciplinary action against students before they were enrolled as advocates.

Mr. Kumar said that at the most, the BCI may inquire into the conduct of individual students, but collective punishment cannot ordinarily be imposed on an entire batch for the alleged acts of a few. Pre-enrolment conduct may become relevant where it attracts a statutory disqualification or otherwise legally affects eligibility, but mere expression of an opinion or peaceful protest cannot by itself justify denial of enrolment.

What have courts said on BCI’s powers over enrolment?

In the case of Indian Council Of Legal Aid & Advice vs Bar Council Of India & Anr on 17 January, 1995, The Supreme Court of India dealt with a challenge to a Bar Council of India rule barring persons above 45 years of age from enrolment as advocates. The Court held that the BCI could not use its rule-making powers under Section 49 of the Advocates Act to introduce an additional disqualification for enrolment that was not provided for under the Act. It also held that enrolment of advocates falls within the domain of the State Bar Councils and struck down the rule as ultra vires the Advocates Act and violative of Article 14.

In the judgment, the court observed that, “It seems Parliament, while enacting the Act, created agencies at the State level as well as at the Central level in the form of State Bar Council of India and invested them with rule making powers on diverse matters touching the legal profession, presumably because it must have realised that matter pertaining to the profession are best left to informed bodies comprising members of the said profession. However, while doing so it provided for basic substantive matters, e.g., eligibility for entry into the profession (Section 24) disqualification for enrolment (Section 24A), authority entitled to grant admission (Sections 25 and 26), the authority which can remove any name from the roll (Section 26A), etc., and placed them within the domain of a State Bar Council. Thus it is the State Bar Council which alone must decide on the question of enrolment of an applicant on its roll.”

The Court also noted that “It is, therefore, within the exclusive domain of the State Bar Councils to admit persons as advocates on their rolls or to remove their names from the rolls.”

What’s the status now?

The BCI Council subsequently modified the Chairman’s order and said that all NALSAR 2026 graduates would be entitled to enrol with the State Bar Council of their choice.

“With the blanket restriction now withdrawn, NALSAR’s 2026 graduates are presently entitled to seek enrolment in the ordinary course. Even the so called inquiry have been withdrawn. So no further action against them is possible. To debar a law graduate from enrolment, there should be some pre-existing disqualification as provided in the Advocates Act and Rules governing enrolment.” said Mr. Kumar.

World.title: CEO killing: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to stalking charges
World.content:
Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty on Friday (August 14, 2026) to federal stalking charges in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

Mangione entered the plea at a hastily scheduled hearing in Manhattan federal court, which is ongoing. This resolves one of two cases against him in connection with Thompson’s death.

Mangione is scheduled to go on trial on September 8 on state murder charges. With his guilty plea in federal court, his lawyers could seek to have the state case thrown out on double jeopardy grounds.

Authorities say Mangione stalked Thompson, 50, then shot him outside a New York City hotel on December 4, 2024, as the executive walked to UnitedHealth Group’s annual investor conference.

Surveillance video of the killing showed a masked gunman shooting Thompson from behind. Police say “delay,” “deny” and “depose” were written on the ammunition, mimicking a phrase used to describe how insurers avoid paying claims.

World.title: Girl’s father murdered by gang after he objected to stalking
World.content: In a shocking incident, a 45-year-old man was allegedly murdered after he objected to a 21-year-old man stalking his teenage daughter at Watrap in Virudhunagar district on Friday. The police said Ayyanar of Kottayur East Colony lived with his family. His 17-year-old daughter had complained about a 21-year-old man, Periyasamy, stalking her. As it was annoying and disturbing, Ayyanar had objected and shouted at Periyasamy, the prime accused. On Friday, when Ayyanar was walking along the street, Periyasamy, his brother Alaguraja, his wife Pechiammal and a few others allegedly picked up a wordy altercation with him. During the altercation, Periyasamy allegedly attacked Ayyanar with a knife on his back. Ayyanar, who sustained serious injuries, collapsed. On information, his daughter and son rushed to the spot. The Watrap police arrived and sent the body to the Government Hospital for post-mortem. The police registered a case of murder and arrested the three suspects. The weapon was also seized. A hunt was on to nab a few more accused in the case.

World.title: Two killed in alleged Kuki extremists’ attack in Manipur
World.content:
Alleged Kuki extremists attacked a Liangmai Naga village in Manipur’s Kangpokpi district on Friday (August 14, 2026) morning, killing two people and injuring two others.

The incident at Langka Naga village in the Kuki-majority district marked the return of violence to the restive State.

The Working Committee of Tangkhul Naga Long (WC-TNL), an apex body of the Tangkhul community, claimed that 50 gunmen, backed by extremist groups Kuki National Front (KNF) and Kuki Revolutionary Army (KRA), attacked the village at around 7.30 a.m.. The two outfits are among the 25 Kuki-Zomi armed groups that signed Suspension of Operations agreements with the Centre in 2008.

The WC-TNL said the Naga men killed were identified as Wiriliangbou Chawang, 35, and Kawidinang Abonmai, 54. The injured were Maliangjinang Abonmai, 50, and Namthiulungbou Prinmai, 45.

The Naga organisation said the KNF and the KRA engaged in armed violence against the Nagas after Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand issued a 15-day deadline for armed volunteers to surrender their weapons.

“All this while, the Naga civil volunteers have maintained restraint, restricting themselves in defending the village and protecting the innocent civilians,” the WC-TNL said, asking the State government to act against the “armed Kukis and their militants involved in ambush, abduction, extortion, loot, arson and killings”.

The hills of Manipur have been witnessing incidents of killings and arson, involving the Kukis and Nagas, since February. The violence has been largely in Kangpokpi and Ukhrul districts.

Government accountability

The WC-TNL said the inability of the government to act against the Kuki extremists would be construed as a strategic political movement against the Nagas by the present dispensation in Manipur.

Condemning Friday’s attack, the Liangmai Naga Council, Manipur, declared an immediate “total shutdown” across all Liangmai Naga-inhabited areas of the State until further notice. It appealed to all members of the committee to remain calm and united, and urged the authorities to bring the attackers to justice.

The Liangmai Nagas have recently been at the receiving end of the Kuki-Naga conflict in Manipur following the killing of three Thadou church leaders in Kangpokpi district on May 13. The killing triggered a hostage crisis, which ended with the recovery of the bodies of six Liangmai Naga captives on June 10.

Meanwhile, the security forces recovered more than 2,000 live rounds of ammunition and five firearms during a joint search operation in Manipur’s Kakching district on Friday. The firearms included three INSAS rifles.

Friday also saw the Central Reserve Police Force expanding its security arrangements for the movement of essential supplies along the Jiribam-Imphal route (National Highway 37). The force deployed additional escorts for 424 loaded trucks and fuel tankers amid a severe transport crisis.

On Thursday, stranded truckers called a 24-hour strike after a driver was found dead in his vehicle. The truckers said they were running out of cash to buy food, water, and medicines due to blockades and landslides that were impeding the movement of goods-carrying vehicles on the highway.

World.title: Arjun Ayanki taken into custody in threat case
World.content:
The Kuttampuzha police in Ernakulam took Arjun Ayanki into custody for allegedly threatening the SHOs of Kothamangalam and Oonnukal through social media.

The police took him into custody after producing a warrant at the Thalassery Sub Jail. Ayanki, who had been in police custody for allegedly insulting the Home Minister on social media, was produced before the Thalassery Chief Judicial Magistrate Court on Friday (August 14). After the court remanded him again, the Kuttampuzha police reached the jail and took him into custody.

Meanwhile, the police seized in Taliparamba the car allegedly used by Ayanki while he was absconding. The car, which belongs to his relative, was found abandoned in Taliparamba and taken into police custody.

World.title: Jharkhand student protesters plan ‘Tiranga Yatra’ to spread message of unity
World.content:
Students protesting against alleged irregularities in Jharkhand’s recruitment examinations are planning to take out a ‘Tiranga Yatra’ to celebrate India’s 80th Independence Day in Ranchi on Saturday (August 14, 2026).

JPSC-JSSC Reform Manch leader Ravindra Paswan said the “indefinite” protest, which entered its 21st day on Friday, will continue until the government accepted their demands.

“On Independence Day, we have organised a Tiranga Yatra. Students from all districts of Jharkhand will come here to participate in this march. The aim is to convey a message of unity and patriotism,“ Mr. Paswan said.

Kumar Rajat, Sub-Divisional Officer of Ranchi Sadar, and Dhananjay Kumar, Additional District Magistrate (Law and Order), went to the protest site to gather information about the march.

The march will begin at 9.30 a.m. from Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium, where the students are camping, and will pass through Kachhari Chowk, Nucleus Mall, Lalpur Chowk, Plaza Chowk, Firayalal Chowk, and Shaheed Chowk before returning to the stadium, the students said.

Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha (JLKM) leader Devendra Kumar Mahto, in a video message from the Ranchi Sadar Hospital, alleged that a few people were trying to “weaken” the protest. He urged protesting students to continue with the agitation for the “sake of reforms” in competitive examinations.

“I am under treatment at Sadar Hospital, Ranchi and continuing my hunger strike. Today is the 12th day. After the lathi-charge during the Vidhan Sabha March on August 10, I was brought to Sadar Hospital, and it has been four days now,” Mr. Mahto said in the video posted on X.

“I have been continuously urging the hospital management of Ranchi Sadar to transfer me to the protest venue, Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium, where my student friends are sitting in a peaceful protest,” he added.

Mr. Mahto demanded an inquiry into the lathi-charge on students during the August 10 rally. “I demand legal action against the official responsible for giving the order of lathi-charge,” he said, adding that the protesting students should not worry about his health.

Also Read: Agitating students accuse govt. of withholding health details of Devendra Mahto to weaken stir

“At present, the most important thing is the reform in the recruitment process, which has collapsed in Jharkhand. It is really painful that in every exam, there is a paper leak, irregularities and jobs are being offered on recommendations,” he said.

He added that the “soul of Jharkhand is being sold” with these jobs. “Jharkhand is in danger, and you all have to save it. I will appeal to the officials of the State government that power comes and goes in democracy. Do not become a slave and follow the instructions of the government blindly,” Mr. Mahto said.

In a related development, the police continued examining video footage to identify miscreants involved in violence during the Vidhan Sabha March on Monday (August 10). The police have registered FIRs against more than 500 unnamed protesters.

World.title: PM Shehbaz briefs President Zardari on Pak-Saudi-Turkiye defence pact
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called on President Asif Ali Zardari in Islamabad on Friday and briefed him on a recently signed defence pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, according to a statement issued by the Presidency.

For his part, President Zardari “expressed his best wishes for the effective implementation of the tripartite agreement with regard to defence cooperation, regional peace and stability and promotion of the security of the Muslim ummah”, the Presidency’s statement on its X account said.

He also appreciated PM Shehbaz’s and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir’s efforts for “further strengthening the longstanding fraternal relations between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan into a robust strategic partnership”, the statement added.

The joint defence agreement, signed on August 7 in Makkah, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empowers its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.

Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia will form political and military mechanisms under the defence pact , Turkiye’s defence ministry said on Thursday, adding the alliance would also deepen defence industry cooperation.

Both Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Dar have said the pact is defensive in nature, with the latter saying that it is also “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Saturday said Turkiye expected Egypt to join the pact “in the next stage”, telling the Anadolu state news agency only “a few technical issues” stood in the way.

Egypt has not commented on the agreement nor on the remarks by Fidan.

Meanwhile, Kuwait , Bahrain and Somalia are among the countries that have welcomed it. Iran’s comments also took a rather positive tone, stressing its stance of pursuing “security mechanisms based on cooperation between regional countries”.

Counter-terrorism also discussed

Apart from discussions on the Makkah pact, “the professional capabilities of the security forces and law enforcement agencies in operations against Fitna-al-Hindustan and Fitna al-Khawarij were appreciated” during Friday’s meeting, the statement by the Presidency said.

The state has designated Balochistan-based terrorist groups as Fitna-al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan, and Fitna al Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan.

The meeting’s participants reiterated the “resolve to eradicate the scourge of terrorism” from the country, the statement said, adding that foreign and interior affairs were also discussed.

President Zardari also emphasised “the need for effective measures to provide relief to the people” in light of the current regional situation. He also stressed the need for “uninterrupted supply of essential commodities and their availability at reasonable prices”.

He “expressed the hope that Pakistan’s effective diplomatic efforts for the promotion of regional and global peace would further strengthen the country’s international standing, and that its positive impacts would be reflected in the national economy and the lives of the people”, the Presidency’s statement said.

The meeting was also attended by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Interior and Narcotics Control Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Punjab Assembly Speaker Malik Muhammad Ahmad Khan and Senator Sherry Rehman.

World.title: Petroleum dealers postpone planned strike as govt approves margin revision
World.content:
The Pakistan Petroleum Dealers’ Association (PPDA) on Friday called off its plans to begin a strike on Saturday after the government approved a proposed revision in the dealers’ margins.

The nod for the revision was also confirmed by the finance ministry in a statement, which did not specify the amount.

The Economic Coordination Committee had “deliberated on the matter regarding revision of dealers’ margins on motor spirit and high-speed diesel” during a meeting chaired by Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb, the statement said, adding that a revision of the margin had been approved.

Meanwhile, the PPDA said the government had increased the petroleum dealers’ margin by Rs1.34 per litre, bringing the total margin to Rs10 per litre.

The PPDA had threatened the strike, demanding an eight per cent increase in the petroleum dealers’ margin. Currently, the dealers’ margins are Rs8.64 per litre.

As the PPDA Chairman Bakhsh announced during a press conference in Karachi that they were calling off the strike, he also said that petroleum product prices may once again be revised every 7 or 15 days, instead of being changed daily.

Last month, the government announced that it would start revising fuel prices on a daily basis, rather than the weekly system that had been in vogue in recent months. The government on Thursday rejected the dealers’ demand for monthly price fixing, adding that it will continue the daily price-fixing mechanism for petroleum products.

In its Friday statement, the PPDA said it “had postponed Saturday’s planned strike based on the government’s assurances”.

“However, [the PPDA chairman] warned that the association would continue its protest until all of its demands were accepted,” the statement added.

The association’s vice chairman, Tariq Hassan, further said that “because dealers had not received an increase in their margin for the past three years, approximately $50 million belonging to petroleum dealers remains outstanding with the government”.

On Wednesday, the PPDA issued a 72-hour ultimatum to the government over its failure to fulfil promises made by the petroleum minister to resolve their issues, especially the increase in margin to eight per cent on the retail sale price of petrol.

The association had warned that if the government failed to meet its demands within 72 hours, petrol pumps across the country would shut down indefinitely from 6am on Saturday (August 15) and would not reopen until those demands were met.

A delegation of petroleum dealers had also held brief talks with Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik in Islamabad on Wednesday.

In the meeting, the minister had assured the delegation that a Rs1.34 per litre increase in dealers’ margin, which had been pending for two years, had already been sent to the ECC and was awaiting approval from the Federal Cabinet.

World.title: World leaders extend greetings to Pakistan on Independence Day, hail bilateral ties
World.content:
Felicitations poured in from other nations on Friday as Pakistan celebrated 79 years of independence.

World leaders and diplomats, from the Iranian president to US State Secretary Marco Rubio, not just wished Pakistan and its people on the country’s 80th Independence Day, but also took the opportunity to hail Islamabad’s ties with their countries.

Saudi Arabia’s King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman congratulated President Asif Ali Zardari, wishing the government and people of Pakistan steady progress and prosperity, according to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).

King Salman also praised the “strong relations” between the two countries, highlighting the “shared commitment to advancing cooperation across all fields”, SPA reported.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in a message to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, described Pakistan’s Independence Day as a valuable opportunity to honour the achievements of the nation, reaffirming Tehran’s firm resolve to further strengthen its relations with Pakistan, Iran’s IRNA news agency reported.

He also expressed “readiness to take more effective steps to advance bilateral ties” and “secure the common interests of both sides”, the report said.

It added that Pezeshkian noted that the “shared interests of the Iranian and Pakistani nations have become inextricably interwoven, a reality that underscores the need for greater synergy and closer cooperation” and stressed that a “new turning point has begun in deepening and expanding the longstanding and strategic relations” between Tehran and Islamabad.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi congratulated his Pakistani counterpart, Ishaq Dar, according to IRNA.

The state-run Iranian news agency reported that Araghchi said that continued political consultations and the strengthening of economic, trade, border, security, and cultural cooperation between the two countries would pave the way to leverage existing capacities and secure their shared interests.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in his message on Pakistan’s Independence Day, appreciated “the partnership between our nations and the bonds of friendship between our peoples”.

“Together, through our cooperation on regional mediation, critical minerals, energy, counterterrorism, cultural heritage, and trade and investment, we are turning potential into progress and delivering real results for Americans and Pakistanis alike,” Rubio said.

In Islamabad, US Chargé d’Affaires Natalie Baker met Dar and congratulated him.

Turkiye’s Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz also congratulated Pakistan and posted on X: “Our relations with Pakistan are based on an exceptional brotherhood nourished by our shared history, common values, and our determination to stand by each other in difficult times”.

He noted that the recent defence agreement between Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had “added a new dimension” to relations between Ankara and Islamabad.

Turkiye’s foreign ministry also extended felicitations to the “friendly and brotherly Pakistan”.

Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, in a message to President Zardari, congratulated Pakistan on Independence Day, the Qatar News Agency reported.

Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a phone call with Dar and “extended warm greetings on Pakistan’s Independence Day to the leadership, government and people of Pakistan, and conveyed his best wishes for continued peace, progress and prosperity,” the FO said in another post.

Chinese ambassador to Pakistan, Jiang Zaidong, met Dar, congratulated him and reaffirmed the “close and time-tested ties between” Islamabad and China, according to the FO.

Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin congratulated President Zardari and PM Shehbaz, commending Pakistan-Russia relations.

“I am confident that we will continue our constructive joint efforts to further strengthen the entire spectrum of our partnership for the benefit of the friendly peoples of Russia and Pakistan, and in the interests of enhancing international security and stability,” a post on the Russian embassy’s X account quoted him as saying.

UK High Commissioner to Pakistan Jane Marriott, in a meeting with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, “conveyed warm wishes” on Pakistan’s Independence Day, the Foreign Office (FO) said on X.

Sultan of Oman Haitham bin Tarik and Kuwait’s Crown Prince Sheikh Sabah Al Khaled Al Hamad Al Sabah congratulated Pakistan in their messages to President Zardari.

Somalia’s Foreign Ministry also extended congratulations to Pakistan.

In a post on X, the ministry said, “The Federal Republic of Somalia congratulates the government and people of Pakistan on their 79th Independence anniversary, reaffirming our commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation and friendship between our two nations”.

Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in a statement posted on X, congratulated the Pakistani government and people, adding that “Romania remains committed to further strengthening our bilateral relations, including under the EU-Pakistan framework”.

Georgia, meanwhile, expressed its “cordial wishes for peace and prosperity of Pakistani people”, adding that it was looking forward to “further advancing our friendly relations”.

Azerbaijan also extended “heartfelt congratulations to the brotherly people and the government of Pakistan”.

World.title: Balochistan home minister unhurt as convoy comes under attack in Mastung
World.content:
QUETTA: Six people, including three police personnel, were injured in an armed attack on the convoy of Balochistan Home Minister Mir Ziaullah Langove in Mastung on Friday.

A senior police official told Dawn that the home minister remained unhurt in the attack, which occurred as his convoy reached the Khad Kocha area of Mastung. He said that Langove was on his way to Quetta from Kalat.

The official added that six people sustained bullet injuries in the attack, three of whom were police personnel.

Nawab Raisani Memorial Hospital’s Dr Sana also confirmed to Dawn that six injured had been brought to the hospital and two of them were in serious condition. She said two of the others were referred to Quetta.

Security forces have cordoned off the area and launched a search operation.

Langove, who is from the Balochistan Awami Party, was sworn in as provincial home minister in March.

Langove had also served as the provincial home minister previously, but his appointment was declared null and void after he was de-notified on August 21, 2024.

World.title: Afghan soil being used against Pakistan, Naqvi tells Norway FM as two discuss counterterrorism cooperation
World.content:
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Friday met with Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide, where the two sides discussed counterterrorism cooperation, particularly the use of Afghan soil in terror attacks against Pakistan.

Eide arrived in Pakistan a day earlier on a two-day visit — the first by a Norwegian foreign minister in a decade.

According to a handout issued by the interior ministry, the two leaders discussed strengthening bilateral relations and the regional situation. Naqvi and Eide also agreed to improve cooperation in counterterrorism, prevention of illegal immigration, police training, and mutual legal assistance.

The two sides held discussions on the situation in neighbouring Afghanistan and the activities of proscribed organisations operating from the neighbouring country.

During the meeting, Eide lauded Pakistan’s “constructive and active” role in the US-Iran war. The two sides also discussed measures taken against illegal immigration to Europe from Pakistan.

“Pakistan’s effective measures have led to a 47 per cent reduction in illegal immigration to Europe,” the statement quoted Naqvi as saying, adding that “a zero-tolerance policy has been adopted against illegal immigration”.

He said that Pakistan’s measures against illegal immigration were also appreciated by the European Union.

“Promoting legal immigration is very important for effectively curbing illegal immigration,” he said.

According to the statement, Naqvi told Eide that “Afghan soil is continuously being used for terrorism in Pakistan” and that Pakistan stood “as a wall” between the world and terrorist elements.

“Everyone must work together for the complete eradication of terrorism.” Naqvi was quoted as saying. He also told Eide that his visit would be an “important milestone” in strengthening bilateral relations between Norway and Pakistan.

In the meeting, Eide appreciated the “active role” of the Pakistani diaspora in Norway and their contributions in sectors ranging from politics to health.

Minister of State Talal Chaudhry and other senior officials were present at the meeting as well, the statement added.

On Thursday, Eide held a series of engagements with top civilian and military leadership, where the two sides discussed expanding cooperation in trade, investment, technology, climate resilience, maritime affairs, skilled labour and security, while also exchanging views on regional developments.

World.title: Trump's envoy Jared Kushner to visit Israel to bridge gaps on Gaza plan
World.content:
US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner will visit Israel next week in hopes of bridging gaps on a Gaza plan rejected by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, officials said Friday.

Kushner and Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative for Gaza of Trump’s so-called Board of Peace implementing the deal, will visit both Israel and key mediator Egypt.

The trip comes after Netanyahu publicly rejected a 15-point plan announced by Mladenov in which Hamas agreed to hand over its weapons to a new Palestinian governing committee in Gaza.

A Board of Peace official said Kushner and Mladenov hoped for “constructive conversations” on advancing Trump’s overall peace plan that began with the October 2025 declaration of a ceasefire, which has reduced but not ended Israeli strikes in Gaza.

“The United States and Israel agree on the end state, which is a demilitarised Hamas,” the official said on condition of anonymity.

“We will hear the concerns that have been raised and talk about next steps.

“What is critical is that we both agree on the desired outcome and are finding ways to accelerate progress.”

The latest part of the Gaza plan, to which Hamas agreed in late July, would start a phased Israeli withdrawal from much of the Gaza Strip, according to an initial version released by the Board of Peace.

Mladenov later backtracked and said that Israel would not need to pull out troops until a complete Hamas disarmament.

Netanyahu had vowed no pullout and has voiced scepticism that Hamas would disarm, saying it should destroy weapons in a verifiable way.

World.title: Indian firm to make fighter jet engines with Rolls-Royce
World.content:
India’s Reliance Industries and Britain’s Rolls-Royce announced on Friday plans to jointly design and manufacture engines for New Delhi’s multirole indigenous fighter jet programme.

Reliance Industries Limited, India’s largest private sector company, has been expanding into defence production in military aerospace and advanced munitions to support Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ‘Make in India’ initiative.

India, one of the world’s largest arms importers, has made the modernisation of its defence forces a top priority, with repeated pushes to boost domestic production.

Rolls-Royce builds engines for commercial use by the world’s biggest aircraft manufacturers Airbus and Boeing, as well as for fighter jets.

The pair of industry giants issued a joint statement announcing “their strategic intent to partner and offer capabilities for the design, development, manufacturing and delivery of a sovereign indigenous combat engine for India’s Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme”.

The statement did not reveal the scale of investment the two companies will make for the partnership.

The AMCA is India’s flagship fifth-generation stealth multirole fighter jet, developed locally for its air force.

The partnership “marks a major milestone towards building a robust, self-reliant aerospace ecosystem in the country,” the statement quoted Rolls-Royce Chief Executive Tufan Erginbilgic as saying.

“Together, we aim to build an enduring national capability that can make India self-reliant and, over time, globally competitive in advanced propulsion technologies,” said Reliance Executive Director Anant Ambani.

Under Modi, India has prioritised modernisation of its military “driven by a self-reliant and future-ready defence sector”, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh told soldiers on Friday on the eve of the country’s 80th independence day.

Last month, India approved the purchase of a range of military equipment worth $5.46 billion, including missiles, electronic warfare systems and kamikaze drones.

New Delhi, over the last decade, has sought to reduce its dependence on Russia, its traditional main supplier of military equipment, turning to other countries like the United States and France, as well as boosting domestic production.

India is also rapidly modernising its navy with domestic production of ships and submarines.

A four-day conflict with Pakistan last year highlighted the need for Delhi to upgrade its defence capabilities.

Earlier this year, New Delhi approved the purchase of $39 billion worth of defence equipment, including Rafale jets from France.

India’s current defence budget is $85 billion.

World.title: Pakistan's leadership stresses need for unity, reforms as nation celebrates Independence Day
World.content:
Pakistan’s civilian and military leadership has stressed the need for unity and reforms as the nation celebrates 79 years of independence today.

According to state-run Radio Pakistan, the day dawned with a 31-gun salute in Islamabad and a 21-gun salute at the provincial headquarters. A change of guards ceremony was also held at the mausoleum of Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah in Karachi.

Flag hoisting ceremonies were also held at the Supreme Court and the Federal Constitutional Court in Islamabad.

‘Pakistan’s security linked to peace in our neighbourhood’

In his message, President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to Quaid-i-Azam, those behind the Pakistan Movement and those who sacrificed their homes, security and livelihoods in the struggle for a homeland.

“But independence is not only a historic achievement. It is also a responsibility that each generation must carry forward. The Pakistan that was created through the democratic will of its people must continue to grow stronger, more secure and more prosperous. Our task is not only to remember what earlier generations achieved, but to add to it through our own work,” he said.

The president said that the past year had reminded citizens of the strength of the Pakistani nation.

Recalling last year’s brief military conflict with India, he said, “The events surrounding Marka-i-Haq demonstrated that Pakistan seeks peace, but also possesses the resolve and capacity to defend its sovereignty and national interests. The lesson of strength is ultimately a lesson of responsibility. A country that can defend itself must also use its strength to prevent conflict, protect peace and serve the interests of its people.”

He said that the security and stability enjoyed today had come at a great cost, paying tribute to the martyrs of the armed forces, law enforcement agencies and police.

“Their courage and commitment have helped safeguard our nation against external aggression and the threat of terrorism. The people of Pakistan remain deeply grateful for their service,” he said.

He also highlighted Pakistan’s efforts to facilitate dialogue in the region.

“Pakistan has effectively used its channels of communication, its geographical location and diplomatic capital to encourage dialogue and de-escalation at a time when wider conflict could have serious consequences for the region and the world,” he said.

He reiterated that all disputes must be ultimately addressed through dialogue and diplomacy.

“Our security is linked to the peace and stability of our neighbourhood and the world at large. Pakistan will continue to support efforts that reduce tensions, protect regional stability and create conditions for cooperation,” he said.

The president also went on to say that the country must focus on the work that will determine Pakistan’s future.

“We must strengthen our economy, create greater opportunities for our young people, improve education and skills, strengthen institutions through a series of governance, economic and social reforms to ensure that the benefits of development and democracy reach every part and community of the country,” he said.

“Pakistan’s greatest strength is its young people. Across the country and around the world, they are demonstrating their talent in science, technology, business, education and the creative industries. Our responsibility is to give them the education, skills and opportunities they need to realise their potential. By investing in our youth today, we are investing in Pakistan’s future,” he added.

“For ordinary Pakistanis, national progress is measured in practical terms. It means a young person finding the skills and opportunity to build a career. It means a family being able to access quality education and healthcare. It means farmers, workers, traders and businesses being able to plan for the future with greater confidence. The strength of Pakistan will ultimately be judged by whether our national progress improves the lives of its people,” President Zardari said.

He also voiced Pakistan’s support for the people of occupied Kashmir, saying Pakistan will continue to support a peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with the aspirations of its people and the relevant United Nations resolutions.

On Afghanistan, the president said that Pakistan had always respected and supported the national sovereignty of our neighbour Afghanistan and expected the same reciprocity.

“It is sad that the current interim regime of Afghanistan is allowing and supporting a cocktail of terror groups to use their soil for launching attacks against neighbouring countries including Pakistan. It is sad the Taliban regime of Afghanistan is collaborating with India in launching terror attacks against Pakistani civilians and security personnel. They are doing this to distract us from the peace building efforts of Pakistan, recognised by the entire world,” he said.

“I warn them to stop these evil actions against the people of Pakistan and assure all and sundry that the armed forces of Pakistan are capable of defeating these evil designs,” he said.

He ended his message by calling on the nation to contribute to the country’s progress in whatever field they serve.

‘Pakistan committed to defending its national interests’

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also began his message by paying tribute to the founding leaders of Pakistan, saying the nation owed the fulfilment of its dream of an independent homeland to their vision, statesmanship and sacrifices.

Highlighting the government’s economic achievements over the past two-and-a-half years, PM Shehbaz said the country had successfully navigated challenging circumstances to achieve economic stability and was now moving towards becoming a developed economy.

He noted that remittances from overseas Pakistanis had increased by $11.3 billion over the past two years, which he termed a reflection of their confidence in government policies.
