“We will soon present a draft of the relevant legislative amendments addressing these issues,” he said, without specifying what changes the amendments would introduce.

Border crossings: more people entered than left

Nelli Davtyan, acting head of the Migration and Citizenship Service, also spoke to journalists. She recalled that last year Armenia recorded a “significant positive figure” in the difference between the number of citizens entering and leaving the country. The figure stood at 8,660.

In the first half of this year, the difference between entries and exits stood at 1,347.

“There were 871,409 entries and 870,062 exits. If we compare this with figures for the first half of previous years, last year’s figure was -20,065, while in 2024 it was -22,893,” Davtyan noted.

She stressed that the figure usually rises in the second half of the year. This happens because seasonal migrant workers return home after leaving the country for temporary work. They usually leave in early spring and return in autumn. Davtyan therefore described a positive figure already in the first half of the year as “exceptional”.

More than 6,000 people granted temporary residence permits

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia had transformed from a country that “sends” migrants abroad into a country that receives migrants. “The second major trend is the growing interest in Armenia among foreign nationals,” he noted.

Nelli Davtyan said the Migration and Citizenship Service had received 9,534 applications for one-year temporary residence permits: “Of these, 6,059 were approved. Compared with previous years, the number of applications has almost tripled. The proportion of approved applications has also nearly tripled.”

According to Davtyan, the number of applications for three-year residence permits has also increased, although more modestly: “In previous years, the figure stood at 1,500-1,700, while in the first half of this year it had already reached 2,085.”

Armenia implementing 53 EU recommendations on visa liberalisation

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia was actively cooperating with the European Union on visa liberalisation. He recalled that Armenia received its first report on the implementation of the action plan in May 2026. The report gave a fairly positive assessment of the steps taken by the Armenian government.

“The EU presented us with 53 recommendations. To complete our work, we divided them into specific actions. We broke down the recommendations so that we could clearly identify the steps we need to take to implement them,” Kazaryan explained.

Based on the 53 recommendations, an Armenian working group drew up a list of 117 actions. More than half of them have already been completed.

The recommendations form part of the first stage of the visa liberalisation action plan. This stage covers legislation and policy development only. The authorities expect to assess how effectively Armenia has implemented the first stage by early 2027 or during the first half of the year. If the results prove positive, work on the second stage will begin.

Rise in applications for Armenian citizenship

World.title: Myth Detector: 230 fake social media accounts created to create illusion of support for Georgian PM’s statements
World.content:
Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

1On 2 August, marking the 18th anniversary of the 2008 August War, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze held a briefing. He focused in particular on what he described as the spread of “Russophobia” in Georgia and the role of the so-called “deep state” in this process.

After the briefing, pro-government messages began circulating widely on social media. Various media outlets also published visual materials promoting these messages.

According to a study by Myth Detector, 230 fake accounts took part in the campaign. The organisation analysed likes on social media posts, as well as the photos and activity of the profiles that shared them. It identified signs of coordinated and suspicious behaviour that, according to the study, aimed to increase support for specific government narratives.

The study also says the profiles were designed to appear as if they belonged to different socio-demographic groups. Some accounts used photographs depicting idyllic family life to make themselves appear more trustworthy.

Profile photos were generated using artificial intelligence (AI)

According to Hive Moderation, a tool for detecting AI-generated images, there was more than a 90% probability that all 230 profile photos had been generated using AI. In some cases, the probability reached 100%. A visual inspection also identified features typical of AI-generated images, including unnatural shapes of hands and fingers, as well as certain distortions.

The photos repeat the same settings and compositions

Some accounts use identical or very similar photos, including the same images with minor changes. The visual design of different accounts also repeats similar photography styles and details. These include photos with a consistent aesthetic, featuring Tbilisi in the background, a glass of wine or a cup of coffee, a hand touching the head, or similar compositional choices. The accounts also use images showing people having fun, relaxing or taking part in sports to create an impression of authenticity. In some cases, different accounts use the same first and last names.

An illusion of broad support is created through artificially diverse social and demographic profiles

The campaign creates the impression that it brings together people of different ages, appearances and interests. The profiles include young and older people, supporters of conservative and alternative views, as well as religious people, family-oriented users, sports enthusiasts and people who enjoy outdoor activities.

AI-generated accounts use real workplaces and educational institutions to make their profiles appear more credible

Most profiles list places of education and employment, including the Tbilisi Transport Company, various Georgian insurance companies, commercial banks, microfinance organisations, government agencies and municipal services.

Different accounts show identical behaviour

Most profiles list a date between 20 and 24 July 2026 as the date they began living in Georgian cities, although some accounts appear to have been created earlier.

Profile activity focuses on the same messages

The activity of the suspicious accounts, particularly their likes, is concentrated on posts featuring conspiracy claims by the ruling party’s chairman about the “party of global war”, the “deep state’s plan” and the “opening of a second front”. They also engage with the narrative about “Russophobia”, suggesting an artificial increase in the level of support.

Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

World.title: Russia no longer attracts Armenian migrant workers as they look for new opportunities in Europe
World.content:
Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

The geography of labour migration from Armenia is changing. Russia, which until recently remained the main destination, has become less attractive. The main reasons are Russia’s economic downturn, driven by the war in Ukraine, and the depreciation of the rouble.

Many migrants are now returning from Russia to Armenia. Some are trying to find work in their home villages or in the capital, while others are looking for new opportunities, particularly in Europe. The direction of labour migration is changing, with European countries becoming increasingly popular.

Work visa for Poland

After two years working at a meat-processing plant in Poland, 40-year-old Serob (name changed) returned to Armenia for a month. He came to prepare all the necessary documents and take his wife and children with him to Warsaw.

“I received a three-year residence permit and the right to work. Living away from my family is difficult. I decided that we should be together. I should also say that Poland has become one of the first steps towards the European labour market for many people. Many of my friends work in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and other countries on legal work visas. I was also offered a job in the Netherlands, but I decided to stay in Poland,” he says.

Serob is a butcher. He was also in demand in Armenia. However, he says his salary there was not enough to support his family:

“I had friends who worked as butchers in Europe. They told me that the profession was in demand there and well paid. Gradually, I started thinking: why not try going to Europe and working there? I also had a lot of debts and loans. I went to Poland on a work visa. The process moved slowly. The Polish embassy invited me for an interview a year after I submitted my application.”

A recruitment agency then sent his details to a meat-processing company. Representatives of the company interviewed Serob online. During the video call, he demonstrated his professional skills to the employer, including how he deboned meat.

“The employer liked my work and sent me a contract and the necessary documents. The embassy then approved my work visa. At first, I lived in a house in Poland with people of different nationalities. They all worked for the same company and lived in separate rooms. Later, when my financial situation improved, I moved into a separate flat with a friend from Armenia. I sent most of my earnings to my family to help resolve our financial problems. I did not work in a shop or at a market. I worked at a specialised meat-processing plant with refrigerated storage facilities. It is physically demanding work,” the butcher says.

He notes a shortage of butchers in the European labour market, which creates demand for migrants with the necessary skills. Meat-processing plants employ workers from Ukraine, Argentina, Azerbaijan and Armenia.

“Many Armenians are now going to European countries for work. And not only to meat-processing plants. When I flew to Poland, I met some women who worked as pastry chefs on the plane. They were also travelling to Poland under legal employment contracts. Many Armenians also work in shops. These are people who speak foreign languages. In any case, I am happy. I will return to work in a month, this time with my family,” Serob says.

Working at a German medical clinic with an Armenian degree

Doctors, teachers and highly skilled professionals in various fields are also in demand on the European labour market. Dentist Edgar Mirzoyan has been living and working in Germany for nine months.

Edgar Mirzoyan

“One day, my nurse told me that her friend worked in Germany and that they might need a dentist. I simply gave her my contact details and forgot about it. Some time later, they contacted me. At the same time, I started learning German. The whole process took two years: learning the language, preparing documents and taking exams. Finally, I moved to Germany. By the way, getting my Armenian degree recognised in Germany seemed more realistic and achievable than in other European countries,” Edgar says.

At the same time, the 30-year-old dentist studied not only the professional requirements but also the overall situation in the country, including its economy, level of safety and even happiness index.

“Geography also influenced my final decision. It was important for me to stay connected to Armenia. You can get from Germany to Armenia in just a few hours. In this sense, Europe was a much more convenient destination for me than, for example, Canada. Before moving to Germany, I had a completely different idea of what it would be like. Of course, everyone’s experience is different. Some doctors who arrived at the same time as me had a much harder journey. A lot depends on which city you move to, who your employer is and who you interact with. Everyone has their own experience,” he says.

Edgar started working two days after arriving in Germany. Some time later, his wife also joined him.

“Before moving to Germany, I registered in advance to take a language exam. They tested my knowledge of medical German. I passed the exam successfully. After that, I received a temporary licence valid for two years. I can work during this period, but I must work under the supervision of an experienced doctor.

However, the process of having my degree fully recognised is still under way. The authorities compare my entire university curriculum, the number of hours I completed and the subjects I studied with the German curriculum. I applied for this process while I was still in Armenia. They only started reviewing my documents after two years of waiting. If they find differences between the curricula, I will have to make up the gaps. It is not yet clear how significant those differences will be,” the doctor says.

According to Edgar, working in Germany has its own particularities. Berlin is a multicultural city, and his patients include not only Germans. About 30 per cent are Armenians and Yazidis, while another 30 per cent are Russians and Ukrainians.

Edgar continues to practise in Armenia as well:

“I can take leave twice a year. I come to Armenia, mainly perform implant procedures and surgeries, and then return to Germany. I have many patients who wait for me to come back. They book appointments in advance, I come and perform the surgery, and the next stage of treatment takes place three to six months later, when I can return again.”

When labour migration is a family choice

For many people who move to Europe, leaving is a decision about their family’s future, improving their living conditions and trying to build a new life in a different environment.

Vergine (name changed) chose this path. She has lived in the Czech Republic with her husband for seven years and now has two children.

“First, my husband moved to Prague on a work visa. He started working in the security department of a shopping centre. Two years later, I joined him. We made the decision consciously, after carefully considering everything. We wanted to settle down and continue our lives in a European country. In this sense, the Czech Republic seemed like a suitable option, and we are very happy with our choice,” Vergine says.

Before moving to the Czech Republic, the couple worked at Zvartnots Airport.

“At first, I worked at a language centre as an English teacher. Then my second child was born here. Of course, there were many difficulties. We lived in a foreign country without support from relatives and with a small child, but we managed. I now work as an English teacher at a school,” she says.

The young family does not plan to return to Armenia for now, but they regularly visit their relatives.

“We have the right to live and work here, but I am sure that one day we will definitely return,” Vergine says.

Changing migration patterns

According to Tatevik Bezhanian, an expert with the migration programme of the charitable organisation Armenian Caritas, Armenia currently has no statistics showing how many people leave for European countries to work.

One reason is that Armenia has no intergovernmental labour migration agreements with EU countries. Bulgaria is the only exception. In addition, most people who leave for Europe find jobs through private recruitment agencies, and the state does not register this process.

“You will not find this data in official statistics. On the other hand, we also do not have a migration card system under which people have to state when entering or leaving the country that they are going abroad to work. They may not indicate the purpose of their departure at all,” Bezhanian says.

She says this problem is not unique to Armenia. Internationally, governments mainly register migrant workers arriving in their countries because they can manage these migration flows. Countries that pursue targeted labour migration policies, sign bilateral agreements and organise the recruitment of their citizens abroad usually have comprehensive data on those who leave. The Philippines and Uzbekistan are among them, for example.

Tatevik Bezhanian notes that even when Armenian authorities want information about labour migrants leaving for Russia, they have to rely on official Russian statistics:

“If the geography of labour migration expands, we will have to approach the relevant authorities in countries such as Poland, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. We will need to obtain data and determine how many Armenian citizens work there.”

Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

World.title: Opinion on Georgian petrol in Abkhazia: ‘If needed, it’s possible’
World.content:
The indirect consequence of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries has been a fuel crisis in Abkhazia, which in recent years has been buying petrol from Russia.

After struggling with shortages for two weeks, Abkhazia decided to buy petrol from Georgia. Given the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, this was a rather “unorthodox” move, but at the same time the only viable way out of the situation.

In a blog post, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz outlet Chegemskaya Pravda, discusses whether Abkhazia can trade with Georgia.

Inal Khashig: “Abkhazia has been grappling with a petrol shortage for the past two weeks. There is virtually no fuel left in the country. Government assurances that the situation is under control and that a new shipment of petrol is about to arrive have done little to reassure people — if anything, they have only deepened the pessimism. Queues at petrol stations stretch as far as the eye can see.

And then petrol arrived from an unexpected source — Georgia.

Tbilisi says the government has nothing to do with it and that it is entirely a private business matter. Sukhumi, for its part, says that when the country is facing a fuel shortage, it will not prevent petrol tankers from entering from Georgia. After all, there is precedent for this kind of economic contact: during the difficult 1990s, we supplied Georgians with relatively cheap fuel.

This particular fuel crisis has once again brought an enduring Abkhaz question to the fore: should we trade with an enemy state or not?”

To me, it is quite straightforward: if this kind of cooperation is vital for the country as a whole, its economy and the well-being of its people, then it is justified. Sukhumi has, after all, cooperated with Tbilisi in the energy sector throughout the post-war years, and no one objects because there is no alternative. This cooperation is vital to both Abkhazia and Georgia.

And now, when the whole of Abkhazia — and with it the country’s economy — has ground to a halt because of the lack of petrol, refusing to buy fuel from the Georgians looks like outright posturing.

Incidentally, I think the government’s argument that Abkhazia actively sold petrol to Georgia in the 1990s is a very good one. At the time, war-ravaged Abkhazia was under a severe blockade: Russia under Boris Yeltsin had effectively sealed us off on all sides. Nothing could be brought in or taken out. About the only thing permitted was taking mandarins across the border in handcarts, with Abkhaz women effectively serving as beasts of burden.

Abkhazia’s tiny budget was funded by selling timber and scrap metal to Turkey, as well as by smuggling fuel into Georgia.

The latter involved considerable risk and loss of life, as fuel tankers had to travel towards the Georgian border through the Gali district, which was unstable at the time. But there was effectively no other way of bringing even a little money into the state coffers. Whatever anyone may say, those modest revenues helped Abkhazia survive at the time.

And yes, we traded with Georgia then because we had to.

And we need to do so now to protect the country from a fuel crisis.

And in future, we need to take similarly responsible steps, even if they run counter to established dogmas. Rigid dogma is not the best guide to action in crises like the one we are facing now.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Analysts say Ukraine is preparing a large-scale offensive
World.content:
Ukraine Launches Large-Scale Offensive

Based on reporting by Novosti Donbassa

Ukrainian defense forces have liberated 19 settlements across several sectors of the front, according to DeepState, a Ukrainian battlefield monitoring project, which reported the advances after updating its combat map.

According to the analysts, Ukrainian forces have regained control of Zelenyi Hai, Novokhatske, Hrushevske, Tolstoi, Zirka, Yalta, Piddubne, Myrne, Voskresenka, Sichneve, Vorone, Ternove, Berezove, Stepne, Kalynovske, Pryvillia, Zlahoda, Rybne and Krasnohorske.

In addition, Ukrainian troops pushed Russian forces back in six other settlements: Novopavlivka, Novoheorhiivka, Novomykolaivka, Novohryhorivka, Zaporizke and Pryvilne.

The Ukrainian military also released video footage from settlements it said had been liberated in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions.

exchange

World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: Luigi Mangione admits killing UnitedHealthcare CEO
World.content:
Luigi Mangione has admitted to fatally shooting a health insurance executive and pleaded guilty to two federal charges of stalking the executive with the intent to kill him.

The guilty plea will avert a federal trial in the closely watched case over the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, a brazen crime that was condemned by public officials but became emblematic of Americans' frustration with health insurance industry practices.

It could also allow Mangione, 28, to seek dismissal of state murder charges and delay an upcoming trial in that case.

US District Judge Margaret Garnett told Mangione that if he pleaded guilty, he could face a maximum sentence of life in prison on each count. Judge Garnett set Mangione's sentencing for December 18.

Mangione's lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, said there was no plea agreement with prosecutors.

Mr Thompson led UnitedHealth Group's insurance unit before he was shot dead in the early morning of December 4, 2024, outside the New York City hotel where an investor conference was taking place.

In court today, Mr Thompson's widow, Paulette, sat in the front row of the gallery with other members of his family.

Brian Thompson's widow Paulette was in court to see Luigi Mangione admit the shooting. (Reuters: David Dee Delgado)

Mangione told the court that he researched details of UnitedHealthcare's annual investor conference in December 2024 after suffering a broken back and navigating the health insurance system.

He said he then used a 3D printer to make part of a gun and travelled to New York with the intent of killing Mr Thompson.

"I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died," Mangione said.

Graphic footage of the killing and a five-day manhunt for a suspect made the case a media fixture and social media sensation. Mangione was arrested in Pennsylvania.

No possibility of death penalty

He had previously pleaded not guilty in April 2025 to murder, weapons and stalking charges brought by Manhattan federal prosecutors.

Judge Garnett threw out the murder and weapons charges over legal technicalities in a surprise ruling in January 2026.

Luigi Mangione's to-do list revealed in court The documents shed new light on the steps the 27-year-old may have taken — or planned to take — to avoid capture after UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson's killing last year.

The decision eliminated the possibility that Mangione would face the death penalty in the federal case, though he still faces a possible sentence of life without parole if convicted on the remaining stalking charges.

His federal trial was most recently set for January.

Mangione separately pleaded not guilty in December 2024 to state terrorism, murder, weapons and forgery charges brought by Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg.

The terrorism charges were thrown out by a judge in September 2025. A trial in that case is scheduled for September 8 before Justice Gregory Carro in Manhattan.

Mangione would face 25 years to life in prison if convicted of second-degree murder.

The guilty plea in the federal case could allow Mangione to seek dismissal of the murder charge under New York's double jeopardy law, which protects people from being prosecuted twice for the same conduct.

Mr Bragg's office would oppose the move, arguing that the murder charge is legally distinct from the federal charges. Whoever loses would likely seek an emergency appeal.

Reuters

World.title: Tourists among those evacuated from Croatia as wildfires stretch across Europe
World.content:
A wildfire engulfed homes in a picturesque Croatian resort overnight, killing one person, injuring 40 and forcing 1,200 to evacuate, officials said, as the EU warned that pockets of "very extreme" wildfire conditions stretched across the continent.

Hundreds more were evacuated from a beach resort in northern Greece and from a village in southwest France, while a major grass fire engulfed houses in England, officials said.

England's Stourbridge saw multiple homes lost after a grass fire began on the hottest day of the year. (Reuters: Temilade Adelaja)

Record-breaking heat and drought that scientists link to climate change have created ideal conditions for wildfires across Europe this summer, especially in France, Spain and Greece. The Balkans region has also endured several heatwaves.

Flames turn night sky red

Local residents and tourists described scenes of chaos as they fled in their cars from a fire outside Omis, a scenic town on Croatia's prized Dalmatian coast surrounded by trees and rocky hills.

Mario Vukucis stands next to his brother's burnt-out cafe and bar in Stanici, Croatia. (Reuters: Antonio Bronic)

"The flames were licking both sides of the road. When I got a little further around the bend and looked, I saw flames shooting up from under my hood. The car was on fire!" said local resident Ljubica Uglesic.

Nearly 300 fire fighters were deployed to a blaze in Croatia. (Reuters: Antonio Bronic)

The fire, which turned the night sky red, appeared to have calmed on Friday morning, said Chief Fire Commander Slavko Tucakovic.

Authorities found one charred body while, of 40 people treated in the nearby hospital in Split, seven were in a serious condition, the hospital said.

Dinghies help in rescue from Greek seaside town

In northern Greece, people wearing face masks, some clutching children or pets, boarded dinghies and boats in the seaside town of Siviri as the fire devoured a forest and columns of smoke turned the cloudless sky a dark grey.

The coastguard said that more than 300 people had been evacuated by boat from the town, which sits on a peninsula of woodland, olive groves and beaches south of Greece's second city, Thessaloniki.

Those forced to flee found shelter through the Red Cross and tourists were among the evacuees. (Reuters: Alexandros Avramidis)

More than 140 firefighters, nine aircraft and seven helicopters were deployed to battle flames, while fishing vessels took part in the evacuation.

In Britain, Simon Markey was playing golf in Stourbridge, in central England, when he saw a fire start in a field nearby and spread quickly across the golf course despite efforts by firefighters to contain it.

It reached an area of houses, said local resident Paul Nash, whose neighbour's house burned down.

Ten homes were burnt in fires in England, while two fire fighters and a child were taken to hospital. (Reuters: Temilade Adelaja)

"I heard a scream, and all the trees along the railway track were exploding. They weren't just setting fire, they were exploding. So we just grabbed everything and left," Mr Nash said.

In France, authorities evacuated 525 people from the village of Luglon after a wildfire broke out in the southwestern Landes region, not far from an area already devastated by major blazes this summer.

Fires near Bordeaux have remained consistent throughout summer. (AP: Emma Da Silva)

Rescue services in Spain late on Thursday launched an operation to remove the remains of three kings who ruled the Aragón region in the 11th ​century from a monastery threatened by a wildfire.

An even larger fire in Huelva, in southern Spain, has burned 31,000 hectares so far and forced the evacuation of 700 people.

Only 100 kilometres from a region which saw 50,000 hectares fire-damaged last month, the south of France continues to burn. (Reuters: Stephanie Lecocq)

Firefighting planes in Spain have clocked more than 8,200 hours flying time so far this year, exceeding the number of hours flown in 2025, when a record 393,000 hectares of land burned, Spain's Environment Minister Sara Aagesen said on Bluesky.

'Very extreme' wildfire condition across Europe

The European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service warned of "very extreme" conditions across a large area of central and eastern Europe, with additional pockets over southern Britain, Ireland, northern France and southern Sweden, in its outlook for the week to August 19.

By Friday a fire in Germany had affected 300 hectares of land and encroached on residential homes. (Reuters: Timm Reichert)

The average high across Western Europe on Friday was forecast to be 31.2 degrees Celsius (88 degrees Fahrenheit), which is 8 C (14 F) above what was typical from 1961 to 1990, data from the Reuters Climate Monitor showed. The temperature for Europe as a whole was 1.6 C (2.9 F) above the 1961-1990 average, it said.

The hot, dry summer is also taking a heavy toll on agriculture. Relentless heat and drought could halve this year's French maize harvest and reduce European Union production to its smallest in decades, according to analysts.

Reuters

World.title: Deborah Mailman becomes first Indigenous inductee to Logies Hall of Fame
World.content:
Deborah Mailman is set to become the first Indigenous person to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame.

"This means everything," Mailman, a Bidjara and Maori actor, tells ABC Radio National's Awaye!

"For me and for our mob, this isn't just recognition for me.

"It's recognition for everyone who's gone before me, who changed things for someone like me to be doing the work that I'm doing."

On Sunday Mailman will become the sixth woman to join the list in just over 40 years, following recent inductees Rebecca Gibney (2024) and Magda Szubanski (2025).

"Times are changing, thankfully, but it's 2026," Mailman says.

"To be the first [Indigenous person] — it's long overdue. Not just for me, but for anyone in this industry."

Mailman sees the milestone as a reflection of how Australian TV has changed in the last 10 to 20 years.

"Where the most exciting storytelling is coming from is the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander sector," she says.

"It's just getting stronger and stronger … look at the skill that's there, that has been nurtured over a long time, to get to the point where we have so many of our mob doing incredible work."

2026 Logie nominations The annual awards show also introduced a new category honouring Australian sports journalists, named after legendary commentator Bruce McAvaney.

Mailman picked up her most recent Logie in 2024, taking out best lead actress in a drama for playing renegade politician Alex Irving in ABC TV's Total Control.

It was her sixth, following industry and publicly voted wins for shows including Mabo, Redfern Now and Mystery Road.

Speaking to ABC Arts at the Logies that year, she described how it felt to win the award for the show's final season in the year of the failed Voice to Parliament referendum.

"Over the four or so years [of making Total Control], we had a new prime minister, throw a pandemic in the middle of it, and then the country voted no," she said.

"To be part of this production that kept us [Indigenous peoples] in that focus, that kept our narrative strong, that meant everything to me. That meant everything to all of us who are part of it."

A foot in the door

Mailman's first Logie came in 2002 for her first small-screen role as the optimistic and generous Kelly Lewis in share house drama The Secret Life of Us, an award she won again in 2004.

She started her acting career on the stage, which saw her co-write and star in the seminal play The 7 Stages of Grieving in 1994, before she played Nona in director Rachel Perkins's film Radiance in 1998, landing her an AFI Award (now AACTA) for best lead actress.

Three years later she scored her breakthrough TV gig with The Secret Life of Us.

Mailman looks back fondly at making the show, which catapulted its cast, including Gold Logie winner Samuel Johnson and 2026 Logie nominee Claudia Karvan, into the mainstream.

"That experience really gave me my training in front of a camera," Mailman says.

"It introduced me to the art of filmmaking."

Mailman with her Secret Life of Us co-stars, including Claudia Karvan and Joel Edgerton. (Supplied: Network Ten)

She especially loved how relatable the storylines felt, not just to her and the rest of the cast, but to the audience.

"It was such a big new adventure for me and I just loved every moment of it," Mailman says.

There, at that apartment building in St Kilda, Mailman met lifelong friends and collaborators.

"It was my first real foot into the [screen] industry," she says.

"To be supported in the way that I have been, right from the get-go, has been really important."

Telling First Nations stories

After The Secret Life of Us, Mailman featured as Lorraine in Redfern Now (earning another Logie), as a guest star of sketch series Black Comedy, and in movies including the musicals Bran Nue Dae and The Sapphires.

In 2012 Mailman starred as Lorraine in Redfern Now. Four years later, she picked up the Logie for most outstanding actress for the telemovie. (Supplied: ABC TV)

More recently she's played Kerry in Mystery Road, Aunty Linda in Indigenous superhero series Cleverman, and a nun in Warwick Thornton's award-winning The New Boy.

Roles like these are just a handful of the Indigenous-led projects Mailman has taken on throughout her career.

"That's where a lot of my work has gravitated towards: working with my own mob and telling stories that matter to me and my family and many communities around the country," she says.

She sees it as a kind of correction after First Nations stories were excluded from Australian screens for many years.

"Our voices weren't there," Mailman says.

"Now to be part of that canon of storytelling that shows the breadth and diversity and dynamic of who we are as people and our culture and what our stories are means everything to me."

Mailman is proud to follow in the footsteps of other Indigenous trailblazers on both screen and stage, including Justine Saunders (The Fringe Dwellers), Kylie Belling (Until the End of the World) and National Black Theatre founders Bob Maza and Gary Foley.

"They were instrumental in providing opportunities that are there for me now," she says.

Mailman also admires other Indigenous community leaders and activists who are not from the performing arts world.

"They're the people I have to thank because they fought the hard fight," she says.

Mailman feels privileged to potentially inspire the next generation of First Nations actors and creatives, alongside her peers and collaborators Perkins and Leah Purcell (The Drover's Wife).

"A whole bunch of us grew up professionally together," Mailman says.

"I'm part of that community and I'm proud of that.

"I'm really proud I'm still doing what I'm doing and that I've been part of this group of artists who've led by example."

Celebrating Blak excellence

Mailman joins the Logies Hall of Fame in a year dominated by Indigenous stories and storytellers.

Half of the nominees for most popular new talent are First Nations actors: 10-year-old Eloise Hart (Mystery Road: Origin, Goolagong), Lila McGuire (Goolagong) and Tamala (Ghosts Australia).

2026 Logies: First Nations excellence With strong representation of Indigenous talent in this year's Logie nominations, actor Lila McGuire says it's a "very important time" and "a gift for young mob".

The same is true for best lead actor in a drama, with Hunter Page-Lochard (Reckless), Mark Coles Smith (Mystery Road: Origin), and Rob Collins (RFDS); and best supporting actor, with Clarence Ryan (Mystery Road: Origin) against Thomas Weatherall, nominated twice (Heartbreak High; The Narrow Road to the Deep North).

Meanwhile, Goolagong is up for best miniseries, Mystery Road: Origin for best drama program, and Miranda Tapsell's Top End Bub for best scripted comedy.

For Mailman, being recognised in the same year as so many Indigenous nominees makes being inducted into the Hall of Fame this year even more special.

"That speaks volumes to me," she says.

" It's so exciting to have that many of our actors be acknowledged in this way, which demonstrates absolutely their excellence in their craft. "

It also means being inducted in front of close friends such as Collins.

"There's going to be mob in the room!" Mailman says.

"It's going to be a real joy to have that energy, to know that everyone else is being celebrated along with me.

"It's just a big warm hug."

World.title: Multi-million dollar art recovered after three-minute Italian museum heist
World.content:
Three century-old paintings believed to have been stolen by an organised gang have been recovered, months after the criminals broke into an Italian museum in a three-minute heist.

The fine artworks are the 1919 impressionist painting Fish by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cézanne's 1887 Still Life with Cherries, and the 1922 Odalisque on the Terrace by Henri Matisse.

Authorities said the Cézanne was valued at six million euros ($9.79 million), the Renoir at three million euros ($4.89 million), and the Matisse at 20,000 euros ($32,665).

Fish by Pierre-Auguste Renoir. (Reuters: Supplied/Fondazione Magnani Rocca)

Italy's Carabinieri, the domestic police force, and its cultural heritage protection unit confirmed in a statement on Friday, local time, the paintings were discovered during searched ordered by prosecutors.

The police did not provide details of the searches, but said investigations into the heist were ongoing.

Cup And Plate Of Cherries by Paul Cezanne. (Reuters: Supplied/Fondazione Magnani Rocca)

How Italy's three-minute art museum heist unfolded

The heist at the Italy's Magnani Rocca Foundation, located about 20 kilometres south of Parma in the country's north, took place on the night of March 22, according to police.

Odalisque on the Terrace by Henri Matisse. (Reuters: Supplied/Fondazione Magnani Rocca)

Authorities at the time said they believed the masked thieves forced open an entrance door, while local media reported they managed to take the paintings in less than three minutes before escaping across the museum's gardens.

In the days after the heist, Italy's La Repubblica newspaper reported the thieves entered the museum's grounds via an unlit, country access road after sawing three bars off a back gate.

They then forced the building's front door open with a crowbar and accessed the museum's French Room on the upper floor by breaking down its doors, the outlet said.

CCTV from inside the museum shows the masked thieves removing the works of art from the walls of an upper floor room. (Reuters: Supplied/Carabineiri Parma)

The newspaper said an interior alarm startled the group, who then fled and were believed to have lost a fourth painting — the three million euro ($4.9 million) Paysage de Cagnes also by Renoir — during their escape.

Carabinieri officers and private security contractors who arrived at the museum later said they spotted the group on thermal imaging cameras while inside the building, but were unable to stop them fleeing.

The Magnani Rocca Foundation was established by art historian Luigi Mangini in 1977, aimed at promoting cultural activities around art, music and literature.

The security vision also shows the thieves running through an open foyer area to escape through a window. (Supplied: Carabineiri Parma)

The foundation hosts Mr Mangini's collection of art and also includes works by Dürer, Rubens, Van Dyck, Goya and Monet.

Apart from its showcased art, the building is known for its spacious gardens, often roamed by a muster of white peacocks.

Mr Mangini lived in the greenhouse on the villa's grounds until his death in 1984.

Experts stunned by theft of 'recognisable' art

During its investigation of the heist, the Carabinieri's RIS forensic agency and the force's dedicated art recovery squad analysed CCTV footage from the villa on the night of the theft.

Magnani Rocca Foundation museum villa is renowned for its spacious gardens and white peacocks. (Instagram: Francesca Fietta/magnanirocca)

La Repubblica reported in April that authorities believed the gang consisted of up to five people, who police were trying to "height match" as part of identikit efforts.

One source told Reuters they had been surprised at the thieves' choice of works of relatively low value from the museum's permanent collections.

The ⁠lack of commercial insurance in Italy for paintings like those that were stolen is not uncommon, market sources say.

Art historian Silvia Evangelisti told La Repubblica the heist was "a very strange theft".

"These works are so recognisable that it's impossible to imagine the market they could be sold on," she said.

"They could have stolen older works, which Luigi Magnani's precious and refined collection is full of.

"Perhaps they were disturbed by their location on the first floor; they were in a hurry to act so they could escape more quickly."

Italian art expert Claudio Strinati echoed that sentiment.

"Renoir's painting — for example — is very beautiful but, within the context of the foundation as a whole, it isn't among the most important works," he told The Associated Press.

Simone dall'Orto, the mayor of the Traversetolo commune to the south-east of the museum, said the thievery had "dismayed" local residents.

"It affects not only an artistic heritage of extraordinary value, but the very identity of our community," he said.

The crime also followed a series of high-profile heists at major European museums, including the stunning theft in October of French crown jewels and other items worth 88 million euros ($143.7 million) from the Louvre in Paris.

ABC/Wires

World.title: NATO fighter jet shoots down a drone over Latvia
World.content:
A NATO fighter jet shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace, a spokesperson from the alliance says, confirming earlier statements by Latvia's defence ministry and military.

The military alliance has launched an investigation, the spokesperson said on Friday, local time, as concerns grow in Europe over unauthorised drone activity — particularly along the military alliance's eastern flank bordering Russia, whose war in Ukraine grinds on.

Ukraine's drone attacks on Russia could backfire Ukraine is firing drones deep inside Russian territory almost every day since June, but some analysts argue it could give Vladimir Putin an excuse to escalate his war.

It was not immediately clear where the drone shot down over Latvia had come from.

"We can confirm that two Italian Eurofighter jets were scrambled earlier today in response to a drone over Latvian airspace," a NATO spokesperson said.

"One of the Eurofighters shot down the drone," they added, saying that "two Turkish F-16 fighter jets were also scrambled" and all aircraft "were operating under NATO command".

Earlier on Friday, Latvia's defence ministry wrote on X that NATO "fighter jets have successfully shot down a foreign unmanned aerial vehicle that had entered Latvia as a result of Russian electromagnetic warfare".

Both Russia and Ukraine are relying on heavy use of drones to launch attacks in the four-year conflict.

Latvia, an EU and NATO member state of about 1.9 million inhabitants, shares a border with Russia to the east.

It and other countries along NATO's eastern flank including Romania and Poland have suffered repeated incursions into their airspace.

Russia dismisses Black Sea ceasefire

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks in recent weeks against commercial ships in the Black Sea. (Reuters: Victor Sayenko)

Russia on Friday dismissed the idea of a ceasefire with Ukraine in the Black Sea, saying it saw no grounds for "half-measures" that would offer a respite to the other side.

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks in recent weeks against commercial ships in the Black Sea, driving world grain prices higher.

Ukraine's drones could crash Russian banks On the outskirts of Russian cities, warehouses belonging to the country's largest online retailer are being struck by Kyiv's drones, with some analysts saying it could lead to a financial crisis.

In a statement, Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Ukraine of "brazen acts of terrorism" against shipping, while making no mention of Russia's own attacks.

"We view these attacks as a deliberate policy aimed at destabilising civilian shipping in the Black Sea region to further escalate tensions and prolong the conflict, all with the blatant acquiescence of regional neighbours," Ms Zakharova said.

"At the same time, we see no signs of improvement in the situation and, consequently, no grounds for half-measures that merely grant the Kyiv regime a temporary breathing space."

Ms Zakharova said she was commenting on a statement by Türkiye's foreign minister in a media interview that Ankara had put proposals to both Russia and Ukraine for a moratorium on military operations in the Black Sea.

She said Russia had received no formal proposal from Türkiye.

No peace talks on Ukraine have taken place since February, when the United States went to war with Iran and broke off its efforts to mediate between Moscow and Kyiv.

3 dead and 20 injured in latest attacks on Ukraine

Ukrainian rescuers working to extinguish a fire in a damaged residential building following an air attack in Donetsk. (AFP: Ukrainian Emergency Service)

Russia attacked 12 Ukrainian regions overnight, wounding dozens of people, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

In Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, a Russian glide bomb demolished six floors of a 10-story apartment block, killing one person and wounding 16 others, he said.

North Korea benefits from Russia alliance Almost two weeks ago, what is believed to be a North Korean missile was fired in an attack that killed a Ukrainian family. It could be part of a major escalation in North Korea's involvement in the war in Ukraine.

Russian jet-powered drones also struck a home in northern Ukraine on Friday, local time, killing a 29-year-old woman and her nine-year-old son, officials said.

A Russian strike in northern Ukraine's Sumy region also wounded four other people, including the dead boy’s father and grandmother, who were hospitalised with severe burns, the regional military administration chief said.

Ukrainian forces, meanwhile, extended their long-range strike campaign against Russian infrastructure, hitting the port of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region north of Moscow and starting a brief fire, its governor said.

Ust-Luga is one of Russia's largest oil and gas export terminals located more than 800 kilometres from Ukraine.

It has been a frequent target of Ukrainian drone attacks this summer, as Kyiv seeks to undermine Russian oil exports that provide Moscow with vital revenue for its war effort.

The Russian Defense Ministry said its air defences on Friday intercepted 553 Ukrainian drones over 18 Russian regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the waters of the Azov and the Black seas.

ABC/wires

World.title: Cory Bernardi condemned for anti-trans slur, labelling protesters 'incels'
World.content:
A social media video from One Nation MP Cory Bernardi in which he uses an anti-trans slur and describes protesters as a "bunch of incels" has been condemned by organisers of yesterday's SA rally against his party.

WARNING: This story contains language that some readers could find offensive.

Hundreds of people, many of them school students, attended Thursday's event outside SA parliament, which was part of nationwide protests against One Nation and its leader Pauline Hanson.

Mr Bernardi, who was elected to the Legislative Council at the March state election, appeared on the steps of parliament, where he began filming the event before roaming through the protest.

In a video from the event which he later posted on social media, he repeatedly shouted "it's a tranny", and at one point referred to the protesters as "a bunch of incels".

Sam Ats and Jordan Armstrong were among the organisers of the anti-One Nation protest. (ABC News: Kathryn Bermingham)

One of the organisers of the SA event, Year 11 student Sam Ats, described Mr Bernardi's comments towards the protesters as "appalling".

"Cory Bernardi is a 56-year-old man who is bullying teenagers and high-schoolers, calling them slurs, recording them without their consent to bully and intimidate people who are trying to make their voice heard," the 17-year-old said.

Another organiser, university student Jordan Armstrong, who identifies as a transgender man, also condemned Mr Bernardi's behaviour towards the protesters.

"Calling them slurs and harassing them, it's actually quite embarrassing for him," he said.

"It was pretty pathetic."

Jordan Armstrong described Mr Bernardi's comments as "pathetic". (ABC News: Kathryn Bermingham)

The rally on the steps of South Australia's parliament on North Terrace was one of several protests across the country against One Nation's national leader Pauline Hanson.

Protesters repeatedly chanted "f*** Pauline Hanson".

Asked whether that was inflammatory, Sam Ats responded: "I'd say that saying, 'There's no such thing as a good Muslim' is inflammatory."

Mr Bernardi posted two videos from the event on Instagram, including one in which he described the protesters as an "assortment of weirdos", adding that there were "some 'furries' there".

"I saw some weird-looking chick with pointy elf ears on, uh there was plenty of transvestites and things like that, and they're all chanting for a socialist agenda," he said.

"There were oldies there, and I say oldies, people my age, helping these kids."

Cory Bernardi wandered through the protest while filming on his phone. (Instagram)

In a second video, filmed on the steps of parliament, he described the protesters as "total losers" who "don't want to be at school today" and as "a bunch of incels who are now promoting socialism".

"I'm just going to go down there and say g'day," he said to his phone camera, before roaming through the protest and approaching attendees.

"Why aren't you chanting?" he asked one teenager.

That video was accompanied by Taylor Swift's song I Knew It, I Knew You, which was written for the film Toy Story 5.

The use of the music coincides with controversy in the US, where some of the songs of the pop star, who has been outspoken against conservative politics in recent years, have been removed from social media videos posted by Donald Trump's campaign and the White House.

Corey Bernardi records a video on the steps of Parliament House. (ABC News)

Mr Bernardi was also the subject of chants on Thursday. After he approached young attendees, protesters began chanting "f*** Cory Bernardi".

Mr Bernardi later told media that the protesters "don't know what they're talking about" and described the gathering as "an assortment of incels, unintelligent, unemployable people".

The ABC has contacted Mr Bernardi and One Nation for comment.

World.title: Freo locks up minor premiership after downing Crows in thriller
World.content:
Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Caleb Serong played a starring role as Fremantle snared just the second minor premiership in the club's history with a 24-point win over Adelaide in Perth.

Scores were level early in the final quarter of Friday night's blockbuster following Crows forward Riley Thilthorpe's second goal of the night.

But buoyed by a thundering 55,010-strong crowd, Fremantle did what it has done all season — blowing its rival off the park with a devastating burst.

Michael Frederick started the run when he nailed a tough set shot after being tackled high.

Jye Amiss (centre) kicked 5.1 in the win while Josh Treacy (right) took six contested marks. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Although Josh Treacy, Luke Jackson and Andrew Brayshaw missed their shots after that, Amiss bobbed up for his fifth goal of the night by snapping from the goalsquare.

And when Isaiah Dudley dodged and weaved his way through three Crows players before unleashing a successful snap, the margin was 22 points and it was game over.

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox rubbed it in by roughing up an opponent and then pointing to the scoreboard after kicking a goal in the dying minutes of the 16.16 (112) to 13.10 (88) win.

The triumph boosted Fremantle's record to 19-3, securing the club a second minor premiership to go with their 2013 efforts.

It also meant Fremantle will end the home-and-away season with a perfect 12-0 record at Perth Stadium.

Adelaide (14-8) now faces a huge battle to snare a top-four berth, with the loss even leaving them vulnerable to slipping into the dreaded wildcard spots from seventh to 10th.

Amiss finished with 5.1 in a powerful display, Josh Treacy was huge with six contested marks but a wayward 1.4, Dudley kicked three goals, while Serong was influential with 29 disposals, 12 clearances, 536m gained and two goals.

Crows playmaker Izak Rankine racked up a monster 14 disposals in the opening term on the way to 39 possessions, 10 clearances, 717m gained and one goal.

Adelaide star Izak Rankine finished the match with a game-high 39 disposals. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Adelaide had an interesting lead-in to the match, with players forced to evacuate their hotel just hours before bounce down due to a fire alarm going off in their hotel.

Amiss missed an early set shot sitter from 15m out as Adelaide skipped out to a two-goal lead.

But Amiss soon made amends, nailing three other set shots for the term — from 50m, 40m and 35m — to give Fremantle a 13-point edge by quarter time.

Fremantle led by just five points at half-time, and the third quarter was a rollercoaster ride featuring four lead changes and five occasions when the scores were even.

Fremantle skipper Alex Pearce suffered a huge scare when his heavily-strapped left knee hyper-extend during a collision, leaving him hobbled for the next couple of minutes.

The action was fierce and fast, but it was Fremantle who produced more of the memorable moments.

Treacy hurt himself while completing a team-lifting tackle on Max Michalanney.

The Fremantle powerhouse dusted himself off after a few deep breaths and kicked a goal moments later.

Serong nailed a goal from just inside the centre square following a dazzling series of handballs from the Dockers.

And when Brayshaw dribbled one through with the outside of his right boot, Fremantle turned for home with a seven-point edge.

The Dockers kicked five goals to three in a powerful final term to wrap up top spot on the ladder with one round to spare.

World.title: Tasmanian woman charged over alleged 'series' of attempted poisonings
World.content:
A 43-year-old South Launceston woman has been charged over what police allege is a "series of attempted poisonings".

Tasmania Police allege that over a period of months, the woman had delivered "intentionally contaminated drinks to a 47-year-old man on several separate occasions".

"The man did not consume the drinks and was not physically injured," police said on Friday night.

The man and the woman "were known to each other", police said, and "there is no indication that contaminated drinks were sent to any other person".

Police said on Friday they had charged the woman with two counts of attempted unlawfully administering poison with intent to harm.

She has been detained to appear in court.

World.title: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty in federal case, admits killing insurance CEO
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaCrime Luigi Mangione pleads guilty in federal case, admits killing insurance CEO Jack Queen August 15, 2026 — 2:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Luigi Mangione has admitted in court to fatally shooting a health insurance executive and pleaded guilty to two federal charges of stalking the executive with the intent to kill him. The guilty plea will avert a federal trial in the closely watched case over the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, a brazen crime that was condemned by public officials but became emblematic of Americans’ frustration with health insurance industry practices. It could also allow him to seek dismissal of state murder charges and delay an upcoming trial in that case. Luigi Mangione appears for a pre-trial hearing at Manhattan Criminal Court in New York on August 11. Steven Hirsch/Pool New York Post via AP US District Judge Margaret Garnett told Mangione that if he pleaded guilty, he could face a maximum sentence of life in prison on each count. Garnett set Mangione’s sentencing for December 18.



Mangione’s lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, said there was no plea agreement with prosecutors. Thompson led UnitedHealth Group’s insurance unit before he was shot dead in the early morning of December 4, 2024, outside the hotel where an investor conference was taking place. Thompson’s widow sat in the front row of the gallery with other members of his family. Mangione, 28, said in court that he researched details of UnitedHealthcare’s annual investor conference in December 2024 after suffering a broken back and navigating the health insurance system. He said he then used a 3-D printer to make part of a gun and travelled to New York with the intent of killing Thompson. “I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” Mangione said. Stickers in support of Luigi Mangione outside New York City’s federal court on Friday. Bloomberg



Graphic footage of the killing and a five-day manhunt for a suspect made the case a media fixture and social media sensation. Mangione was arrested in Pennsylvania. He had previously pleaded not guilty in April 2025 to murder, weapons and stalking charges brought by Manhattan federal prosecutors. Garnett threw out the murder and weapons charges over legal technicalities in a surprise ruling in January 2026. The decision eliminated the possibility that Mangione would face the death penalty in the federal case, though he still faces a possible sentence of life without parole if convicted on the remaining stalking charges. Related Article Crime Luigi Mangione is tipped to plead guilty to stalking. What does that mean for his murder trial? His federal trial was most recently set for January. Mangione separately pleaded not guilty in December 2024 to state terrorism, murder, weapons and forgery charges brought by Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg. The terrorism charges were thrown out by a judge in September 2025. A trial in that case is scheduled for September 8 before Justice Gregory Carro in Manhattan. Mangione would face 25 years to life in prison if convicted of second-degree murder.



The guilty plea in the federal case could allow Mangione to seek dismissal of the murder charge under New York’s double jeopardy law, which protects people from being prosecuted twice for the same conduct. Bragg’s office would oppose the move, arguing that the murder charge is legally distinct from the federal charges. Whoever loses would likely seek an emergency appeal.
