World.title: I’m not really into traumatic superhero stories, but Lanterns had me in its grip
World.content:
★★★ CultureTV & radioStreaming I’m not really into traumatic superhero stories, but Lanterns had me in its grip Jared Richards August 15, 2026 — 2:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lanterns ★★★ Superheroes and mortals alike return to the same question in HBO Max’s gritty, psychological take on DC’s Green Lantern franchise: “Are you afraid?” The three words become a mantra for John Stewart (Aaron Pierre, Rebel Ridge; The Morning Show), a Lantern-in-training assigned to follow around Earth’s long-standing Lantern, Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler, Friday Night Lights). Together, they investigate a strange shooting in Nevada with suspected intergalactic links. Kyle Chandler as Green Lantern Hal Jordan in Lanterns. Warner Bros Without mental resolve, these intergalactic law officers can’t use their weapons – a magical emerald green ring that lets them fly and create objects, force fields and more out of sheer mind power. But fear itself is the powering force of Lanterns, a show that examines how it is used to justify acts of love, war and hatred across interpersonal relationships and intergalactic colonialism alike.



Created by Chris Mundy (Ozark) and produced by Damon Lindelof (Watchmen; The Leftovers) and DC writer Tom King, Lanterns is a detective drama first and a superhero show second, though there’s a solid amount of cheesy jokes and quips. Don’t worry: that dark, moody edge isn’t an excuse for terrible lighting or filters. Lanterns offers crisp visuals. Editor's pick ★★★★

Review Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage At first, John and Hal couldn’t seem more opposite. While Hal’s decades of power and fame has left him arrogant and smarmy, John is comparatively robotic, a stoic ex-military man emotionally cauterised by a traumatic childhood. In Lantern’s opening scene, he barely reacts when his father draws a close-range rifle in their backyard for a William Tell trick, shooting an apple atop his head. Both men are fearless, but through flashbacks across the seven of eight episodes offered for review, it’s revealed that their mental fortitude is not equal. As in the comics, John is a black man, one told as a boy that Hal and other white men are “privileged enough to not know fear”. That tension – of resentment at Hal’s ability to be a fool in public, such as getting arrested on purpose for the purposes of their investigation – is one of Lantern’s most intriguing, understated qualities.



With a weekly release schedule, it’s easy to imagine casual audiences might drop off, as early episodes find John cold and Hal a touch too irritating. At least the other characters – including Kelly Macdonald as a local sheriff, and Nathan Fillion reprising his role from Superman as an abrasive Lantern – agree on that last point, too. Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler in Lanterns. As someone not particularly drawn to a trauma-led take on a lesser-known superhero, I found Lanterns gripping enough. It’s a balanced blend of cheesy one-liners, engaging action and emotional depth, with lots to love for fans of DC or superhero stories more broadly. Lanterns streams on HBO Max from August 17.

World.title: Deborah Mailman makes history as first Indigenous person inducted into Logies Hall of Fame
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Sunday night, Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame, as well as only the sixth woman. “I had a moment of almost bursting into tears,” she says. “I couldn’t quite understand it all, to be honest. It took some time for it to land because I was like, ‘Are you sure?’ I had to re-read the email and go, ‘Hang on, what?’ And then when I started thinking [about it], I got really quite emotional about it.” Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame on Sunday night. Jessica Hromas/eyevine/Headpress The award, which began in 1984, recognises “outstanding and continued contribution and enrichment to Australian television culture by an individual, a group of individuals, or a program”. Mailman will be one of three inductees on the night, with the other two revealed during the ceremony. For Mailman – whose breakthrough came in the 1998 film Radiance, followed by roles in the TV series The Secret Life of Us, Redfern Now, Cleverman, Offspring and Total Control, as well as the films Rabbit-Proof Fence, The Sapphires and Bran Nue Dae – the fact she is the first Indigenous person to receive the honour is a source of enormous pride but also conflicted emotion. Related Article Logies Full list of nominees at the 2026 Logie Awards “This is not being disrespectful ... but it’s a long time coming,” she says. “And I don’t mean that for just for me, but in terms of us as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in this country, and in this industry, because I’m a beneficiary of the many people who have gone before me and who’ve worked their asses off for someone like me to be a beneficiary and to have these opportunities, so I acknowledge that I’m only here because of the hard work that’s gone before.”



The fact that she is only one of six women to receive the honour – joining Magda Szubanski, Rebecca Gibney, Kerri-Anne Kennerley, Noni Hazlehurst and Ruth Cracknell – is also something Mailman wanted to acknowledge. “I don’t know if there’s any sort of sugarcoating that,” she says. “I mean, it has been an industry built for some time for certain people. But now we’ve seen in the past decade or so, even longer than that, when we look at storytelling in this country and where that excitement has been for some time, and the voices that haven’t been there before, and the representation around so many voices that have never had a foot in the door, that’s what it’s about.” Deborah Mailman with her The Secret Life of Us co-stars (from left) Samuel Johnson, Joel Edgerton, Spencer McLaren and Abi Tucker at the 2002 Logie Awards, at which Mailman won most outstanding actress in a drama series. Getty Images Deborah Mailman with her most outstanding actress Logie in 2004. Paul Harris Deborah Mailman at the 2024 Logie Awards, where she won Best Lead Actress in a Drama for Total Control, with her co-star Rachel Griffiths. Getty Images That Mailman, 54, has become one of the most recognisable and beloved faces on screen is still a surprise to her. Growing up in Mount Isa, she only took to acting when faced with the alternative: business studies. “I didn’t choose it to become an actor,” she says, laughing. “I just thought, ‘Yeah, I didn’t want to do that, so I’ll try this [drama].’ And I just had two really great teachers throughout high school that saw something or supported me, and I just loved drama. I wasn’t an academic, I was average at best, and … I was very shy and that helped with my confidence.”



Related Article ★★★★

Review Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage In many ways, Mailman’s life can be measured in firsts: her first screen role, in Radiance, landed her the Australian Film Institute award for best actress in a leading role, making her the first Indigenous woman to do so; her first TV role in The Secret Life of Us, in which she played student Kelly Lewis, landed her Logies for outstanding actress in a drama series in 2002 and 2004. She has won six Logies in total, including for the TV film Mabo, the ABC dramas Redfern Now, Mystery Road, Total Control and the Nine shark drama Bite Club. “I still pinch myself that I’m still in this industry – and I’m still in love with it,” she says. “It’s a hard industry to be a part of, and when I signed up at 17 years of age, I had no idea what this was going to look like for me. And the fact that I’m still here and still getting great opportunities, and getting really good work, that’s not lost for me.” Deborah Mailman, pictured with Rachel Maza, in Radiance, the film for which she made history as the first Aboriginal actress to win the Australian Film Institute Award for best actress in a leading role. She still gets approached the most by fans of The Secret Life of Us, and Play School, and in many ways still considers herself to be a “shy kid”, so it’s no great surprise to hear that she is “really, really, really nervous” about the prospect of standing on stage on Sunday, with all eyes turned in her direction. “This is doing my head in,” she says. “Having been at these events before, you’re part of a production, you’ve got your co-workers, your colleagues around you, and you’re celebrating together. This is a very different feeling, and, yeah, I’m really, really, really nervous, but I’m also trying to just enjoy what this is about as well.” Maybe she could channel her Total Control character, the fearless senator Alex Irving, and just get up there and let them have it?

World.title: Rabbitohs sink Bulldogs’ finals chances with dominant win
World.content:
So that is that.

With three-and-a-half rounds of football still remaining, the top eight has all but been decided.

Loading

This is a rivalry often celebrated on a Good Friday, but for Canterbury this is a very black one indeed. With everything to play for, Cameron Ciraldo’s team didn’t register a point until Enari Tuala went over in the 63rd minute. By then, it was too little, too late.

In defeating Canterbury, Souths have effectively ended their season and extended their own. While there may be some permutation that would allow the Bulldogs to scrape into the play-offs, so poor is their for-and-against that you can effectively put a line through them.

Asked if he was still hopeful of qualifying for the post-season, Ciraldo replied: “Hope’s not a strategy.

“All we can control is how we play next Saturday night. That’s all we can worry about now, we can’t worry about anything else.”

In climbing, at least temporarily, above Newcastle into sixth spot, the Rabbitohs have almost certainly booked their first finals appearance since 2022.

David Fifita scores against Canterbury. Getty Images

Thursday night’s Roosters-Panthers clash – the best game of the year to date – was a defensive masterclass. Inspired by what they had witnessed just 24 hours earlier, Souths showed similar resolve on their line.

Canterbury captain Stephen Crichton seemed try-bound early, only for Jack Wighton to somehow contort his body under the ball to make a save. Jethro Rinakama was also bound for glory, only for Cameron Murray to produce an equalling stunning stop. It is a fair turnaround for a side that conceded over 29 points per game since Round 18.

“They are vital, they make a difference in a game,” Souths coach Wayne Bennett said about the desperation on the goal-line.

“Stopping them on the tryline from getting the ball down, everyone gets confidence from that … It’s a state of mind. They can do it, they don’t always want to do it.

“They are learning how to win, these guys, what works for them and what doesn’t. Today they applied it for 80 minutes and got a great result.”

The best defensive stop of the night, however, belonged to Crichton. His decision to invade the space of referee Ashley Klein proved a try-saving one.

Under the pump for much of the opening quarter, the Rabbitohs were rewarded for not cracking. David Fifita, the best on ground, pounced on a Cody Walker grubber to open the scoring. Only moments earlier, a similar grubber from Lachlan Galvin went dead-in-goal.

Loading

Fifita and Crichton, meanwhile, kept finding each other. The Maroons forward ran straight over the top of his opponent in the eighth minute, the collision of the night. Crichton, to his credit, didn’t back down and had a few personal wins of his own, like the penalty he milked from the back-rower late in the opening half.

Walker also had a hand in the second try, yet another example of the ball singing along that lethal left edge. If there is a better job in rugby league than being Alex Johnston, we are yet to find it.

Canterbury needed to start the second half well. Souths kicked off and the ball – and the Bulldogs’ finals prospects – slipped through Bailey Hayward’s hands.

It’s a good thing this didn’t come down to goal-kicking. Bud Sullivan kicked just the seventh goal of his career, and then appeared to injure his groin in attempting an eighth. A decade after making his NRL debut, it was left to Matt Dufty to stand over the tee for the first time. Late in the game, there was an opportunity to extend the lead beyond two converted tries with a penalty goal. Bereft of options, they tapped and scored. It will be an area of concern for the tighter, more important games that lay ahead.

World.title: Strict bail conditions for Setka after being charged for a third time
World.content:
Former construction union boss John Setka made menacing posts on social media about a former CFMEU administrator, suggesting he take “anti-c--- tablets”, police allege. The 61-year-old was arrested on Friday morning and faced the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court later in the evening, where prosecutors applied to have Setka’s existing bail revoked. Loading During his subsequent application for bail, the court heard that on Monday, Setka had taken to Instagram to share nine images directed at senior figures of the CFMEU. “Images posted depicted the following: an image of Murray Furlong, the general manager of the Federal Commission, two memes with a couple sitting at a park and the title saying ‘say goodbye to being a c---’, and a smaller medication image labelled ‘anti-c---’ tablets,” the investigating police officer told the court.



The court also heard two images of Mark Irving, the former administrator of the CFMEU, and an image of Matthew McGowan, the current assistant administrator and head of the Victorian branch, were posted by Setka. Further images depicted Elizabeth Lukin, a consultant within the construction industry, and McGowan’s wife, as well as other union figures. Setka was on Friday morning charged with using a telecommunications device to menace, using a telecommunications device to offend and two charges of committing an indictable offence while on bail. The former union boss was first arrested in November and charged with seven counts of using a carriage service to menace, harass and offend the union’s government-appointed administrator, Mark Irving, KC. He was charged a second time, in February, over allegations he issued a threat on Christmas Day to an official from the Albanese government-backed administration that took control of the CFMEU in 2024. The court on Friday heard about the alleged offending that prompted Setka’s first arrest in November last year, with emails sent from his account allegedly telling the administrator that he would “come to the CFMEU office whenever he pleases”.



“[Setka] told the administrator to go f--- their mothers with Nick McKenzie,” the investigating officer said, referring to The Age’s senior investigative reporter. “The accused signed off the email saying that if the administrator leaks any more information that he will fix it himself.” The court heard that following his arrest on Friday morning, Setka “made admissions to posting on social media, and made admissions that it came from his account”. “When the accused was asked about if the social media posts would offend the recipients, he said if that hurts their feelings, he ‘wouldn’t give two f---s and that’s their problem’.” The court heard Setka would pose an unacceptable risk of endangering the safety and welfare of other people, and will “continue to make social media posts”.



“We’re not just talking about that isolated post. We’re looking at a pattern of behaviour from the accused,” he said. John Setka is facing further charges. Victoria Police Defence lawyer Lee Ristivojevic, for Setka, told the court the prosecution’s case was “weak”. “It’s submitted that the nature of the allegations, of the charges, that if he was to be found guilty, he’s not likely to receive a term of imprisonment for the offences,” she said. “We say that it is not a serious example of the offence.” Ristivojevic said Setka had “what I’d described as a positive bail history in terms of court orders”, and that it was “not suggested he’s breached any conditions of bail”. She further submitted that a compelling reason to release Setka on bail was that he provides essential care for his elderly mother.



Related Article Updated

Building Bad Setka charged with harassing a CFMEU administrator Magistrate Nicole Spicer ultimately granted Setka’s bail application, noting that none of the alleged victims had sought personal safety intervention orders. “I do consider that the risk can be brought to an acceptable level by the imposition of conditions targeted to make clear that the particular behaviour that you have allegedly engaged in in making social media commentary of a personal and allegedly harassing nature simply cannot occur whilst you are subject to the grant of bail,” Spicer said. She imposed bail conditions that Setka “not threaten or harass any employee or representative of the CFMEU administrator, or any person named in criminal charges” against him. She further ordered him not to “make posts or comments on any social media platform which are threatening, intimidating or use obscene language directed towards or about such individuals”. Police established Operation Hawk in mid-2024, in response to this masthead’s Building Bad series, which exposed criminal behaviour and corruption in the CFMEU. As in the comics, John is a black man, one told as a boy that Hal and other white men are “privileged enough to not know fear”. That tension – of resentment at Hal’s ability to be a fool in public, such as getting arrested on purpose for the purposes of their investigation – is one of Lantern’s most intriguing, understated qualities.



With a weekly release schedule, it’s easy to imagine casual audiences might drop off, as early episodes find John cold and Hal a touch too irritating. At least the other characters – including Kelly Macdonald as a local sheriff, and Nathan Fillion reprising his role from Superman as an abrasive Lantern – agree on that last point, too. Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler in Lanterns. As someone not particularly drawn to a trauma-led take on a lesser-known superhero, I found Lanterns gripping enough. It’s a balanced blend of cheesy one-liners, engaging action and emotional depth, with lots to love for fans of DC or superhero stories more broadly. Lanterns streams on HBO Max from August 17.

World.title: Deborah Mailman makes history as first Indigenous person inducted into Logies Hall of Fame
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Sunday night, Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame, as well as only the sixth woman. “I had a moment of almost bursting into tears,” she says. “I couldn’t quite understand it all, to be honest. It took some time for it to land because I was like, ‘Are you sure?’ I had to re-read the email and go, ‘Hang on, what?’ And then when I started thinking [about it], I got really quite emotional about it.” Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame on Sunday night. Jessica Hromas/eyevine/Headpress The award, which began in 1984, recognises “outstanding and continued contribution and enrichment to Australian television culture by an individual, a group of individuals, or a program”. Mailman will be one of three inductees on the night, with the other two revealed during the ceremony. For Mailman – whose breakthrough came in the 1998 film Radiance, followed by roles in the TV series The Secret Life of Us, Redfern Now, Cleverman, Offspring and Total Control, as well as the films Rabbit-Proof Fence, The Sapphires and Bran Nue Dae – the fact she is the first Indigenous person to receive the honour is a source of enormous pride but also conflicted emotion. Related Article Logies Full list of nominees at the 2026 Logie Awards “This is not being disrespectful ... but it’s a long time coming,” she says. “And I don’t mean that for just for me, but in terms of us as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in this country, and in this industry, because I’m a beneficiary of the many people who have gone before me and who’ve worked their asses off for someone like me to be a beneficiary and to have these opportunities, so I acknowledge that I’m only here because of the hard work that’s gone before.”



The fact that she is only one of six women to receive the honour – joining Magda Szubanski, Rebecca Gibney, Kerri-Anne Kennerley, Noni Hazlehurst and Ruth Cracknell – is also something Mailman wanted to acknowledge. “I don’t know if there’s any sort of sugarcoating that,” she says. “I mean, it has been an industry built for some time for certain people. But now we’ve seen in the past decade or so, even longer than that, when we look at storytelling in this country and where that excitement has been for some time, and the voices that haven’t been there before, and the representation around so many voices that have never had a foot in the door, that’s what it’s about.” Deborah Mailman with her The Secret Life of Us co-stars (from left) Samuel Johnson, Joel Edgerton, Spencer McLaren and Abi Tucker at the 2002 Logie Awards, at which Mailman won most outstanding actress in a drama series. Getty Images Deborah Mailman with her most outstanding actress Logie in 2004. Paul Harris Deborah Mailman at the 2024 Logie Awards, where she won Best Lead Actress in a Drama for Total Control, with her co-star Rachel Griffiths. Getty Images That Mailman, 54, has become one of the most recognisable and beloved faces on screen is still a surprise to her. Growing up in Mount Isa, she only took to acting when faced with the alternative: business studies. “I didn’t choose it to become an actor,” she says, laughing. “I just thought, ‘Yeah, I didn’t want to do that, so I’ll try this [drama].’ And I just had two really great teachers throughout high school that saw something or supported me, and I just loved drama. I wasn’t an academic, I was average at best, and … I was very shy and that helped with my confidence.”



Related Article ★★★★

Review Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage In many ways, Mailman’s life can be measured in firsts: her first screen role, in Radiance, landed her the Australian Film Institute award for best actress in a leading role, making her the first Indigenous woman to do so; her first TV role in The Secret Life of Us, in which she played student Kelly Lewis, landed her Logies for outstanding actress in a drama series in 2002 and 2004. She has won six Logies in total, including for the TV film Mabo, the ABC dramas Redfern Now, Mystery Road, Total Control and the Nine shark drama Bite Club. “I still pinch myself that I’m still in this industry – and I’m still in love with it,” she says. “It’s a hard industry to be a part of, and when I signed up at 17 years of age, I had no idea what this was going to look like for me. And the fact that I’m still here and still getting great opportunities, and getting really good work, that’s not lost for me.” Deborah Mailman, pictured with Rachel Maza, in Radiance, the film for which she made history as the first Aboriginal actress to win the Australian Film Institute Award for best actress in a leading role. She still gets approached the most by fans of The Secret Life of Us, and Play School, and in many ways still considers herself to be a “shy kid”, so it’s no great surprise to hear that she is “really, really, really nervous” about the prospect of standing on stage on Sunday, with all eyes turned in her direction. “This is doing my head in,” she says. “Having been at these events before, you’re part of a production, you’ve got your co-workers, your colleagues around you, and you’re celebrating together. This is a very different feeling, and, yeah, I’m really, really, really nervous, but I’m also trying to just enjoy what this is about as well.” Maybe she could channel her Total Control character, the fearless senator Alex Irving, and just get up there and let them have it?

World.title: Rabbitohs sink Bulldogs’ finals chances with dominant win
World.content:
So that is that.

With three-and-a-half rounds of football still remaining, the top eight has all but been decided.

Loading

This is a rivalry often celebrated on a Good Friday, but for Canterbury this is a very black one indeed. With everything to play for, Cameron Ciraldo’s team didn’t register a point until Enari Tuala went over in the 63rd minute. By then, it was too little, too late.

In defeating Canterbury, Souths have effectively ended their season and extended their own. While there may be some permutation that would allow the Bulldogs to scrape into the play-offs, so poor is their for-and-against that you can effectively put a line through them.

Asked if he was still hopeful of qualifying for the post-season, Ciraldo replied: “Hope’s not a strategy.

“All we can control is how we play next Saturday night. That’s all we can worry about now, we can’t worry about anything else.”

In climbing, at least temporarily, above Newcastle into sixth spot, the Rabbitohs have almost certainly booked their first finals appearance since 2022.

David Fifita scores against Canterbury. Getty Images

Thursday night’s Roosters-Panthers clash – the best game of the year to date – was a defensive masterclass. Inspired by what they had witnessed just 24 hours earlier, Souths showed similar resolve on their line.

Canterbury captain Stephen Crichton seemed try-bound early, only for Jack Wighton to somehow contort his body under the ball to make a save. Jethro Rinakama was also bound for glory, only for Cameron Murray to produce an equalling stunning stop. It is a fair turnaround for a side that conceded over 29 points per game since Round 18.

“They are vital, they make a difference in a game,” Souths coach Wayne Bennett said about the desperation on the goal-line.

“Stopping them on the tryline from getting the ball down, everyone gets confidence from that … It’s a state of mind. They can do it, they don’t always want to do it.

“They are learning how to win, these guys, what works for them and what doesn’t. Today they applied it for 80 minutes and got a great result.”

The best defensive stop of the night, however, belonged to Crichton. His decision to invade the space of referee Ashley Klein proved a try-saving one.

Under the pump for much of the opening quarter, the Rabbitohs were rewarded for not cracking. David Fifita, the best on ground, pounced on a Cody Walker grubber to open the scoring. Only moments earlier, a similar grubber from Lachlan Galvin went dead-in-goal.

Loading

Fifita and Crichton, meanwhile, kept finding each other. The Maroons forward ran straight over the top of his opponent in the eighth minute, the collision of the night. Crichton, to his credit, didn’t back down and had a few personal wins of his own, like the penalty he milked from the back-rower late in the opening half.

Walker also had a hand in the second try, yet another example of the ball singing along that lethal left edge. If there is a better job in rugby league than being Alex Johnston, we are yet to find it.

Canterbury needed to start the second half well. Souths kicked off and the ball – and the Bulldogs’ finals prospects – slipped through Bailey Hayward’s hands.

It’s a good thing this didn’t come down to goal-kicking. Bud Sullivan kicked just the seventh goal of his career, and then appeared to injure his groin in attempting an eighth. A decade after making his NRL debut, it was left to Matt Dufty to stand over the tee for the first time. Late in the game, there was an opportunity to extend the lead beyond two converted tries with a penalty goal. Bereft of options, they tapped and scored. It will be an area of concern for the tighter, more important games that lay ahead.

World.title: Strict bail conditions for Setka after being charged for a third time
World.content:
Former construction union boss John Setka made menacing posts on social media about a former CFMEU administrator, suggesting he take “anti-c--- tablets”, police allege. The 61-year-old was arrested on Friday morning and faced the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court later in the evening, where prosecutors applied to have Setka’s existing bail revoked. Loading During his subsequent application for bail, the court heard that on Monday, Setka had taken to Instagram to share nine images directed at senior figures of the CFMEU. “Images posted depicted the following: an image of Murray Furlong, the general manager of the Federal Commission, two memes with a couple sitting at a park and the title saying ‘say goodbye to being a c---’, and a smaller medication image labelled ‘anti-c---’ tablets,” the investigating police officer told the court.



The court also heard two images of Mark Irving, the former administrator of the CFMEU, and an image of Matthew McGowan, the current assistant administrator and head of the Victorian branch, were posted by Setka. Further images depicted Elizabeth Lukin, a consultant within the construction industry, and McGowan’s wife, as well as other union figures. Setka was on Friday morning charged with using a telecommunications device to menace, using a telecommunications device to offend and two charges of committing an indictable offence while on bail. The former union boss was first arrested in November and charged with seven counts of using a carriage service to menace, harass and offend the union’s government-appointed administrator, Mark Irving, KC. He was charged a second time, in February, over allegations he issued a threat on Christmas Day to an official from the Albanese government-backed administration that took control of the CFMEU in 2024. The court on Friday heard about the alleged offending that prompted Setka’s first arrest in November last year, with emails sent from his account allegedly telling the administrator that he would “come to the CFMEU office whenever he pleases”.



“[Setka] told the administrator to go f--- their mothers with Nick McKenzie,” the investigating officer said, referring to The Age’s senior investigative reporter. “The accused signed off the email saying that if the administrator leaks any more information that he will fix it himself.” The court heard that following his arrest on Friday morning, Setka “made admissions to posting on social media, and made admissions that it came from his account”. “When the accused was asked about if the social media posts would offend the recipients, he said if that hurts their feelings, he ‘wouldn’t give two f---s and that’s their problem’.” The court heard Setka would pose an unacceptable risk of endangering the safety and welfare of other people, and will “continue to make social media posts”.



“We’re not just talking about that isolated post. We’re looking at a pattern of behaviour from the accused,” he said. John Setka is facing further charges. Victoria Police Defence lawyer Lee Ristivojevic, for Setka, told the court the prosecution’s case was “weak”. “It’s submitted that the nature of the allegations, of the charges, that if he was to be found guilty, he’s not likely to receive a term of imprisonment for the offences,” she said. “We say that it is not a serious example of the offence.” Ristivojevic said Setka had “what I’d described as a positive bail history in terms of court orders”, and that it was “not suggested he’s breached any conditions of bail”. She further submitted that a compelling reason to release Setka on bail was that he provides essential care for his elderly mother.



Related Article Updated

Building Bad Setka charged with harassing a CFMEU administrator Magistrate Nicole Spicer ultimately granted Setka’s bail application, noting that none of the alleged victims had sought personal safety intervention orders. “I do consider that the risk can be brought to an acceptable level by the imposition of conditions targeted to make clear that the particular behaviour that you have allegedly engaged in in making social media commentary of a personal and allegedly harassing nature simply cannot occur whilst you are subject to the grant of bail,” Spicer said. She imposed bail conditions that Setka “not threaten or harass any employee or representative of the CFMEU administrator, or any person named in criminal charges” against him. She further ordered him not to “make posts or comments on any social media platform which are threatening, intimidating or use obscene language directed towards or about such individuals”. Police established Operation Hawk in mid-2024, in response to this masthead’s Building Bad series, which exposed criminal behaviour and corruption in the CFMEU. World.title: Firefighters battle blaze at Gloriavale Christian Community
World.content:
Firefighters were battling a blaze at the Gloriavale Christian Community late on Friday night.

Fire and Emergency said the fire in the remote community on the South Island's West Coast was reported shortly before 9pm.

One crew arrived to find a building at the site well involved on fire.

FENZ shift manager Simon Lyford said the building was "some distance" from Gloriavale's hostels, and they had no concerns with people sleeping on site on Friday night.

As of 10.30pm, FENZ said they had isolated power from the building and four of the crews were dealing with the fire from inside the building.

When the fire was reported, the caller said everyone had been evacuated from the building, FENZ said. They were not aware of any injuries.

Five fire crews, four fire trucks and two tankers were on site late on Friday night.

The fire was not being treated as suspicious.

World.title: Young child dies after dog attack in Aranui, Christchurch
World.content:
A young child has died after a dog attack in Christchurch on Friday afternoon.

Senior Sergeant Dan Overend said emergency services were called to Basingstoke Street in Aranui around 4:45pm after reports of a child sustaining serious dog bite injuries.

"Upon arrival, emergency services located a young child in a critical condition.

"Despite the immediate efforts of first responders, and a member of the household, the child sadly died at the scene."

Overend said the dog involved was known to the occupants of the address and lived at the property.

"Police remain at the address carrying out a scene examination, and enquiries into the circumstances that led to this tragic incident are ongoing.

"Occupants of the address are assisting police with enquiries."

World.title: Experts call for meth safety policy u-turn after 'huge increase' in contamination
World.content:
The debate around methamphetamine contamination in homes has reignited, with the authors of a new study calling for a policy u-turn over safe thresholds.

'The impact of New Zealand's 2018 methamphetamine policy on residential contamination' was published in the New Zealand Medical Journal on Friday.

The 2018 policy raised the threshold for what was deemed acceptable from 0.5μg of methamphetamine per 100cm2 to 15μg - higher than accepted levels in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia, the report said.

In an analysis of more than 420 homes, researchers from Unitec and the University of Waikato found a "substantial" rise in meth contamination since the policy change.

The report said there could be several factors behind the trend, including a potential increase in "clandestine" meth labs that was also driving increased consumption of the drug, and the policy change leading to less vigilance about the risk.

The report noted that methamphetamine use continued to rise, according to last year's New Zealand Drug Trends Survey.

The study's lead author Dr Muhammad Irfan said people could be passively exposed to meth by living in homes where the drug had been smoked or manufactured.

Meth use in NZ breaks records - why? Afternoons Download MP3 10m

He said fears about the effect of this exposure on health - particularly in children - were what prompted testing in New Zealand in 2010.

"Children are crawling ... might be touching the surface of the carpet ... putting their hands in their mouth. Their health is .. in danger because of the meth contamination."

Irfan said the cost of methamphetamine testing and a need to house people were factors in a review of the threshold in 2018, and in May that year the new levels were adopted.

He said the "huge increase" in contamination since should trigger a tightening of restrictions again, if not to pre-2018 levels then to the 1.5μg threshold recommended by Environmental Science and Research (now known as PHF Science) in 2019.

Overseas research has found passive exposure to methamphetamine could lead to eye and respiratory infections in children as well as some psychological effects, Irfan said.

Further research on the health impact was needed to establish a contamination threshold that accurately accounted for the risk, he said. In the meantime the acceptable level should be lowered, he added.

The study's release comes after neighbours in a Lower Hutt suburb raised concerns that potential buyers of a Kāinga Ora home were left in the dark about its history as a "meth lab".

The 'for sale' sign outside the Kāinga Ora property on Naenae's Langford Street. RNZ

'Jury still out' on health effects

Speaking to RNZ earlier this week, emeritus professor of toxicology at University of Canterbury Ian Shaw said the "jury's still out" on the health effects of living in a meth-contaminated home.

While he could not comment on this particular study or its findings, he was currently part of a research team - contracted by a New Zealand company - looking into the effects of meth exposure.

"As far as I'm aware, we don't really know whether residues of methamphetamine in houses have any effect on people that might live in those houses later. So we need ... a definitive study to determine that."

Shaw said the current statutory limits for meth contamination appeared fairly arbitrary.

Professor Ian Shaw Supplied

"I don't think that we have set ... that threshold based on the knowledge that below that amount will have no effect on you and above that amount it might have an effect on you."

In his opinion, the effect on people who were living in a home where meth had been smoked was very low.

"Cutting your bread on a bread board that someone smoked meth next to ... you would get really low doses," he said.

"But at the other end of the spectrum you might have a house ... that's a meth lab ... then the amounts of methamphetamine contaminating that home could be very significantly greater."

Shaw said those homes could give people a "reasonable-sized" dose of the drug.

World.title: 'Send help': Doctor's plea to Health NZ as hospital struggles to cope with demand
World.content:
Palmerston North ED doctor puts out plea for help to Health NZ Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

A Palmerston North emergency department doctor is urging Health New Zealand to "send help" after an extraordinarily busy day.

"It's been kind of a hectic day with the waiting room. I think we have close to 20 to 30 patients," Dr Dusty Bratton told Checkpoint on Friday afternoon.

Bratton was speaking as a member of the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists (ASMS).

Patients had contacted RNZ to say they had been waiting up to 17 hours to be seen at the ED. Bratton said one patient had to wait up to 27 hours.

When he arrived at the hospital in the morning, he found 20 patients with nowhere to be examined. People were even resorting to leaving the ED because of the wait times, he said.

Bratton did not know if this was normal for Palmerston North, having moved to the area a year ago from the US.

He said Kiwis were experiencing longer wait times and more "bedblock" - time spent over-capacity - than people in the US, which could lead to "bad outcomes" for patients.

"It doesn't seem to flow quite as well."

Staff were picking up extra shifts to help combat the wait times but that was not sustainable, he said.

Healthcare workers have taken to protesting in recent years as hospitals struggle to cope with demand. Kim Baker Wilson / RNZ

"[Staff are] just trying to help out as much as they can. They're staying late, coming in early."

He had personally worked an extra three shifts in two weeks.

Bratton doubted Palmerston North would be able to reach the government's target of seeing 95 percent of patients within six hours.

"The number of patients we have are greater than the number of spaces we have."

The ED needed more beds and space to admit and see patients, he said.

There was pressure to reach discharge targets and make numbers look better on paper, but Bratton did not know if that always resulted in decisions that were in the patients' best interests.

In the last month, Palmerston North Hospital has added an extra 14 beds and an assessment room to the department.

Bratton said this had not solved "bedblock" issues, however.

Asked what his message was to Health NZ, he replied: "Send help - that's all I got."

Health NZ responds to concerns

Health NZ group director of operations at Counties Manukau Dr Vanessa Thornton admitted they were "going to have to put our thinking caps on and do more" in response to wait times during flu season.

"We are starting to think about what we're going to do next year already with respect to this," she told Checkpoint.

"I think it's a really challenging time and the staff are doing a great job.

"Just this week compared to last week we've had 1500 more presentations to EDs across the country, and most of that is related to viral load and flu, particularly influenza A," she said.

Dr Vanessa Thornton RNZ / Dan Cook

Palmerston North Hospital was one of many struggling with "unprecedented demand" due to winter illness, she said. Even her own, Middlemore Hospital, had seen patients facing eight-hour waits on Friday morning.

Most hospitals were not close to the current target of 95 percent of people being seen within six hours, she said.

She wanted to reassure the public that they would not be sent home early to help meet that target.

"All patients that are urgently needing critical care are seen as a priority, but some will wait longer to be seen for treatment," she said.

World.title: Flights cancelled as fog hits Wellington Airport
World.content:
Wellington Airport says fog has caused several flight cancellations on Friday evening.

MetService said a southerly wind had pushed a low cloud shelf into Wellington over the past few hours on Friday evening.

Passengers are being advised to check directly with their airline for the latest information before travelling to the airport.

Meteorologists earlier said as temperatures cool in the evening, a thick bank of mist could sink to surface levels.

The cloud bank was expected to last through the afternoon to the early hours of Saturday morning.

Meteorologist Alwyn Bakker earlier said the southern coast of Wellington would be most exposed - including the harbour and airport.

"So you get that sea fog when sea surface temperatures and air temperatures are very close together.

"So with a southerly the air is cooled down, the sea takes a little bit longer to cool down water - it hangs on to heat better than air essentially."

He said low visibility might impact flights, depending on how much moisture builds in the air.

"Basically, planes like to see the ground before they land."

Auckland Airport affected by fog on Friday morning

Fog restrictions were in place at Auckland Airport this morning.

By 7.20am, several domestic regional flights had been cancelled as well as some arrivals.

A number departing had been delayed as well as arriving.

Of the main trunk domestic flights, one to Christchurch had been delayed, as had an arrival from Dunedin.

World.title: Households cut health insurance, despite rising claim payouts
World.content:
New Zealanders are cutting back on their health insurance, just as the amount being paid out in health insurance claims increases.

A report commissioned by the Financial Services Council showed 9 percent of people with health insurance terminated their policies last year, up from 7 percent in 2022.

At the same time, the average health insurance claim paid per member increased from $1097 in 2021 to $1921 in 2025.

"The evidence shows insurance is already providing billions of dollars of funding, expanding access to care and protecting families from the financial consequences of illness and death. The opportunity for government is to recognise and strengthen that contribution as part of a more resilient New Zealand health system," Financial Services Council chief executive Kirk Hope said.

Health insurance premiums have risen sharply recently, up almost 75 percent in the past five years alone.

Hope said it was problematic that, as health insurance usage was increasing and treatment costs were rising, households were struggling with the cost of cover.

"Just as New Zealand needs every part of the health system working better together, people are cutting back the very cover that helps them access care sooner."

People who completely dropped their health insurance would usually need to go back through the underwriting process to take it out again, which could mean pre-existing conditions were not covered.

Kirk Hope RNZ / Richard Tindiller

About 35 percent of adults have private health insurance.

Of those, 43 percent are covered through an employer or group scheme.

Hope said the Government could help by removing fringe benefit tax from employee-funded insurance.

"It's a very effective way, it's community-rated and it's not underwritten so it's a very effective way for people to get access if the employer is providing low-cost or no-cost health insurance for them, but it's very expensive for employers because they have to incur a 50 percent to 70 percent tax on premiums."

World.title: Southland says it is missing the love when it comes to South Island infrastructure
World.content:
Southland businesses meet to hear politicians’ plans Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Business people from across the South Island have met in Christchurch for the first South Island election conference to hear from politicians about their plans for the Mainland.

They covered a range of topics from transport, productivity, infrastructure and immigration, with National announcing its election plan for the South Island.

But the head of the Southland Chamber of Commerce said she still felt her region was badly overlooked and its potential underestimated.

While other parts of the country might be struggling with high unemployment rates, the Southland Chamber Commerce said its region is grappling with how fill a bout 4000 skilled jobs.

Chief executive, Sheree Carey, said there was about 10 billion dollars in new investment and eight major projects in the pipeline, including a data centre and a mineral plant, but Southland wasn't getting it's fair share of infrastructure spending.

"We need some serious consideration from government, and all the parties really, on what can we do for Southland, because if they want to double exports and increase GDP, then Southland is the region that is well on its way. So we need that support back," said Carey.

Sheree Carey said the region could do with improvements to its roading, housing, schools and social services, but she feels there was more focus on Canterbury and Queenstown.

"If they look at all the stats we are the ones that are leading in every statistics that you can see, in growth and exports and everything, and where is the love? Southland wants some love as well," Carey said.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said National's South Island plan will build more reliable transport and regional connections and help to grow exports.

National Party members and Christopher Luxon speak to media during a stand-up in Christchurch on Friday. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

The Infrastructure Minister, Chris Bishop, said the plan showed that National was backing the south.

"The Rolleston Rail intermodal rail and freight hub, here in Christchurch, leaning into public transport in Queenstown by way of a gondola. There are three different solutions on the table there. I think we need to think creatively about Queenstown transport issues. There is a strategic network plan being developed by NZTA now, but the simple reality is we just can't keep adding lanes and lanes in Queenstown," Bishop said.

He said the plans build on other investments already underway, including the new Dunedin and Nelson hospitals, and the Brougham Street upgrade in Christchurch.

Labour's Kieran McAnulty said the biggest infrastructure mistake governments make is announcing plans, only to drop them or press pause because of politics or a lack of funding.

"The way we have approached this is first and foremost recognise that the country is sick to the gut of things stopping and starting constantly. There is too much of it. We are never going to get where we need to get if it keeps happening. And people won't have the confidence to run the businesses in the way they want to, if they don't have the confidence that things will be followed through," McAnulty said.

He said Labour wants all Crown projects to go through the Infrastructure Commission's independent assurance process to stop that happening.

The chief executive of Business Canterbury, Leeann Watson, said the two main parties have a lot in common on the issue of infrastructure.

"If there is one part of our conference today where we wanted to see alignment it is in that future investment and infrastructure. Having good bipartisan support to provide a long term plan and some certainty is really important and we saw that today," Watson said.

World.title: Fiji court rules COI report into Malimali appointment was unlawful, null and void
World.content:
The Fiji High Court has ruled that the Commission of Inquiry report into the appointment of Barbara Malimali as FICAC Commissioner, in its entirety is null and void.

Justice Dane Tuiqereqere also found that the COI report was unlawful, and that its adverse findings are irrational and have been quashed

It's also been found that President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu and Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka failed to provide the applicants with natural justice.

Malimali challenged the report with former Attorney General Graham Leung, and lawyers Wylie Clarke and Laurel Vaurasi.

Local media said the judge has determined that the President, the Prime Minister and the Commission of Inquiry, breached principles of natural justice for not giving the applicants the opportunity to respond to the adverse findings against them.

Fiji Village News said Justice Tuiqereqere ruled that the work of the Commission of Inquiry after 1st February 2025, including the report is ultra vires or unlawful.

He found that the extension of the Commission of Inquiry beyond 31st January 2025 was ineffective.

As a result, the actions of the Commissioner after that date, including the completion of his report dated 1st May 2025, were unlawful, Fiji Village News stated.

Fijian Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka making a case for the 20 percent salary reduction for all 55 MPs in parliament last week. 30 April 2026 Facebook / Parliament of the Republic of Fiji

Justice Tuiqereqere has also found that adverse findings and recommendations against the applicants including Malimali, former Attorney General Graham Leung and lawyers Wylie Clarke and Laurel Vaurasi were unlawful, including those relating to a meeting at the FICAC office on 5th September 2024.

'Praise God for the win'

The applicants had further challenged the decision by the President, on the advice of the Prime Minister, to release the Commission of Inquiry report publicly.

Malimali and her lawyer Tanya Waqanika are on the island of Kadavu and responded to the ruling in a Facebook post, saying justice has been served.

"Praise God for the win," Waqanika said in her post.

"It has been a hard battle fighting to clear Barbara Malimali's name from the COI taxpayer funded $4m (and counting) crocodile hunting failed expedition.

"Barbara Malimali and me are here in my village and we just received the news that we WON our HBJ No 9/26 Judicial Review case against the Fiji Government (well, all the Respondents names are Govt representatives).

The judge also said the COI Chair, David Ashton-Lewis, should have provided a draft of the adverse findings against the applicants to them and an opportunity to respond before compiling the report.

The Commission of Inquiry was the brainchild of Rabuka.

In June, the High Court rejected the Prime Minister's attempt to stall its ruling that the country's former anti-corruption chief was illegally sacked.

World.title: Quick hits: Tempers flare as Aussies wilt, Starc's heart-in-mouth moment
World.content:
Mitchell Starc vents his frustration at a Bangladeshi batter, while a star is born on treacherous Darwin turf.

Here are the quick hits from another torrid day for Australia against Bangladesh.

1. Smith grounds one

Smith downed a chance in the morning session. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

There is toiling, and then there is whatever the Australian bowlers were doing during the first session of day two.

The much-vaunted Aussie quartet, with Cam Green and Beau Webster in support, combined for just a single wicket during the opening two hours of play.

The ball found its way past Bangladeshi willow on a few occasions, but for the most part, chances were at a premium.

So, it was far from an ideal time for the usually so-reliable hands of slipper-supreme Steve Smith to let him down.

But with rookie opener Tanzid Hasan already past 50 and Australia having just taken their first wicket of the day, Smith floored one.

Tanzid edged a Nathan Lyon delivery into the elbow of Alex Carey, the ball ricocheted towards slip, and a diving Smith was unable to gather cleanly.

It was far from a sitter, but one Smith will be disappointed to have missed.

Tanzid given a life on 62.

2. Tanzid Hasan's maiden Test ton

Coming into this series, there were serious questions surrounding Bangladesh's opening pair, with the Tigers having struggled to nail down a reliable top two in recent years.

Up steps Tanzid Hasan, the 25-year-old opener playing just his second Test match.

Tanzid was considered and composed against the much-vaunted Australian attack, providing the foundation for a brilliant Bangladeshi team effort.

Tanzid completed a sparkling maiden century on day two. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

He already had an ODI century to his name, having scored 107 against Pakistan in Mirpur in March, and he also has scored five first class tons for an average of 39.60.

Talk about nervous 90s, though.

First, Pat Cummins whacked the 25-year-old on the arm with a vicious, 140km/h bouncer.

Then, Tanzid almost holed out to the substitute fielder at long off when on 96, skying a Lyon slower ball with a lofted drive that plugged in the outfield after falling just short of the fielder.

He moved to 99 with a neat clip, and then celebrated his century with a push down the ground off Lyon, a superb hundred celebrated accordingly.

3. The Darwin turf bites at the Australians

Starc got tangled in the turf while taking a catch. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

However, Tanzid was unable to turn his maiden Test ton into a truly big one, holing out to Lyon only a matter of balls later.

But Australian hearts were in Australian mouths as Mitchell Starc slid to make the catch and then flipped over ungainfully.

Starc, wincing as he got up, looked to be in some discomfort, and the replays showed that the Darwin turf may have been to blame.

The fast-bowler's knee had been caught in the grass, with a cloud of dust and thatch of grass disengaging from the ground.

Starc was tangled up awkwardly by the Darwin turf. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Thankfully, Starc appeared to recover well, but it wasn't the first time the Marrara Stadium outfield had appeared a little loose, with the ever-energetic Marnus Labuscagne ripping out his fair share of greenery.

With the surface only likely to disintegrate more dramatically over the coming three days, both teams should be wary of not getting twisted up in the outfield.

4. Steve Smith's hat-trick of slip catches

Australia desperately needed something to happen to interrupt the Bangladesh momentum — and it arrived with the new ball.

Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and then Pat Cummins all extracted edges with the new pill, claiming the wickets of Hossain Shanto (84), Litton Das (0) and Mushfiqur Rahim (36) as Bangladesh crumbled from 3-297 to 6-308.

And all three of them were caught by Steve Smith at second slip, making dramatic amends for his earlier fumble.

That trio of catches put Smith level with Joe Root with 218 catches, the most ever by a non-wicketkeeper in Test cricket.

Australia's pacemen are worth their weight in gold, but Smith certainly pays his way in the field to help them out.

5. 'Get off the wicket!'

Tempers flared late on it Darwin. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

With that new-ball blitz an increasingly distant memory, and with the Australian bowlers beginning to wilt in the late Darwin sun, the hosts' frustration was on full display late in the evening session.

Into the 103rd over of the innings, Starc was bowling to all-rounder Mehidy, who was well set and intent on seeing the day through.

Mehidy set off for a single and came very close to colliding with the Australian spearhead.

Starc wasn't impressed.

"It's my follow through, not your follow through. Get off the wicket," Starc could be heard saying through the stump mic.

"I didn't see!" Mehidy could be heard saying during the next over, still perhaps apologetic about the near-collision.

But of course, the all-rounder shouldn't be taking the altercation personally.

The Australians' frustration was all of their own making.

6. You call that a knife?

Nathan Lyon used a knife to clean his spikes. (Supplied: Fox Sports)

There's nothing worse as an athlete than getting mud or grass caught between your cleats or spikes.

Nathan Lyon clearly had this issue during the second session, when going through his usual array of warm ups and stretches on the boundary at Marrara Oval.

But what can you do about it when in the middle of a Test match as you're about to prepare for a bowling spell?

Turns out, you ask someone in the kitchen if they have a spare a butter knife they don't mind soiling with some outfield dirt.

Much like the Northern Territory's best known international export, Crocodile Dundee, one can almost imagine one of the locals querying Lyon's choice of implement with quips like "you call that a knife …"

World.title: NRL top eight all but locked in after Souths win
World.content:
Canterbury have been left needing a minor miracle to make the NRL's top eight after succumbing to a 22-6 defeat at the hands of South Sydney.

Led by a rampaging David Fifita, the Rabbitohs took a major step towards returning to the finals for the first time since 2022 with a workmanlike victory at Stadium Australia on Friday night.

But the Bulldogs' hopes of featuring in September are all but over.

Should North Queensland see off Parramatta on Saturday, Cameron Ciraldo's men will be four points adrift of the finals places with just three full rounds of the regular season left to play.

Canterbury take on St George Illawarra, Penrith and Brisbane to round out their campaign and will no doubt look back on this loss to Souths as a game that got away.

Stephen Crichton, Jethro Rinakama, Lachlan Galvin and Jacob Preston were all either held up or stopped short of the line in the first half.

And as South Sydney, who moved up to sixth, pulled away in the second half, the Bulldogs didn't have the firepower to go with them.

The Rabbitohs withstood plenty of early pressure but struck in the 23rd minute when Fifita, who finished with 144m and six tackle busts, pounced on a Cody Walker grubberkick.

Walker was the conductor for their second as the Bunnies shifted from right to left, the veteran playmaker sending Tallis Duncan through a hole to set up Alex Johnston.

The Rabbitohs were far too clinical for the wasteful Bulldogs. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

Souths led 10-0 at halftime after Preston was penalised for a double movement and they moved out of touching distance from the restart.

Dogs hooker Bailey Hayward dropped the kick-off and Duncan crashed over on the left edge on the ensuing set.

Rinakama trudged off with a knee issue soon afterwards and the Bunnies pushed ahead further through winger Campbell Graham.

Missing a recognised goalkicker — Souths converted just one of their five tries — kept Canterbury alive though.

Enari Tuala finally scored on the hour mark but Canterbury's attack didn't have the spark to trouble Wayne Bennett's side, who completed the win with a well-deserved Matt Dufty try two minutes from fulltime.

Earlier, Manly's 'Fozball' fever dream is officially over after the Dolphins became the first team to hold the Sea Eagles scoreless at Brookvale Oval in 33 years.

In a match that failed to reach any real heights, the Dolphins had enough strike to pull away late and win 22-0, leapfrogging them above Cronulla into fourth spot.

The Dolphins' win did come at some cost, with in-form second-rower Connelly Lemuelu limping from the field in the second half with a hamstring injury.

But the story of the night was the Sea Eagles, whose finals hopes are now virtually over after six straight losses.

AAP

World.title: Boxer dies more than a decade after fight leaves him with brain injury
World.content:
Prichard Colón, a former boxer who was left with severe brain damage after a fight more than a decade ago, has died aged 33.

His father, Richard Colón, confirmed his son's death in a Facebook post on Thursday.

The post did not detail the Puerto Rican boxer's cause of death.

World Boxing Organization (WBO) president Gustavo Olivieri posted a tribute to Colón on social media.

"Today, the WBO solemnly joins his family and all those who had the privilege of knowing, supporting, and loving him in mourning his passing," Mr Olivieri said.

What happened to Prichard Colón?

Colón was injured in a boxing match against Terrel Williams in Virginia in the US in October 2015.

Born in Florida, US, Colón kicked off his boxing career in Puerto Rico, where he won five amateur titles.

He was considered a "rising star" in the lead-up to the nationally televised match, ESPN reports.

Here's how a report from Reuters described the match at the time:

"An online video of the fight showed Williams, a 31-year-old fighter from Los Angeles, punching Colón in the back of the head in the seventh round, a shot that appeared to stun Colón, who was briefly examined in his corner. "Williams was penalised for the illegal punch. "Colón was then knocked down twice in the ninth round. "He was disqualified after the ninth round. "His corner mistakenly took off his gloves, thinking it was the final round and that the fight was complete."

After the match, Colón needed assistance to walk to his dressing room after the match.

He said he felt dizzy, vomited and then "passed out", according to a report from the Washington Post.

Colón was rushed to hospital where he underwent surgery to relieve pressure on his brain, spending seven months in a coma.

He was 23 years old.

Prichard Colon, left, and Terrel Williams during the fight. (Getty Images via AFP: Patrick Smith)

In 2016, the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation determined there was no wrongdoing on the part of organisers of the fight, the Washington Post reported.

"No one action [or failure to act] can be identified that is so apparent or egregious to justify holding accountable any one person," the regulator said in a statement.

Signs of hope

In 2017, nearly two years after the fight, Colón was still in what doctors described as a persistent vegetative state, according to an article from ESPN.

He needed around-the-clock care.

At the time, his parents told the US broadcaster they hoped Colón would regain some brain function despite the challenges he faced.

"I do believe in miracles," his father said.

By 2019, Colón had made significant progress, according to another article by the Washington Post.

After months of therapy, he was able to communicate using facial gestures, verbal sounds and a computer that tracked his eye movements.

He could pedal on a recumbent bike, and his competitive spirit was driving him to take steps with assistance in a friendly rivalry with a fellow patient.

"He gets tired and impatient like anyone, and some of his days are better than others," Washington Post reporter Kent Babb wrote.

"What's clear is that he's made it this far, beyond where anyone thought he would, because of good coaching."

'Extraordinary fighting spirit'

News of the former boxer's death triggered an outpouring of grief in the boxing world.

"Prichard's life was defined by courage, perseverance, and an extraordinary fighting spirit," Mr Olivieri said.

"His story transcended the ring and deeply touched the boxing community, which stood by him throughout the years with respect, admiration, and hope."

The WBO paid tribute to Colón's "resilience" as well as "the unwavering love of his family".

Tributes to Prichard Colón were posted to social media after news of his death broke. (Facebook: World Boxing Organization-WBO)

ABC with Reuters

World.title: Australia's Grace Kim makes fast start at LPGA event
World.content:
Australian golfer Grace Kim has continued her hot run with a stellar opening round at the LPGA Tour's Portland Classic.

Fresh off two straight top-10 finishes, Kim is just one stroke behind Colombian leader Mariel Galdiano after the first round at the Columbia-Edgewater Country Club.

Playing an all-out attack, the major champion collected seven birdies and an eagle to finish the day in a seven-way tie for second.

The world number 38 also needed only 24 putts, the fewest of any player in the field.

Kim started with a three-birdie stretch after starting her round on the 10th hole.

"Having that three-birdie start is just a nice feeling to kick-start things," the 25-year-old said.

"A lot of us out here are pretty straight, fairways and greens.

"But in terms of holing all those putts, knowing that the greens roll quite true … it's really nice to just put a stroke on it and see where it would normally go."

Kim is in a batch at 6-under, including Augusta National women's amateur champion Maria Jose Marin, Arpichaya Yubol and Olivia Cowan.

The 20-year-old Marin landed five-straight birdies on the front nine.

"I reached a flow state that I haven't reached in a while," she said.

"After the British Open I didn't play my best golf, and I think getting that confidence back with this round is all that I needed."

One shot behind them and tied for ninth is Australian Robyn Choi (67), who sprang to life on the back nine.

After going out in even par with a birdie and bogey, Choi stormed home with four consecutive birdies beginning on the 12th. She then added another on the 17th to rocket up the field.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Fellow Australian Steph Kyriacou (72) had a solid round of even par, but will have to play well with the cut projected to be around 1-under.

American pacesetter Galdiano's opening 65 featured nine birdies.

Galdiano, a 28-year-old from Hawaii, is making her fourth LPGA Tour start of the year.

"Every start on the LPGA means a lot to me, so just enjoy the moment, really," she said.

World.title: Fraser officially enters Carlton coaching race after mid-year turnaround
World.content:
Josh Fraser has presented to the Carlton hierarchy after officially entering the club's process to find its full-time coach.

After a stunning run of 10 wins from 12 matches since becoming interim coach when Michael Voss left the club in May, Fraser has Carlton on the cusp of the most unlikely finals appearance.

Although he has delivered a perfect on-the-job audition, Fraser was still required to pitch to the Blues' coaching panel on Wednesday.

Loading...

Untried assistants Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong) have been through the process, with Fraser only formally putting his hand up this week.

"A fortnight ago, the club came to me and asked me to be a part of this coaching process," Fraser said today.

"Then this week, I was in a position to go back to the club and accept that offer to go through the process.

"I presented to the coaching panel this week."

At his first press conference when taking over from Voss, Fraser was adamant he was not interested in being Carlton's coach beyond this season.

But after a wildly successful 12 weeks in charge, buoyed by enthusiastic fans, Fraser could not turn down the opportunity.

"I have said, previously, that I've been ambitious to be a senior coach," Fraser said.

"I've been fortunate to be able to sit in the chair and consolidate some of my thinking; get some opportunity exposure to the role that otherwise you wouldn't normally get.

"It's been something that's been crystallising in my mind and my thoughts.

"Really confident that I'm ready to assume the responsibility of being a senior coach.

"There are 19 jobs to be a senior (AFL) coach.

"I'm as excited about this group as a lot of our Carlton supporters will be."

Joyous Blues fans were chanting "we want Fraser" as the Blues steamrolled St Kilda on Sunday night to put themselves in the box seat to earn a spot in the wildcard round.

If they defeat the Western Bulldogs, who will be without superstar captain Marcus Bontempelli on Sunday, the Blues will lock in their spot in the top 10.

It has been one of the more remarkable in-season turnarounds in AFL history, with Carlton 1-8 when Fraser took over.

"It can disrupt the club at times, when there's a significant change, like when you lose a coach, and you bring another coach in mid-season," Fraser said.

"That speaks to the culture that's been here, but I'm grateful for all the support I've had around me."

AAP

World.title: Bangladesh grinds Australia into the Darwin dirt as rookie scores sparkling ton
World.content:
Australia's much-vaunted bowling attack has been ground into the Darwin dirt, experiencing another torrid day against Bangladesh at Marrara Stadium.

Led by a sparkling maiden Test ton to rookie-opener Tanzid Hasan, Bangladesh lost just five wickets on day two, reaching stumps on 6-351 and 153 first-innings runs ahead of their hosts.

After an opening day that saw Australia bowled out for a well below-par 198, Pat Cummins's men picked up where they left off on day two, struggling for ideas and inspiration against a disciplined Bangladeshi batting line-up.

Mitchell Starc took the only wicket in an energy-sapping morning session for Australia, while Steve Smith was uncharacteristically slow in reacting to a deflected Tanzid edge, that, if taken, would have seen the opener depart for 62.

Tanzid, playing just his second Test match, took 188 balls to reach his century, and brought it up with a push back past Nathan Lyon after a nervous period in the 90s.

Tanzid completed a sparkling maiden century on day two. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

However, the 25-year-old threw his wicket away only a matter of balls later, caught in the deep after mistiming an ill-advised slog against Lyon for 101.

That was the only wicket to fall in the second session as captain Najmul Hossain Shanto, who had shared a 93-run partnership with Tanzid, continued to take the fight to the Australians alongside 39-year-old, 103-Test veteran Mushfiqur Rahim.

Bangladesh's lead by the time the new ball was taken stood at 91, with seven wickets remaining.

Starc instantly got the new ball talking, sending the first ball swinging past the bat and stumps of Shanto to the giant left hander's complete disbelief.

But it was Hazlewood who made the breakthrough in his first over, finding the edge of Shanto to have him caught at second slip by Steve Smith for 84.

Starc got in on the act three overs later, having Litton Das caught behind, also by Smith, for a 12-ball duck.

Then Pat Cummins joined the party to find the edge of Mushfiqur, and give Smith a third consecutive catch, Australia's three great pacemen striking with fearsome force to reduce Bangladesh from 3-297 to 6-308.

That third catch put Smith level with Joe Root on 218 catches, the most ever in Test cricket by a non wicketkeeper.

But Australia once again toiled as the lacquer faded from the new ball, with six-wicket hero from day one, Hasan Mahmud (13 not out), providing able support to all-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz, who reached stumps on 32.

World.title: EPL side walks off as Spanish club kicks penalty into open net
World.content:
Fulham's preseason match against Málaga turned out to be not too friendly after the English club walked off and coach Álvaro Arbeloa was shown a red card for complaining to the referees.

The match had finished 2-2, after the La Liga side Málaga FC equalised in the 90th minute.

At full-time, the Premier League outfit walked off the pitch while Málaga stayed on, believing a penalty shootout should decide the winner.

Malaga striker Jauregi then kicked a penalty into an open net before celebrating in front of the home fans.

In a post on X, Fulham said both teams had agreed before the match that no penalty shootout would follow a draw.

"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw," Fulham wrote on X.

On their club website, Malaga said it believed a shootout was on the cards.

"Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract," the La Liga club said.

World.title: Payne's fame began as a joke. Now his shirt has sparked a bidding war
World.content:
Just a few months ago, few soccer fans outside New Zealand and Australia knew Tim Payne's name. Now they are bidding thousands of dollars for the jersey off his back.

The shirt Payne wore in his debut for Club Olimpia, a Paraguayan soccer powerhouse, has become a coveted piece of match-worn memorabilia since the club put it up for auction online five days ago.

With bidding set to close, the leading offer has climbed above 21 million in Paraguay's currency, the guarani, equivalent to around $5,000.

Viral Kiwi star meets Argentine influencer who boosted following to 5M New Zealand soccer player Tim Payne has met social media influencer Valen Scarsini after the Argentine encouraged his fans to follow the unheralded All Whites player.

It is the latest development in the unlikely rise of the 32-year-old defender, who entered the World Cup with just over 4,000 followers on Instagram and emerged as one of the tournament's biggest social media sensations.

Before representing New Zealand at the World Cup, Payne spent most of his career out of the limelight, playing for low-profile clubs in New Zealand before playing 143 A-League matches for Wellington. He also spent two years with England's Blackburn Rovers but never made a major appearance because of work-permit problems.

Then Argentine soccer influencer Valen Scarsini, known online as El Scarso, went searching for what he called the World Cup's "least-known soccer player".

Scarsini settled on Payne, whose Instagram account had 4,715 followers at the time, and encouraged his more than 2 million followers across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube to follow Payne, flood his posts with supportive comments and mention his name everywhere.

Loading Instagram content

Within days, Payne's following skyrocketed, eventually topping 5.4 million — more than the entire population of his native New Zealand. The surge in online fame helped carry Payne to Paraguay, where he signed with national club champion Olimpia on a one-year deal in June, ending a seven-year stint with Wellington Phoenix.

Payne gave legions of new fans another reason to cheer him during his August 2 debut against Asunción club Rubio Ñu, scoring minutes after coming off the bench to help Olimpia win 5-0.

Now the signed jersey from that match is drawing the sort of interest usually reserved for far more established names — though the leading offer remains a far cry from the millions of dollars paid for jerseys worn by Argentine superstar Lionel Messi and other soccer greats.

"I know exactly what it means to wear these stripes and play in this shirt, and that's why I want to give it to a true Olimpista (Olimpia fan)," Payne said in a video launching the auction.

AP
